Union of India ) .RESPONDENTS Through the Secretary, ) Ministry of Finance, Government ) of India, North Block, ) New Delhi – 110 001. ) ) 2. Deputy Commissioner of ) Income Tax – 1(3)1, Aayakar Bhavan ) M. K. Road, ) Mumbai – 400 020. ) ) 3. Additional Commissioner of ) Income Tax – 1(3), Aayakar Bhavan, ) M. K. Road, ) Mumbai – 400
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the statutory requirements of section 245 of the Income-tax Act before adjusting Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against outstanding demands. The case arose in AY 2019-20 and concerned a refund/stay-of-demand dispute; the court specifically criticized the Department’s approach to treating its order as not covering matters dealt with by the ITAT on the ground that the Union of India was not a party, calling that justification unacceptable and inconsistent with the conduct expected of a model litigant.

From a compliance perspective, the key requirement reaffirmed is that before any refund is adjusted against a tax demand under section 245, the Department must follow the procedure mandated by that section rather than simply making an adjustment unilaterally. The judgment signals that authorities cannot rely on technical arguments to avoid the effect of a High Court order where the substance of the dispute requires compliance, and that departmental actions in refund adjustment matters are subject to judicial scrutiny. No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines were stated in the excerpt, but the operative compliance point is that refund adjustments must be lawfully and transparently made in conformity with section 245 and the court’s direction, especially where related stay/refund proceedings are already pending or decided.

rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that a writ petition could be maintained in Bombay even though the challenged income-tax order had been passed by Delhi authorities, because the assessee was based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arose there. For compliance purposes, the more important ruling is that a notice under section 148 and a reassessment order under section 147 issued in the name of an amalgamated company that had already ceased to exist are **void and without jurisdiction**; this is not treated as a mere procedural defect.

The Court specifically rejected the argument that the defect could be cured under section 292B, and it also held that the assessee’s participation in the reassessment proceedings does **not** validate the proceedings or create any estoppel against law. In practical terms, if a company has been amalgamated before reassessment proceedings are initiated, tax notices and reassessment orders must be issued, if at all, in the name of the surviving entity; action taken against the non-existent predecessor entity is invalid.

The case concerned AY 2012–13, and the Court’s decision was pronounced on April 9, 2021 and published on April 24, 2021. The ruling reinforces a key compliance control point for corporate restructuring: once an amalgamation takes effect, the company should ensure tax records, PAN-related communications, and litigation notices are promptly aligned with the successor entity’s name so that any future assessment or reassessment proceedings are not directed at a dissolved legal person.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). Facts: The assessee company filed its return of income for AY 2013-14 in question which was subjected to scrutiny assessment. In the course of assessment proceedings, it was gathered by the AO that one M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL) amalgamated with the assessee company under the scheme of amalgamation.
rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held in **DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.** that **section 56(2)(viib)**, which taxes a private company on **excess share premium received over fair market value**, does **not apply** where shares are issued to shareholders pursuant to a **scheme of amalgamation**. The case involved **AY 2013–14**, with the tribunal’s decision **pronounced on April 13, 2021** and published on **April 24, 2021**.  

On the facts, the assessee-company had filed its return for AY 2013–14, and during scrutiny the Assessing Officer found that **M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL)** had amalgamated into the assessee under an approved amalgamation scheme. In that process, the assessee issued shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The tax department sought to treat the value arising from the amalgamation as **deemed income** under section 56(2)(viib), effectively characterizing the issuance as if there were an unjustified premium over face value.  

The tribunal rejected that approach, stating that the purpose of section 56(2)(viib) is to tax **unexplained or excessive premium received by private companies on issuance of shares where the shares do not carry corresponding underlying value**, not to cover share issuance mandated by an amalgamation scheme. It held that the **notional excess of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be treated as share premium** for this deeming provision. The decision also referred to **AS-14 issued by ICAI** and **CBDT Circular No. 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012** in support of the treatment of amalgamation accounting and share issuance as distinct from taxable premium.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where shares are issued **solely because of a bona fide amalgamation approved under a scheme**, the transaction should not ordinarily be exposed to **section 56(2)(viib)** tax on alleged excess fair market value. However, the ruling is limited to the facts of amalgamation-related issuance and does not change the general rule that **unjustified share premium in ordinary equity issuances** can still be scrutinized under section 56(2)(viib).

This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns **section 50C of the Income-tax Act**, which deems the **stamp duty valuation** of transferred property to be the sale consideration for **capital gains** purposes when the stated sale price is lower than the stamp valuation. The Tribunal stated that the **third proviso to section 50C**, inserted by the **Finance Act, 2018**, creates a tolerance band under which section 50C will **not apply if the difference between stamp duty value and actual consideration does not exceed 5%**; this tolerance was later **increased to 10% by the Finance Act, 2020**. Although those amendments were described as prospective, the Tribunal held them to be **curative in nature** and therefore applicable **retrospectively from 1 April 2003**, the date section 50C was originally introduced.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that where a property transfer’s **stamp duty value is up to 10% higher than the declared sale consideration**, the declared consideration should be accepted at face value and the **anti-avoidance substitution mechanism under section 50C should not be triggered**. The case was an appeal for **Assessment Year 2011–12** in the matter of **Maria Fernandes Cheryl vs. ITO (International Taxation 2(3)(1), Mumbai)**, with the Tribunal’s pronouncement dated **15 January 2021** and publication on **17 April 2021**. The ruling is relevant to taxpayers and tax teams handling **immovable property transfers**, especially where there is a small gap between contractual consideration and stamp duty value, because it supports using the statutory tolerance band rather than mechanically substituting stamp value for capital gains computation.

The Supreme Court held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 because Section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act applicable “as far as may be.” As a result, where a corporate debtor makes a written and signed acknowledgement of debt before expiry of the limitation period, that acknowledgement can extend the limitation period for filing an insolvency application. The Court also clarified that an entry in the debtor’s books of account, including a balance sheet entry, can constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18, provided it is read together with the notes annexed to or forming part of the balance sheet and the auditor’s report.

This decision specifically reverses the NCLAT Full Bench ruling in V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund, which had taken a contrary view on balance-sheet acknowledgements. The Court reaffirmed the basic limitation principle that once time begins to run, it cannot be stopped except by a legally recognized process. For compliance purposes, this means companies facing potential debt enforcement or insolvency exposure should treat balance-sheet disclosures, related notes, and auditor commentary as potentially legally significant acknowledgements that may revive or extend limitation periods for creditors. The judgment was pronounced on April 15, 2021 and published on April 17, 2021.

In this case, the refusal to accept the declaration was held improper because the record did not show that the taxpayer fell into any of the statutory exclusion categories. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **DCIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd.** examined the **third proviso to section 254(2A)** of the Income-tax Act, which had provided for **automatic vacation of a stay granted by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) after 365 days**, regardless of who caused the delay in hearing the appeal. The Court held that this rule was **unconstitutional** because it was **discriminatory and manifestly arbitrary**: it could punish an assessee even when the ITAT could not hear the appeal in time for reasons beyond the assessee’s control, and it could also benefit the Revenue even when the Revenue itself was responsible for the delay.

As a result, the Court struck down the offending operation of the proviso and directed that the provision be **read down** by deleting the word **“even”** and the words **“is not”** after the phrase **“delay in disposing of the appeal”**. In practical compliance terms, a stay granted by the ITAT **does not automatically lapse merely because 365 days have passed**; the stay will stand vacated **only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. This means the focus shifts to **fault-based delay** rather than a strict time-based expiration.

For corporate taxpayers with pending appeals and stay orders before the ITAT, the decision materially affects **stay-of-demand management**: companies no longer face automatic loss of stay solely due to passage of time beyond 365 days if they are not at fault for the delay. At the same time, the ruling preserves the possibility of vacation of stay where the assessee’s conduct is responsible for delaying disposal. There is **no new filing deadline or compliance formality created by this judgment**, but it is important for legal and tax teams to document which party caused any adjournments or hearing delays so that stay protection can be defended if challenged.

rows.summary:
This Delhi High Court ruling in **CIT v. D. K. Garg** concerns **Section 68 of the Income-tax Act** and the treatment of **accommodation entries**, **cash credits**, and the taxpayer’s attempt to claim the benefit of **peak credit**. The Court held that an accommodation entry provider who seeks peak-credit relief must make a **full and candid disclosure of all facts within his knowledge** about the credit entries in the relevant accounts; this includes explaining **the source of every deposit**, **the destination of every payment**, and the movement of funds through the account structure. In practical terms, the assessee must be able to show that money was moved **through banking channels** from the creditor’s bank account to the assessee’s bank account, that the **identity of the creditors** is established, and that the money later paid out from the assessee’s account returned to the creditors’ accounts; this is the **primary onus** on the assessee under Section 68.

The decision is especially relevant to entities or individuals involved in **entry-providing / paper-entity transactions** or other arrangements where cash is introduced and converted into cheques or bank transfers. The Court emphasized that a taxpayer cannot claim the benefit of peak credit merely by asserting that only the highest outstanding balance should be taxed; instead, the taxpayer must first produce a clear and credible explanation of the entire transaction flow and the linked accounts involved. Where the taxpayer fails to do this, the unexplained credits remain liable to be treated under Section 68. The case date is **AY 1995–96**, with the judgment pronounced on **4 August 2017** and published on **16 August 2017**.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court’s decision in **ADIT v. E-Funds IT Solution Inc.** addresses when a foreign company will be treated as having a **Permanent Establishment (PE) in India** under **Article 5 of the India–U.S. DTAA (1990)** for tax purposes. The tax authority had held that the U.S. companies had a **fixed place PE in Delhi** and were therefore taxable in India on income earned through that alleged PE; the CIT(A) also upheld the assessments, additionally reasoning that the companies had **service PE** and **agency PE** status under Article 5.

The Supreme Court explained the law on **fixed place PE, service PE, and agency PE**, and rejected the idea that mere **close association, dependence, or integrated business relationship** between the U.S. company and Indian group entities is enough to create a PE. It held that the correct test is whether the foreign enterprise itself has a sufficiently permanent **place of business in India through which its own business is carried on**, and that the **functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed** test is **not the proper test** for determining a location/fixed-place PE. The Court therefore clarified that a foreign company does not automatically become taxable in India just because related Indian entities perform support functions or because there is operational dependence between the entities.

For compliance purposes, the key practical takeaway is that **foreign enterprises using Indian affiliates or service providers are not automatically exposed to Indian PE risk solely because of group linkage or business dependence**. PE exposure must be assessed based on the actual facts showing whether the foreign company has a **fixed place**, **service presence**, or **agency relationship** in India within the meaning of the treaty, rather than relying on generalized notions of economic presence or business integration. The judgment is dated **October 24, 2017** (pronouncement), with publication on **October 25, 2017**.

rows.summary:
This circular explains how the GST return filings for July and August 2017 were to be handled during the initial rollout period, when the normal monthly return sequence under sections 37, 38, and 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 and rules 59, 60, and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017 was temporarily disrupted. Ordinarily, registered persons had to file outward supply details in FORM GSTR-1 by the 10th of the next month, inward supply details in FORM GSTR-2 by the 15th, and the monthly return in FORM GSTR-3 by the 20th; however, the GST Council extended the filing dates for GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 for July and August 2017 and allowed a simplified return in FORM GSTR-3B for those two months, to be filed by the notified due dates after payment of tax.  

The circular also notes that taxpayers using transitional credit under section 140 of the CGST Act for their July 2017 liability had to file FORM GST TRAN-1 on or before 28 August 2017, and that this credit would be posted to the electronic credit ledger and could be used to discharge tax liability. Because FORM GSTR-3B was filed instead of the normal return sequence while the GSTR-1/GSTR-2 due dates were extended, the circular says the system would later reconcile the information furnished in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 with the amounts reported in GSTR-3B once those returns were filed.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the simplified GSTR-3B filing did not replace the underlying reporting obligations permanently; it was an interim mechanism for the initial GST months, with reconciliation to follow once the regular statement/return data became available. The document is addressed to all Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax and all Principal Directors General/Directors General, indicating that field formations were expected to apply and oversee this reconciliation framework.

No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 27 August 2017 by the Ministry of Finance, clarifies how lottery tickets are to be classified and taxed under GST because assessees were encountering return-filing and tax-payment problems due to a coding mismatch. The circular states that, under the CGST Act, 2017, supply of lottery is treated as a **supply of goods**, even though the GST rate notifications had shown the classification entry for lottery as “-”. For compliance purposes, the government clarifies that this “-” should be read as **“Any Chapter” of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975**, and that lottery must be taxed under the applicable GST rate notifications accordingly.

The circular specifically resolves the issue that the lottery description was appearing as goods while the code allotted in the system was under services, which had prevented some taxpayers from uploading returns or depositing tax on time. It emphasizes that return filing is linked to the rate of tax applicable to the supply, and that there is no ambiguity on the applicable lottery tax rate. The prescribed GST rate for lottery is confirmed as **12% or 28%, as the case may be**, depending on the relevant notified category.

This clarification applies to the GST framework under **CGST, IGST, UTGST, and SGST** rate notifications and is directed to all Central Tax field formations and systems officials. From a compliance standpoint, entities dealing in lottery tickets should ensure their tax classification and return-filing treatment align with the “Any Chapter” classification and the correct notified rate, so tax can be paid and returns filed without system errors or delay.

It is hereby clarified that any registered person who has received a minimum foreign inward remittance of 10% of export turnover in the preceding financial year is eligible for availing the facility of LUT provided that the amount received as foreign inward remittance is not less than Page 2 of 5 Rs. one crore. This means that only such exporters are eligible to LUT facilities who have received a remittance of Rs. one crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is a higher amount, in the previous financial
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the rules for exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax by furnishing either a bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT), under section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, in response to inconsistent interpretations of Notification No. 16/2017–Central Tax dated 7 July 2017 and earlier GST circulars. The key policy clarification is that the LUT facility is no longer limited to manufacturer exporters: **any registered person** may use LUT **if** they received foreign inward remittance in the preceding financial year equal to **at least 10% of export turnover, and in any case not less than Rs. 1 crore**; the circular states this effectively means the exporter must have received **whichever is higher: Rs. 1 crore or 10% of export turnover** in the previous financial year. If that threshold is not met, the exporter must export under a **bond** rather than LUT.

The circular also clarifies the process for using and accepting the bond/LUT. The bond must be **executed on non-judicial stamp paper** for an amount determined as per the relevant bond format, and the exporter is required to furnish a **bank guarantee** along with the bond only to the extent required by the proper officer, not as a blanket requirement for all exporters. It further states that the LUT can be furnished on the exporter’s own letterhead in the prescribed format, and it must be accepted by the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner. The circular instructs tax officers not to insist on unnecessary guarantees or documentation beyond what the notification and circular require.

Another important compliance clarification is that the LUT/bond is a **pre-export** undertaking: it must be furnished **before exports are made** under the zero-rated/without payment route. The circular also explains that exports under bond/LUT are subject to the condition that the exporter will comply with the export provisions, including export of goods or services within the prescribed time limits and maintenance of proof of export. If the exporter fails to comply, the bond can be enforced for tax, interest, and any other applicable amount. The circular is intended to create uniformity across field formations, so compliance teams should ensure exporter eligibility is checked against the prior-year remittance threshold and that the correct instrument—LUT or bond—is used before undertaking exports without payment of integrated tax.

A clarification has been soughtas to whether bond to be furnished for exports is a running bond (with debit / credit facility) or a one-time bond (separate bond for each consignment / export). It is observed consign
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the bond/LUT procedure for **exports of goods or services without payment of integrated tax** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. It was issued by the **CBEC GST Policy Wing on 7 July 2017** under **section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017** to ensure uniform implementation after complaints from exporters and field offices about difficulties with the prescribed process. The core requirement is that any registered person making such zero-rated exports must furnish either a **bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in FORM GST RFD-11** before exporting without IGST payment.

The circular then distinguishes who may use an LUT and who must furnish a bond. It points to **Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 01-07-2017**, which specifies the class of exporters eligible to export under LUT, together with the applicable conditions and safeguards. **Exporters not covered by that notification must furnish a bond instead of an LUT.** The circular also reiterates that the **procedure for submission and acceptance of the bond was already laid down in Circular No. 2/2/2017-GST dated 4 July 2017**.

For the bond itself, the document requires that it be executed on **non-judicial stamp paper** of the **value applicable in the State where the bond is furnished**. A key clarification sought by the field was whether export bonds should be a **running bond with debit/credit facility** or a **separate one-time bond for each consignment/export**. The circular notes this issue and explains that the bond mechanism is intended to operate as a running bond, so exporters do not have to execute a fresh bond for every shipment.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that exporters making zero-rated supplies without IGST must first check whether they qualify for LUT under the 1 July 2017 notification; if not, they must arrange a bond in RFD-11 on the correct state stamp paper and follow the prescribed submission/acceptance process from the earlier circular. The circular is not imposing a new tax rate or deadline, but it does require adherence to the LUT/bond framework as a precondition to exporting without paying integrated tax.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 5 July 2017 by the Central Board of Excise and Customs (GST Policy Wing), assigns “proper officer” status for specific GST functions under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (and related rules) to designated Central Tax officers, for matters other than registration and composition. It applies by virtue of section 2(91) of the CGST Act, read with section 20 of the IGST Act and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act, and it is intended to clarify which officer rank may legally exercise particular powers under the Act/rules.

For Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns the functions under section 67(7) and the proviso to section 78. For Additional or Joint Commissioners of Central Tax, it assigns powers under sections 67(1), (2), (5), and (9); sections 71(1) and (2); the proviso to section 81; the proviso to section 129(6); and rule 139 sub-rules (1) to (4) and rule 140(2). For Deputy or Assistant Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns a broader set of functions, including sections 54(5), (6), (7), and (10); section 60(1), (2), and (3); sections 63, 64(1), and 65(6); and multiple powers under section 74, including sub-sections (1), (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (9), and (10), with the listing continuing on the next page. 

From a compliance standpoint, the practical impact is that taxpayers and company compliance teams must ensure that notices, orders, demands, recovery actions, inspections, access requests, search/seizure-related actions, refund-related actions, and other proceedings under the cited provisions are handled by the correct officer rank, because authority is being formally allocated to those officers. The circular does not set new monetary thresholds, tax rates, or filing deadlines; instead, it is an internal administrative authorization that determines which GST officer is empowered to act under the listed sections and rules, effective from the date of the circular itself, 5 July 2017.

Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters on the issue of difficulties being faced while supplying the goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax and filing the FORM GST RFD -11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in), because of which exports are being held up. 2. Whereas, as per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, any registered person availing the option to supply goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax shall furnish, prior to export, a bond or a Letter of Undertaking. This bond or Letter of Undertaking is required to be furnished in FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal. Further, Circular No. 26/2017- Customs dated 1 st July, 2017 has clarified that the procedure as prescribed under rule 96A of the said rules requires to be followed for the export of goods from 1 st July, 2017. 3. Another issue being raised by various stakeholders is that the Bond/Letter of Undertaking is required to be given through the proper officer which is to be furnished to the jurisdictional Commissioner as per sub-rule (1) of rule 96A of the said rules. Taking cognizance of the fact that a large number of such Bonds/Letter of Undertakings would be required to be filed by the registered exporters who would be located at a distance from the office of the jurisdictional Commissioner, it is understood that the furnishing of such bonds/undertakings before the jurisdictional Commissioner may cause hardship to the exporters. 4. Thus, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (
rows.summary:
This circular addresses practical problems exporters were facing after GST implementation when supplying goods or services for export **without payment of integrated tax** and then trying to file **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST common portal. The government notes that these difficulties were causing export shipments to be held up, so it clarifies the procedure for furnishing the required **bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** under **rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**.

The core requirement is unchanged: any **registered person** choosing to export **without paying integrated tax** must furnish, **before export**, a **bond or LUT** in **FORM GST RFD-11**. The circular also confirms that, for **export of goods**, the rule 96A procedure applies **from 1 July 2017**, consistent with **Circular No. 26/2017-Customs dated 1 July 2017**.

The new operational relaxation is that the bond/LUT does **not** need to be physically filed before the **jurisdictional Commissioner**, which had created hardship because many exporters are located far from that office. Instead, the circular allows this filing to be handled through the **proper officer** / jurisdictional tax administration mechanism in a way that avoids travel and administrative delay, so exporters can complete the requirement more easily and prevent export disruption.

For compliance purposes, the document is important because it confirms that exporters using the **zero-rated export without IGST payment route** must still ensure a valid **bond or LUT is in place before export**, but the process is being administratively simplified to reduce delays. The effective date tied to the export procedure is **1 July 2017**, and the requirement remains to use **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST portal.

rows.summary:
This circular amends Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST dated 9 February 2018 on the question of who is the “proper officer” for adjudicating show cause notices issued under sections 73 and 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the IGST Act, 2017. It responds to two prior central tax notifications: Notification No. 02/2022-Central Tax dated 11 March 2022, which had already given certain Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners in specified Central Tax Commissionerates all-India jurisdiction to adjudicate DGGI-issued show cause notices, and Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax dated 25 November 2024, which expanded that arrangement to more such officers by substituting Table V in Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax. The 27/2024 notification took effect on 1 December 2024, and this circular is issued on 4 December 2024 to align the CBIC circular with that expanded adjudication framework.

The operative change is that paragraph 7.1 of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST (as previously amended by Circular No. 169/01/2022-GST dated 12 March 2022) is substituted. The new text begins by stating that, for show cause notices issued by officers of the Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (DGGI), there may be cases where a single notice is issued to multiple noticees. In such cases, adjudication is to be handled in line with the all-India jurisdiction empowered officers specified under the amended notification framework, rather than being confined by the normal territorial jurisdiction approach.

For compliance purposes, the practical impact is on the adjudication of DGGI-issued show cause notices under sections 73 and 74: companies or other noticees facing such notices may have their matters adjudicated by the centrally empowered Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax designated under Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax as amended, including the broader set added by Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax. The document does not create a new tax rate, penalty, filing deadline, or monetary threshold; its significance is procedural and jurisdictional, clarifying which officers are authorized to adjudicate DGGI notices, including where one notice covers multiple noticees. The compliance team should therefore ensure that any DGGI show cause notices received on or after the effective change are tracked with attention to the designated adjudicating authority, and that internal responses, representation strategy, and escalation paths reflect this all-India jurisdiction framework.

(Supreme Court of India) Substance Over Label: “Advance” Given as Security Is Earnest Money Liable to Forfeiture; Refund Cannot Be Granted Without a Specific Prayer u/s 22-Supreme Court Summary: The Supreme Court held that an amount described in an agreement as “advance money” may, in substance, constitute earnest money if it was paid as security for due performance of the contract. Such earnest money can be forfeited upon the purchaser’s default where the agreement contains a clear, reasonable & reciprocal forfeiture clause. The Court further held that refund of earnest money cannot be granted in a suit for specific performance unless such relief is specifically claimed, as required u/s 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Agreement, Advance & Alleged Default The purchaser entered into an agreement dated 25.07.2007 for purchase of a property situated at Kengeri, Bengaluru, for ₹55.50 lakh. He paid ₹20 lakh through two cheques as advance & agreed to pay the balance ₹35.50 lakh within four months. The agreement expressly provided that if the purchaser failed to pay the balance consideration within the stipulated period, the advance would be forfeited. Conversely, if the vendors failed to execute the sale deed despite the purchaser being ready to perform, they would refund double the advance amount. The purchaser claimed that he approached a bank for finance but was advised to obtain the original title documents & probate of an unregistered Will under which the vendor had acquired the property. According to him, the vendors failed to furnish the required documents despite repeated requests. The vendors, ho
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that an amount described in a sale agreement as “advance” can still be treated in substance as **earnest money/security for performance** if the surrounding terms show it was paid to secure completion of the contract, and not merely as a partial price payment. In this case, the purchaser agreed on **25.07.2007** to buy property in Kengeri, Bengaluru, for **₹55.50 lakh**, paid **₹20 lakh** by two cheques, and undertook to pay the remaining **₹35.50 lakh within four months**. The agreement expressly stated that if the purchaser failed to pay the balance within that period, the advance would be **forfeited**; if the vendors defaulted despite the purchaser being ready and willing, they had to refund **double the advance**. The Court found this reciprocal forfeiture/refund structure to be clear and reasonable, and accepted that the ₹20 lakh advance functioned as earnest money liable to forfeiture upon the purchaser’s default.

The Court also addressed the procedural point under **Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963**, holding that a court **cannot grant refund of earnest money in a suit for specific performance unless the plaintiff specifically asks for that relief in the pleadings**. In other words, a general prayer for specific performance is not enough to obtain a refund of earnest money if the contract fails; the refund must be expressly sought. The purchaser had argued that he was unable to complete payment because the vendors allegedly did not provide original title documents and probate relating to an unregistered Will, but the Court’s ruling emphasizes that, where the agreement contains a valid forfeiture clause and the purchaser defaults, the earnest money can be forfeited unless the purchaser both proves entitlement to relief and properly pleads the refund claim. This decision is relevant for companies, property sellers, and contracting parties because it confirms that contractual “advance” payments may be treated as forfeitable security deposits depending on the agreement’s substance, and that litigants seeking money back in a specific performance suit must include a **specific prayer for refund**.

(Supreme Court) Democratic Control Stops Where Depositors’ Safety Begins: Supreme Court Upholds RBI’s Five-Year Supersession Power u/s 36AAA Over Multi-State Co-operative Banks SEO Title: Supreme Court Upholds RBI Power to Extend Co-operative Bank Board Supersession SEO Description: Supreme Court holds RBI can extend supersession of a multi-State co-operative bank Board beyond six months and its original tenure. Summary: The Supreme Court has held that RBI’s power u/s 36AAA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to supersede the Board of Directors of a multi-State co-operative bank is not restricted by the six-month ceiling prescribed under Article 243ZL(1) of the Constitution. RBI may extend the supersession from time to time for an aggregate period of up to five years, even beyond the original tenure of the elected Board, where such regulatory intervention is necessary to protect depositors, preserve financial stability & secure proper management of the bank. Supersession of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank’s Board Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd. was originally registered under the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960. It commenced banking activities in 1965 & became a scheduled bank in 1988. Following amalgamation with co-operative banks situated in Gujarat & Karnataka under directions issued by RBI, it acquired the status of a multi-State co-operative bank. The appellants were elected to the Bank’s Board in May 2019 for a statutory term of five years. On 24.11.2023, RBI invoked section 36AAA(1) & (2
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that RBI’s supersession power over the board of a multi-State co-operative bank under section 36AAA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is not confined to the six-month limit in Article 243ZL(1) of the Constitution. Instead, RBI may extend a board supersession from time to time for an aggregate period of up to five years, where necessary to protect depositors, maintain financial stability, and secure proper management of the bank. This means that for affected multi-State co-operative banks, RBI can lawfully continue board supersession well beyond the ordinary six-month constitutional ceiling applicable to co-operative societies when the statutory banking-regulation framework is being applied.

The case involved Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., which began as a Maharashtra co-operative society bank, later became a scheduled bank, and after amalgamation with co-operative banks in Gujarat and Karnataka attained the status of a multi-State co-operative bank. The appellants had been elected to its board in May 2019 for a five-year statutory term, but on 24.11.2023 RBI invoked section 36AAA(1) and (2) to supersede the board. The Court upheld RBI’s action and the legality of extending the supersession period, confirming that the regulator’s intervention can outlast the original elected board term if required for depositor protection and sound banking governance.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that multi-State co-operative banks are subject to RBI’s enhanced supervisory powers under the Banking Regulation Act, and board governance cannot be assumed to be protected by the Constitution’s six-month supersession limit alone. If RBI determines that a bank’s condition warrants intervention, the board may remain superseded in repeated extensions for up to five years in total, creating a prolonged period in which ordinary board control is displaced by RBI-appointed administration. This decision underscores the need for banks in this category to maintain strong governance, capital, and prudential compliance, because regulatory non-compliance or financial weakness can trigger sustained loss of board control and ongoing RBI oversight.

rows.summary:
This Himachal Pradesh High Court decision concerns a tax department appeal filed 31 days late against an ITAT Chandigarh order dated 25.02.2025 in ITA No. 413/Chd/2024, SBS Biotech Unit-II v. The Pr. CIT-1 Chandigarh. The Court allowed the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax-1’s request for condonation of delay, holding that the delay was sufficiently explained and arose from the case records being with the Income Tax Officer at Parwanoo, the need to obtain and forward opinion for approval, issuance of instructions to Standing Counsel, the authorised signatory being at Chandigarh, and intervening festival breaks. The Court found this sequence showed bona fide conduct, diligence, prompt action, and “sufficient cause,” and emphasized that the explanation covered the entire period of delay.

For compliance purposes, the key legal holding is that a short, nominal delay in filing an income-tax appeal can be condoned where the party shows genuine and diligent pursuit of the appellate remedy; at the limitation/condonation stage, the court should not assess the merits of the proposed appeal. The Court distinguished much more extreme delay cases relied on by the respondent, including Shivamma, which involved 3,966 days’ delay, and Managing Committee of Namrata Girls High School, which involved an aggregate delay of about 11 years, indicating those authorities did not control a 31-day delay supported by a detailed explanation.

The decision also notes the relevance of Section 260A(2A) of the Income-tax Act, underscoring that delay-condonation under the appellate framework remains available where sufficient cause is shown. There are no new filing deadlines or procedural rules created by this judgment, but it reinforces that tax authorities and other appellants should be prepared to document the full chronology of delay and the reasons for it, because a complete, credible explanation may justify condonation even when the appeal is filed after the prescribed time.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court decision concerns **New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA)** and its tax status, not a private developer penalty. The Income Tax Department had issued **notices under Section 142 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on 28.07.1998 and 08.08.1998**, and NOIDA challenged them on the ground that it was a **local authority** and therefore exempt from income tax under **Section 10(20)** and **Section 10(20A)**. The Allahabad High Court initially accepted NOIDA’s position on **14.02.2000**, holding that NOIDA was a local body and covered by the exemption under **Section 10(20A)**, although it did not decide the separate Section 10(20) issue; later, the High Court’s **Division Bench judgment dated 28.02.2011** dismissed NOIDA’s writ petition, and the review was rejected on **04.11.2011**, leading to the appeal before the Supreme Court.

For compliance purposes, the material point is that the case turns on whether an authority created under the **U.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976**—here, NOIDA, constituted by notification dated **17.04.1976**—is entitled to tax exemption as a local authority under the pre-amendment income-tax provisions. The court’s discussion is anchored in the statutory framework of the 1976 Act and the impact of the **Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992** on the status of such development authorities. Any organization structured like NOIDA, or similarly created under a state industrial/urban development statute, would need to assess whether it can claim local-authority-style tax exemptions and whether it remains exposed to income-tax notices and compliance obligations under Section 142.

The Court found that the Commission relied upon a detailed report filed by the AO on the last date of hearing, passed its order on the very next day without permitting the assessee to respond, deviated from the statutory procedure & suffered from a reasonable likelihood of bias. Despite the abolition of the Settlement Commission, the Court directed the Interim Board for Settlement to treat the restored application as pending & decide it afresh within six weeks. Search, returns & settlement application The assessee-company was engaged in purchasing & selling dates, oats & honey and manufacturing syrups, jams & squash under the brand name “Lion Dates.” A search u/s 132 was conducted on 17.07.2013 at its business premises & the residences of its directors. Statements were recorded u/s 132(4), followed by another statement u/s 131. Notices u/s 153A were issued for AYs 2008-09 to 2013-14, while a notice u/s 148 was issued for AY 2007-08. The assessee filed the required returns but claimed that certain mistakes had occurred while offering additional income on its consultant’s advice. The assessee filed an application u/s 245C(1
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court held that the Settlement Commission’s rejection of Lion Dates Impex (P) Ltd.’s settlement application under section 245D(4) could not stand because the process was unfair and procedurally defective. The assessee had been subjected to a search under section 132 on 17.07.2013 at its business premises and the residences of its directors, statements were recorded under sections 132(4) and 131, and reassessment/notice proceedings followed for AYs 2008-09 to 2013-14 under section 153A, with a section 148 notice also issued for AY 2007-08; after this, it filed a settlement application under section 245C(1). The Court found that the Commission relied on a detailed report submitted by the Assessing Officer on the last date of hearing, then passed its rejection order the very next day without giving the assessee any meaningful opportunity to review or rebut that report, which violated the statutory procedure and amounted to a denial of hearing. It also held that the circumstances gave rise to a reasonable likelihood of bias, because the case was effectively decided on material introduced at the end of the hearing without fair participation by the taxpayer.

Although the Income Tax Settlement Commission itself has since been abolished, the Court directed that the restored settlement application be treated as pending before the Interim Board for Settlement and be reconsidered afresh. The Interim Board must decide the matter within six weeks. For compliance purposes, the key point is that settlement proceedings must follow a fair, adversarial process: if the department files last-minute material, the applicant must be given a real chance to respond before any adverse decision is made, and decision-makers must avoid any appearance of bias or pre-judgment.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | No E-Way Bill on an Internal Stock Transfer? No Section 129 Penalty Either
rows.desc: Summary: The Thiruvananthapuram Bench of the GST Appellate Tribunal in M.S. Steels v. Commissioner of Kerala State GST, (2026) 45 Centax 257, considered whether penalty under Section 129 of the CGST/KGST Act, 2017 could be imposed where goods were moved from one registered premises to another registered premises of the same assessee under the same GSTIN without an e-way bill. M/s M.S. Steels, a partnership firm dealing in steel goods, moved TMT bars from its own premises to its own godown on 13.06.2022 under Delivery Challan No. M120. The vehicle was intercepted and the goods were detained under Section 129(1) solely for want of an e-way bill, resulting in a penalty of Rs. 1,34,640 under Section 129(3), with no tax demand. The Tribunal held that the movement was not a “supply” under Section 7 because there was only one entity, no second person and no consideration. Consequently, Section 9 was not attracted and there was no “tax payable” on which the Section 129 penalty could be computed. The Tribunal rejected the Revenue’s contention that “tax payable” was merely a yardstick for penalty and also rejected the finding that the transaction was “not genuine” merely because the e-way bill was absent. At the same time, the Tribunal clarified that the e-way bill requirement continues for movement for reasons other than supply under Rule 138(1)(ii), and that the appropriate consequence for such a documentation lapse lies under Section 122(1)(xiv), rather than the tax-linked machinery of Section 129. The appeal was allowed and the Order-in-Appeal was set aside with consequential relief. No E-Way Bill on an Internal Stock Transfer? No Section 129 Penalty Either Analysis of M.S. Steels v. Commissioner of Kerala State GST, (2026) 45 Centax 257 (Tri. – GST – Kerala) Table of Contents▸ 1. Introduction 2. Facts of the Case 3. Question of Law 4. The Statutory Scheme 5. Findings of the Tribunal 5.1 A same-GSTIN movement is not a “supply” 5.2 No supply means no tax, and no tax means
rows.summary:
The Thiruvananthapuram Bench of the GST Appellate Tribunal in **M.S. Steels v. Commissioner of Kerala State GST, (2026) 45 Centax 257** held that **Section 129 penalty under the CGST/KGST Act, 2017 cannot be imposed where goods are moved between two registered premises of the same assessee under the same GSTIN, solely because no e-way bill was generated**. The facts involved **M/s M.S. Steels**, a partnership firm dealing in steel goods, which moved **TMT bars** from its own premises to its own godown on **13.06.2022** under **Delivery Challan No. M120**; the vehicle was intercepted, the goods were detained under **Section 129(1)** for want of an e-way bill, and a penalty of **Rs. 1,34,640** was levied under **Section 129(3)**, with **no separate tax demand** raised.

The Tribunal found that this internal transfer was **not a “supply” under Section 7**, because there was only **one legal entity**, there was **no second person**, and there was **no consideration**. As a result, **Section 9 (the charging provision for GST)** was not triggered, and therefore there was **no “tax payable”** on which a penalty under **Section 129** could be computed. The Tribunal expressly rejected the Revenue’s argument that “tax payable” is only a penalty benchmark and also rejected the characterization of the movement as “not genuine” merely because the e-way bill was absent.

At the same time, the Tribunal clarified an important compliance point: **the e-way bill requirement still applies to movements that are not supplies, if they fall within Rule 138(1)(ii)**. However, where the problem is only a documentation lapse in such a non-supply movement, the Tribunal said the proper consequence would lie under **Section 122(1)(xiv)**, not under the tax-linked detention and penalty mechanism of **Section 129**. The appeal was **allowed**, the **Order-in-Appeal was set aside**, and the assessee received **consequential relief**.

rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court (Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri) dealt with a writ petition by Umen Chandra Roy concerning entitlement to Input Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with Section 16(5). The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the Court noted was within the statutory cut-off contemplated by Section 16(5), and later filed a rectification application on January 12, 2026 seeking the ITC benefit. That rectification request was rejected by the revenue authority on April 8, 2026 because it was said not to have been filed within the period prescribed in a departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024 read with a circular dated October 15, 2024.

The Revenue challenged the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai order dated 8 February 2023, which had dismissed the Revenue’s appeal against the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Pune order dated 23 March 2022. The Assessing Officer made an addition of Rs.7,47,00,000/- by disallowing the provision for major repairs. The assessee contended that the liability accrued over the period and that the expenditure could be provided for on the basis of reliable estimates. The CIT(Appeals) examined the Concession Agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38 and 39, and
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held, in **PCIT v. ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd.**, that a **scientifically estimated provision for major repairs** under a road BOT concession can be allowable for income-tax purposes, and it **dismissed the Revenue’s appeal under Section 260A** of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The dispute related to **Assessment Year 2015-16** and arose after the Assessing Officer disallowed a **provision for major repairs of Rs. 7,47,00,000**, increasing taxable income, even though the assessee had reported a **book loss of Rs. 4,48,91,467** and an **income-tax loss of Rs. 8,46,64,672**.

The assessee was a **special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) arrangement** and toll collection, operating under a **30-year concession agreement with the Government of Maharashtra**. Under that agreement, the assessee was **contractually required to carry out major repairs during the concession period**, with the **first major repair due after seven years (in the eighth year)** and the **last repair in the 30th year**. The assessee argued that the repair liability **accrued over time** and that it was therefore proper to create a provision based on **reliable scientific estimates**, rather than waiting until the actual expense was incurred.

In support of its position, the assessee also relied on **CBDT Circular No. 9/2014**, dealing with expenditure on the development of roads/highways under BOT agreements. The CIT(A), after examining the **Concession Agreement—particularly Articles 17, 37, 38, and 39—**accepted the assessee’s claim, and the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai, affirmed that view in its order dated **8 February 2023**. The High Court found no error in that approach and upheld the Tribunal’s order dated **8 February 2023** as well as the CIT(A)’s order dated **23 March 2022**.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that entities engaged in **BOT road projects or similar concession arrangements** should carefully review their contracts to determine whether they have **binding, periodic obligations for major repairs** and whether those liabilities can be **reasonably estimated and recognized over the concession period**. The case confirms that where the obligation is contractual and the estimate is supportable, a provision may be defensible; however, the allowance depends on the **specific concession terms and the quality of the estimate**, not on a blanket rule for all infrastructure projects.

The Appellant/Applicant submitted that it had filed an appeal before the First Appellate Authority in APL-01 and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, stating that the Department was undertaking recovery proceedings. The Respondent-State Government drew the Bench’s attention to its submissions dated 28.07.2026 and, particularly, to APL-02, which had been rejected on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, being the First Appellate Authority. The Registry raised a defect because the GSTAT appeal had been filed before the rejection order of the First Appellate Authority came into existence. After hearing both sides and examining the records, the Bench found that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 had been filed on 19.03.2026, whereas no order under Section 112(1) of the CGST Act, 2017 was then in existence because the First Appellate Authority had not yet passed its order. The central question before the Bench was whether an aggrieved person could approach GSTAT under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017 in the absence of an order passed under Section 107 or Section 108. The Bench reproduced the substance of Section 112(1), under which an aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order passed unde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that an appeal to GSTAT is not maintainable if it is filed before the First Appellate Authority has passed its order under Section 107 of the CGST Act, 2017. In this case, Pankajam Plastics filed an appeal in APL-01 before the First Appellate Authority and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, saying the Department had begun recovery proceedings. However, the record showed that the First Appellate Authority’s order rejecting APL-02 was not passed until 24.06.2026, so when the GSTAT filing was made, no appealable order under Section 107 or Section 108 existed. The Registry had flagged this as a defect, and the Bench agreed that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 could not be entertained because Section 112(1) allows an appeal to the Tribunal only against an order already passed by the lower authority.

For compliance purposes, the decision means taxpayers cannot pre-emptively file a GSTAT appeal merely because recovery proceedings are underway or because they expect an adverse first appellate outcome; the statutory precondition is the existence of an actual order from the First Appellate Authority or other qualifying order under the Act. The ruling reinforces that the timing of the appeal is critical: a GSTAT appeal filed before the Section 107/108 order comes into existence is procedurally defective and liable to be rejected as not maintainable. Companies facing GST disputes should therefore track the exact date of the appellate order, preserve the order copy, and file the Tribunal appeal only after the order is formally passed and available.

rows.summary:
The document summarizes an anti-profiteering proceeding under Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017 concerning M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. and its “Vertex Panache” project, after a homebuyer complaint alleged that GST input tax credit (ITC) benefits were not passed on to buyers following the introduction of GST effective 01.07.2017. The Standing Committee referred the matter to the DGAP, whose initial report found alleged profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010, made up of Rs. 65,17,866 as base profiteering plus Rs. 7,82,144 in GST, said to be due to 140 eligible homebuyers. Vertex Homes argued that the apparent ITC benefit was offset by significant increases in construction costs, pointing to a budgeted construction cost of Rs. 1,56,94,91,872 versus actual expenditure of Rs. 1,61,06,72,320, which it said reflected a net cost increase of Rs. 4,11,80,448 including indirect costs.

The company further identified sharp inflation in key materials used in the project: Ready-Mix Concrete increased by 19.87%, sand by 62.98%, and bricks by 73.17%. It claimed that, based on actual quantities and actual costs, the extra expense attributable to these major inputs alone was Rs. 3,49,87,499, materially eroding any ITC-based benefit. In support, the respondent relied on the Delhi High Court’s decision in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, especially paragraph 118, to argue that price increases driven by genuine commercial factors do not amount to profiteering merely because tax incidence has reduced or ITC has become available. The respondent also submitted a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 from M/s Tukaram & Co. The material point of the document is that the dispute concerns whether GST ITC gains were actually retained by the developer or were neutralized by legitimate construction-cost escalation; the case is being used to test the application of Section 171 in the real-estate sector, particularly for homebuyers in projects launched around the GST transition date of 01.07.2017.

rows.summary:
This GST anti-profiteering case concerns M/s Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd., against whom a complaint alleged that the company did not pass on the benefit of the GST rate reduction on “MI LED Television 4A 80 cm” from 28% to 18%, effective 01.01.2019 under Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31.12.2018. The matter was referred by the Standing Committee on Anti-Profiteering to the DGAP under Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017, and the DGAP reviewed invoices and outward taxable supplies for the pre-rate-cut period 01.11.2018 to 31.12.2018 and the post-rate-cut period 01.01.2019 to 31.12.2019. On its initial analysis, the DGAP found profiteering of ₹7,79,947, later reduced to ₹5,58,891 after accepting credit notes totaling ₹2,21,056 issued to 174 customers for cancelled orders or returned goods.

A key dispute before the GST Appellate Tribunal was whether the respondent had actually passed the GST benefit to customers through Electronic Gift Vouchers (EGVs). The respondent produced EGV screenshots, an Excel mapping of vouchers to customer orders and invoices, and later credit notes; however, the DGAP initially objected that the EGVs appeared conditional, time-bound, and restricted, and that the system description “Offers and cash back” did not by itself prove transfer of the GST benefit. The Tribunal nevertheless held that the EGVs were a valid mode of passing on the GST benefit, accepted the voucher-based evidence along with the mapping provided, and treated them as an actual consumer benefit transfer rather than an impermissible substitute. The Tribunal also accepted the additional credit-note adjustments already recognized by the DGAP.

As a result, the Tribunal ordered the respondent to deposit only the remaining profiteered amount of ₹10,241 into the Consumer Welfare Fund. For compliance teams, the material takeaway is that the anti-profiteering obligation attached to the 01.01.2019 GST rate reduction was not limited to cash refunds; properly documented Electronic Gift Vouchers could be accepted as evidence of benefit transfer, provided there is traceable linkage to the affected customer orders/invoices. The order underscores the need to maintain contemporaneous records showing how each customer received the benefit, because unsupported or inadequately mapped voucher schemes may still be challenged even where the business intends them as a pass-through mechanism.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: Summary: The article examines the restriction of input tax credit under Section 17(5)(c) and (d) of the CGST Act on works contract services, goods and services used for constructing immovable property, and the statutory exceptions for plant and machinery and construction not undertaken on a taxable person’s own account. It explains the meaning of immovable property through the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act and judicial tests concerning the nature, object, intention, functionality, permanency and marketability of annexation. It also discusses ITC eligibility for movable installations, HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems and other business equipment, and recommends separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery and movable goods to reduce the risk of denial of otherwise eligible credit. Table of Contents▸ Background: Blocked credit under section 17(5)(c/d) Comments: What is immovable property? Movable vs immovable property test-various judgements The principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Bharti Airtel Limited v The Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune Eligibility to Input tax credit and immovable property under GST Way ahead and conclusion Possible issues when there is a Single contract for construction of building and supply of machineries, other moveable goods: ACTION POINTS FOR ITC OPTIMISATION: Show all 10 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background: It is being observed that the assesses are receiving notices requiring to reverse/pay back ITC availed pertaining to newly constructed building projects used for business operations[such as factory premise/warehouses], alleging such credit is restricted being of nature of “immovable property”. However in addition to civil works, such projects involve installation of electrical fittings, cabling, STP, security, fire fighting, machines for manufacture of
rows.summary:
The document explains that GST input tax credit is frequently being challenged by tax authorities when taxpayers claim credit on costs tied to newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses, on the theory that the credit relates to “immovable property” and is therefore blocked under Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act. It states that credit is generally not available for works contract services and for goods or services used in constructing immovable property on a taxpayer’s own account, but there is an important statutory exception for “plant and machinery” and for construction that is not undertaken for the taxpayer’s own account. The article emphasizes that determining whether something is immovable depends on legal tests drawn from the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act, and case law, focusing on factors such as the nature of the item, the object of annexation, intention, functionality, permanency, and marketability, rather than simply whether an item is attached to a building.

A major compliance point is that business installations embedded in or connected to a building are not automatically ineligible for ITC just because they are installed on-site. The document specifically discusses items such as HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, cabling, security systems, and other business equipment, noting that some of these may qualify as movable or as plant and machinery depending on how they are installed and used. The article warns that where a single contract covers both civil construction and supply/installation of machinery or movable goods, the tax officer may attempt to deny credit across the package or treat the whole project as blocked credit, creating a higher litigation risk.

To reduce that risk, the article recommends structuring procurement and invoicing so that civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods are covered under separate, independent contracts and separate invoices. This is presented as an ITC-optimization and documentation control measure, not merely a drafting preference, because clean separation of scope helps support the argument that eligible machinery or movable installations should not be tainted by ineligible immovable-property construction. The article also suggests that businesses engaged in factory, warehouse, or similar infrastructure projects should review the legal characterization of each installation item before claiming credit, rather than assuming all costs inside a constructed facility are blocked.

No new statutory deadlines or rate changes are described in the text provided, but the compliance implication is immediate: taxpayers with existing or planned construction projects should reassess past and current ITC positions, especially where notices have already been issued demanding reversal of credit on newly constructed facilities. The practical takeaway is that a business should document the functional nature and separability of equipment at the time of contracting and installation, since the availability of ITC turns on whether the expenditure is truly for immovable property or instead for eligible plant, machinery, or other movable business assets.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court: Mere Words “Fraud” or “Suppression of Facts” in a GST Show Cause Notice Are Not Enough to Invoke Section 74 Summary: The Supreme Court in M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors. held that merely using the expressions “fraud” or “suppression of facts” in a GST show cause notice is insufficient to invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act. M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam challenged an SCN dated 13.06.2025 concerning FY 2018-19 and raising a demand of Rs.1,52,56,431/-. The company argued that the ordinary limitation period applicable under Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025 and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without identifying any conduct constituting fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Although the department sought to explain the allegations through its counter affidavit, the Court refused to consider those subsequent explanations. It reiterated that the legal validity of a notice must be determined from the notice itself and that deficiencies affecting jurisdiction cannot be cured through pleadings filed later before a court. The SCN contained only a bland reference to “fraud or concealment of facts” without explaining how fraud was inferred or concealment detected. The use of the expression “or” also indicated uncertainty regarding the allegation being made. Holding that the foundational facts and reasoning supporting the invocation of the extended limitation period must be disclosed in the notice, the Supreme Court set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order as well as the SCN and restrained the department from proceeding further on its basis. Table of Contents▸ Background of the Case What the Company Argued What the Department Argued What the Supreme Court Held Key Takeaways for Practitioners Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background of the Case This case deals with a Show Cause Notice (SCN) iss
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST department cannot invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by inserting the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts” in a show cause notice; the notice itself must set out the factual basis showing why that exceptional provision applies. In **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.**, the taxpayer challenged an **SCN dated 13.06.2025** for **FY 2018–19** demanding **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, arguing that the ordinary limitation under **Section 73** had already expired on **28.02.2025** and that the department had invoked **Section 74** mechanically without stating any conduct amounting to fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression. The Court agreed and emphasized that the validity of an SCN must be judged from the notice itself; the department cannot later “fix” jurisdictional defects by giving a fuller explanation in a counter affidavit or other court filings. It noted that the notice only contained a vague reference to “fraud or concealment of facts,” without explaining what was allegedly concealed, how fraud was inferred, or what facts supported the allegation, and the use of the word “or” showed uncertainty about the very basis of the charge. As a result, the Supreme Court **set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order and quashed the SCN**, and it **restrained the department from proceeding further** on that notice.  

For compliance teams, the practical point is that any GST notice seeking to use the longer **Section 74** window must contain specific, disclosed facts in the notice itself; a generic accusation of fraud is not enough to preserve the department’s extended limitation claim. Entities facing GST demands should scrutinize whether the department has clearly pleaded the factual ingredients needed for Section 74 and whether the normal Section 73 limitation has already expired, because a vague notice may be vulnerable to challenge at the threshold.

The authorised representative also submitted that an E-Way
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench held that goods transported without an E-Way Bill can still attract detention and Section 129 penalty where the surrounding facts suggest possible tax evasion, and it restored the tax and penalty that had been cancelled by the first appellate authority. The case involved 132.90 cubic feet of iron goods moved by M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly under Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018; the vehicle was intercepted by the Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018, and the driver did not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception. The tax authorities had imposed tax of Rs. 47,844 and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844 under Section 129(3) of the UPGST Act, 2017, but the first appellate authority later set aside both amounts by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018.

On appeal, the Department argued that transportation without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated Rule 138 of the GST Rules and that later production of the tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment did not erase the original non-compliance. It also argued that the interception, the nature of the goods, the route, and the later documents together supported an inference of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal’s order summary indicates that the key issue was whether the factual circumstances justified restoring the Section 129 levy despite the assessee’s later documentary support.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that for intra-State movement of goods covered by the GST e-way bill framework, the E-Way Bill must accompany the consignment at the time of transit; producing invoices or return records after detention may not prevent penalty exposure if the vehicle is intercepted without the required document. This decision reinforces that detention proceedings under Section 129 can be sustained where officials view the lapse as more than a mere technical defect, especially when the goods, route, or conduct raise evasion concerns.

rows.summary:
This CESTAT Chennai order (Final Order Nos. 42436–42438/2018, pronounced 18.09.2018) deals with three connected service tax appeals involving real estate developers in Tamil Nadu: Real Value Promoters Pvt. Ltd., Ceebros Property Development, and Prime Developers. The core dispute was whether their construction activities should be taxed as **Works Contract Service** under the post-1.6.2007 composition scheme, or instead as **Commercial or Industrial Construction Service / other taxable service**, with the department alleging short-payment of service tax for certain projects. For Real Value Promoters, the department specifically challenged the tax treatment of three projects—**Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, and Surya Skanda**—arguing that the contracts were not properly classifiable as works contracts and that the assessee had not validly opted for the composition scheme.

The tribunal focused on the legal position that the department had attempted to split the transaction into separate parts—supply of materials on one side and construction/service on the other—and to deny works contract treatment on that basis. The tribunal held that where a construction agreement involves both transfer of property in goods and provision of construction/service elements, it is to be treated as a **works contract** rather than a pure service contract, and therefore the applicable taxation must follow the works contract regime rather than being reclassified as commercial construction merely because the assessee separately accounted for supply and service components. In substance, the order rejects the department’s attempt to treat these contracts as non-works contracts simply because of the manner in which the consideration or components were structured.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that developers executing **composite construction projects after 1.6.2007** should assess whether their contracts legally constitute works contracts and, if so, whether they have properly followed the **composition scheme opt-in requirements** and related tax payment methodology for the projects at issue. The ruling turns on the nature of the contract and the existence of both goods and service elements, and it directly affects service tax exposure for real estate/construction businesses that had been paying under the works contract composition method while the department sought reclassification. The order does not announce a new filing deadline or rate change in the text provided, but it is important because it confirms the tribunal’s view that **separate supply and construction arrangements do not automatically take a contract outside works contract treatment** if, in substance, the arrangement is a composite works contract.

rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in a GST-fraud-related criminal case involving an allegedly non-existent/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries. The case was registered as Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC; the Court’s decision concerns pre-trial release only and does not decide the merits of the alleged GST fraud.

The applicant argued he was not the owner of the firm, was not named in the FIR, had no connection with the alleged fraud, and was not a beneficiary; his name allegedly appeared only through the statement of Sakeel Khan. He also relied on the fact that he had no prior criminal history apart from this case and had been in custody since 05.04.2026, with trial unlikely to conclude soon because of heavy court pendency.  

The State and the GST Department opposed bail, but the Court, after considering the allegations, evidence on record, and the parties’ submissions, found that the applicant was entitled to bail during the pendency of trial. The document does not set out any new GST compliance rule, filing obligation, penalty rate, or operational threshold; its practical significance is that it reflects judicial treatment of alleged GST-fraud prosecutions and the Court’s willingness to grant bail where the accused disputes ownership/benefit and where the FIR and alleged bogus-firm timeline are remote from each other.
