rows.summary:
The CESTAT Delhi decision concerns a municipality’s liability for service tax on two revenue streams during the period April 2009 to July 2014: (1) amounts collected for allowing advertisers to use municipal land for hoardings, and (2) rent/licence fees collected from various immovable properties, including vacant land, let or licensed to agencies, persons, and traders. The Department had demanded service tax of **Rs. 39,22,945**, plus **interest, penalties, and late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns**, and both the adjudicating authority and Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand before the matter went to the Tribunal. The facts also show the municipality received **Rs. 3,06,738** from hoarding-related receipts between **April 2009 and June 2012** and **Rs. 3,39,22,974** as rent from immovable properties between **April 2009 and July 2014**, with the dispute spanning both the **pre-negative-list** and **post-negative-list** service tax regimes.

On the immovable-property issue, the municipality argued that “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been wrongly interpreted, relying on the view in **Cuddalore Municipality v. Joint Commissioner of GST & Central Excise** that the words **“any other person”** mean a person other than the owner, and that **vacant land was excluded** from the relevant taxable definition. It also argued that **arrears of rent** had been subjected to the **wrong service tax rate**. On the advertisement/hoarding receipts, the municipality contended that it was not providing an advertisement service as such; rather, it was only collecting **statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961** for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings.

The Tribunal held that the **hoarding-space/advertisement-related receipts were taxable**, rejecting the municipality’s characterization as merely a statutory licence fee and treating the activity as falling within the service tax net. However, the title of the decision makes clear that the Tribunal **quashed the extended-period service tax demand**, which means the Department could not sustain the demand for the longer look-back period based on the facts alleged in the case. For compliance purposes, the key takeaways are that municipal bodies can face service tax exposure on receipts from allowing hoardings/advertising use of land, but the ability to invoke the **extended limitation period** is vulnerable and must be supported by the statutory requirements for suppression/misstatement or similar grounds; any demand relating to renting/licensing arrangements must also be tested against the exact statutory definition in force for the relevant period, including the treatment of **vacant land**, the identity of the recipient, and the applicable **rate** for any arrears.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court dealt with a writ petition filed by Sankaran Mekala challenging a demand order dated 16.07.2026 issued for Assessment Year 2015-16 under sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The petitioner asked the Court to quash the demand and to direct the Income Tax Department to reopen the e-filing portal so she could upload her return in compliance with an earlier Madras High Court order dated 09.02.2026 in W.P. In that earlier case, the Court had directed her to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and respond to the section 148 notice; she says she complied in part by depositing Rs. 5 lakhs, but could not upload the return because of technical problems with the portal.

For proof, the petitioner produced evidence of the Rs. 5 lakh payment, other supporting documents she had filed, and a screenshot showing the portal upload failure. The Revenue accepted notice, and the Court accepted the petitioner’s evidence of the technical inability to upload the return. On that basis, the High Court held that the interests of justice required giving her another opportunity to comply with the earlier order, rather than penalizing her for the portal issue. The writ petition was therefore disposed of with a direction allowing her to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 through the reopened portal access, so she could complete the filing that had been ordered earlier.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017 in full. The customs demand of Rs. 2,16,93,068, along with consequential interest, and the penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each imposed under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties imposed on the co-appellants, were held unsustainable because the Revenue did not produce reliable, corroborative evidence to support the allegations.

The case arose from a DEEC licence issued under the EXIM Policy 1997–2002 that allowed duty-free import of 5,350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5,000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue’s theory was that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that maize had been fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the required steel products. The Tribunal rejected that allegation, relying on multiple pieces of record evidence: special permission for exports through Ghojadanga LCS, customs examination of the export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, DRI Chennai’s confirmation that the goods were manufactured by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission to segregate and export unprocessed scrap, the undisputed realization of export proceeds, and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority.

A significant point noted by the Tribunal was that the CBI had also investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and had filed a final report stating that the available evidence indicated that the exports had in fact been made, which further undermined the customs case. For compliance purposes, the decision underscores that allegations of diversion or sham exports under an advance authorization/DEEC-type scheme must be backed by concrete, corroborated evidence; where exports are documented, examined by customs, certified by excise, supported by foreign-buyer permission, paid for, and formally discharged by DGFT, a demand for duty, interest, and penalties is unlikely to survive appellate review.

(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered a challenge to a customs penalty of Rs. 425,27,99,100/- imposed on Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya by the Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat under Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962. The penalty arose from an allegation that a consignment of natural diamonds had been mis-declared as lab-grown diamonds to pay a lower tariff. The Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025 was challenged before the Gujarat High Court, but the challenge failed when the High Court dismissed the appeal on 20.01.2026. The matter then reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court did not enter into the merits of the underlying customs dispute. Instead, the appellant contended that several judgments and articles relied upon by the second respondent in the Order-in-Original had been generated using Artificial Intelligence. The Court independently verified the material relied upon in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied upon case laws that were either non-existent or had fake citations. The Court further found that some case laws which did exist did not lay down the legal propositions attributed to them. The Court observed that the material appeared to be a hallucination of AI. This discovery led the Supreme Court to rely upon its recent decision in Pooja Ramesh Singh Vs Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd., where the Court had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards producing, citing or relying upon artificial-intelligence-generated precedents without verification. The Supreme
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court set aside the customs penalty proceedings in this matter after finding that the Order-in-Original was materially tainted by reliance on fake or misattributed legal authorities that appeared to have been generated by artificial intelligence. The underlying customs case involved a penalty of **₹425,27,99,100** imposed by the **Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat** on **Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya** under **Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962**, based on an allegation that a shipment of **natural diamonds** had been misdeclared as **lab-grown diamonds** to secure a lower tariff. The **Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025** had already been challenged before the **Gujarat High Court**, which dismissed the challenge on **20.01.2026**, after which the matter was taken to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court did **not** decide whether the customs allegation itself was correct. Instead, it examined the authorities cited in the customs order and found that the second respondent had relied on **case laws that were non-existent or had fake citations**, and that some cases that did exist did **not support the legal propositions attributed to them**. The Court characterized the material as appearing to be an **AI “hallucination”** and relied on its recent decision in **Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd.**, which adopted a **zero-tolerance approach** to producing, citing, or relying on **AI-generated precedents without verification**.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that adjudicating authorities and litigating parties must verify all cited legal authorities before relying on them in orders, pleadings, or appeals; fake citations or AI-generated references can undermine the validity of the decision-making process and lead to the order being set aside. This decision underscores the need for rigorous citation-checking and source verification in customs and other regulatory proceedings, especially where large monetary penalties and statutory enforcement actions are involved.

rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three related writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited by common order dated 24.04.2026, all arising from GST issues for the 2019–2020 tax period. One petition challenged an impugned order/reply dated 29.05.2024, another challenged the show cause notice dated 31.05.2024 issued in Form GST DRC-01, and the third challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 together with the consequential Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the GST enactments that extended the limitation period. A key development was that, after the writ petitions were admitted, the Court granted interim protection on 13.08.2024 and directed/received a detailed report from the jurisdictional State Tax Officer dated 27.01.2026. The Court recorded that the officer’s report prima facie supported the petitioner’s position, and based on that report and the subsequent developments, the Court closed the matters rather than continuing the limitation challenge litigation. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that the Court’s handling of this case turned heavily on the factual/legal conclusion in the State Tax Officer’s report, which appears to have undermined the department’s position in these proceedings.

The document does not indicate any new prospective GST filing, payment, or reporting rule for all taxpayers; rather, it concerns the validity of a limitation extension under Section 168A and a specific DRC-01 notice for one taxpayer and tax period. However, it is relevant to compliance teams because it shows that limitation-extension notifications and the resulting show cause notices can be challenged, and that the department’s own factual report can be decisive in determining whether proceedings survive judicial scrutiny. The dates and instruments that matter here are 31.03.2023 (Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax), 29.05.2024 (impugned order/reply), 31.05.2024 (DRC-01 show cause notice), 13.08.2024 (interim protection), 27.01.2026 (State Tax Officer report), and 24.04.2026 (final common order disposing of the writ petitions).

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan** set aside an appellate order dated **27.02.2026** that had rejected the taxpayer’s **GST appeal as time-barred**, and directed the Appellate Authority to hear and decide the appeal **on merits** rather than dismissing it on limitation. The petitioner had also sought relief against an earlier order dated **07.02.2024** and restoration of its GST registration, but the key compliance point from the reported outcome is that the Court accepted that the appeal delay should be excused because the taxpayer’s inability to file in time was linked to **medical reasons beyond its control**. The Court’s direction was **conditional**: the appeal is to be entertained subject to the petitioner depositing **late fees, penalty, and other statutory deposits as admissible**.

The decision relies heavily on prior Rajasthan High Court precedent, especially **M/s. Pratap Power Spares v. Union of India & Ors.**, where the Court had already held that a **99-day delay** could be condoned after allowing relaxation within the **120-day limit under Section 107 of the CGST Act**, provided the appeal was filed within **30 days** after such relaxation. The petitioner also cited other supportive Rajasthan High Court rulings, including **M/s. Molana Construction Company**, **Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, Central GST**, **RPC PSIPL JV** (two decisions), and **M/s. Kakar Automobiles**, to argue that procedural delay should not defeat substantive appellate review when the delay arose from circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that this judgment reinforces that **GST appellate deadlines may be relaxed in exceptional cases involving bona fide medical hardship**, but only through judicial intervention and not as an automatic right. It also underscores that, even where delay is excused, the taxpayer may still be required to make the **statutory monetary deposits** tied to the appeal before the authority is directed to examine the case on merits.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Jagdish Prasad Agrawal v. Union of India** addressed the legality of **blocking Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the Electronic Credit Ledger under Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. The petitioner, a partnership firm, had challenged the blocking of its **IGST ITC**, including a **negative balance**, and sought a declaration that the blocking was illegal and void, plus restoration/re-credit of any ITC that had been unlawfully adjusted against the demand. By the time of hearing, the respondents conceded that the **Electronic Credit Ledger had already become operational again**, because the blocking had **ceased by operation of law after one year**, so the live dispute was whether the original blocking was valid.

The Court focused on the procedural safeguards under **Rule 86A**, and the respondents were **unable to show that those mandatory requirements had been followed before the ITC was blocked**. They admitted the omission was a **bona fide mistake** and also acknowledged that, although the authority may have had reasons to act, **no proper reasoned order** had been passed and **no opportunity of hearing** had been given to the petitioner before the credit was blocked. In substance, the ruling underscores that ITC blocking under Rule 86A cannot be done informally or mechanically: the department must comply with the rule’s mandatory preconditions and record proper reasons before restricting a taxpayer’s Electronic Credit Ledger.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that **ITC blocking under Rule 86A is not self-executing or discretionary without process**; the department must be able to justify the action through **documented, reasoned decision-making**, and the measure is **time-limited, expiring after one year**. The case confirms that where blocking is imposed without following Rule 86A safeguards, the action is vulnerable to challenge, and taxpayers may seek restoration of credit and related relief. The respondents’ statement that any future blocking would be done properly indicates that the Court viewed compliance with Rule 86A’s procedure as essential, not optional.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Allows CENVAT Refund Where Credit Was Not Challenged Under Rule 14
rows.desc: CESTAT Chandigarh allows Agilent’s CENVAT refund, holding Rule 5 refund cannot be denied where credit was not challenged under Rule 14.The post CESTAT Allows CENVAT Refund Where Credit Was Not Challen
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chandigarh allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd’s appeal against denial of refund of unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The company was a 100% export-oriented service provider supplying Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers under service agreements and exporting those services without payment of service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed a refund under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, but the department rejected ₹78,79,939 of the claim on the theory that credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services did not have a nexus with the exported output services.

The Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position that taking CENVAT credit, using it, and seeking refund are separate issues, and held that where the department had not first challenged the credit’s availment under Rule 14, it could not later deny the Rule 5 refund by re-litigating eligibility of the underlying credit. It also accepted the broader argument that the disputed services could qualify as “input service” under Rule 2(l), and that a strict direct nexus with the exported output service was not required in the manner applied by the lower authority. As a result, the refund denial was set aside and the appeal was allowed, confirming that export-oriented service providers cannot be denied Rule 5 refunds merely by questioning, at the refund stage, credits that were never separately disallowed or recovered under Rule 14.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Hyderabad Sets Aside Tax on Pharma Regulatory Approval Support Services
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad set aside service tax on foreign bank charges and regulatory documentation, holding no recipient relationship and no scientific consultancy classification.The post CESTAT Hyderabad Se
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad, in **Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise**, set aside Service Tax demands, interest, and penalties raised by the department in an **Order-in-Original dated 28.08.2014** for **2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012**. The case involved two principal allegations: first, that charges deducted by **foreign/intermediary banks** while export proceeds were remitted from overseas buyers constituted taxable **“Banking and Other Financial Services”** received by the exporter under the **reverse charge mechanism**; and second, that payments made for overseas regulatory approval-related support allegedly amounted to **“Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services.”**

On the banking issue, the Tribunal held that **mere reduction in export realization because foreign banks deducted charges does not, by itself, make the exporter the recipient of banking services**. The department had argued that because the appellant ultimately received a net amount after deductions, it must have received and paid for banking services; the Tribunal rejected this as insufficient. It emphasized that there was **no evidence of any contract, engagement, or obligation by Aurobindo Pharma to pay the foreign banks for services rendered to it**, and therefore no service provider–service recipient relationship could be established.

The Tribunal also relied on the appellant’s own earlier favorable precedent, **Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020**, to support its conclusion that such bank deductions in export transactions are not automatically taxable on the exporter. As a result, the demand raised on that basis was not sustainable.

On the second issue, the Tribunal held that **services related to obtaining foreign regulatory approvals for pharma products do not fall under “Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services” merely because they involve technical or expert assistance**. The ruling indicates that compliance, documentation, and approval-support services for overseas pharmaceutical regulatory processes were wrongly classified by the department under that taxable category for the relevant period. The consequence for compliance teams is that, for the period covered by the case, **export-related bank deduction charges and pharma regulatory approval support services were not treated as taxable service receipts on the facts found by the Tribunal**, and the associated **tax, interest, and penalties were set aside**.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Mumbai Deletes Section 112(a) Penalty on Customs Hawaldar for Lack of Proof
rows.desc: CESTAT Mumbai sets aside Section 112(a) penalties on a deceased Customs Hawaldar where co-accused statements and phone records did not establish involvement.The post CESTAT Mumbai Deletes Section 112(
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai decision in **Ranjita Rajendra Bane v. Commissioner of Customs** sets aside personal penalties imposed on the deceased customs officer’s legal representative because the department failed to prove any actionable role by the officer in the smuggling operation. The case arose from the recovery of smuggled gold from the **gent’s toilet at Pune International Airport** after passengers arrived from **Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52 on 16.08.2018**; the department alleged that **Rajendra Bane, then a Customs Hawaldar**, had facilitated the offense even though he was on **sanctioned leave** and at his native place near Ratnagiri. The original adjudication had imposed penalties of **₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962**, relying mainly on **Section 108 statements**, statements of co-accused/accomplices, **telephone call records**, and the recovery of gold from the airport and a passenger.  

For compliance purposes, the important point is that the Tribunal found the evidence too weak to sustain a penalty: the officer’s alleged involvement was not established by any direct material, and the defense version—that he had actually informed the Superintendent on duty at the airport about the suspected activity and that the source was protected as confidential informer communication—was not properly disproved. The Commissioner (Appeals) had rejected this explanation, but the Tribunal held that suspicion and derivative statements were insufficient to fasten personal liability under **Section 112(a)** without proof of active participation, aiding, or knowledge. The practical compliance takeaway is that penalties against customs personnel or other individuals alleged to have assisted smuggling must be supported by concrete, corroborated evidence of involvement; mere association, call records, or untested statements from co-accused will not necessarily be enough to survive appellate scrutiny. No new filing deadline, regulatory change, or prospective procedural requirement is announced in this case; it is a fact-specific appellate ruling on the evidentiary threshold for imposing customs penalties.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Patna HC Remits Nukkad Natak GST Exemption Issue to Appellate Authority
rows.desc: Patna High Court sets aside a delayed GST appeal order and directs the Appellate Authority to decide the Nukkad Natak exemption issue on merits.The post Patna HC Remits Nukkad Natak GST Exemption Issu
rows.summary:
The Patna High Court dealt with a GST dispute involving M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, a registered taxpayer that performs Nukkad Natak (street plays) for public awareness programmes, mainly on assignments from government departments. For financial year 2022-23, the department issued a notice under Section 73 of the CGST Act based on gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100 received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya, and the adjudicating authority later confirmed tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452 by order dated 20.08.2025. The petitioner appealed under Section 107(1), but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on 28.02.2026 solely because it was filed 21 days late.

The petitioner argued that a later Collectorate, Gaya memo dated 28.11.2025 (Memo No. 322) clarified that GST was not applicable to receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak, and that Nukkad Natak teams consisting of 4, 6, 8, or 10 members were exempt from the GST regime. In substance, the petitioner was asking the High Court to consider whether the exemption/clarification defeated the tax demand, rather than letting the case end on a procedural delay in appeal. The High Court did not decide the GST exemption merits itself; instead, it remitted the matter to the Appellate Authority for reconsideration, so the appeal issue was sent back for fresh handling in light of the later memo and the taxpayer’s arguments. For compliance purposes, the case highlights that GST exposure was asserted on government-linked Nukkad Natak receipts, that the disputed demand covered tax, interest, and penalty of Rs. 1,63,452, and that the procedural issue was a 21-day appeal delay, but the ultimate exemption question remains to be determined by the appellate forum.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for Fresh Verification
rows.desc: GSTAT Bengaluru remands an FY 2018-19 ITC mismatch dispute for invoice-wise verification, fresh adjudication and mandatory personal hearing.The post GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the matter back for fresh verification in a case involving alleged excess input tax credit (ITC) of ₹2,33,502 for financial year 2018–19. The disputed credit comprised ₹1,16,751 CGST and ₹1,16,751 SGST, and the department had also levied interest of ₹2,03,730 and penalty of ₹23,350, taking the total demand to ₹4,60,582. The taxpayer, M/s. N. R. Builders, a proprietary concern engaged in quarrying and sale of crushed stones, argued that the apparent mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A was not wrongful ITC but credit on invoices pertaining to FY 2017–18 that was availed in FY 2018–19 within the time allowed under Section 16(4).  

On procedure, the taxpayer challenged the demand because no personal hearing was actually granted and no notice in FORM GST ASMT-10 preceded the proceedings; the record instead showed a pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A dated 22.01.2024, followed by a show cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 issued under Section 73. The show cause notice itself recorded the date, time, and venue of personal hearing as “NA,” and the proper officer then confirmed the demand ex parte. The First Appellate Authority upheld that confirmation, but the Tribunal found that the lower authorities had not adequately examined the taxpayer’s explanation that the credit related to earlier-year invoices and therefore could have been admissible within the statutory time limit.  

The practical compliance outcome is that a GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A mismatch, by itself, was not treated as conclusive proof of inadmissible ITC in this case; the matter must be re-verified with reference to invoice dates and the Section 16(4) timing rules before disallowing credit and imposing consequential tax, interest, and penalty. The order also highlights that where the show cause notice does not provide an actual hearing opportunity and the case is decided ex parte, the taxpayer can successfully press for remand on procedural fairness grounds.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Review major GST changes from September 2025 to September 2026 covering Finance Act amendments, rates, refunds, GSTAT appeals and judgments.The post Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Admin
rows.summary:
The document reviews GST developments in India from September 2025 to September 2026 and says this was a high-change period spanning legislation, tax rates, refunds, return filing, appellate remedies, and case law. The Finance Act, 2026 amended the rules on post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds, and appellate arrangements, and it also omitted section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act, which had dealt with intermediary services; however, the amendments to sections 15, 34, and 54 of the CGST Act are not yet operative because they still await notification. For rates, the earlier compensation cess regime was withdrawn and specified tobacco and pan masala products were moved into the 40% GST slab, completing the rate rationalisation recommended by the 56th GST Council; companies dealing in those products must therefore apply the new effective tax treatment rather than the prior cess structure.

On refunds, the framework for provisional refunds was expanded on a risk-based basis, meaning refund processing now depends more on risk assessment than a purely manual or uniform approach. For compliance and filings, the return architecture increasingly requires pre-filing verification and reconciliation, supported by GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System, so businesses must ensure invoice matching and internal review before submission to reduce mismatch and exposure. The document also notes that GSTAT benches became operational, and revised limitation dates were prescribed for legacy appeals, which is important for taxpayers with pending or older dispute matters because appeal windows may now be governed by new cut-off dates.

The judicial developments highlighted by the document include rulings that clarified buyer exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, the statutory timelines applicable to detention orders, and the prospective application of penalty-related pre-deposit requirements. In practical terms, this means compliance teams should not assume that supplier default eliminates buyer risk, and they should treat detention and penalty appeal deadlines as strictly time-sensitive. Finally, the document notes that the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026 and that proposals on ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance were under consideration; these proposals are not law unless and until formally implemented, so they should be tracked but not relied upon as operative requirements.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why are bona fide buyers denied GST input tax credit when sellers fail to deposit tax? Analysis of Sections 16(2)(c) and 76 of the CGST Act.The post Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaul
rows.summary:
The document explains that under **section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act**, a buyer’s right to claim **input tax credit (ITC)** depends on the supplier actually having **paid the GST to the government**. As a result, even a **bona fide purchaser** who has a valid invoice, has received the goods or services, has paid the full consideration including GST, and has filed returns properly can still be forced to **reverse ITC** if the supplier defaults on depositing the tax. The document contrasts this with **section 76**, which separately authorizes the GST department to recover **tax collected but not deposited** directly from the person who collected it, along with **interest and penalty**.

It notes that, in practice, authorities often proceed against **compliant buyers** instead of defaulting sellers because buyers are easier to identify, are usually still active in the GST system, and have traceable assets, while suppliers may have shut down, vanished, or been shell entities. The department also uses **automated GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B mismatch detection**, which makes buyer-side action administratively simpler than pursuing recovery from the seller. The Supreme Court in **Bhandari Scrap Traders** upheld the constitutional validity of section 16(2)(c), confirming that ITC is a **statutory benefit** that can be conditioned on supplier tax payment.

From a compliance perspective, the document warns that although there is a direct recovery route against defaulting suppliers under section 76, current enforcement may still target the purchaser, so businesses should assume buyer-side exposure remains real. It recommends that buyers preserve strong evidence of due diligence and transaction genuineness, including **supplier verification records, invoices, proof of receipt of goods/services, e-way bills, transport documents, banking/payment records, and GSTR-2B/GSTR-3B reconciliation**. The document also says a fairer enforcement approach would be to prioritize recovery from the defaulting supplier and reserve ITC denial for cases involving **collusion, fraud, or failure to prove genuineness**, but until legislation or binding precedent changes the position, buyers should be prepared to substantiate every ITC claim with complete documentary support.

rows.summary:
GSTN has removed a portal-level validation that previously blocked taxpayers from filing an appeal where a demand order showed the demand amount as “NIL” or “Zero.” This matters for situations where the taxpayer had already paid the disputed amount before the demand order was issued, so the order itself shows no outstanding monetary demand even though the taxpayer still disputes the underlying liability, findings, or legal basis recorded in the order. As a result, affected taxpayers can now file an appeal in Form GST APL-01 against the relevant demand order even when the order displays NIL or Zero demand.

The update was issued by Team GSTN on September 7, 2026. The advisory specifically says taxpayers who were earlier unable to appeal because of the GST Portal restriction may now proceed with filing, and any query or technical issue in doing so can be raised with the GST Helpdesk. Form GST APL-01 is the prescribed appeal form before the First Appellate Authority under GST law.

For compliance purposes, the ordinary statutory timeline under Section 107 of the CGST Act, 2017 still applies: the appeal must generally be filed within three months from the date the order is communicated, with a further condonable period of one month available in appropriate cases. The document also notes the usual pre-deposit requirement for appeals under GST, namely deposit of the admitted amount of tax, interest, fine, fee, and penalty in full, along with the prescribed pre-deposit amount, before the appeal can be pursued.

rows.title: Finance | From First Enquiry to Final Invoice: Digitising the Modern Professional Practice
rows.desc: Tax and legal practices all run on the same rhythm — enquiry, intake, deadlines, time, invoice — held together by a patchwork of tools. Here is why a growing number of firms are consolidating that entire lifecycle into a single system, and what they gain by doing so. Every professional practice — whether it advises on tax, law, or compliance — runs on the same underlying rhythm. A client makes contact. Details are gathered and verified. Work is carried out against deadlines that cannot be missed. Time and costs accumulate. And eventually an invoice goes out, ideally reflecting everything that was actually done. For decades that rhythm has been held together by a patchwork of tools: a folder structure on a shared drive, a register or two, a spreadsheet for time, an accounting package for billing, and a great deal of institutional memory living in individual inboxes. That arrangement works, in the sense that the work gets done. But it quietly taxes a firm in ways that rarely appear on any statement. Information is re-entered at every handover. A deadline recorded in one person’s calendar is invisible to everyone else. A file handed over informally is a file no one can find when it matters. And the effort of holding it all together grows faster than the practice itself. As firms take on more clients and more colleagues, the cracks in a fragmented system begin to show. The response, increasingly, is consolidation: moving the whole lifecycle — from the first enquiry to the final invoice — into a single system where every piece of information sits in one place and every module works from the same data. It is a shift many practices are now making, and the logic behind it is worth understanding whether or not a firm is ready to act on it today. Table of Contents▸ Why one system beats five Client data, captured once and verified Deadlines and documents in one place Time that turns into revenue Security is part of the service Starting the shift Advertisement (adsbygoogle = wi
rows.summary:
This document is not a regulatory change or a formal financial rulemaking; it is an industry-oriented explanation for tax, law, and compliance practices about why many firms are digitising and consolidating operations into a single practice-management system. Its central point is that firms are moving away from a patchwork of tools—shared-drive folders, registers, spreadsheets for time recording, accounting software for billing, and information kept in individual inboxes—because that fragmented setup causes re-entry of data, makes deadlines invisible across the team, creates files that cannot be found when needed, and increases operational strain as the firm grows. The “change” being described is therefore a process and systems change: consolidating the full client lifecycle from first enquiry through intake, deadline tracking, work delivery, time capture, and final invoicing into one integrated platform where all modules draw from the same data.

The document says this consolidation is being adopted by a growing number of firms across tax, legal, and broader compliance practices, but it does not impose a legal obligation, set a compliance deadline, or specify statutory thresholds, rates, or filing dates. The compliance relevance is operational: a firm should understand that a single system can reduce duplication of work, improve visibility of deadlines and files across personnel, and ensure invoices reflect work actually performed because time and cost data are captured in the same environment as the matter record. It also highlights security as part of the service, implying that consolidated systems are expected to support better control over client information and reduce the risks that come from information dispersed across email, spreadsheets, and shared folders.

No formal enforcement date or required implementation timetable is given. The practical takeaway for a compliance team is that the document is advocating a governance and workflow redesign rather than announcing a new rule: if a firm chooses to modernize, it should evaluate whether its current process still relies on manual handoffs, duplicate data entry, and siloed deadline tracking, since those are the inefficiencies and control gaps the article identifies as the main drivers for change.

The document warns taxpayers not to assume that a tax audit is avoided simply because they mostly transact digitally or because their profits are low; the enhanced business audit threshold of **Rs. 10 crore** under **Section 63 of the Income Tax Act, 2025** (corresponding to **Section 44AB of the Income Tax Act, 1961**) applies only if **both cash receipts and cash payments stay within 5% of their respective totals**. In other words, digital turnover alone does not automatically qualify a business for the higher threshold, and the cash-percentage condition must be checked separately on both the receipt side and the payment side. The document also emphasizes that taxpayers can mistakenly think losses or very low profits remove audit exposure, but the **presumptive taxation provisions under Section 58 of the Income Tax Act, 2025** (corresponding to **Sections 44AD, 44ADA, and 44AE of the 1961 Act**) can still create **books-of-account and audit requirements** if the relevant statutory conditions are met, including cases where reported profits fall below the prescribed presumptive rates or where lock-in and related eligibility conditions apply. 

It further notes that taxpayers often miscalculate **turnover or gross receipts**, confuse the thresholds applicable to **business versus profession**, and fail to recognize that whether an activity is classified as a business or a profession affects which audit test applies. The compliance takeaway is that tax audit status should be evaluated **throughout the year**, not treated as a year-end checklist item: entities need to monitor the nature of receipts and payments, identify what counts as cash versus non-cash, and verify whether their activity, turnover/gross receipts, and presumptive-tax status trigger audit or books obligations. No new filing date or separate deadline is stated in the excerpt, but the document clearly expects ongoing compliance review under the cited provisions.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Bhagyashree Abhijit Bhatkhande Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) No Return, No Advance Tax, No Appeal?—ITAT Directs CIT(A) to First Decide Applicability of s.249(4)(b) Before Burying ₹99.38 Lakh Appeal The controversy The assessee, Ms. Bhagyashree Abhijit Bhatkhande, did not file her return of income u/s 139(1) for AY 2018-19. Information available on the Insight Portal showed that she had jointly purchased an immovable property along with Mr. Abhijit Bhatkhande for a total consideration of ₹1.89 crore. Based on this information, proceedings were initiated by issuing notice u/s 148A on 6 August 2024. After passing an order u/s 148A(d), the AO issued notice u/s 148 on 29 August 2024. The assessee did not file a return in response to the notice u/s 148. The subsequent statutory notices, communications & show-cause notices issued during the reassessment proceedings also remained unanswered. Property purchase treated as unexplained The property was situated at Borivali West, Mumbai, and had been purchased under a registered deed dated 10 November 2017. The AO called upon the assessee to explain the source of investment and furnish the registered document, bank statements & supporting evidence. In the absence of compliance, the AO treated the investment as unexplained. After including stamp duty, registration charges & incidental expenses, the total cost was computed at ₹1,98,76,240. Since the property was jointly acquired, the assessee’s share was taken at 50%, namely ₹99,38,120. The assessment was accordingly completed u/s 147 r.w.s. 144 & 144B, determining the assessee’s inco
rows.summary:
This ITAT Mumbai order concerns AY 2018-19 and an addition of ₹99,38,120, being the assessee’s 50% share of a jointly purchased Mumbai property that the Assessing Officer treated as unexplained investment. The assessee had not filed a return under section 139(1), did not file any return in response to the section 148 notice, and also did not respond to the reassessment notices, communications, or show-cause notices; the reopening began with a section 148A notice dated 6 August 2024, followed by a section 148 notice dated 29 August 2024 after the section 148A(d) order. The property at Borivali West, Mumbai was bought under a registered deed dated 10 November 2017 for a stated consideration of ₹1.89 crore, but after adding stamp duty, registration charges, and incidental expenses, the AO computed total cost at ₹1,98,76,240 and attributed half to the assessee; the reassessment was completed under sections 147/144/144B on that basis.

For the appeal, the key issue was not the tax addition itself at this stage, but whether the first appellate authority could dismiss the appeal for non-compliance when the assessee had not filed a return. The ITAT held that the Commissioner (Appeals) must first examine the applicability of section 249(4)(b), which can bar an appeal where no return has been filed and tax due on admitted income has not been paid, before disposing of the matter on a procedural default basis. As a result, the ITAT remanded the matter to the CIT(A) for fresh consideration of that threshold issue and for disposal in accordance with law.

From a compliance perspective, the case highlights that failure to file a return and failure to respond to reassessment notices can expose a taxpayer to ex parte reassessment and unexplained investment additions, but appellate dismissal cannot be presumed without first testing the statutory bar under section 249(4)(b). No change in substantive tax law is announced here; rather, the decision clarifies the required sequence for appellate handling in cases involving non-filing and reassessment.

Savla had returned an income of only ₹2,24,666 and, therefore, lacked the financial capacity to advance ₹1.30 crore. According to the AO, confirmations and evidence establishing the creditworthiness of the persons who had provided funds to her were not satisfactorily produced. The entire loan was consequently treated as an unexplained cash credit u/s 68, taxable at 60% u/s 115BBE, besides initiation of penalty proceedings u/s 271AAC(1). Family funding trail questioned The assessee explained that the funds received by Mrs. Nisha J. rows.summary:
The document summarizes an ITAT Mumbai decision for AY 2017-18 involving Deluxe Recycling India Private Limited, where the company had received an unsecured loan of ₹1.30 crore from Mrs. Nisha J. Savla, sister of one of its directors, and the Assessing Officer treated the amount as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The assessee had produced the lender’s confirmation, income-tax return, bank statement, and ledger account, and explained that Mrs. Savla had sourced the money from family members, an HUF, and share sale proceeds; however, the AO rejected the explanation primarily because Mrs. Savla herself had reported only ₹2,24,666 of income and, in the AO’s view, had not proven capacity to lend ₹1.30 crore. On that basis, the AO added the full loan amount as income under section 68, applied tax at 60% under section 115BBE, and initiated penalty proceedings under section 271AAC(1).

The ITAT’s holding, as reflected in the title and summary, was that low returned income by itself cannot justify treating a loan as unexplained without examining the full fund trail. The key compliance-relevant point is that the tribunal accepted repayment/fund-trail evidence and restored the issue of the ₹1.30 crore addition, indicating that the source of the lender’s funds and the movement of money through bank accounts matter more than the lender’s standalone declared income figure. The document does not provide a regulatory filing deadline or new rule effective date; it is a case-law outcome relevant to how section 68 assessments should be defended or challenged in similar unsecured loan situations, particularly where money comes through relatives, HUFs, and share-sale proceeds. For compliance teams, the practical implication is that related-party loans should be documented with complete banking trails, source-of-funds evidence for the lender, and supporting records for any layered funding, because the tax authority may still challenge the transaction if the fund trail is incomplete.

rows.title: Income Tax | Assured-Margin Model: Nil Valuation of Real Services Leads to Double TP Adjustment
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12661 Case Name Red Hat India Private Limited Vs Assessment Unit (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Red Hat India Private Limited Vs Assessment Unit (ITAT Mumbai) TPO Cannot Value Real Services at Nil by Remote Control: Assured-Margin Model Makes Separate Line-Item Adjustment a Double Blow The Mumbai ITAT has held that where an assessee operates under an assured-margin model & its overall segmental profitability is benchmarked under TNMM, an international transaction forming an integral part of the operating costs of that segment cannot ordinarily be benchmarked separately by determining its ALP at nil. Such a separate disallowance distorts the assured-margin arrangement & results in a double TP adjustment. Open-Source Software—but Not a Free Business Model Red Hat India distributed open-source software subscriptions & provided related training, consulting, software development and IT-enabled services. Under its subscription segment, Red Hat India paid royalty at 3% of revenue to Red Hat USA for the use of trademarks, trade names & domain names. It also paid a service fee structured to ensure that Red Hat India earned an assured operating margin of 1.4% of subscription revenue. Under the services segment, the fee arrangement ensured an assured operating margin of 13.5%. If Red Hat India’s profitability fell below the agreed margin, the AE was required to make a reverse payment to restore that margin. For AY 2021-22, the TPO proposed cumulative TP adjustments of ₹97.12 crore relating to royalty & service fees, software development services, ITeS & back-office, sales and marketing support services. For AY 2022-23, the corresponding adjustments aggregated to ₹105.68 crore. ALP of Su
rows.summary:
This case concerns Red Hat India Private Limited, which operated under an **assured-margin model** for its Indian business, with its cross-border service arrangements benchmarked through TNMM at the segment level. In the subscription segment, Red Hat India paid **royalty at 3% of revenue** to Red Hat USA for use of trademarks, trade names, and domain names, and also paid a service fee structured so that Red Hat India earned an **assured operating margin of 1.4% of subscription revenue**; in the services segment, the arrangement ensured an **assured operating margin of 13.5%**. The agreement also provided that if profitability fell below the agreed margin, the associated enterprise had to make a **reverse payment** to restore the margin.

For **AY 2021-22**, the Transfer Pricing Officer proposed cumulative adjustments of **₹97.12 crore** for royalty and service fees, software development services, ITeS and back-office services, and sales and marketing support services; for **AY 2022-23**, the corresponding adjustments aggregated to **₹105.68 crore**. The key dispute was that the TPO sought to value an international transaction that was part of the operating costs of the segment at **nil ALP** on a separate line-item basis, even though the overall segment was already benchmarked under TNMM and the arrangement itself was designed to deliver a fixed margin. The Mumbai ITAT held that in an assured-margin structure, an integral transaction within the segment’s operating costs should not ordinarily be benchmarked separately at nil, because doing so distorts the contractual margin mechanism and effectively creates a **double transfer pricing adjustment**.

From a compliance perspective, the decision is significant for taxpayers using **segment-level TNMM or assured-margin models**: if an intercompany charge is embedded in a broader tested segment whose profitability is already protected by a contractual margin and true-up mechanism, tax authorities should not normally impose a second adjustment by independently valuing that embedded charge at nil. The ruling therefore reinforces the need to evaluate transfer pricing on the basis of the actual structure of the arrangement, the segmental benchmarking method adopted, and any contractual margin-correction provisions, rather than isolating an internal charge and disregarding the agreed profit-protection mechanism.

rows.title: Corporate Law | SC: Security Advance Is Earnest Money, Liable to Forfeiture; Refund Requires Specific Prayer
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12662 Case Name K. R. Suresh Vs R. Poornima & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); K. R. Suresh Vs R. Poornima & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Substance Over Label: “Advance” Given as Security Is Earnest Money Liable to Forfeiture; Refund Cannot Be Granted Without a Specific Prayer u/s 22-Supreme Court Summary: The Supreme Court held that an amount described in an agreement as “advance money” may, in substance, constitute earnest money if it was paid as security for due performance of the contract. Such earnest money can be forfeited upon the purchaser’s default where the agreement contains a clear, reasonable & reciprocal forfeiture clause. The Court further held that refund of earnest money cannot be granted in a suit for specific performance unless such relief is specifically claimed, as required u/s 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Agreement, Advance & Alleged Default The purchaser entered into an agreement dated 25.07.2007 for purchase of a property situated at Kengeri, Bengaluru, for ₹55.50 lakh. He paid ₹20 lakh through two cheques as advance & agreed to pay the balance ₹35.50 lakh within four months. The agreement expressly provided that if the purchaser failed to pay the balance consideration within the stipulated period, the advance would be forfeited. Conversely, if the vendors failed to execute the sale deed despite the purchaser being ready to perform, they would refund double the advance amount. The purchaser claimed that he approached a bank for finance but was advised to obtain the original title documents & probate of an unregistered Will under which the vendor had acquired the property. According to him, the vendors failed to furnish the required documents despite repeated requests. The vendors, ho
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **K. R. Suresh v. R. Poornima & Ors.** held that a payment described in a contract as “advance money” can still be treated in substance as **earnest money** if it was paid as security for the purchaser’s performance of the agreement. In this case, the purchaser agreed on **25.07.2007** to buy property in Kengeri, Bengaluru for **₹55.50 lakh**, paid **₹20 lakh** by two cheques, and undertook to pay the remaining **₹35.50 lakh within four months**. The agreement expressly stated that if the purchaser failed to pay the balance within the stipulated period, the advance would be **forfeited**; conversely, if the vendors failed to execute the sale deed despite the purchaser being ready and willing, they would have to **refund double the advance amount**. The purchaser later alleged that he could not obtain bank finance because he needed the original title documents and probate of an unregistered will, while the vendors argued that he simply defaulted.

For compliance and contract-drafting purposes, the key legal point is that **substance prevails over label**: calling a payment an “advance” does not prevent it from being treated as earnest money if the agreement shows it was intended as security for performance. The Court found the forfeiture clause enforceable because it was **clear, reasonable, and reciprocal**—meaning the agreement protected both sides by providing forfeiture if the buyer defaulted and double refund if the sellers defaulted. As a result, where the purchaser fails to perform within the contractual deadline, the seller may be entitled to forfeit the amount paid as earnest money, subject to the contract terms and proof of default.

The Court also clarified an important procedural requirement under **Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963**: in a suit for **specific performance**, a party cannot obtain **refund of earnest money** unless that relief is **specifically prayed for** in the pleadings. In other words, a litigant seeking only specific performance cannot later secure a refund of earnest money as an incidental benefit unless the plaint expressly asks for that alternative or additional relief. For corporate transaction teams, this means sale agreements should state deposit/forfeiture/refund terms unambiguously, and litigation pleadings must include specific prayers for refund if that remedy may be needed.

rows.title: Income Tax | Low Income Doesn’t Mean Low Creditworthiness: AO Must Investigate U/s 68
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12660 Case Name Amogh Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2012-13 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Amogh Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. Vs ITO (ITAT Mumbai) Low Returned Income Is Not Low Creditworthiness: Once Section 68 Documents Are Filed, AO Must Investigate—Not Speculate Summary: The Mumbai ITAT has deleted additions aggregating to ₹4.95 crore u/s 68, holding that the creditworthiness of an investor or lender cannot be judged solely from the income returned during one particular year. Once the assessee furnishes confirmations, PAN, ITR acknowledgements, bank statements & ledger accounts establishing the three ingredients of section 68, the burden shifts to the Revenue to conduct an independent enquiry. The AO cannot reject documentary evidence merely on suspicion without exercising the powers available u/s 131 or 133(6). [Section 68 – TaxGuru] Share Application Money & Loans Treated as Unexplained The assessee, a private limited company engaged in the business of builders & developers, filed its return declaring nil income under the normal provisions & book profit of ₹16,538 u/s 115JB. During assessment, the AO called upon the assessee to explain: Share application money of ₹3.86 crore received from ten parties; & Unsecured loans of ₹1.09 crore received from Divine Construction Company & Mangesh Construction. The AO noticed that confirmations were initially filed only from six out of the ten share applicants. Five confirmations were signed by a common signatory. He also found discrepancies between certain loan confirmations & the balances appearing in the assessee’s books. Consequently, the AO treated the entire amount of ₹4.95 crore as unexplained cash credits u/s 68. A
rows.summary:
This ITAT Mumbai ruling in **Amogh Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. v. ITO** is a taxpayer-favorable section 68 decision for an assessment year **2012–13** case involving a **private limited builder/developer**. The assessee had returned **nil income under the normal provisions** and **book profit of ₹16,538 under section 115JB**, but the Assessing Officer (AO) added back **₹4.95 crore** in total under **section 68**—comprising **₹3.86 crore of share application money from 10 parties** and **₹1.09 crore of unsecured loans from Divine Construction Company and Mangesh Construction**—on the theory that the credits were unexplained.

The ITAT deleted the addition, holding that **low returned income in a particular year does not by itself prove low creditworthiness** of an investor or lender. The key compliance lesson is that once the assessee provides the standard section 68 evidence—**confirmations, PAN, ITR acknowledgements, bank statements, and ledger accounts**—the legal burden shifts to the Revenue, and the AO must make a real inquiry rather than reject the evidence on suspicion alone. In this case, the AO had noted that confirmations were initially available from only **6 of the 10 share applicants**, that **5 confirmations were signed by a common signatory**, and that there were alleged mismatches between some loan confirmations and the assessee’s books, but the Tribunal found that these issues did not justify treating the full amount as unexplained without further investigation.

The Tribunal specifically criticized the AO for **not using statutory enquiry powers under sections 131 or 133(6)** to test the genuineness and creditworthiness of the parties before making the addition. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that when capital/share application money or unsecured loans are received, the company should maintain complete third-party documentation and banking trail; if those records are produced, the tax authority must independently verify them and cannot rely only on an assumption that a low-income return equals no creditworthiness.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Restricts Section 271AAB Penalty on Unreconciled Jewellery to 10%
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12657 Case Name Rohan M. Thakkar, Legal Heir of Late Mahesh N. Thakkar v. DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Where unreconciled jewellery is admitted as undisclosed income during search, the concessional penalty rate under Section 271AAB(1)(a) may apply when the disclosure is substantively complied with, even though the income was omitted from the original return but included in a revised return before completion of assessment. Summary: The ITAT Mumbai considered whether jewellery valued at ₹29,75,000 found during a search under Section 132 constituted undisclosed income under Section 271AAB and, if so, whether penalty was leviable at 10% under Section 271AAB(1)(a) or at 30% under Section 271AAB(1)(c). During the search on 18 November 2015, jewellery aggregating to ₹3,71,28,639 was found at residential premises and bank lockers, of which jewellery weighing approximately 1,250 grams and valued at ₹29,75,000 could not be reconciled with wealth-tax returns, valuation reports or other contemporaneous records. In his statement under Section 132(4), the assessee admitted that the jewellery was unrecorded and offered ₹29,75,000 as income. Although the amount was inadvertently omitted from the original return, it was included in a revised return filed on 30 November 2017 before completion of assessment on 29 December 2017, and the corresponding tax was paid. The Assessing Officer levied penalty at 30% under Section 271AAB(1)(c), amounting to ₹8,92,500, which was confirmed by the CIT(A). The Tribunal held that the jewellery constituted undisclosed income because it was found d
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that unreconciled jewellery found during a search can still be treated as “undisclosed income” for purposes of Section 271AAB, but the penalty rate may be limited to 10% under Section 271AAB(1)(a) where the taxpayer has substantively complied with the disclosure conditions. In this case, during a search under Section 132 on 18 November 2015, jewellery worth ₹3,71,28,639 was found at the assessee’s residence and in bank lockers, and jewellery weighing about 1,250 grams valued at ₹29,75,000 could not be matched to wealth-tax returns, valuation reports, or other contemporaneous records. The assessee admitted in a Section 132(4) statement that this jewellery was unrecorded and offered ₹29,75,000 as income; although this amount was missed in the original return, it was later included in a revised return filed on 30 November 2017, before the assessment was completed on 29 December 2017, and tax on the amount was paid.

The Assessing Officer had imposed penalty at 30% under Section 271AAB(1)(c), resulting in a penalty of ₹8,92,500, and the CIT(A) upheld that view. The Tribunal disagreed with the higher penalty rate and ruled that, because the assessee had admitted the amount during search, later reflected it in a revised return before assessment completion, and paid the due tax, the case fit the concessional penalty framework rather than the higher-rate default provision. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that search-found, unreconciled assets like jewellery can trigger Section 271AAB exposure, but timely admission, correction through a revised return before assessment finalization, and tax payment can materially affect the penalty rate, reducing it from 30% to 10% in the Tribunal’s view. The ruling applies to AY 2016–17 and is relevant to entities or individuals dealing with search assessments, unexplained assets, and post-search return revisions.

Summary: The Ahmedabad Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal considered whether, for A.Y. 2025-26, rebate under the first proviso to Section 87A could be denied to the extent tax liability included Short Term Capital Gain chargeable under Section 111A. The assessee had declared total income of Rs. 6,95,720/-, including STCG of Rs. 1,54,411/-, and claimed rebate of Rs. 25,000 under Section 87A. While processing the return under Section 143(1), the CPC restricted the rebate to Rs. 12,066/-, and the Addl. CIT(A) upheld the adjustment, relying upon CBDT Circular No. 13/2025 dated 19.09.2025. The Tribunal examined the statutory language applicable to A.Y. 2025-26 and found that Section 87A did not contain an express exclusion of income chargeable at the special rate under Section 111A. It noted that the Finance Act, 2025 subsequently amended Section 87A with effect from 1st April 2026, corresponding to A.Y. 2026-27, and inserted a restriction concerning tax payable at the rates under Section 115BAC(1A). The Tribunal held that the subsequent amendment could not be applied retrospectively and that an administrative circular could not impose a substantive restriction absent from the statute applicable to the relevant assessment year. Following the reasoning in Jayshreeben Jayantibhai Palsana v. ITO and relying also upon the
rows.summary:
For AY 2025-26, the ITAT Ahmedabad held that an assessee cannot be denied the Section 87A rebate merely because part of the total income consists of short-term capital gains taxable at the special rate under Section 111A. In this case, the taxpayer reported total income of Rs. 6,95,720, including STCG of Rs. 1,54,411, and claimed the full Section 87A rebate of Rs. 25,000; however, the CPC, while processing the return under Section 143(1), reduced the rebate to Rs. 12,066, and the Addl. CIT(A) sustained that reduction by relying on CBDT Circular No. 13/2025 dated 19.09.2025.

The Tribunal found that, for the relevant year, Section 87A itself did not contain any express prohibition against claiming the rebate when income includes gains taxed under Section 111A. It held that a circular cannot create a substantive disqualification that is not present in the statute, and it rejected the attempt to deny the rebate on that basis for AY 2025-26. The Tribunal also noted that the Finance Act, 2025 later amended Section 87A with effect from 1 April 2026, i.e. from AY 2026-27, by inserting a specific restriction related to tax payable under Section 115BAC(1A); because that amendment was prospective, it could not be used to justify restricting the rebate for AY 2025-26.

The practical compliance takeaway is that, for returns for AY 2025-26, taxpayers with income that includes STCG under Section 111A were still eligible to claim the Section 87A rebate if otherwise within the statutory conditions applicable for that year, and processing adjustments or appellate denials based solely on the presence of Section 111A income were not upheld by this ruling. This decision also underscores that administrative guidance such as the CBDT circular cannot override the unamended statutory text for the year in question.

Core Issue: The Tribunal considered three principal issues: the addition arising from the difference between receipts reflected in Form 26AS and the receipts declared in the return, the addition under Section 68 in respect of outstanding trade creditors representing credit purchases, and the rejection of books of account followed by estimation of net profit. Facts: The assessee was engaged in civil contract work and had declared receipts in the return which differed from the gross receipts reflected in Form 26AS. The assessee explained that certain deductors had deducted TDS on the gross amount inclusive of service tax, whereas service tax was separately accounted for and was not offered as income. The assessee also had outstanding balances payable to suppliers against purchases made on credit. During assessment, the Assessing Officer questioned these creditors and ultimately treated certain outstanding balances as unexplained cash credits. The AO also rejected the books of account and estimated the net profit on the ground that all vouchers were not produced, despite the assessee having furnished books, ledgers and major vouchers electronically. AO/CIT(A) Finding: The Assessing Officer made an
rows.summary:
In **Punit Goel v. ACIT-2 (ITAT Lucknow)** for **AY 2016-17**, the Tribunal dealt with three tax-compliance issues arising from a civil contractor’s assessment: a mismatch between receipts reported in **Form 26AS** and receipts declared in the return, an addition under **Section 68** for outstanding trade creditors, and rejection of books of account followed by **profit estimation**. The assessee explained that the 26AS figure was higher because some deductors deducted TDS on amounts **including service tax**, while the assessee excluded service tax from income; the case summary does not state that the Tribunal made an adverse finding on this point, but it confirms this was one of the disputes examined.

The key ruling for compliance purposes is that **where purchases are accepted as genuine, the related unpaid trade creditors cannot be added as unexplained cash credits merely because some suppliers did not respond to notices**. In other words, once the underlying purchases are accepted, outstanding balances owed to suppliers on those purchases do not automatically become Section 68 additions just because the assessment officer could not secure confirmations from every creditor. The Tribunal also rejected the approach of **rejecting the books and estimating net profit solely because all vouchers were not produced**, where the assessee had already furnished the **books of account, ledgers, and major supporting vouchers electronically**.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that contractors and other businesses should keep documentation linking **credit purchases, supplier balances, and the underlying invoices/ledgers** so that trade creditors can be defended if questioned. At the same time, the ruling suggests that incomplete voucher production alone should not justify book rejection where core accounting records are available and purchases are otherwise accepted, but it remains important to retain and be able to produce supporting evidence for material expenses and credit balances.

Summary: The ITAT Delhi disposed of nine Revenue appeals and nine Cross Objections filed by the assessee against the consolidated order of the CIT(A), Noida dated February 2, 2026, concerning Assessment Years 2014-15 to 2022-23. The Tribunal held that for AYs 2014-15 to 2018-19, the escaped income represented only the profit embedded in alleged unaccounted purchases, which was below the ₹50 lakh threshold prescribed under Section 149(1)(b), and therefore notices under Section 148 issued beyond three years were without jurisdiction and were quashed. The Tribunal also held that the AY 2022-23 assessment framed under Section 143(3), instead of the special reassessment mechanism under Sections 147/148, was void ab initio and quashed it. However, the assessee’s challenge based on the 30-day period provided in the notices under Section 148 was rejected because the notices were issued on March 29, 2023, when the applicable provision permitted the Assessing Officer to specify the period for filing the return, with the three-month requirement introduced only from April 1, 2023. The Tribunal rejected the cross-examination ground, finding that the assessee had not demonstrated that any specific request for cross-examination had been made during assessment proc
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi in **JCIT (OSD) vs. Ramesh Kumar** dealt with reassessment disputes covering **Assessment Years 2014-15 through 2022-23** and disposed of **nine Revenue appeals and nine cross-objections** arising from a consolidated CIT(A), Noida order dated **February 2, 2026**. The core compliance holding is that where the alleged “unaccounted purchases” are matched by corresponding sales, the amount that can be treated as escaped income is only the **embedded profit element**, not the full purchase value; because that profit element was found to be **below ₹50 lakh**, the Revenue could not validly reopen the older assessments beyond three years. In particular, for **AYs 2014-15 to 2018-19**, notices issued under **Section 148** after the three-year period were held to be **without jurisdiction and were quashed** because the escaped income did not meet the statutory threshold under **Section 149(1)(b)**.

The Tribunal also addressed a separate procedural issue for **AY 2022-23** and held that the assessment made under **Section 143(3)** was invalid because, on the facts, the case required the special reassessment route under **Sections 147/148**; the assessment was therefore declared **void ab initio** and quashed. On the assessee’s objection that the Section 148 notices allowed only **30 days** to file returns, the Tribunal rejected the challenge because the notices were issued on **March 29, 2023**, when the then-applicable law still allowed the Assessing Officer to specify the filing period; the stricter **three-month** requirement became effective only from **April 1, 2023** and therefore did not apply. The Tribunal also rejected the cross-examination argument, finding that the assessee had not shown a specific request for cross-examination during the assessment proceedings, so no procedural violation was established on that ground.

Summary: The Supreme Court has held that RBI’s power u/s 36AAA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to supersede the Board of Directors of a multi-State co-operative bank is not restricted by the six-month ceiling prescribed under Article 243ZL(1) of the Constitution. RBI may extend the supersession from time to time for an aggregate period of up to five years, even beyond the original tenure of the elected Board, where such regulatory intervention is necessary to protect depositors, preserve financial stability & secure proper management of the bank. Supersession of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank’s Board Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd. was originally registered under the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960. It commenced banking activities in 1965 & became a scheduled bank in 1988. Following amalgamation with co-operative banks situated in Gujarat & Karnataka under directions issued by RBI, it acquired the status of a multi-State co-operative bank. The appellants were elected to the Bank’s Board in May 2019 for a statutory term of five years. On 24.11.2023, RBI invoked section 36AAA(1) & (2
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that RBI’s power under section 36AAA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to supersede the Board of Directors of a multi-State co-operative bank is not confined by the six-month limit in Article 243ZL(1) of the Constitution. Instead, where RBI considers supersession necessary for depositor protection, financial stability, and proper bank management, it may extend the supersession from time to time for an aggregate period of up to five years, even if that period goes beyond the original tenure of the elected board.

The case involved Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., which began as a Maharashtra co-operative society bank, became a scheduled bank in 1988, and later acquired multi-State co-operative bank status after RBI-directed amalgamations with co-operative banks in Gujarat and Karnataka. The appellants had been elected to the bank’s board in May 2019 for a statutory five-year term. On 24.11.2023, RBI invoked section 36AAA(1) and (2) to supersede the board, and the Supreme Court upheld RBI’s authority to do so.

For compliance purposes, the ruling confirms that multi-State co-operative banks remain subject to RBI’s enhanced supervisory intervention powers notwithstanding the board’s elected tenure or constitutional time limits applicable to co-operative governance. The key operational takeaway is that RBI may lawfully continue supersession and related management control measures for a cumulative period of up to five years, so banks and board members must treat RBI directions during supersession as binding for the full permitted period. This decision reinforces that depositor safety and regulatory stability can override democratic board-control arguments in the co-operative banking context.
