The Pr. CIT-1 Chandigarh. The Department explained that the delay arose because the case records were with the Income Tax Officer, Parwanoo, opinion was sought and forwarded for approval, instructions were thereafter issued to Standing Counsel, the authorised signatory was at Chandigarh and festival breaks intervened. The High Court found that the explanation covered the entire period of delay and demonstrated bona fide, diligence, promptitude and sufficient cause. It distinguished the Supreme Court decisions relied upon by the respondent, including Shivamma, involving 3966 days’ delay, and Managing Committee of Namrata Girls High School, involving cumulative delay of about 11 years. The Court held that the nominal 31-day delay could be condoned and that the merits of the proposed appeal should not be examined at the stage of deciding the condonation application. It further held that Section 260A(2A) of the Incom
rows.summary:
The Himachal Pradesh High Court held that a **31-day delay** in filing a tax appeal under **Section 260A** could be **condoned** where the appellant shows a **bona fide, continuous, and adequately explained effort to pursue the appeal**. Here, the appellant was the **Principal Commissioner of Income Tax-1**, seeking to appeal an ITAT Chandigarh Bench “B” order dated **25.02.2025** in **ITA No. 413/Chd/2024 (SBS Biotech Unit-II v. Pr. CIT-1 Chandigarh)**. The Department explained that the delay occurred because the case records were with the **Income Tax Officer, Parwanoo**, an opinion had to be obtained and forwarded for approval, instructions were then issued to **Standing Counsel**, the **authorized signatory was in Chandigarh**, and **festival holidays/breaks** also intervened.

The Court accepted this explanation as covering the **entire period of delay** and as evidence of **diligence, promptitude, and sufficient cause**, emphasizing that the delay was nominal and not indicative of neglect. It distinguished Supreme Court cases cited by the respondent, particularly **Shivamma** (where the delay was **3,966 days**) and **Managing Committee of Namrata Girls High School** (where the cumulative delay was about **11 years**), noting that those authorities involved far more extreme delays and were not controlling on a short, explained delay like this one. The Court also stated that the **merits of the proposed appeal cannot be examined at the stage of deciding a condonation application**; the only question was whether the delay was sufficiently explained.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that in **income-tax appellate matters**, a **short procedural delay** may still be excused if the department or appellant can document a **step-by-step, bona fide timeline** showing why the filing was not completed on time. The decision specifically reinforces that **Section 260A(2A)** supports condonation where there is **sufficient cause**, and that courts may be more willing to condone modest delays when the record shows active pursuit rather than inaction.

rows.summary:
The document is a Supreme Court of India judgment concerning whether the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) was entitled to income-tax exemption as a “local authority” or development authority under the Income Tax Act. NOIDA, constituted under the U.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976 by notification dated 17.04.1976, challenged notices issued by the Income Tax Department under Section 142 of the Income Tax Act dated 28.07.1998 and 08.08.1998; its position was that it was exempt under Section 10(20) and/or Section 10(20A). The Allahabad High Court had initially allowed NOIDA’s writ petition on 14.02.2000, holding that it was a local body covered by Section 10(20A), but the case was later appealed, and the Supreme Court judgment noted here is reviewing that tax-exemption issue.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the document is not imposing a new forward-looking regulatory filing requirement; it is an appellate judgment addressing whether an authority like NOIDA falls within an income-tax exemption category and whether the Income Tax Department could issue and pursue Section 142 notices. The facts recited show the disputes arose from the tax authority’s attempt to obtain information/participation through those notices, while NOIDA argued its statutory status exempted it from tax. Because the excerpt ends before the Supreme Court’s final holding, the material compliance takeaway from this text alone is limited to the existence of the exemption dispute, the statutory basis invoked, and the relevant dates of the notices and High Court ruling.

Summary: ITAT Ahmedabad disposed of the assessee’s appeal for AY 2020-21 by directing her to approach the Principal Commissioner under Section 119(2)(b) for permission to file a revised return and claim a ₹1,50,000 deduction under Section 80C. The assessee had filed her return on 30.12.2020 declaring total income of ₹63,98,501, which was processed under Section 143(1) by the CPC on 25.11.2021, resulting in a demand of ₹9,81,370. She subsequently filed a rectification application under Section 154 on 08.08.2022, pointing out that deduction under Section 80C for an investment of ₹1,50,000 in a Fixed Deposit had not been allowed. The CPC passed a rectification order on 25.07.2025 determining income at ₹63,98,500, but did not allow the deduction because no such claim had been made in the original return. The CIT(A) dismissed the assessee’s appeal. Before the Tribunal, the assessee submitted that the omission was inadvertent, that the ₹1,50,000 investment had actually been made during the year and was eligible for Section 80C deduction, and requested either restoration to the Assessing Officer for verification or permission to pursue relief under Section 119(2)(b). The Tribunal held that, since
rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held that where a taxpayer omitted a valid deduction claim from the original return, that claim ordinarily cannot be introduced through a rectification application under Section 154 unless there is a clear “mistake apparent from the record.” In this case, the assessee for AY 2020–21 had filed the return on 30.12.2020 declaring total income of ₹63,98,501, which was processed under Section 143(1) by CPC on 25.11.2021 and led to a demand of ₹9,81,370. She later filed a Section 154 rectification request on 08.08.2022 seeking allowance of a ₹1,50,000 deduction under Section 80C for a fixed deposit investment, but CPC’s rectification order dated 25.07.2025 did not grant the deduction because the claim had not been made in the original return; the CIT(A) also rejected the appeal.

The Tribunal accepted that the assessee claimed the omission was inadvertent and that the ₹1,50,000 investment was allegedly made during the year and otherwise eligible under Section 80C, but it did not grant the deduction directly in the Section 154 proceeding. Instead, it directed that the proper course was to approach the Principal Commissioner under Section 119(2)(b) and seek condonation/permission to file a revised return so the deduction could be claimed through that route. For compliance purposes, the key point is that an unclaimed deduction like this one is not automatically recoverable through rectification; if a taxpayer has documentary evidence that an eligible deduction was missed in the original return, the remedy indicated by this decision is to seek condonation under Section 119(2)(b), subject to the authority’s acceptance.

The decision affects taxpayers and their advisors handling post-filing correction requests, especially where a substantive deduction or exemption was omitted from the original return but the underlying transaction was allegedly genuine and eligible. It also underscores the procedural distinction between correcting an apparent arithmetical/record error under Section 154 and seeking relief to make a late claim through the condonation mechanism under Section 119(2)(b).

Summary: ITAT Chandigarh partly allowed the appeal of Haploos Plyboards Private Limited for AY 2017-18, holding that the ₹100 lakh surrendered during a survey, comprising ₹90.40 lakh for excess stock and ₹9.60 lakh for excess cash, was required to be assessed as business income and could not be subjected to the higher rate under Section 115BBE. The assessee, engaged in manufacturing ply and ply board, had surrendered the amount during a survey conducted at its business premises on 21 September 2016 and had offered the surrender as “business income” in its computation. The Assessing Officer nevertheless applied the higher rate under Section 115BBE. The Tribunal noted that the assessee had no other source of income and that its statement recorded under Section 133A accepted the discrepancy and offered the additional amount as “misc. business income”. Relying on A.P. Knit Fab v. DCIT, the Tribunal held that where excess stock had a clear nexus with the assessee’s regular business and no independent undisclosed asset existed, the surrendered amount constituted business income and was subject to the normal rate of tax. The Tribunal further relied on the Rajasthan High Court decision in Deepak Maratha, which held that the amen
rows.summary:
For AY 2017-18, the ITAT Chandigarh held that a ₹1 crore surrender made during a survey at Haploos Plyboards Private Limited’s business premises had to be treated as business income, not as income taxable at the special enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The surrender consisted of ₹90.40 lakh for excess stock and ₹9.60 lakh for excess cash found during the survey conducted on 21 September 2016, and the company had already offered this amount in its return/computation as “business income” / “misc. business income.” The Assessing Officer’s attempt to tax the amount under section 115BBE was rejected because the excess stock and cash were found to have arisen from the assessee’s regular manufacturing business, the assessee had no other source of income, and there was no separate undisclosed asset or independent source justifying treatment as deemed income of the kind covered by section 115BBE. The Tribunal relied on prior case law, including A.P. Knit Fab and Deepak Maratha, to say that where surrendered amounts have a direct nexus with normal business activity and are voluntarily disclosed as business income, they are taxable at the normal business rate rather than the punitive section 115BBE rate. The decision also clarifies the timing point that the amended 60% rate under section 115BBE applies only from AY 2018-19, so it could not be applied in this AY 2017-18 case.  

From a compliance perspective, the key implication is that survey surrender amounts should be carefully documented and characterized based on their true source: if excess stock or cash is traceable to regular operations and is accepted in the books/return as business income, the taxpayer can argue against section 115BBE treatment. At the same time, the ruling underscores that the tax position depends on the factual nexus to business activity, so companies should maintain inventory, cash, and survey-response records that clearly connect any discovered discrepancy to the ordinary course of business.

rows.summary:
This Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Kolkata decision concerns assessment year 2014–15 and arises from an assessment order under section 143(3) dated 30 December 2016. The assessee challenged, among other things, an addition of Rs. 12,01,950 made under section 50C on the sale of property, arguing that the stamp-value deeming difference should not apply in full. The Tribunal held that the statutory 10% tolerance band under section 50C applies retrospectively, and on that basis deleted the section 50C addition; for compliance purposes, the key point is that property-transfer valuations for pre-amendment years may benefit from the 10% safe-harbor treatment where the declared consideration is within that margin of the stamp duty value.

The same appeal also involved a disallowance/addition of Rs. 31,46,527 relating to alleged bogus or pre-arranged share-trading loss. The assessee contended that the loss was supported by material evidence and not based on suspicion, while the tax authorities had treated it as non-genuine. From a compliance perspective, the document indicates that share-loss claims can still be scrutinized for genuineness and may be disallowed if the department views them as arranged or unsupported, so documentation of trade execution, counterparties, market transactions, and commercial rationale remains critical.

The order identifies the parties as Chandra Prakash Jhunjhunwala versus DCIT, CC-3(4), Kolkata, with the assessee represented by counsel and the Revenue by the Departmental Representative. The hearing took place on 18 June 2019 and the order was pronounced on 9 August 2019. No new filing deadline or procedural rule is created in the text beyond the appellate ruling itself, but the decision is material for assessing historical section 50C exposures and for evidencing share-trading losses in income-tax compliance reviews.

rows.summary:
This decision concerns an income-tax settlement application filed by Lion Dates Impex (P) Ltd. after a search under section 132 on 17 July 2013 at its business premises and the residences of its directors. The search led to statements under sections 132(4) and 131, followed by notices under section 153A for assessment years 2008-09 through 2013-14 and a notice under section 148 for AY 2007-08. The company responded by filing the required returns and then moved an application under section 245C(1) before the Settlement Commission, stating that some additional-income disclosures had been made incorrectly on consultant advice.

The Madras High Court held that the Settlement Commission’s rejection of the application under section 245D(4) could not stand because the process was unfair and procedurally flawed. In particular, the Assessing Officer filed a detailed report on the last date of hearing, and the Commission passed its order the very next day without giving the assessee any meaningful opportunity to review or rebut that report. The Court also found that the Commission had departed from the statutory procedure and that the circumstances gave rise to a reasonable likelihood of bias, making the proceeding an “ambush” rather than a fair adjudication.

As a result, the High Court set aside the rejection order and restored the settlement application. Although the Settlement Commission has since been abolished, the Court directed the Interim Board for Settlement to treat the restored application as pending and to decide it afresh within six weeks. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that settlement proceedings must allow a genuine opportunity to respond to adverse material, especially when new departmental reports are introduced at the last stage, and a decision made without that opportunity may be vulnerable to being quashed for denial of hearing and bias.

Summary: The ITAT Mumbai dismissed the Revenue’s appeal against the order of the National Faceless Appeal Centre for A.Y. 2022-23, upholding deletion of additions of Rs.6,00,70,268/- towards sundry creditors under section 41(1) and Rs.44,28,000/- towards unsecured loans under section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The assessee, engaged in export of granites, marbles, construction material and textile products, had originally declared total income of Rs.22,73,190/-, while the Assessing Officer determined total income at Rs.6,76,69,848/- after making additions towards sundry creditors, brokerage expenses and unsecured loans. The Tribunal noted that the assessee subsequently furnished creditor-wise details, confirmations, purchase particulars and bank statements showing discharge of substantial creditor balances in the succeeding financial year. Relying upon CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P.) Ltd., it held that section 41(1) requires remission or cessation of liability and that subsequent payment of creditor balances negated the inference of cessation during the relevant year. Regarding unsecured loans, confirmations, PAN particulars, returns of income and bank statements supported the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of the creditors, a
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that the tax department could not make additions merely because certain confirmations or supporting papers were not produced during assessment if the surrounding evidence shows the liability or loan is real. In this case, the Revenue’s appeal was dismissed and the order of the National Faceless Appeal Centre was upheld for Assessment Year 2022–23, deleting a **Section 41(1)** addition of **Rs. 6,00,70,268** relating to sundry creditors and a **Section 68** addition of **Rs. 44,28,000** relating to unsecured loans. The assessee, an exporter of granites, marbles, construction material, and textile products, had returned income of **Rs. 22,73,190**, while the Assessing Officer had assessed income at **Rs. 6,76,69,848** after also adding brokerage expenses and the disputed creditor and loan balances.

For the sundry creditors, the Tribunal accepted that the assessee later furnished creditor-wise details, confirmations, purchase particulars, and bank statements, and that substantial creditor balances were actually discharged in the succeeding financial year. Applying the principle from **CIT v. Sugauli Sugar Works (P.) Ltd.**, the Tribunal held that **Section 41(1)** applies only where there is an actual **remission or cessation of liability**; mere non-furnishing of confirmations during assessment, by itself, does not prove that the liability ceased in the relevant year. The later payments were important evidence that the creditors had not been written off or extinguished during the year under review.

For the unsecured loans, the Tribunal found that the assessee had produced confirmations, PAN details, income-tax returns, and bank statements, which established the **identity, creditworthiness, and genuineness** of the lenders. The addition under **Section 68** was therefore not sustainable on suspicion alone, because documentary evidence supported the loans. The practical compliance takeaway is that where creditor or lender documentation exists and can be reconciled through bank records and subsequent payments, the department cannot treat the amounts as unexplained or as ceased liabilities solely due to incomplete production at the assessment stage.

rows.desc: SFIO and ED can investigate the same factual matrix under distinct statutes; key principles, adjudication tracks and judicial position explained.The post 41 FAQs on SFIO-ED nexus for investigations an
rows.summary:
The document explains the relationship between the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in India, emphasizing that both agencies may investigate the same underlying facts, but under different laws and for different legal purposes. SFIO generally proceeds under company-law/fraud investigation powers, while ED proceeds under money-laundering and related enforcement statutes; the key compliance point is that a single corporate event or transaction can trigger parallel proceedings from both agencies, and an SFIO investigation does not prevent ED from independently examining the same factual matrix.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical implication is that companies, directors, officers, and other connected persons may face dual-track scrutiny arising from the same conduct, with separate evidence demands, summons, and adjudication consequences depending on which statute is being applied. The document highlights the “adjudication tracks” and the judicial position, indicating that compliance defenses, record retention, and response strategy should be built to handle parallel investigations rather than assuming one agency’s action will subsume the other’s.

No specific monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, effective dates, or new procedural amendments are stated in the provided text. The main takeaway is the need to maintain robust documentation, ensure consistency in statements and disclosures across agencies, and treat any SFIO inquiry as potentially escalating into or overlapping with ED enforcement if the facts suggest financial irregularity, fraud, or money-laundering exposure.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Fourth Amendment Rules 2026 Permit Inventory E-Commerce Exports
rows.desc: Fourth Amendment to FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019 permits inventory-based e-commerce exports of Indian-made goods subject to FTP 2023.The post FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Fourth Amendment Rules
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs has notified the **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026** by **S.O. 4870(E) dated 2 September 2026**, issued under **clauses (aa) and (ab) of section 46(2) of FEMA, 1999**. The amendment takes effect **from the date of publication in the Official Gazette** and further amends the **Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019**.

The substantive change is the insertion of **serial number 15.2.5 in Schedule I** of the 2019 NDI Rules. This new provision expressly allows an **e-commerce entity** to operate an **inventory-based model of e-commerce solely for exporting goods or products manufactured or produced in India**. The permitted exports must be carried out in accordance with the **Foreign Trade Policy 2023**, the **Handbook of Procedures (HBP)**, and the **Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods & Services) Regulations, 2015**.

For compliance purposes, the amendment also creates an exception to existing e-commerce restrictions: the limitations on **Business-to-Consumer (B2C) transactions** and on the **inventory-based model of e-commerce** found in **serial numbers 15.2.1 to 15.2.4** do **not apply** when the goods or products are exported through e-commerce under this new export-specific permission. In practical terms, entities involved in India-origin product exports via e-commerce should review whether their model now falls within the newly permitted export-only inventory structure, while activities not tied to export of Indian-manufactured/produced goods remain subject to the earlier restrictions.

The notification also notes the regulatory history of the principal NDI Rules: they were originally published on **17 October 2019** and have been amended multiple times up to **S.O. 3030(E) dated 12 June 2026**. No separate compliance deadline beyond immediate commencement on Gazette publication is stated in the text.

rows.title: Corporate Law | ECLGS 5.0: ₹2.55 Lakh Crore Credit Support for MSMEs, Non-MSMEs and Airlines
rows.desc: PIB Backgrounder details ECLGS 5.0, offering government-backed credit guarantees, additional working capital and support to MSMEs, non-MSMEs and airlines.The post ECLGS 5.0: ₹2.55 Lakh Crore Credit Su
rows.summary:
The PIB Backgrounder on **Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) 5.0**, posted on **5 September 2026**, explains a government-backed credit support scheme approved on **5 May 2026** and implemented by **NCGTC** to provide additional financing to businesses impacted by external disruptions. The scheme is designed to facilitate up to **₹2.55 lakh crore** of additional credit through **Member Lending Institutions** and applies to **MSMEs, eligible non-MSME business borrowers, and scheduled passenger airline companies**.

For **MSMEs**, the scheme provides **100% guarantee coverage** and permits additional credit generally up to **20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding during Q4 FY 2025–26**, subject to a maximum of **₹100 crore per borrower**. For **eligible non-MSMEs**, the coverage is **90%**, with the same general credit limit structure of up to **20% of peak fund-based working capital outstanding in Q4 FY 2025–26**, also capped at **₹100 crore per borrower**. For **scheduled passenger airline companies**, the scheme provides **90% guarantee coverage** and allows additional credit up to **100%**, subject to a ceiling of **₹1,500 crore per borrower**; any borrowing above **₹1,000 crore** is tied to specified equity conditions.

The scheme remains operational until **31 March 2027** or until guarantees totaling **₹2.55 lakh crore** have been issued, **whichever occurs first**. Repayment terms differ by borrower type: **MSME and eligible non-MSME loans** have a **five-year tenure including a one-year moratorium**, while **airline loans** have a **seven-year tenure including a two-year moratorium**. As of **20 August 2026**, the scheme had already issued **6,73,979 guarantees** covering **₹2,50,024 crore**, with MSMEs accounting for **97.3% of guarantees by number** and **80.79% of the guaranteed amount**.

The Backgrounder also notes that the government has conducted outreach efforts and that applications/access are available through the **Jan Samarth Portal**. For compliance purposes, the key points are that eligibility, guarantee percentage, loan caps, tenure/moratorium, and airline equity conditions are all scheme-specific requirements that lenders and borrowers must follow, and the scheme is nearing its overall issuance cap based on the reported utilization figures.

rows.title: Corporate Law | CCPA Imposes ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Dial4Trade for Online Listing and Sale of Ammonium Nitrate Without Mandatory Safeguards
rows.desc: CCPA penalises Dial4Trade ₹10 lakh for listing and facilitating sale of Ammonium Nitrate without licence verification, buyer checks and safety disclosures.The post CCPA Imposes ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Dia
rows.summary:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a **₹10 lakh penalty** on **Dial4Trade Technologies Private Limited** for **facilitating the online listing, hosting, advertising, and sale of ammonium nitrate** without the safeguards required for a regulated explosive substance. The CCPA also ordered the company to **immediately stop listing, hosting, advertising, or otherwise facilitating the sale of ammonium nitrate** and **any other substance classified as an explosive under the Explosives Act, 1884**. This is not just a narrow product-specific issue: the order is directed at the platform’s conduct in enabling sale of a hazardous substance through its marketplace.

In its review, the Authority found multiple compliance failures: the platform did **not adequately disclose the seller’s valid PESO licence details**, did **not verify the buyer’s identity or licensed status**, did **not provide traceability mechanisms** for transactions as expected under the **Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012**, and did **not warn users about the legal restrictions and consequences of unauthorized possession**. The listing also used **images depicting explosions and blast effects**, which the CCPA treated as aggravating the misleading nature of the presentation. The Authority held that an online product listing made available to the public qualifies as an **“advertisement” under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, and that presenting a regulated explosive as if it were an ordinary consumer product without the mandatory disclosures amounts to a **misleading advertisement and unfair trade practice**.

The CCPA rejected Dial4Trade’s argument that it was merely a **B2B marketplace/intermediary** and therefore not responsible for the content or sale. The Authority emphasized that **marketplace e-commerce entities remain subject to the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020** and must comply with the prescribed **due-diligence obligations**, including the checks and disclosures relevant to regulated goods. The action is part of a broader **sector-wide examination of online platforms dealing with hazardous chemicals and explosive substances**, so other platforms handling similar products should expect scrutiny and should review whether they have the required licensing verification, buyer validation, traceability, and warning controls in place.

rows.title: Corporate Law | EPFO Invites PF Trusts to Seek Retrospective Exemption Regularisation under EPF Scheme 2026 Amnesty
rows.desc: EPFO invites eligible PF Trusts to seek retrospective regularisation of exempt status under EPF Scheme 2026 Amnesty provisions by 28 December 2026.The post EPFO Invites PF Trusts to Seek Retrospective
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Labour & Employment has introduced a one-time amnesty under the EPF Scheme 2026 to allow retrospective regularisation of the exempt status of provident fund trusts that were recognised under the Income Tax Act, 1961 but never obtained a formal exemption order under section 17 of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 or section 143 of the Code on Social Security, 2020. The scheme was notified on 29 June 2026, and the operational application guidelines were issued by EPFO circular on 11 July 2026. The amnesty window remains open for six months from notification, ending on 28 December 2026, so affected PF Trusts must apply within that period if they want to regularise past exempt status.

The scheme is intended to give PF Trusts a route to cure historical exemption gaps and, after retrospective regularisation, choose whether to operate going forward as an exempt establishment or an unexempt establishment. It also provides relief from certain requirements under the Code on Social Security, 2020, specifically waiving or relaxing the minimum employee headcount requirement, corpus size requirement, and the three-year compliance rule for qualifying trusts seeking regularisation. EPFO is actively conducting outreach to likely beneficiaries and stakeholders, including the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, professional bodies, and establishments, and it has also coordinated with the Income Tax Department to verify which PF Trusts are recognised for income tax purposes and how that aligns with EPF/CoSS coverage and exemption status. PF Trusts that fall into this category are specifically invited to apply under the 11 July 2026 EPFO circular; the document notes that no independently verified public reproduction of that circular was identified, but the operative compliance point is that eligible trusts should use the EPFO procedure before the 28 December 2026 deadline.

rows.title: Corporate Law | EPFO VISHWAS 2026 Scheme Offers Reduced EPF Damages for Long-Pending Disputes
rows.desc: EPFO urges eligible establishments to settle long-pending EPF damages disputes under VISHWAS, 2026 at substantially reduced rates by 28 December 2026.The post EPFO VISHWAS 2026 Scheme Offers Reduced E
rows.summary:
The Government of India’s EPFO VISHWAS, 2026 Scheme is a one-time settlement mechanism for resolving long-pending disputes over damages/penalties for delayed Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) contributions at reduced rates. It applies only to eligible employer cases relating to delays in PF contributions arising before 14 June 2024, and the document says it can cover matters that are already pending before courts or tribunals, EPFO penalty orders where recovery is still pending, penalty notices that have been issued but no final order has yet been passed, and instances where payment delays were recorded but no penalty notice has yet been issued.

The scheme is open until 28 December 2026, and the document expressly says this deadline will not be extended. Under the settlement formula, damages are calculated at 0.25% per month for delays of up to two months, 0.50% per month for delays of more than two months but up to four months, and 1% per month for delays beyond four months; this is described as much lower than the normal penalty regime, which may reach 37% per year. Employers are first required to clear all outstanding interest on the delayed PF contributions before they can use the scheme.

The compliance process is: eligible employers must apply online through the EPFO Employer Portal using the dedicated VISHWAS, 2026 module, after which the system computes the revised damages. Once the calculation is generated, the employer is given 15 days to make payment, with an automatic additional 15-day extension available where needed. After payment is confirmed, EPFO issues a digitally signed Settlement Certificate, and the relevant court or tribunal proceeding is then treated as closed.

Operationally, EPFO has set up dedicated VISHWAS Cells and Helpdesks at all 153 Regional Offices to support applications and settlements. The document also notes that the Bombay High Court (Pune Bench), Madras High Court, and Kerala High Court have issued directions encouraging or requiring eligible establishments to avail themselves of the scheme in certain proceedings, which means employers with litigation in those jurisdictions should review whether they are covered and act before the 28 December 2026 cut-off.

rows.title: Corporate Law | IRDAI Warns Public Against Fraudulent Website Impersonating Bima Bharosa/IGMS
rows.desc: IRDAI cautions policyholders against igmsirdai.online and urges use of only the official Bima Bharosa portal for insurance grievances.The post IRDAI Warns Public Against Fraudulent Website Impersonati
rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued Public Notice No. IRDAI/PPGR/BB/2026-27/25 dated 4 September 2026 warning that the website **“igmsirdai.online”** and its complaint-registration webpages are **not official IRDAI platforms** and appear to be impersonating IRDAI’s insurance grievance system/Bima Bharosa/IGMS. The notice says the matter is under examination and that IRDAI is initiating or taking action as permitted by law, but it does not announce any new penalty or filing rule for regulated entities.

For compliance purposes, the operative requirement is that **policyholders, the general public, and other stakeholders should not use the suspect website**, should not register complaints there, and should **not provide personal, policy, financial, banking, KYC, OTP, password, or any other sensitive information** unless they have independently verified the site’s authenticity. They are also cautioned **not to make payments or respond to requests for banking credentials or OTPs** received through such a site or related communications.

IRDAI instructs users to **register and track insurance grievances only through the official Bima Bharosa portal**. Anyone who has already submitted personal, policy, or financial information via the suspected website is advised to take immediate precautionary steps and, where appropriate, report the incident to **cybercrime or other law-enforcement authorities**.

IRDAI further states it will **not be responsible for losses or disclosure of information** resulting from interaction with unauthorized or fraudulent websites impersonating IRDAI. The notice is a public-warning and consumer-protection communication rather than a rulemaking circular, but compliance teams should treat it as confirmation that any internal or customer-facing references to grievance portals must point only to the official Bima Bharosa channel and should be checked against phishing/impersonation risks.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | ICAI President’s Message: Advancing Financial Literacy, Global Professional Pathways & Financial Empowerment
rows.desc: ICAI President highlights financial literacy, global mobility, IFSC opportunities, public finance, tax, audit quality and professional initiatives for 2026.The post ICAI President’s Message: Advancing
rows.summary:
The President’s message frames India’s financial-system evolution as a shift from basic financial inclusion to active financial participation and, ultimately, financial empowerment, and it ties that shift directly to the profession’s role in promoting financial literacy, trust, and informed decision-making. It notes progress such as a higher Financial Inclusion Index, expanded account ownership, and the continued reach of government and digital rails like Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, Aadhaar-enabled services, UPI, digital payments, insurance, pensions, and investment products. At the same time, it warns that “financial literacy” must now cover much more than saving and using bank accounts: it should include planning, protection, borrowing/credit, investment, taxation, financial planning, and digital safety, because users are increasingly exposed to phishing, impersonation, fraudulent investment schemes, misinformation, and AI-enabled manipulation.

For ICAI, the message presents financial-literacy outreach as an ongoing compliance-and-public-interest mission rather than a one-off campaign, citing initiatives such as Vittiya Gyan, Investor Awareness Programmes, Project Vanijya, and outreach to rural and tribal communities. It also signals continuing engagement on professional development and regulatory capacity-building, including ICAI’s international participation (such as the IFAC Board Meeting in India and the ICAI International Conference–ASEAN), professional pathways with ISCA, WOFA 2026, public-finance workshops, new IFSCA-related certificate courses, and the MoU with the Department of Higher Education, Government of Madhya Pradesh. Additional items mentioned include the All India Leadership Summit, financial-reporting and audit-quality initiatives, the revised Guidance Note on Tax Audit under Section 44AB, the I-Kar Pe Charcha mobile application, ICAI’s strategy meeting, and regional conferences.

The message does not announce a single new binding regulatory rule with a specific effective date, rate, or threshold in the text provided; instead, it functions as a strategic update and call to action. The core compliance takeaway for professionals is that ICAI is emphasizing stronger competence in financial literacy, fraud awareness, and digital-risk awareness, alongside continued attention to audit, tax-audit, reporting-quality, and public-finance capability. The closing appeal is to convert financial literacy from mere awareness into a sustained movement for financial empowerment in support of a more confident, resilient, and financially empowered Viksit Bharat.

rows.title: Income Tax | Compensation Received Six Years Late: Karnataka HC Directs Condonation for TDS Refund
rows.desc: Karnataka HC directs PCIT to decide Section 119(2)(b) delay condonation where land acquisition compensation was received after title dispute resolution.The post Compensation Received Six Years Late: K
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that, where compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land was not actually received until years after the relevant assessment year because of a title dispute, the taxpayer’s inability to reflect that compensation in the original return should be addressed through condonation of delay under section 119(2)(b) of the Income-tax Act rather than by rigidly denying the refund claim. In this case, the petitioner, claiming as legal heir of the original owners, said he was entitled to compensation for 3 acres and 20 guntas in Survey Nos. 87/3 and 87/4 at Kothanur Village, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bengaluru South Taluk, which had been acquired by the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB) under the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966. The compensation payment was delayed for years due to a dispute over title, and only after a civil court decree resolved the title in his favor did the KIADB deposit/disburse the compensation; the petitioner then sought treatment of the compensation as exempt under section 96 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, and also sought refund of TDS deducted by KIADB.  

The court directed the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Bengaluru-3, to examine and decide the assessee’s application for condonation of delay in filing the revised return for Assessment Year 2019-20. The practical compliance point is that the refund claim depends on whether the delayed receipt of compensation can be brought into the tax computation through condonation under section 119(2)(b), because the compensation was received only in 2025 even though the return year at issue was AY 2019-20. For corporate or institutional compliance teams handling land acquisition payouts, the decision reinforces that where compensation is legally exempt and TDS has been withheld, late receipt caused by a bona fide dispute may justify a condonation-based revised return/refund route, and the tax authority must specifically consider that request rather than summarily rejecting the refund claim on timing grounds.

rows.title: Company Law | Annual ROC Compliance 2026: Beyond AOC-4 and MGT-7
rows.desc: Annual ROC compliance FY 2025-26 covering AGM, AOC-4, MGT-7, KYC, XBRL, DPT-3, MSME-1, penalties and pre-filing reconciliation.The post Annual ROC Compliance 2026: Beyond AOC-4 and MGT-7 appeared firs
rows.summary:
The document says FY 2025–26 annual ROC compliance should be treated as a full corporate compliance closure exercise, not just the mechanical filing of AOC-4 and MGT-7/MGT-7A. It covers the entire sequence from finalisation and audit of financial statements, Board approval, Board’s Report and AGM, through annual financial-statement and annual-return filings, auditor-related filings, and event-based or periodic compliances such as DPT-3, MSME-1, director KYC, CSR, share capital, charges, and related-party transactions. The key compliance message is that companies should first reconcile their internal records and statutory filings, then identify and rectify exceptions, and only then approve and file the annual ROC documents.

A major change highlighted is the revision of the “small company” thresholds effective 1 December 2025: the limits have increased to ₹10 crore paid-up capital and ₹100 crore turnover. Because of this, companies need to re-check whether they qualify for MGT-7A instead of MGT-7, whether XBRL filing applies, and whether MGT-8 certification is required, rather than relying on older threshold-based checklists. The document also notes that director KYC has shifted from an annual filing requirement to a three-year cycle, effective 31 March 2026, so companies must determine which directors fall into the new DIR-3 KYC cycle and ensure the correct filing timing.

The summary emphasizes that AOC-4 must match the signed financial statements exactly, and MGT-7/MGT-7A must agree with statutory registers, share capital records, and MCA master data. Similar pre-filing reconciliations are required for borrowings reported in DPT-3, MSME dues reported in MSME-1, related-party transactions, charges, CSR disclosures, and share capital changes. The article also flags the continuing obligation to comply even where there has been no business activity, meaning inactive companies are not automatically exempt from annual ROC obligations. It additionally warns that failures can trigger additional filing fees, statutory penalties, and in some cases director-disqualification consequences.

The document further stresses the need for consistency across books of account, GST returns, Income-tax filings, and MCA records, indicating that annual ROC compliance should be validated against the company’s broader regulatory footprint. In practical terms, the recommended workflow is: review all applicable compliances, reconcile source records with MCA requirements, identify and correct mismatches, obtain approvals, and then file the forms. For a compliance team, the main takeaway is that FY 2025–26 filings should be managed as a coordinated year-end compliance closure exercise with updated threshold checks and cycle-based director KYC planning, rather than as isolated ROC forms filed at the deadline.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Calcutta HC Allows Extension of ITC Rectification Time Under Section 16(5)
rows.desc: Calcutta High Court quashes ITC rectification rejection, holding notification timelines cannot override Section 16(5) of the CGST Act.The post Calcutta HC Allows Extension of ITC Rectification Time Un
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court, Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri, dealt with a writ petition by Umen Chandra Roy concerning entitlement to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) under Section 39 of the CGST Act, read with Section 16(5). The petitioner had filed the relevant return up to November 30, 2021, which the Court treated as being within the statutory cut-off contemplated under Section 16(5), and later submitted a rectification application on January 12, 2026 seeking the ITC benefit. That rectification request was rejected by the revenue authority by order dated April 8, 2026 on the ground that it was not filed within the period said to be prescribed by a departmental circular/notification dated April 8, 2024, read together with a circular dated October 15, 2024.

A key point in the judgment is that the Court records an apparent drafting/correction issue: paragraph 3 referred to the applicable period as “six weeks,” but a later correction order dated August 21, 2026 stated that this should be read as “six months,” and also corrected the word “communication” to “circular.” The petitioner’s legal argument was that the rectification filing period could be extended because Section 16(5) itself does not prescribe a specific deadline for filing such a rectification application. The revenue’s position was that the original order dated March 6, 2024 had been served on the petitioner the same day by post, and it disputed the petitioner’s timing/entitlement on that basis.

For compliance purposes, the document is significant because it addresses whether an administrative time limit imposed through circulars can bar rectification-based ITC relief under Section 16(5) where the statute itself does not set a filing deadline. The operative dates and deadlines referenced in the dispute are March 6, 2024 (original order), April 8, 2024 and October 15, 2024 (departmental circular/notification framework), November 30, 2021 (return filing cut-off noted by the Court), January 12, 2026 (rectification application), April 8, 2026 (rejection order), and August 21, 2026 (correction order changing “six weeks” to “six months”). The document does not provide the final merits outcome beyond these facts, but it clearly indicates that the enforceability and length of the rectification window for Section 16(5) ITC claims was the central compliance issue.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Chennai Rejects DR Objection Over Counsel’s CIC Appearance
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai rejects the conflict objection, remands ₹80.32 lakh management fee TP issue, upholds 80IA relief and disallows delayed PF/ESI.The post ITAT Chennai Rejects DR Objection Over Counsel’s CIC
rows.summary:
This document is a Madras High Court judgment dated 27.03.2017 in appeals filed by the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central 2, Chennai, against Ennore Cargo Container Terminal Pvt. Ltd. for Assessment Years 2007-08 and 2010-11, challenging a common ITAT order dated 12.05.2016. The Revenue’s main tax issue was whether the company was entitled to deduction under Section 80IA(4) for its Container Freight Station (CFS) operations after the statutory amendment to Section 80IA(4) inserted an Explanation with effect from 01.04.2002 that omitted the phrase “any other public facility of similar nature.” The Revenue also argued that the assessee was not actually “developing” infrastructure facilities and was only acting as a custodian handling and moving containerized import/export cargo at the CFS, rather than operating a qualifying infrastructure facility.

For AY 2007-08, the Revenue additionally questioned the ITAT’s treatment of a deemed dividend issue under the Income-tax Act. The document excerpt does not provide the full reasoning or the final outcome of the High Court’s decision on the substantive tax issues, but it does establish that the appeals were brought under Section 260A and that the core compliance issue for similarly situated businesses is the availability of Section 80IA(4) infrastructure deductions for CFS-related activities in light of the post-01.04.2002 wording of the provision. Entities operating CFS or similar logistics/infrastructure facilities should note that the dispute turns on whether their role is sufficiently “development” of infrastructure versus mere custody/handling services, and whether the amended statutory language supports deduction eligibility for their activity.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | CA Association Seeks Extension of Tax Audit and ITR Due Dates for AY 2026-27
rows.desc: Chartered Accountants Association Jalandhar requests extension of Tax Audit Reports, Forms 10B/10BB and audit-related ITR due dates for AY 2026-27.The post CA Association Seeks Extension of Tax Audit
rows.summary:
The Chartered Accountants Association, Jalandhar has written to the Finance Minister requesting an extension of the statutory due dates for AY 2026-27 filings. Specifically, it seeks more time to file Tax Audit Reports, Forms 10B and 10BB, and other audit-related reports, and asks for corresponding relief by pushing out the Income-tax Return filing deadlines that depend on those audit submissions. The document is not itself a rule change; it is a representation urging the government to revise existing deadlines because, in the Association’s view, taxpayers and professionals need more time to complete audit and return compliance.

The letter is addressed to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, and is dated September 06, 20265 as printed in the document. It references AY 2026-27 and frames the request as being made “on behalf of taxpayers.” The requested extension would affect entities and taxpayers required to undergo tax audit, entities filing Forms 10B/10BB, and the associated income-tax return filing obligations that follow from those reports. No specific extension length, revised date, threshold, rate, or procedural form change is proposed in the excerpt provided; the substance is simply a request for a postponement of the due dates.

rows.title: Income Tax | Bombay HC Upholds Deduction for Scientifically Estimated Major Repairs Provision
rows.desc: Bombay High Court holds provision for major road repairs allowable where contractual liability is certain and estimate is scientifically reliable.The post Bombay HC Upholds Deduction for Scientificall
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court upheld the tax treatment of a scientifically estimated provision for major repairs made by ECA Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd., a special purpose vehicle engaged in road construction and toll collection under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) concession with the Government of Maharashtra. For Assessment Year 2015-16, the company had reported a book loss of Rs. 4,48,91,467 and an income-tax loss of Rs. 8,46,64,672, but the Assessing Officer added back Rs. 7,47,00,000 by disallowing the provision created for future major repairs. The assessee argued that its 30-year concession agreement required major repairs throughout the concession period, with the first such repair due after seven years (in the eighth year) and the last in the 30th year, so the liability accrued over time and could be recognized through a reliable estimate rather than only when cash was actually spent.

The Court’s ruling matters for compliance because it confirms that, where a contractual obligation exists and the amount can be estimated scientifically, a provision may be deductible even if the repair cost has not yet been incurred in cash. The assessee relied on its BOT concession terms and on CBDT Circular No. 9/2014, which addresses expenditure incurred for development of roads/highways under BOT arrangements. The Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Pune, had already accepted the assessee’s position after reviewing the concession agreement, including Articles 17, 37, 38, and 39, and the ITAT, Mumbai dismissed the Revenue’s appeal on 8 February 2023; the High Court then rejected the Revenue’s further appeal under Section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

For taxpayers in similar BOT infrastructure arrangements, the key compliance takeaway is that the tax deductibility of a repair provision depends on the existence of a binding contractual repair obligation and supportable estimation methodology, not merely on actual payment timing. The decision does not announce a new filing deadline or rate change, but it reinforces that entities operating road concessions should maintain robust documentation showing why the liability has accrued, how the estimate was computed, and how the concession agreement specifically obligates the repairs over the life of the project.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Appeal Filed Before Section 107 Order Is Passed Not Maintainable: GSTAT Chennai
rows.desc: GSTAT Chennai held that a Section 112 appeal filed before the first appellate order existed was not maintainable, dismissing it with liberty to refile.The post GST Appeal Filed Before Section 107 Orde
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench held that an appeal filed before the First Appellate Authority had passed its order is not maintainable under Section 112 of the CGST Act, 2017. In this case, Pankajam Plastics had filed an appeal in APL-01 before the First Appellate Authority and also filed the GSTAT appeal in APL-05 on the same day, 19.03.2026, claiming that the department had already started recovery proceedings. However, the record showed that the First Appellate Authority’s order rejecting APL-02 was actually passed later, on 24.06.2026 by the Deputy Commissioner, CT Appeals, meaning no appealable order under Section 107/108 existed when the GSTAT appeal was lodged. The Registry had flagged this as a defect, and the Tribunal agreed that Filing No. 2026133/10100/0064 was premature because Section 112(1) permits an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal only against an order already passed under Section 107 or Section 108.  

For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that a taxpayer cannot bypass the statutory sequence by filing a Tribunal appeal before the first appellate order exists, even if recovery action is being initiated. The operative procedural requirement is that an aggrieved person must first have an actual order from the First Appellate Authority before invoking the GSTAT under Section 112. No filing deadline or monetary threshold was set in this decision; the key requirement is timing and maintainability of the appeal, not the merits of the underlying tax dispute.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Bombay HC Declines Interim Relief Over GST Recovery Citing Unjustified Delay
rows.desc: Bombay HC rejects interim relief to Best Agrolife over GST recovery notices, citing delay, while seeking Revenue’s response on ignored representations.The post Bombay HC Declines Interim Relief Over G
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court dealt with a GST recovery dispute involving Best Agrolife Limited after a notice dated 25/03/2025 required payment of tax and interest within seven days, warning that recovery proceedings under Section 79 of the Maharashtra GST Act, 2017 would begin if payment was not made. The company did not pay in response to the notice; instead, by email dated 11/04/2025, it said it had issued credit notes under Section 34 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with Rule 53 of the CGST Rules, 2017 for returned goods and rate differences, and that these credit notes were reflected through the e-invoice portal and used to adjust outward tax liability against earlier sales periods. It argued that this only reduced output tax liability and did not create any actual tax shortfall because the liability had already been discharged, and it supported that position with a GSTN-generated “Tax Liability Report” for April 2022 through February 2025 and a “NEGATIVE LIABILITY STATEMENT” for 01/09/2024 to 27/03/2025 showing negative sales/negative liability carried on the portal and automatically adjusted against later liabilities.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the court did not grant interim relief against recovery, and the existence of portal-based negative liability, credit-note adjustments, or retrospective set-off claims did not excuse the taxpayer’s failure to pay within the seven-day deadline in the demand notice. The matter shows that when a tax officer issues a demand notice under the MGST framework and expressly threatens Section 79 recovery, the taxpayer must respond promptly and substantively; simply asserting that credit notes were raised and that later portal adjustments offset the liability may not be enough to stop recovery action. The document therefore highlights a practical compliance risk: companies using credit notes for returns or rate differences should ensure that their GST returns, e-invoice reporting, and liability adjustments are fully aligned and promptly documented, because delays or unresolved mismatches can still trigger immediate recovery proceedings.

rows.title: Income Tax | Pune ITAT Restores ₹1.73-Crore Penalty U/s 271(1)(c) on Capital Expenditure Claim
rows.desc: ITAT Pune restores ₹1.73 crore penalty after holding retiring partner settlement payment was capital expenditure and inaccurate particulars were furnished.The post Pune ITAT Restores ₹1.73-Crore Penal
rows.summary:
This order concerns a penalty dispute under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2014-15 involving **M/s. Sarsan Developers, Pune**, a partnership firm engaged in land development. The firm filed its return on **29.11.2014** declaring **nil income**, but in the assessment completed under **section 143(3)** by the Assessing Officer on **23.12.2016**, an addition of **₹5,60,73,319** was made. That amount had been claimed as part of development expenses and represented a payment to a retiring partner, **Kumar Housing Corporation Limited**, which the department treated as a capital expenditure rather than a revenue business expense.

The key compliance issue is that the firm had originally **debited ₹13,40,50,885 as development expenses**, including the disputed **₹5.60 crore** payment. The Assessing Officer treated the payment to the retiring partner as not allowable in computing business income, and the assessment was finalized at **nil income** only after this addition. The order under discussion is not the assessment itself but the Revenue’s appeal against the **CIT(A)’s order dated 13.12.2019**, which had evidently deleted the penalty; the Pune ITAT has now **restored the penalty**.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that the Tribunal accepted the Revenue’s position that the claim of this **capital expenditure** as a deductible development expense amounted to penalty-exposing conduct under **section 271(1)(c)**. The decision underscores that where a taxpayer claims a large payment to a retiring partner or similar structural payout as a revenue deduction, but the tax authorities view it as capital in nature, the claim can lead not only to disallowance but also to a concealment/inaccurate particulars penalty. The case therefore signals the need for careful tax characterization of partner retirement settlements, restructuring payouts, and development-project expense allocations, with supporting documentation and legal analysis robust enough to defend revenue-deduction treatment. The Tribunal’s order was pronounced on **10.10.2023**.

rows.title: Income Tax | Pune ITAT Quashes Reassessment Over ₹1.47-Crore Deposits and u/s 80P Addition
rows.desc: ITAT Pune quashes reassessment after no addition on cash and time deposits, holding section 80P disallowance was an unrelated new issue.The post Pune ITAT Quashes Reassessment Over ₹1.47-Crore Deposit
rows.summary:
For AY 2018–19, the Pune ITAT held that the reassessment of Ekviradevi Gramin Bigarsheti Sahakari Patsanstha Maryadit could not stand because the Assessing Officer reopened the case on one specific ground but ultimately made an addition on a completely different issue. The reopening was based on portal information that the assessee, a co-operative credit society, had not filed a return and had allegedly made cash deposits of ₹91,86,100 in The RDCC Urban Bank and time deposits/investments of ₹55,50,000, totaling ₹1,47,36,100, which the AO treated as escaped income. After issuing notice under section 148A(b), the AO passed an order under section 148A(d) on 07.04.2022 and proceeded with reassessment, but instead of taxing the alleged deposits, he made a disallowance of ₹7,06,146 under section 80P(2)(a)(i).

The Tribunal quashed the reassessment proceedings, relying on the Bombay High Court ruling in CIT v. Jet Airways (I) Ltd., which requires the AO, if reopening is based on a particular escapement issue, to actually assess that issue; the AO cannot “abandon” the original reason for reopening and then make a fresh addition on an unrelated matter. In practical terms, the decision means that where reassessment is initiated to examine alleged unexplained deposits or similar escaped income, the tax authority must either sustain an addition on that very issue or lose the jurisdictional basis for the reassessment if it shifts to a different disallowance, such as denial of a deduction under section 80P. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that reopening notices and resulting additions must match: a reassessment founded on one alleged item of escaped income cannot be lawfully used as a general opportunity to make unrelated adjustments.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Finds Nil Profiteering as Cost Escalation Offsets GST ITC Benefit
rows.desc: GSTAT accepts DGAP's revised computation and finds nil profiteering after construction cost escalation offsets additional ITC benefit.The post GSTAT Finds Nil Profiteering as Cost Escalation Offsets G
rows.summary:
This GSTAT matter concerned an anti-profiteering allegation against M/s Vertex Homes Pvt. Ltd. in its “Vertex Panache” real estate project, where the applicant alleged that the company did not pass on the benefit of additional input tax credit (ITC) that arose after GST came into force on 01.07.2017, which would amount to a violation of Section 171 of the CGST Act, 2017. The Standing Committee referred the complaint to the DGAP, and the DGAP’s initial report alleged total profiteering of Rs. 73,00,010/-, made up of Rs. 65,17,866/- as base profiteering plus Rs. 7,82,144/- as GST, said to be distributable among 140 eligible homebuyers. Vertex Homes defended itself by arguing that the increase in construction costs had substantially absorbed the ITC benefit, pointing to a budgeted construction cost of Rs. 1,56,94,91,872/- versus actual expenditure of Rs. 1,61,06,72,320/-, a difference of Rs. 4,11,80,448/- including indirect cost.

The company specifically said the cost escalation was driven by major input increases of 19.87% for Ready-Mix Concrete (RMC), 62.98% for sand, and 73.17% for bricks, and claimed that the additional expenditure attributable to these items alone was Rs. 3,49,87,499/- based on actual quantities and costs. It relied on the Delhi High Court’s reasoning in Reckitt Benckiser India Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, especially paragraph 118, to argue that genuine commercial cost increases can justify higher prices even where tax incidence changes or ITC becomes available. The respondent also supported its position with a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate dated 25.06.2026 issued by M/s Tukaram & Co.

On the material provided, the key compliance issue is the anti-profiteering rule under Section 171: businesses affected by GST transition, especially real estate project developers, must pass on the benefit of ITC to recipients unless they can substantiate that other bona fide cost escalations offset that benefit. The document does not provide the final GSTAT outcome or any new rule-making deadline; rather, it records the dispute and the company’s cost-escalation defense against the allegation that ITC benefits were not passed through.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Upholds EGVs as Valid GST Benefit Transfer, Orders ₹10,241 Fund Deposit
rows.desc: GSTAT accepts EGVs as valid GST benefit transfer but directs Sane Retails to deposit ₹10,241 with 18% interest in Consumer Welfare Fund.The post GSTAT Upholds EGVs as Valid GST Benefit Transfer, Order
rows.summary:
This order concerns an anti-profiteering allegation against **M/s Sane Retails Pvt. Ltd.** arising from the claimed failure to pass on the GST rate-cut benefit on **“MI LED Television 4A 80 cm”** after the GST rate was reduced from **28% to 18%**, effective **1 January 2019**, under **Notification No. 24/2018-Central Tax (Rate) dated 31 December 2018**. The complaint was filed by **Shri Rohit Kumar Agrawal** and referred to the **DGAP** by the Standing Committee under **Rule 129 of the CGST Rules, 2017**. DGAP examined invoices and outward taxable supply records for the period **1 November 2018 to 31 December 2018** (pre-rate reduction) and **1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019** (post-rate reduction) and initially found profiteering of **₹7,79,947**.

During the proceedings, after the matter moved from the now-ceased National Anti-Profiteering Authority to the **GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT)**, the Tribunal required the respondent to prove that the alleged profiteered amount had been returned to customers. The company relied on **Electronic Gift Voucher (EGV)** screenshots, an **Excel mapping** linking vouchers to customer orders/invoices, and later **credit notes**. DGAP’s initial objection was that the EGVs appeared **conditional, time-bound, and restricted**, and that the internal label **“Offers and cash back”** did not by itself show that the GST benefit had been passed on.

DGAP ultimately accepted **credit notes of ₹2,21,056** issued to **174 customers** whose orders had been cancelled or whose goods were returned, reducing the alleged profiteering amount to **₹5,58,891**. The respondent argued that the remaining benefit had also been passed on through EGVs and associated customer mappings, and the Tribunal assessed whether those vouchers constituted valid transfer of the GST benefit. The key compliance point from the decision is that the Tribunal treated **EGVs as a valid mode of passing on the GST rate-reduction benefit**, provided there is adequate traceability to the affected customer transactions and the benefit is demonstrably linked to the price reduction obligation.

The order results in a direction for a **₹10,241 fund deposit** (as reflected in the title), indicating a residual amount was required to be deposited rather than fully retained by the company. For compliance teams, the substantive takeaway is that when a GST rate cut applies from a specified effective date, businesses must ensure the benefit is passed on to end customers through a clearly documented mechanism—whether by price reduction, refund, credit note, or voucher—supported by transaction-level evidence; where vouchers are used, the company should maintain documentary linkage showing the voucher corresponds to the specific sale and the statutory benefit has been transferred.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | 57th GST Council Meeting Rescheduled to October 7, 2026: Legal Analysis
rows.desc: 57th GST Council Meeting has been rescheduled to October 7, 2026, due to the BRICS Summit, with implications for GST stakeholders.The post 57th GST Council Meeting Rescheduled to October 7, 2026: Lega
rows.summary:
The GST Council Secretariat has formally rescheduled the 57th GST Council Meeting from **September 12, 2026** to **October 7, 2026** in **New Delhi**. The associated **Officers’ Meeting** will now take place on **October 5 and 6, 2026**, also in New Delhi. The meeting will still be chaired by **Union Finance Minister Smt. Nirmala Sitharaman**, and the document states that the Council’s constitutional mandate, composition, and decision-making framework are unchanged.

The reason given for the postponement is India’s hosting of the **BRICS Leaders’ Summit on September 12–13, 2026** in New Delhi, with the document noting that the security, protocol, and administrative burden would make it impracticable to hold the GST Council Meeting at the same time. No new tax rate, exemption, or enforcement rule is introduced by the rescheduling itself, and the document expressly says the postponement **does not affect existing statutory compliance obligations**.

For compliance teams, the key point is that this is a **date change only**, not a substantive GST law amendment, so current filing, payment, registration, and ITC compliance requirements continue uninterrupted. However, the meeting is still significant because it follows the **56th GST Council Meeting of September 3–4, 2025** and the resulting GST rate restructuring, and it may address further policy changes. One reported issue under consideration is **simplification of GST registration procedures for businesses that pass on input tax credit exceeding ₹2.5 lakh per month**.

Until any official outcomes are issued after the October meeting, affected businesses and advisers should continue monitoring GST Council communications, prepare representations, and be ready for possible procedural or rate-related changes that may emerge from the deliberations.

rows.title: SEBI | SEBI Wants Less Scrutiny of AIF Trustees. Does Its Own Enforcement Record Say Otherwise?
rows.desc: SEBI's AIF Trustee enforcement record raises questions over its proposal to exclude Trustee-related transactions from investor-consent scrutiny.The post SEBI Wants Less Scrutiny of AIF Trustees. Does
rows.summary:
SEBI inspected India Asset Growth Fund, an Alternative Investment Fund registered as IN/AIF2/12-13/0037, on November 14–15, 2022, covering the period April 1, 2021 to March 31, 2022. After issuing its inspection findings on October 30, 2023 and receiving responses on December 19, 2023 and March 13, 2024, SEBI concluded that the fund, its manager, certain officers, and the trustee had committed non-compliances with the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 and related circulars. The noticee group named in the adjudication includes India Asset Growth Fund; Essel Finance Advisors and Managers LLP; Vishnu Prakash Rathore, CEO; Arpan Sarkar, AVP Legal; Jaykishan Kikani, Assistant Manager; and Vistra ITCL (India) Limited as trustee.

The document is an adjudication order under Section 15-I of the SEBI Act, 1992 and Rule 5 of the SEBI (Procedure for Holding Inquiry and Imposing Penalties) Rules, 1995, which means SEBI was assessing whether penalties should be imposed for the observed violations. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the order reflects SEBI’s enforcement position that AIF trustees, managers, and responsible officers are all within the scope of scrutiny when fund-level compliance failures occur, rather than treating the trustee as a passive or lightly reviewed role. The excerpt provided does not yet specify the individual violations or penalty amounts, but it clearly establishes that SEBI found multiple regulatory breaches during the inspection period and proceeded to formal enforcement against both the fund and the connected persons/entities.

rows.title: Income Tax | Cash System u/s 145(1) Accepted, Interest Nexus u/s 57(iii) Must Be Proved
rows.desc: ITAT Hyderabad remands interest deduction claim for verification of IIFL loan utilisation, nexus with interest income and cash accounting.The post Cash System u/s 145(1) Accepted, Interest Nexus u/s 5
rows.summary:
The document summarizes an ITAT Hyderabad decision in **Ravi Kumar Gollapudi v. DCIT** for **Assessment Year 2018-19** involving the tax treatment of **interest expense claimed against interest income under “Income from other sources.”** The assessee filed a return declaring **total income of ₹30,33,940**, and the case was selected for **limited scrutiny**, with a notice issued under **section 143(2)**. During assessment, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had claimed **interest expenditure of ₹65,47,089** against **interest income of ₹58,81,505** reported in the year; the prior year figures were also discussed, with **interest income of ₹65,26,481** reported in the earlier year, while the assessee stated that the remaining interest was received in later years.

The key issue was whether the expense could be disallowed simply because the interest paid in the year exceeded the interest received in that year. The ITAT held that, because the assessee regularly followed the **cash system of accounting**, recognition of interest income on an **actual receipt basis** is permissible under **section 145(1)**, so a year-to-year mismatch between interest paid and interest received cannot, by itself, justify outright denial of the deduction. However, the Tribunal made clear that deduction under **section 57(iii)** is not automatic: the assessee must establish a **direct nexus** between the borrowed funds, the interest-bearing advance, and the income actually offered to tax.

As a result, the Tribunal did **not** accept the disallowance as a matter of principle, but it also did **not** allow the full claim unconditionally; instead, it **remanded the matter** for verification of whether the necessary nexus exists. The amount in dispute discussed by the Tribunal was a **₹13.66 lakh disallowance**, and the compliance takeaway is that taxpayers using the cash system can defer recognition of interest income until receipt, but they still need contemporaneous evidence showing that the borrowed funds were used to generate the taxable interest income to support a deduction under section 57(iii).

rows.title: Corporate Law | CCI Rejects Interim Relief as DG Investigation Into Competition Claims Remains Pending
rows.desc: CCI rejects interim relief sought against allegedly restrictive clauses, holding that granting it during the pending DG investigation would pre-judge the issues.The post CCI Rejects Interim Relief as
rows.summary:
The Competition Commission of India refused to grant interim relief in the matter filed by Smt. Rinima Borah Agarwal against Mrs. India Inc., a sole proprietorship run by Smt. Mohini Sharma. The Informant had invoked Section 19(1)(a) of the Competition Act, 2002, alleging violations of Sections 3 and 4, and the Commission had already, by order dated 02.06.2026 under Section 26(1), directed the Director General to investigate the case.  

In the interim application (IA No. 178A of 2025), the Informant asked the Commission to stay specified clauses in the Participant Terms and Conditions dated 23.10.2024 and the Winner’s Terms and Conditions dated 27.10.2024, and also to restrain Mrs. India Inc. from issuing any communications that would restrict or discourage her from joining or participating in other competitions while the case was pending. The Commission held that these requests were effectively the same as final relief, and granting them before the DG investigation was completed would improperly decide issues that still needed to be investigated and adjudicated.  

Accordingly, the Commission found that interim relief was not appropriate or warranted at that stage and rejected the application. The key compliance implication is that the challenged contractual clauses were not yet stayed, but they had already been identified by the Commission as potentially raising competition concerns and remain under active DG investigation, so the underlying terms and communications are still exposed to scrutiny and possible future relief after investigation.

rows.title: Corporate Law | DNA Evidence Establishes Paternity, Not Consent: Delhi HC Upholds Acquittal
rows.desc: Delhi HC holds DNA proves sexual intercourse, not consent, and upholds acquittal where prosecution evidence leaves reasonable doubt.The post DNA Evidence Establishes Paternity, Not Consent: Delhi HC U
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court, in **KXXXXX v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.** ( **CRL.A. 320/2026** and **CRL.M.A. 10175/2026**, Neutral Citation **2026:DHC:7451**), **dismissed the complainant’s appeal and upheld the respondent’s acquittal** in a sexual-offence prosecution. The Court reiterated that a **DNA report showing biological paternity only proves that sexual intercourse occurred**; it **does not, by itself, prove that the intercourse was non-consensual**, which remained the critical issue in dispute. The case involved allegations of **repeated sexual acts, threats, coercion, and administration of an intoxicating substance**, but the Court accepted the Trial Court’s evaluation that the evidence, including the complainant’s testimony and the surrounding circumstances, contained **material inconsistencies** and that there had been **delay in disclosure/reporting**.

For compliance purposes, the key legal standard reinforced here is the **limited scope of appellate interference with acquittals**: an acquittal should not be disturbed if the Trial Court’s view is a **reasonably possible view**. The High Court said reversal on appeal requires something materially more serious, such as **patent perversity, manifest illegality, misreading of evidence, omission of material evidence, or other compelling and substantial reasons**. The Court relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in **Tulasareddi @ Mudakappa & Anr. v. State of Karnataka & Ors.** for that standard.

The Court also emphasized that, in sexual-offence cases, a complainant’s conduct **cannot be judged through stereotypical assumptions**, and that the **seriousness or gravity of the allegation cannot replace proof beyond reasonable doubt**. In practical terms, the ruling underscores that investigators and litigants should not treat **DNA/paternity evidence as dispositive of consent**, and that prosecution must still independently establish the elements of the offence, especially lack of consent, through reliable and coherent evidence.

rows.title: Income Tax | Wrong Approval Quashes Reassessment, Penalty U/s 270A: Hyderabad ITAT
rows.desc: Wrong Sanction Sinks Reassessment, Penalty Goes Down With the Ship: Hyderabad ITAT Quashes Penalty u/s 270A Where Notice u/s 148 Lacked Approval of Specified Authority u/s 151The post Wrong Approval Q
rows.summary:
The Hyderabad ITAT held that a penalty order under section 270A cannot survive where the underlying reassessment itself was initiated on a legally defective notice under section 148. In this case, the assessee challenged a confirmed penalty of ₹2,13,664 for AY 2018-19, and the Tribunal accepted that the validity of the reassessment proceedings could be examined even in an appeal against the penalty, because the reassessment was the foundation of the penalty. The key defect was that the notice under section 148 had been issued with approval from an authority that was not competent under section 151, so the reassessment order was quashed and the consequential penalty was also set aside.

For compliance purposes, the ruling underscores that reassessment action must be backed by approval from the correct “specified authority” under section 151; if the sanctioning authority is wrong or lacks jurisdiction, the notice and everything flowing from it are vulnerable to challenge. It also confirms that taxpayers may raise such a jurisdictional defect later, even in collateral proceedings against penalty, rather than being confined only to an immediate challenge to the reassessment notice.
