Separately, the Tribunal condoned a 110-day delay in filing the appeal because the assessee showed that the delay resulted from a professional lapse by the Chartered Accountant while the assessee was abroad for pilgrimage, indicating that bona fide, adequately explained filing delays may be excused where supported by an affidavit and credible facts.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility & Risks
rows.desc: GST ITC on immovable property: Section 17(5) restrictions, movable-versus-immovable tests, plant and machinery exceptions, and contract safeguards.The post GST ITC on Immovable Property: Eligibility &
rows.summary:
The document explains the GST input tax credit restriction in Section 17(5)(c) and 17(5)(d) of the CGST Act as it applies to works contract services and to goods/services used for constructing immovable property, and notes that tax authorities are issuing notices demanding reversal of ITC claimed on newly constructed business premises such as factories and warehouses. The core compliance issue is that ITC connected to “immovable property” is generally blocked, but the article emphasizes that not every item installed in a building is immovable, so credits related to separately identifiable plant, machinery, and other movable business equipment may still be eligible if the facts support that characterization. It specifically discusses how immovable property is determined using the General Clauses Act, the Transfer of Property Act, and judicial tests such as the purpose of annexation, the degree and permanency of attachment, functionality, intention, and marketability, which means compliance teams need to assess each asset or installation based on substance rather than simply treating all site work as ineligible.

The article highlights that items such as HVAC systems, sewage treatment plants, electrical installations, fire-safety systems, cabling, security systems, and other business equipment can fall into the movable-or-eligible-credit analysis depending on how they are installed and used, rather than being automatically treated as blocked immovable property. It also notes the statutory exceptions under Section 17(5), including the carve-out for plant and machinery and situations where construction is not undertaken on the taxable person’s own account, which are key points for defending ITC positions. A practical compliance recommendation is to structure procurement and execution through separate, independent contracts and invoices for civil construction, plant and machinery, and movable goods/services, because combining them in a single contract increases the risk that otherwise eligible credit may be denied or disputed by the department.

For compliance purposes, the document does not introduce a new deadline, rate, or filing date; instead, it addresses ongoing eligibility rules and audit/litigation risk under existing GST law. The operational takeaway is that companies building or expanding business facilities should document the legal and functional nature of each installation, segregate billing where possible, and retain evidence supporting why an item is movable or qualifies as plant and machinery so they can justify ITC claims if challenged.

rows.title: Income Tax | Builder Delay Can Trigger TDS Interest for Homebuyers
rows.desc: Homebuyers must deduct TDS on every property installment. Delayed builder intimation can result in interest, notices and filing complications.The post Builder Delay Can Trigger TDS Interest for Homebu
rows.summary:
The document explains that homebuyers paying builders through construction-linked installments can face TDS noncompliance if they do not deduct tax from each installment when due. Under Section 194-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a buyer of qualifying immovable property from a resident seller must deduct TDS at 1% on each payment or credit, whichever occurs earlier, and for covered transactions must file Form 26QB within 30 days from the end of the month in which deduction is made; the buyer must also issue Form 16B to the seller. The document warns that builders may ask for installment payments without mentioning TDS until later, often near possession or the final payment, but that delay does not excuse earlier non-deduction: if TDS was not deducted when required, interest is still charged from the date the tax should originally have been deducted, even if the buyer was unaware of the rule.

It specifically states that under Section 201(1A) of the 1961 Act, interest is 1% per month or part of a month for delayed deduction and 1.5% per month or part of a month for delayed deposit after deduction. It also notes a law change effective 1 April 2026: the corresponding obligation continues under Section 393(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, and Form 141 will replace Form 26QB for applicable transactions. The compliance takeaway is that buyers should track every installment independently, deduct and deposit TDS on time for each payment, and complete the required statement and certificate filings without waiting for builder instructions; otherwise, they may accrue avoidable interest even where the builder did not inform them promptly.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court quashes a GST notice invoking Section 74 as mere use of fraud or suppression without supporting particulars is insufficient.The post Vague Fraud Allegation Cannot Invoke GST Section 74:
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a GST show cause notice cannot validly invoke the extended limitation period under Section 74 of the CGST Act merely by using the words “fraud,” “wilful misstatement,” or “suppression of facts” in a conclusory way. In **M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.**, the company challenged an **SCN dated 13.06.2025** for **FY 2018–19** involving a demand of **Rs. 1,52,56,431**, arguing that the normal limitation period under **Section 73 had expired on 28.02.2025** and that the department had mechanically invoked Section 74 without stating any concrete facts showing fraud or suppression. The Court agreed that the **notice itself must disclose the foundational facts** that justify using the extended period; the legal validity of the SCN is judged on its face, and later explanations cannot cure a jurisdictional defect.

The Court found the SCN deficient because it contained only a vague reference to **“fraud or concealment of facts”** without explaining **what conduct amounted to fraud, how concealment was detected, or what specific facts were allegedly suppressed**. It also noted that the use of the word **“or”** reflected uncertainty as to the exact allegation being made, which further undermined the validity of the invocation of Section 74. The department attempted to justify the notice through its counter affidavit, but the Supreme Court refused to rely on those post hoc explanations, reiterating that a defective notice cannot be repaired through later pleadings in court.

As a result, the Supreme Court **set aside the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s order and quashed the SCN itself**, and it **restrained the department from taking further action on the basis of that notice**. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that when GST authorities seek to proceed under **Section 74** rather than **Section 73**, the notice must contain **specific, stated reasons and factual particulars** supporting fraud, wilful misstatement, or suppression; a bare label is not enough to sustain the extended limitation period or the demand.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Restores Section 129 Penalty for Iron Scrap Moved Without E-Way Bill
rows.desc: GSTAT Lucknow restores tax and equal penalty under Section 129(3) for iron scrap transported without an E-Way Bill.The post GSTAT Restores Section 129 Penalty for Iron Scrap Moved Without E-Way Bill a
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow Bench restored a **Section 129 penalty under the UPGST Act, 2017** for a consignment of **iron goods/scrap moved without an E-Way Bill**, holding that the surrounding facts supported an inference of attempted tax evasion. The case arose from transport of **132.90 cubic feet of iron goods** by **M/s Islam Trading Company, Baheri, Bareilly** under **Tax Invoice No. 29 dated 26.03.2018**; the vehicle was intercepted by the **Mobile Squad, Bareilly on 27.03.2018**, and the driver did **not have the E-Way Bill at the time of interception**. On that basis, the authorities imposed **tax of Rs. 47,844/- and an equal penalty of Rs. 47,844/- under Section 129(3)**.

The first appellate authority had earlier **set aside both the tax and penalty by order dated 24.09.2021 in Appeal No. APL/24/2018**, but the Tribunal reversed that outcome. The Department’s position was that movement without the mandatory E-Way Bill violated **Rule 138 of the GST Rules**, and that later production of the **tax invoice, books of account, GST returns, and proof of tax payment** did not erase the original compliance failure. It argued that the interception circumstances, the nature of the goods, the route, and the subsequent documentary production together indicated an **intention to evade tax**.

For compliance purposes, the important point is that the Tribunal treated **absence of an E-Way Bill during transport as a serious statutory breach that can trigger detention and penalty even if supporting sales/tax documents exist later**. The decision reinforces that businesses moving taxable goods must ensure the **E-Way Bill is generated and available with the vehicle/driver before or during transit as required**, because post-event document submission may not prevent **Section 129 tax and penalty exposure**. The source text also notes an internal **party-description inconsistency** in the order, where the cause title and paragraph references do not align on which side was appellant/respondent, but that inconsistency does not change the substantive holding that the **Section 129 penalty was restored**.

rows.title: Service Tax | Separate Supply and ECIS Contracts Not Works Contracts: CESTAT Delhi
rows.desc: CESTAT holds separate material-supply and erection contracts are not works contracts; free supplies remain excluded from assessable value.The post Separate Supply and ECIS Contracts Not Works Contract
rows.summary:
The Tribunal considered three connected appeals involving developers/construction companies in Chennai and Coimbatore: Real Value Promoters Pvt. Ltd., Ceebros Property Development, and Prime Developers. The department had issued show cause notices alleging short-payment of service tax on their construction projects under **Commercial or Industrial Construction Service** and disputing the assessees’ use of the **Works Contract Service composition scheme** after **1 June 2007**. For Real Value Promoters, the dispute specifically covered four projects, with the department objecting to the tax treatment adopted for **Sananda Brindavan, Sujeet, and Surya Skanda** on the ground that the activity was not a valid works contract and that the appellants had not properly exercised the option required for the composition scheme.

The common legal issue was whether these development/construction arrangements should be treated as **separate supply/construction arrangements plus ECIS-related activity** rather than as a single **works contract** for service tax purposes. The Tribunal’s order addresses the classification dispute that affected how service tax was to be computed, including whether the assessees could lawfully pay tax under the **works contract composition scheme** after **1.6.2007** instead of under the general construction-service category. The order indicates that the department’s demand was based on a view that the contract structure and the nature of the services did not satisfy the requirements for works contract classification.

This decision matters for compliance because it highlights that real estate developers and contractors cannot assume that all construction-linked service arrangements automatically qualify as works contracts merely because they involve construction activity and some material supply. The key compliance point is that tax treatment depends on the actual contractual structure and whether the statutory conditions for the composition route were properly met, including any required election/option formalities. The relevant tax periods are those after **1 June 2007**, when service tax under the works contract composition scheme was being claimed by the appellants, and the order arose from original adjudication orders dated **16.8.2010**, **6.1.2010**, and **10.5.2010** for the respective appellants.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Allahabad HC Grants Bail in GST Fraud Case Involving Non-Existing Firm
rows.desc: Allahabad High Court grants bail to Waseem Akram in alleged GST fraud case involving non-existing firm M/s Super Power Industries, noting the applicant was not named in the FIR.The post Allahabad HC G
rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court granted bail to Waseem Akram @ Monu in a GST-fraud-related criminal case involving an allegedly non-existing/bogus firm, M/s Super Power Industries. The case was registered as Case Crime No. 539 of 2025 at Police Station Brahampuri, District Meerut, under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 120-B of the IPC. The court record, as summarized in the document, indicates that the firm had allegedly been declared bogus in November 2021, while the FIR was lodged later on 04.11.2025, and the applicant argued that he was not the owner of the firm, was not named in the FIR, and was not a beneficiary of the alleged fraud.

From a compliance perspective, the document does not announce a change in GST law or a new regulatory obligation; it is a case-law update showing judicial treatment of alleged GST fraud. The applicant’s name reportedly surfaced only through the statement of Sakeel Khan, and he claimed to have no criminal history other than the present case. He had been in custody since 05.04.2026, and the court noted the heavy pendency of cases and the resulting low likelihood of an early trial conclusion. The bail request was opposed by the State A.G.A. and counsel for the GST Department, but after considering the facts, allegations, record, evidence, and submissions, the court held that the applicant was entitled to be released on bail pending trial.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Holds Municipal Hoarding Space Taxable, But Quashes Extended-Period Service Tax Demand
rows.desc: CESTAT holds municipal hoarding space and commercial property rentals taxable, but sets aside extended-period demand for lack of suppression.The post CESTAT Holds Municipal Hoarding Space Taxable, But
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Delhi decision examines service tax exposure of a municipality for two separate streams of receipts during the period 2009-10 to 2014-15: (1) amounts collected for allowing advertisers to use municipal land/space for hoardings, and (2) rent/licence fees received from leasing or licensing municipal immovable properties, including vacant land, to agencies, persons, and traders. The municipality had received Rs. 3,06,738 from hoarding-related receipts between April 2009 and June 2012, and Rs. 3,39,22,974 from immovable-property rent between April 2009 and July 2014; the Department demanded service tax of Rs. 39,22,945, plus interest, penalties, and late fee for failure to file ST-3 returns. Both the adjudicating authority and the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the demand before the matter reached the Tribunal.

On the renting issue, the municipality argued that “Renting of Immovable Property Service” had been wrongly applied, that the phrase “any other person” in the relevant definition should be read to mean someone other than the owner, that vacant land was outside the taxable definition, and that arrears of rent had been taxed at an incorrect rate. On the hoarding issue, it contended that it was only collecting statutory licence fees under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 for allotting land on which advertisers erected hoardings, rather than providing advertising services in the commercial sense. The Tribunal accepted the municipality’s position on the hoarding receipts and held that the municipal collection for allotment/licensing of space for hoardings was not taxable as an advertising service in the manner alleged by the Department.

At the same time, the Tribunal held that the municipality’s renting/licensing of immovable property was taxable service, meaning the activity of allowing use of municipal immovable property did fall within the service tax net. However, it quashed the extended-period service tax demand, so the Department could not sustain the longer look-back invocation on the facts of the case. The decision therefore leaves municipal bodies exposed to service tax on taxable renting/licensing of immovable property for the relevant period, but it also confirms that hoarding-space collections made as statutory municipal licence fees were not to be treated as the disputed taxable advertising service in this case, and it relieves the assessee from the extended-period demand, along with the associated penalties and late-filing consequences to the extent tied to that extended demand.

rows.title: Income Tax | MEIS Rewards Taxable as Revenue Receipt from AY 2016-17: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai Special Bench holds MEIS rewards taxable as revenue receipts under Section 2(24)(xviii) from AY 2016-17.The post MEIS Rewards Taxable as Revenue Receipt from AY 2016-17: ITAT Mumbai appear
rows.summary:
This ITAT Mumbai Special Bench decision holds that receipts under the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2015 are taxable as revenue receipts under the Income-tax Act from Assessment Year 2016-17 onward because of the amendment to section 2(24) inserting clause (xviii). The key statutory change is that, effective AY 2016-17, “assistance in the form of a subsidy or grant or cash incentive or duty drawback or waiver or concession or reimbursement by the Central Government or a State Government” is included in the definition of income “by whatever name called,” so the tribunal treated MEIS rewards as falling within this expanded income definition. The assessee, Aarti Drugs Ltd., a manufacturer of specialty chemicals and bulk drugs, had originally treated the MEIS benefit as revenue, then argued before the CIT(A) that it was capital in nature; the CIT(A) accepted that view for AYs 2016-17 and 2017-18, but the Revenue appealed, and the Special Bench reversed that position.

The Tribunal’s reasoning was that the character of MEIS depends on the “purpose test” and the scheme’s operation, not on the label “reward.” It found that MEIS is government assistance linked to exports and meant to incentivize and support export activity, which places it within section 2(24)(xviii) for the relevant years, regardless of whether the benefit is described as a reward or incentive under the Foreign Trade Policy. The Revenue had relied on Supreme Court authorities such as Sahney Steel and Ponni Sugars, along with the statutory phrase “by whatever name called,” while the assessee argued MEIS was intended to improve export competitiveness and therefore should be treated as capital; the Special Bench did not accept that characterization for income-tax purposes after the AY 2016-17 amendment. Practically, the ruling means companies receiving MEIS benefits for export transactions from AY 2016-17 onward should treat those receipts as taxable revenue income and not as capital receipts, and should ensure their tax computations, return positions, and any past appellate positions for the relevant years align with this treatment.

rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Dismisses Reassessment Appeal Where Recorded Reasons Produced No Addition
rows.desc: Gujarat HC holds Explanation 3 to Section 147 cannot cure reassessment where no addition is made on the recorded reasons.The post Gujarat HC Dismisses Reassessment Appeal Where Recorded Reasons Produc
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court dismissed the Revenue’s section 260A appeal in **PCIT v. NK Proteins Pvt. Ltd.** concerning **A.Y. 2009-10**, where the reassessment notice under **section 148** had been issued on **09.03.2015**, i.e. **more than four years after the end of the relevant assessment year**. The assessee was a manufacturing company dealing in edible and non-edible oil products and by-products, and its original assessment under **section 143(3)** had been completed on **29.12.2011**. The recorded reasons for reopening referred to two alleged issues: a supposed short disallowance under **section 14A read with Rule 8D**, and alleged income of **Rs. 244.98 crores** said to have been received from **National Stock Exchange Ltd. (NSEL)** through a paper trade arrangement.  

In the reassessment, however, the Assessing Officer did **not** make any addition on either of those recorded grounds; instead, he made a disallowance of **Rs. 13,89,08,810/-** under **section 43(5) read with section 73 and section 40A(2)(b)**, plus an additional **Rs. 1,04,652/-** as an excess disallowance under **section 14A**. The assessee challenged the reopening before the CIT(A), arguing that the reassessment was invalid because no addition arose from the very reasons recorded for reopening. The CIT(A) accepted that position, noting that the **Rs. 244.98 crore NSEL figure** related to an addition made in the assessee’s case for **A.Y. 2011-12**, not the year under appeal, and that the assessee had **not undertaken NSEL transactions in A.Y. 2009-10**; the CIT(A) also held that the original **section 14A** disallowance had already been deleted.  

The High Court upheld the CIT(A) and the Tribunal, effectively confirming that where reassessment is initiated on specific recorded reasons but the final reassessment does not make any addition on those reasons, the reopening cannot be sustained on the basis of unrelated additions made later in the reassessment order. For compliance purposes, the decision is significant for tax audit and reassessment risk management: where reopening is beyond four years and is founded on particular alleged escapement items, the Revenue must be able to connect the final reassessment to those recorded grounds; otherwise, the reassessment is vulnerable to being quashed.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 272A(2)(e) Penalty Cannot Continue Beyond Section 139(4): Chennai ITAT
rows.desc: Chennai ITAT restricts section 272A(2)(e) penalty to the period available for filing a belated return under section 139(4).The post Section 272A(2)(e) Penalty Cannot Continue Beyond Section 139(4): Ch
rows.summary:
The Chennai ITAT held that a penalty for failure to file a return under section 272A(2)(e) cannot keep running indefinitely for a charitable trust once the statutory extended-filing period under section 139(4) has expired. The assessee in this case was a registered charitable trust running an educational institution, and for AY 2013-14 it had not originally filed a return; the Assessing Officer later reopened the matter after noticing cash deposits of Rs. 75,55,200 in the trust’s bank account. In response to the reopening, the trust filed a return declaring nil income and claiming exemption under section 10(23C)(iiiad), and the assessment under section 147 accepted that returned income.

Penalty proceedings were then initiated under section 272A(2)(e) for the original failure to furnish the return. The Assessing Officer imposed a penalty of Rs. 3,04,300, and the CIT(A) upheld it, reasoning that the trust had not complied with section 139(4C), that ignorance of law was no defense, that no revenue loss and no mens rea were irrelevant, and that penalty was mandatory absent reasonable cause under section 273B. Before the Tribunal, the assessee ultimately pressed only one ground, and the ITAT accepted the core legal principle that while penalty may be leviable for failure to file, the default period cannot extend beyond the last date permitted for belated filing under section 139(4). In practical compliance terms, the ruling means that for entities covered by section 139 obligations—here, a charitable trust—the exposure to section 272A(2)(e) penalty is limited to the period of actual default up to the section 139(4) deadline, rather than being calculated as an open-ended continuing default after that point.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITR Upload Failure: Madras HC Accepts Screenshot, Orders Portal Access
rows.desc: Madras High Court sets aside the 16.07.2026 demand and directs the Income Tax Department to reopen the portal for filing the AY 2015-16 return.The post ITR Upload Failure: Madras HC Accepts Screenshot
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court dealt with a writ petition by Sankaran Mekala concerning an income-tax demand order dated 16.07.2026 for Assessment Year 2015-16, issued under sections 147, 271(1)(b), and 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The petitioner had earlier challenged the assessment order dated 16.01.2024 and the notice dated 12.04.2022 in W.P. No. 1242 of 2026; that earlier writ was disposed of on 09.02.2026 with a direction to file the return of income for AY 2015-16 and submit a reply to the section 148 notice. In this later petition, she asked the Court to quash the demand and direct reopening of the income-tax e-filing portal because she claimed she could not upload the return due to technical problems on the portal.

A key compliance-relevant fact is that the petitioner had already deposited Rs. 5 lakhs in purported compliance with the earlier High Court order, and she produced documentary evidence supporting that payment and other filings. She also submitted a screenshot to demonstrate the portal upload failure, and the Court accepted that screenshot as sufficient evidence of the technical issue. The Revenue had notice of the petition and did not disprove the inability to upload.

The Court held that, in the interests of justice, the petitioner must be given another opportunity to comply with the earlier direction to file the return. Accordingly, the writ petition was disposed of with a direction that portal access be restored/reopened so she could file the return of income, rather than treating the failure to upload as a default on the merits. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where a taxpayer can substantiate a bona fide e-filing portal failure with evidence such as screenshots and show partial compliance with a prior court direction, the High Court may permit later filing instead of letting the demand or non-compliance stand uncorrected.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Directs Interest-First Income Tax Refund Adjustment Under Section 244A
rows.desc: Mumbai ITAT holds refund must first adjust interest due under Section 244A before principal tax, dismissing Revenues appeals.The post ITAT Directs Interest-First Income Tax Refund Adjustment Under Sec
rows.summary:
The Mumbai ITAT dismissed the Revenue’s appeals and upheld the CIT(A), NFAC view on how income-tax refunds must be adjusted when the refund amount includes both principal tax and interest under section 244A. The dispute arose in consolidated appeals involving Bank of Baroda for AYs 2003-04, 2005-06, 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10, and 2016-17, with ITA No. 5707/Mum/2025 for AY 2003-04 treated as the lead case. The Revenue argued that, because section 244A does not expressly say otherwise, any refund should be first appropriated against the principal tax component rather than the interest component, and that doing the reverse would create additional interest exposure on the unpaid tax and effectively amount to charging “interest on interest.”

The assessee relied on prior judicial rulings, including decisions in its own case, and argued that the issue was already settled and should be followed on consistency grounds absent any change in facts or law. It also cited supporting rulings involving other taxpayers such as Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, Bank of India, IDBI Bank, Reliance Industries Limited, State Bank of India, and Tata Sons Limited. The Tribunal accepted the assessee’s position and confirmed that the refund adjustment under section 244A must be made interest-first rather than tax-first, rejecting the Revenue’s contrary contention. For compliance purposes, this means that where the department issues a refund under section 244A that includes both tax and statutory interest, the refund amount is to be applied first toward the interest component before being applied to the principal tax liability, and the Revenue cannot insist on a tax-first set-off in these circumstances.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs Duty Demand for Alleged Fake DEEC Exports Set Aside by CESTAT Chennai
rows.desc: CESTAT Chennai sets aside customs duty, interest and penalties as alleged diversion and fraudulent DEEC exports lacked corroborative evidence.The post Customs Duty Demand for Alleged Fake DEEC Exports
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai allowed seven connected appeals filed by Chessman Impex Private Limited and co-appellants and set aside Order-in-Original No. 54992/2017 dated 28.02.2017. As a result, the customs demand of Rs. 2,16,93,068/- along with consequential interest was quashed, and the penalties of Rs. 20 lakh each imposed under Sections 112(a) and 114(i) of the Customs Act, 1962, as well as the penalties imposed on the co-appellants, were held unsustainable.

The dispute arose from a DEEC licence obtained under the EXIM Policy 1997–2002, which allowed duty-free import of 5350 MT of non-alloy re-rollable scrap cuttings against an export obligation of 5000 MT of non-alloy steel bars and rods. Revenue’s allegation was that the imported scrap had been diverted into the domestic market and that maize had been fraudulently exported to Bangladesh under 73 Bills of Export instead of the required steel products. The Tribunal rejected the demand because the department did not produce reliable, corroborative evidence to sustain the fraud allegation.

In reaching that conclusion, CESTAT relied on multiple pieces of supporting evidence: special permission for exports through Ghojadanga land customs station, customs examination of the export consignments, Central Excise certification of AR-4s/ARE-1s, confirmation from DRI Chennai regarding manufacture by Goyal Ispat Ltd., the foreign buyer’s permission for segregation and export of unprocessed scrap, actual realization of export proceeds, and the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate issued by the competent DGFT authority. The Tribunal also noted that the CBI had investigated the same alleged fraudulent exports and filed a final report indicating that the available evidence did not support the allegation of fraud. For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that customs duty demands and associated penalties based on alleged diversion or sham exports must be supported by solid, corroborated evidence, and that documented export clearance, certification, foreign buyer permission, receipt of export proceeds, and DGFT discharge evidence can be decisive in defeating such allegations.

rows.title: Custom Duty | SC Sets Aside ₹425 Crore Customs Penalty Due to Fake AI-Generated Case Laws
rows.desc: Supreme Court sets aside ₹425-crore customs penalty after AI-generated fake citations tainted the adjudication and orders fresh decision.The post SC Sets Aside ₹425 Crore Customs Penalty Due to Fake A
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court set aside a customs penalty of **₹425,27,99,100 (about ₹425.28 crore)** that had been imposed on **Vijay Ghanshyam Gadiya** by the **Additional Commissioner of Customs, Surat** under **Section 114 of the Customs Act, 1962**. The underlying allegation was that a consignment of **natural diamonds** had been wrongly declared as **lab-grown diamonds** in order to secure a **lower customs tariff**, but the Supreme Court did **not** decide that merits issue.

Instead, the case turned on the integrity of the materials relied on in the customs adjudication. The appellant argued that several judgments and articles cited in the **Order-in-Original dated 08.10.2025** were generated using **artificial intelligence**. The Supreme Court independently checked the authorities used by the second respondent and found that some cited case laws were **non-existent** or had **fake citations**, while others existed but **did not support the legal propositions** attributed to them; the Court described this as appearing to be an **AI “hallucination.”**

The matter had already been taken to the **Gujarat High Court**, which dismissed the challenge on **20.01.2026** before the case reached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court relied on its recent ruling in **Pooja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd.**, reiterating a **zero-tolerance approach** to producing, citing, or relying on **AI-generated precedents without verification**. For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that adjudicating authorities and litigants must **independently verify all case law and legal authorities before using them in orders or pleadings**, because reliance on fabricated or misrepresented authorities can lead to the order being undermined or set aside.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras HC Upholds Negative Blocking of Electronic Credit Ledger Under Section 79
rows.desc: Madras HC holds Section 79 permits negative blocking of electronic credit ledger at the post-determination recovery stage.The post Madras HC Upholds Negative Blocking of Electronic Credit Ledger Under
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court upheld the blocking of M/s. Zigma Machinery & Equipment Solutions’ electronic credit ledger, rejecting the petitioner’s challenge to reference No. BL3302250000152 dated 04.02.2025. The company had asked for the blockage to be lifted so it could freely use the input tax credit reflected in its electronic credit ledger, arguing that the blockage was beyond the scope of Section 79 of the CGST Act and that “negative blocking” is not permitted under that section when compared with Rule 86A of the CGST Rules. The petitioner also relied on an interim stay order dated 25.02.2026 in a separate writ petition (W.P. No. 41890 of 2025), but that stay related only to recovery proceedings arising from an assessment order dated 17.03.2023 for the 2017–2020 assessment period.

The Court accepted the Revenue’s position that the 25.02.2026 interim order did not undo or invalidate the earlier 04.02.2025 electronic credit ledger blocking, because the stay only kept recovery proceedings in abeyance and did not address the ledger freeze itself. As a result, the blocking of the electronic credit ledger remained in force, and the petitioner was not granted free utilisation of the input tax credit. For compliance teams, the practical point is that a stay on recovery measures does not automatically解除 or override a separate ledger-blocking action; if the department has already imposed a block on the electronic credit ledger, it may continue independently unless specifically challenged and set aside.

rows.title: Income Tax | Kerala HC Remands Medical PG Stipend vs Salary Dispute for Fresh Assessment
rows.desc: Kerala HC sets aside assessment and remands stipend-versus-salary dispute for fresh consideration after giving the assessee an opportunity to produce documents.The post Kerala HC Remands Medical PG St
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court considered a writ appeal by a medical postgraduate student, Nahas Kakkattummal, challenging an income-tax assessment that treated amounts he received during his MD/MS studies as **salary** rather than **stipend**. The appellant argued that he was an admitted postgraduate medical student, that the payments were **statutorily mandated stipend** under the **National Medical Commission (NMC)** regulations, and that the Assessing Officer had wrongly relied on university documents “blindly” because those documents referred to the payments as salary even though the same communications also certified that he was a **bona fide PG student / Junior Resident**. He also relied on an additional certificate (Ext. P5) supporting his student status and asked, at minimum, for permission to place further documents before the tax authorities.

The High Court noted that the Single Judge had declined to exercise writ jurisdiction and sent the petitioner to the ordinary statutory remedy under the Income Tax Act, 1961, but the appellate court found it appropriate to intervene to ensure the factual issue was properly examined. The court therefore **remanded the matter for fresh assessment** so the Assessing Authority could reconsider whether the receipts were actually stipend or taxable salary, rather than simply accepting the university’s description at face value.

For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that payments made to **medical postgraduate trainees/junior residents** may need to be evaluated based on the governing **NMC rules** and the person’s actual training status, not merely by how an employer/university labels the payment in correspondence or records. The decision underscores a need to maintain documentation showing the recipient’s enrollment/status, the legal basis for the payment, and whether the payment is stipend under mandatory medical education regulations, because those facts may determine the income-tax characterization. The document does **not** state a new general tax rate or threshold; the operative change is the court’s direction for **fresh fact-finding/assessment** on the true nature of the receipts.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Kolkata Remands JDA Capital Gains Dispute for Fresh Merits Adjudication
rows.desc: ITAT Kolkata set aside the CIT(A) order and restored a JDA capital gains dispute for fresh merits adjudication in AY 2015-16.The post ITAT Kolkata Remands JDA Capital Gains Dispute for Fresh Merits Ad
rows.summary:
The Kolkata ITAT’s SMC Bench dealt with an AY 2015-16 reassessment of Sandhya Roy arising from a Joint Development Agreement dated 22.01.2015. The assessee had not filed an original return of income and also did not file any return in response to the section 148 notice issued on 31.03.2022, after which the Assessing Officer completed reassessment under sections 147, 144 and 144B. The AO treated the JDA as a “transfer” under section 2(47), computed the alleged sale consideration at ₹48,68,542 based on fair market value plus cash consideration, assumed a nil cost of acquisition, and assessed long-term capital gains of ₹48,68,542 as total income.

Before the CIT(A) (NFAC order dated 16.02.2026), the assessee challenged both the reopening and the capital-gains addition. On limitation, the assessee relied on the Supreme Court’s reassessment-transition rulings in Union of India vs. Ashish Agarwal and Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajeev Bansal, but the CIT(A) rejected the argument because the section 148 notice was issued on 31.03.2022, i.e., before 01.04.2022, and therefore was not within the category of notices the Department had accepted as time-barred in the Supreme Court proceedings. The CIT(A) accordingly upheld the reassessment framework under the Ashish Agarwal directions.

On the substantive capital-gains issue, the ITAT noted that the dispute required fresh examination on the merits rather than summary affirmation. The Tribunal therefore remanded the matter back for reconsideration, meaning the capital-gains computation arising from the JDA is not finally sustained as decided below and must be re-adjudicated in light of the facts and applicable law. For compliance purposes, the case highlights that JDAs can be treated as transfer events for capital-gains purposes, that reassessment notices issued on 31.03.2022 are being tested against the Supreme Court’s transitional regime, and that taxpayers facing such notices must be prepared to substantiate both the validity of reopening and the correct valuation/capital-gains computation.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Allahabad HC Quashes GST Order for Notice Served Only Through Portal After Cancellation
rows.desc: Allahabad HC quashes GST order for natural justice violation where notice was uploaded only on portal after registration cancellation.The post Allahabad HC Quashes GST Order for Notice Served Only Thr
rows.summary:
The Allahabad High Court quashed a GST demand order passed under **Section 74 of the Uttar Pradesh GST Act, 2017** against **Ved Enterprises, Unnao**, holding that the Department violated natural justice by serving the show-cause notice only through the GST portal after the taxpayer’s registration had already been cancelled. The petitioner’s GST registration had been **cancelled on 16 November 2021**, and the petitioner stated it was no longer carrying on business; in that situation, the Court said the taxpayer could not reasonably be expected to keep checking the portal for notices. The impugned order was dated **28 May 2022** and had been issued by the **Deputy Commissioner, State Tax, Sector-1, District Unnao**.

The Court accepted the petitioner’s reliance on the coordinate Bench decision in **M/s Katyal Industries v. State of U.P.** and agreed with the principle that, where registration has been cancelled, service of notice must be made through **some alternative effective mode** rather than only by portal upload. Because the notice was not properly served, the resulting order was invalid and was **quashed and set aside**. The Department was expressly given liberty to **issue a proper notice** and proceed again **in accordance with law**, meaning any fresh action must comply with valid service requirements and procedural fairness. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that once a taxpayer’s GST registration is cancelled, portal-only communication may be insufficient for adverse proceedings, and authorities must use a service method reasonably calculated to reach the person before passing a demand order.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras HC Closes GST Limitation Challenges After State Tax Officer Report
rows.desc: Madras High Court closes two GST limitation challenges and disposes third after State Tax Officer’s 27.01.2026 report prima facie supports petitioner.The post Madras HC Closes GST Limitation Challenge
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court disposed of three related writ petitions filed by Reckitt Benckiser (India) Private Limited by a common order dated 24.04.2026. All three matters arose from the same GST dispute for the tax period 2019–2020 and centered on the legality of limitation extension under the GST laws: one petition challenged an impugned order/reply dated 29.05.2024, another challenged Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023 and the consequential State Government Orders issued under Section 168A of the GST enactments extending limitation periods, and the third challenged a show cause notice dated 31.05.2024 issued in Form GST DRC-01 for the same tax period. The Court had earlier granted interim protection on 13.08.2024, and after that the jurisdictional State Tax Officer submitted a detailed report dated 27.01.2026.

Based on that report, the Court noted that the officer’s conclusion prima facie supported the petitioner’s position. In light of the later developments and the 27.01.2026 report, the Court closed the writ petitions rather than continuing to adjudicate the limitation challenge. For compliance teams, the practical point is that this decision does not announce a new general GST filing or reporting requirement; instead, it shows that limitation-extension actions under Section 168A, Notification No. 9/2023-Central Tax dated 31.03.2023, and related DRC-01 proceedings for the 2019–2020 period were central to the dispute, but the Court ultimately disposed of the matter after the departmental report. Entities with similar limitation-related GST notices, especially DRC-01 proceedings tied to extended limitation periods, should treat this as a reminder to verify whether the underlying extension mechanism and the factual basis asserted by the department remain defensible in their own cases.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rajasthan HC Allows Delayed GST Appeal Citing Medical Reasons Beyond Taxpayer’s Control
rows.desc: Rajasthan High Court condoned GST appeal delay citing medical reasons beyond the petitioner’s control and directed decision on merits.The post Rajasthan HC Allows Delayed GST Appeal Citing Medical Rea
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court permitted Pokran Co-Operative Marketing Society Ltd. to pursue a delayed GST appeal and set aside the appellate authority’s order dated 27.02.2026, which had rejected the appeal as time-barred. The Court directed the Appellate Authority to hear and decide the appeal on merits, but only after the petitioner deposits the late fees, penalty, and any other statutory deposits that are legally payable. This means the Court treated the delay as excusable in the circumstances, rather than allowing a limitation-based dismissal to stand.

The petitioner had challenged the underlying order dated 07.02.2024 and also sought restoration of its GST registration, so the practical compliance impact is that cancellation/restoration disputes can still be revived through writ proceedings where the taxpayer shows circumstances beyond its control. The Court accepted the petitioner’s reliance on prior Rajasthan High Court decisions, especially the Division Bench ruling in M/s. Pratap Power Spares Vs. Union of India & Ors., where a 99-day delay was condoned after granting relaxation of the 120-day appellate window under Section 107 of the CGST Act, and the appeal was required to be entertained if filed within 30 days. The petitioner also cited other cases supporting condonation in appropriate facts, including M/s. Molana Construction Company, Man Singh Tanwar, RPC PSIPL JV (two decisions), and M/s. Kakar Automobiles.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that while Section 107 limitation issues remain important, the High Court has recognized that medical reasons and similar circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control can justify judicial relief against a strict limitation rejection. Entities facing GST cancellation or adverse orders should document such reasons carefully and be prepared to make all required statutory deposits, because the Court’s relief was conditional and did not eliminate the underlying payment obligations.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rule 86A Safeguards Mandatory for ITC Blocking: Rajasthan HC
rows.desc: Rajasthan High Court finds mandatory Rule 86A requirements were not followed in blocking ITC and warns against future non-compliant action.The post Rule 86A Safeguards Mandatory for ITC Blocking: Raja
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court in **Jagdish Prasad Agrawal vs. Union of India** considered a challenge to the **blocking of Input Tax Credit (ITC) in the petitioner’s Electronic Credit Ledger**, including a blocking of **IGST ITC that resulted in a negative balance**. The petitioner asked the Court to declare the blocking illegal, inoperative, and void, and to direct **re-credit of the Electronic Credit Ledger** for any ITC that had been unlawfully used against the disputed demand.

The key compliance issue was whether the department could block ITC **without following Rule 86A of the CGST Rules, 2017**, which governs restrictions on use of credit in the ledger. The petitioner argued that the blocking had already ceased automatically after the **one-year statutory limit** under Rule 86A, so the ledger had been reactivated, but the real issue remained whether the original block was lawfully imposed. The respondents conceded that the ledger was again operational, but they **could not show that the mandatory Rule 86A requirements had been complied with before the block was made**.

The Court noted that the department admitted the lapse was a **bona fide mistake**, and further admitted that although the officer had reasons for taking action, **no proper reasoned order was passed** and **no opportunity of hearing was provided** to the petitioner before the blocking. On that basis, the decision highlights that **ITC blocking under Rule 86A cannot be done informally or mechanically**; the authority must be able to demonstrate compliance with the rule’s safeguards, including a reasoned basis for action and adherence to the procedural requirements before restricting the credit. The respondents also undertook that **any future blocking would be carried out only in accordance with law**, underscoring that compliance teams should expect the department to follow Rule 86A’s mandatory safeguards before freezing or restricting ITC.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Allows CENVAT Refund Where Credit Was Not Challenged Under Rule 14
rows.desc: CESTAT Chandigarh allows Agilent’s CENVAT refund, holding Rule 5 refund cannot be denied where credit was not challenged under Rule 14.The post CESTAT Allows CENVAT Refund Where Credit Was Not Challen
rows.summary:
The Chandigarh CESTAT allowed Agilent Technologies International Pvt Ltd’s appeal against rejection of a refund claim for unutilised CENVAT credit under Rule 5 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. Agilent was a 100% export-oriented unit providing Business Support Services and Information Technology Software Services to overseas customers under service agreements, and it exported those services without charging service tax under the Export of Service Rules, 2005. It had claimed refund of unutilised credit under Rule 5 read with Notification No. 5/2006-CE (N.T.) dated 14.03.2006 and Section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The specific refund amount in dispute was ₹78,79,939, which the Department had denied on the ground that credit taken on General Insurance Services, Works Contract Services, and Commercial or Industrial Construction Services did not have a sufficient nexus with the exported output services. In its appeal, the taxpayer argued that taking CENVAT credit, using that credit, and seeking refund of unutilised credit are separate stages, and that if the Department did not first challenge the availment of credit under Rule 14, it could not later refuse a Rule 5 refund by questioning whether the credit was eligible in the first place. It also argued that the disputed services qualify as “input service” under Rule 2(l), relying on prior case law, and that a direct one-to-one nexus with the final exported services was not required for refund eligibility.

On that reasoning, the Tribunal accepted the taxpayer’s position and held that refund could not be denied merely by reopening the eligibility of the credit when the Department had not invoked Rule 14 to challenge its availment. The practical compliance takeaway is that for export-oriented service providers claiming Rule 5 refunds, the Department’s failure to contest credit entry at the availment stage can materially weaken a later refund denial based solely on alleged lack of nexus. The decision is case-specific, but it reinforces the need to track whether disputed CENVAT credits were ever formally challenged under Rule 14, because that procedural point may determine whether a subsequent Rule 5 refund can be questioned.

rows.title: Service Tax | CESTAT Hyderabad Sets Aside Tax on Pharma Regulatory Approval Support Services
rows.desc: CESTAT Hyderabad set aside service tax on foreign bank charges and regulatory documentation, holding no recipient relationship and no scientific consultancy classification.The post CESTAT Hyderabad Se
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Hyderabad held that Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. was **not liable to Service Tax under reverse charge** on bank charges deducted by foreign/intermediary banks while export proceeds were transmitted from overseas buyers to the company’s Indian bank account. The Department had treated the deductions as evidence that Aurobindo was the recipient of **“Banking and Other Financial Services”** during **2011-12 and 2012-13 up to June 2012**, and had confirmed service tax, interest, and penalties in the Order-in-Original dated **28.08.2014**; the Tribunal set aside that approach because there was **no proof of any contract, engagement, or payment obligation** between Aurobindo and the foreign banks, and the mere fact that the company received a reduced net remittance did not create a service recipient relationship.

The second dispute involved payments for **regulatory approval-related support services** connected with pharmaceutical products. The Tribunal held that these activities were not taxable as **“Scientific or Technical Consultancy Services”** on the facts presented, and it relied on Aurobindo’s own earlier favorable order, **Final Order No. 30919/2020 dated 09.09.2020**, to reach the same result here. In practical compliance terms, this decision is significant for exporters and pharma companies because it confirms that **bank deductions on export remittances are not automatically taxable under reverse charge** unless there is evidence that the taxpayer actually engaged and was contractually liable to pay the foreign bank for a service, and it also reinforces that **regulatory approval support for pharma products is not necessarily taxable as technical consultancy** merely because it relates to compliance or product approval work.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Mumbai Deletes Section 112(a) Penalty on Customs Hawaldar for Lack of Proof
rows.desc: CESTAT Mumbai sets aside Section 112(a) penalties on a deceased Customs Hawaldar where co-accused statements and phone records did not establish involvement.The post CESTAT Mumbai Deletes Section 112(
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai in **Ranjita Rajendra Bane v. Commissioner of Customs** set aside the **personal penalties of ₹2,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 imposed under Section 112(a) of the Customs Act, 1962** on the deceased customs hawaldar, Rajendra Bane, and the appeal was pursued by his widow and legal successor. The underlying allegation was that Bane had helped facilitate a **gold smuggling operation at Pune International Airport on 16.08.2018**, after passengers arriving from **Dubai on SpiceJet Flight SG 52** were linked to gold recovered from the **gents’ toilet at the airport** and from a passenger. The department relied on **Section 108 statements**, including statements of alleged co-accused/accomplices, **call records from a telephone operator**, and the physical recovery of the gold, while alleging that Bane was not acting innocently despite being on sanctioned leave and at his native place near Ratnagiri.

The defense denied any involvement and maintained that Bane was at his native place on the relevant date; it also argued that the seizure had occurred after he passed information to the Superintendent on duty at the airport, and that the source of that information could not be disclosed because it was allegedly protected informer communication. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected that explanation, but the Tribunal found that the prosecution material did **not provide reliable proof linking Bane to the smuggling conspiracy**. In particular, the Tribunal held that the evidence was insufficient to sustain a finding that he had abetted the offense or knowingly facilitated the smuggling activity, and therefore the Section 112(a) penalties could not stand.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that **personal penalty exposure under Section 112(a) requires provable participation or conscious facilitation**, and the Tribunal would not uphold penalties based only on suspicion, uncorroborated statements, or indirect material where the alleged participant’s involvement is not established. The case also shows that where an officer claims to have acted through confidential informer information, the department still must meet the evidentiary burden needed to impose a customs penalty.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Patna HC Remits Nukkad Natak GST Exemption Issue to Appellate Authority
rows.desc: Patna High Court sets aside a delayed GST appeal order and directs the Appellate Authority to decide the Nukkad Natak exemption issue on merits.The post Patna HC Remits Nukkad Natak GST Exemption Issu
rows.summary:
The Patna High Court considered a GST dispute involving M/s Sri Mant Kala Sanchar Sanskritik Dal, a registered taxpayer that performs Nukkad Natak (street plays) mainly for government-led public awareness programmes. For the financial year 2022-23, the department issued a notice under Section 73 of the CGST Act, 2017 based on gross receipts of Rs. 4,98,100 received from the District Public Relations Officer, Gaya, and the adjudicating authority later confirmed tax, interest, and penalty totaling Rs. 1,63,452 by order dated 20.08.2025. The petitioner appealed under Section 107(1), but the Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on 28.02.2026 solely because it was filed 21 days late.

The petitioner relied on Collectorate, Gaya Memo No. 322 dated 28.11.2025, which it said clarified that GST is not applicable to receipts from sale of tickets by a registered person engaged in Nukkad Natak, and that Nukkad Natak teams consisting of 4, 6, 8, or 10 members are exempt from GST. On that basis, the petitioner argued the exemption issue should be examined on merits rather than being rejected for limitation. The High Court did not finally decide the tax exemption question itself; instead, it remitted the matter back to the Appellate Authority for a fresh decision on merits, with a direction to pass a reasoned order after giving the petitioner an opportunity of hearing. For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that this case highlights a claimed exemption position for certain Nukkad Natak activities and team sizes, but the judicial outcome here is procedural: the appeal revives for reconsideration, and the underlying tax liability of Rs. 1,63,452 has not been conclusively overturned by the High Court in this excerpt.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 54 Shortfall Not Taxable in Original Year: Mumbai ITAT Deletes Penalty
rows.desc: Mumbai ITAT holds Section 54 shortfall was not taxable in AY 2014-15 and deletes penalty of Rs.5,25,923 under Section 271(1)(c).The post Section 54 Shortfall Not Taxable in Original Year: Mumbai ITAT
rows.summary:
The Mumbai ITAT case concerned a penalty of Rs. 5,25,923 levied under section 271(1)(c) for Assessment Year 2014-15 in connection with a section 54 capital gains exemption claim. The assessee had sold a residential house for Rs. 1,35,00,000 and computed long-term capital gain of Rs. 72,19,588, then claimed exemption for the full gain in the return filed under section 139(1). Of the claimed reinvestment, Rs. 68,25,500 was invested with M/s Damodar Suruchi Developers for a proposed residential project and Rs. 10,00,000 was deposited in the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme with SBI; however, the developer’s project later stalled for reasons beyond the assessee’s control, and the assessee ultimately entered into a compromise and purchased another residential property for Rs. 49,95,000.

Because the eventual qualifying reinvestment was lower than the original claimed amount, the assessee accepted that a shortfall of Rs. 24,40,579 was taxable and the Assessing Officer brought that amount to tax in AY 2014-15. At the same time, the Assessing Officer imposed penalty equal to 100% of the tax sought to be evaded under section 271(1)(c), and the CIT(A)/NFAC upheld that penalty on the ground that inaccurate particulars had been furnished. The ITAT deleted the penalty, holding in substance that the shortfall in section 54 exemption was not, by itself, taxable in the original year as a penalty matter and that the assessee’s claim arose from a genuine investment attempt that failed due to circumstances beyond his control rather than from concealment or furnishing of inaccurate particulars. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that an unsuccessful or partially unsuccessful section 54 reinvestment claim, especially where the taxpayer has documented the original investment, deposit into the Capital Gains Accounts Scheme, and later purchase of substitute residential property, does not automatically justify a section 271(1)(c) penalty merely because the full exemption is ultimately denied.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for Fresh Verification
rows.desc: GSTAT Bengaluru remands an FY 2018-19 ITC mismatch dispute for invoice-wise verification, fresh adjudication and mandatory personal hearing.The post GSTAT Remands GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A ITC Mismatch for
rows.summary:
The GST Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench, remanded the matter in **N. R. Builders v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes** for **fresh verification** of an alleged **ITC mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A**. The dispute involved an asserted excess Input Tax Credit of **₹2,33,502** for **FY 2018–19**, split equally into **CGST ₹1,16,751** and **SGST ₹1,16,751**; the department also levied **interest of ₹2,03,730** and **penalty of ₹23,350**, bringing the total demand to **₹4,60,582**. The taxpayer, a proprietorship engaged in **quarrying and sale of crushed stones**, argued that the credit was not in fact excess because it related to **FY 2017–18 invoices** but was claimed in **FY 2018–19** within the time permitted under **Section 16(4)** of the CGST Act.

The Tribunal noted that the taxpayer had also raised **procedural objections**, including that **no personal hearing was granted** and that the proceedings were not preceded by any **FORM GST ASMT-10** notice. The record showed a **pre-intimation in FORM GST DRC-01A dated 22.01.2024**, followed by a **show-cause notice in FORM GST DRC-01 dated 30.01.2024 under Section 73**; the notice itself listed the personal hearing date/time/venue as **“NA”**, and the Proper Officer then confirmed the demand **ex parte**. The **First Appellate Authority** had already dismissed the appeal and upheld the demand before the Tribunal intervened.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the Tribunal did **not** finally decide the merits of the ITC disallowance; instead, it held that the department needed to **examine the taxpayer’s explanation that the invoices were from FY 2017–18 but lawfully availed in FY 2018–19 under Section 16(4)** before treating the GSTR-3B/GSTR-2A difference as inadmissible credit. The case therefore underscores that a mere mismatch between GSTR-3B and GSTR-2A is not automatically conclusive of wrongful ITC and that taxpayers should be able to substantiate the invoice period, timing of availment, and Section 16(4) eligibility. It also highlights the importance of **personal hearing** and proper procedural safeguards in **Section 73** recovery matters, especially where adverse orders are passed ex parte.

rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Allows Section 11(1A) Exemption to Charitable Trust, Quashes Section 264 Rejection
rows.desc: Gujarat HC held Section 11(1A) exemption could not be denied to a charitable trust merely because the claim was omitted from the return and allowed refund with interest.The post Gujarat HC Allows Sect
rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court held that a charitable trust can obtain relief under Section 264 even where it failed to claim a rightful exemption in its original return, and it quashed the Commissioner’s order dated 19.11.2020 that had rejected Sheth Shree Karshandas Halu Dharamshala Jamnagar’s claim for exemption under Section 11(1A). The trust was a public charitable trust registered under the Gujarat Public Trust Act, 1950 and under Section 12A of the Income-tax Act with effect from 01.04.2007; it had sold immovable property for Rs. 4,87,50,000 under a registered sale deed dated 11.07.2011, and the full sale proceeds were invested in a two-year fixed deposit with Canara Bank, Jamnagar, pursuant to conditions imposed by the Joint Charity Commissioner. For A.Y. 2012-13, the trust inadvertently did not claim the Section 11(1A) exemption for reinvestment of capital gains, although it had disclosed the capital gains and paid tax; the return was processed under Section 143(1), which generated a demand of Rs. 19,44,180.  

The court accepted that the capital gains reinvestment fell within the charitable trust exemption framework and emphasized that Section 264 gives the revisional authority broad power to grant relief where an assessee has been over-assessed because of a mistake or omission, particularly when the relevant facts were already disclosed. In reaching that conclusion, the court relied on earlier principles from C. Parikh & Co., Ramdev Exports, and S.R. Koshti, and it effectively confirmed that a taxpayer’s failure to raise a correct exemption claim in the original filing does not by itself bar remedial relief if the legal entitlement is otherwise clear. For compliance purposes, the decision is relevant to charitable trusts and similar exempt entities that dispose of capital assets and reinvest sale proceeds in a manner intended to satisfy Section 11(1A): even if the exemption is omitted in the return, the trust may still seek corrective relief through Section 264, but the underlying facts must support the exemption and the investment/disclosure should be documented.

rows.title: Income Tax | Bogus Purchases & Sales Cannot Justify Entire Purchase Addition; 5% GP Applied: Delhi ITAT
rows.desc: Delhi ITAT upholds reassessment based on survey information exposing bogus transactions, but restricts the addition on alleged bogus purchases by applying 5% gross profit on turnover and allowing cred
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT in **HSB Home Solutions Ltd. v. ACIT** (AY **2012–13**) **partly allowed** the assessee’s appeal and addressed both the **validity of a reopened assessment** and the **quantification of income from alleged bogus purchases/sales**. The Tribunal upheld reopening of the assessment even though it was initiated **after four years**, holding that the reassessment was supported by **subsequent survey information dated 30.11.2018** showing allegedly bogus transactions that had **not been examined in the original assessment**; it also noted that the original assessment order itself recorded that the assessee had **no business activity despite substantial purchases, sales, and disclosed profit**, so the reopening was not merely a change of opinion.

On the merits, the Tribunal held that the Assessing Officer **could not tax the entire purchase amount as undisclosed income** merely because the purchases were alleged to be bogus, especially where the corresponding sales had also been treated as bogus. The amounts involved were **purchases of Rs. 5,81,57,000** and **sales/turnover of Rs. 5,94,91,966**. The Tribunal rejected the argument that transactions routed through banking channels by themselves proved genuineness, because **physical movement of goods and the existence of the counterparties were not established**. Instead, considering the overall facts, it directed the AO to **apply a 5% gross profit rate on the turnover of Rs. 5,94,91,966**, while **giving credit for profit already disclosed by the assessee**.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the decision confirms that where tax authorities have new post-assessment material from survey or similar proceedings, they may sustain reassessment beyond four years, and where alleged bogus purchases and sales are part of the same chain, the income addition may be limited to a profit element rather than the full purchase value. The Tribunal relied on Supreme Court and Delhi High Court authorities such as **New Delhi Television Ltd. v. DCIT, Phool Chand Bajrang Lal v. ITO, ITO v. Lakhmani Mewal Das, High Gain Finvest (P) Ltd., and Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd.**, reflecting the principles governing reopening based on new material and the treatment of unexplained or non-genuine trading transactions.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Ahmedabad Dismisses Revenue Appeals on Goodwill, Electricity & Steam Valuation
rows.desc: ITAT Ahmedabad upheld depreciation claims and benchmarking of captive electricity and steam, dismissing Revenue appeals for AYs 2018-19 and 2020-21.The post ITAT Ahmedabad Dismisses Revenue Appeals on
rows.summary:
The Ahmedabad ITAT dismissed the Revenue’s appeals in **DCIT v. Nirma Limited** for **Assessment Years 2018-19 and 2020-21**, disposing of ITA Nos. **1569 and 1570/AHD/2026** by a common order dated **21.08.2026**. The appeals arose from CIT(A), Ahmedabad-13 orders dated **09.02.2026** passed under **Section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961**. Because the issues were the same across both appeals, the Tribunal heard them together and relied heavily on its own prior rulings in the assessee’s earlier years.

For **AY 2018-19**, one issue was the Revenue’s challenge to the deletion of an addition of **Rs. 4,09,94,465** on account of **depreciation on goodwill** arising from the amalgamation of **Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd.** The Revenue argued that the amalgamating company was a sick, loss-making entity with negative net worth and that the goodwill was only an accounting entry, but the CIT(A) had followed Tribunal decisions already rendered in Nirma’s own case for **AYs 2012-13 to 2016-17**. The ITAT upheld that approach and dismissed the Revenue’s grounds, so the depreciation claim on goodwill stood allowed. The Revenue also disputed deletion of **Rs. 1,73,64,613** relating to **depreciation on brands and names** transferred from a demerged unit, but the CIT(A) again followed earlier Tribunal rulings in the assessee’s favor, and the ITAT affirmed the deletion.

A further major dispute for **AY 2018-19** involved **transfer pricing on inter-unit sale of electricity**, where the Assessing Officer/TPO had proposed an adjustment of **Rs. 1,17,72,05,188**. The case summary indicates that the Revenue’s challenge on this issue was also not accepted by the Tribunal, consistent with the recurring treatment of the matter in the assessee’s favor. Overall, the practical compliance takeaway is that the ITAT continued to endorse Nirma’s tax positions on depreciation for goodwill and intangibles arising from restructuring, as well as its transfer-pricing position on internal electricity transactions, leaving the CIT(A)’s relief intact and rejecting the Revenue’s attempts to restore the additions.

rows.title: Income Tax | IBC Resolution Plan Bars Pending Pre-Approval Income Tax Proceedings: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai allows assessee appeals and dismisses Revenue appeals, holding the approved IBC Resolution Plan barred continuation of pre-approval tax proceedings.The post IBC Resolution Plan Bars Pendin
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that the Income-tax Department could not continue or press pending pre-approval income-tax proceedings against Reliance General Insurance Company Limited, now IndusInd General Insurance Company Limited, once the resolution plan for its parent, Reliance Capital Limited (RCL), was approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Tribunal noted that RCL held about 99.83% of the assessee’s equity during the relevant years, and that RCL was admitted into CIRP by the NCLT, Mumbai on 06.12.2021, which triggered the Section 14 moratorium. The resolution plan submitted by IndusInd International Holdings Limited was approved by the Committee of Creditors in June 2023 and then approved by the NCLT on 27.02.2024 under Section 31 of the IBC; the Income-tax Department had participated in the insolvency proceedings and had raised objections there, including on carry-forward loss issues under the Income-tax Act.

The Tribunal disposed of a consolidated set of appeals covering Revenue’s appeals for assessment years 2011-12 to 2018-19 and 2020-21, and the assessee’s appeals for assessment years 2012-13 and 2020-21, but it did not decide the underlying tax additions on merits because the insolvency resolution issue was treated as determinative. The practical compliance effect is that once the resolution plan was approved, pending tax proceedings based on pre-resolution claims against the corporate debtor/group entity were barred and the Department could not re-litigate matters that should have been dealt with in the CIRP. The decision reinforces that tax authorities must raise and pursue their claims within the insolvency process itself, because a later attempt to continue separate proceedings can be shut down after NCLT approval of the resolution plan.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Jodhpur Deletes ₹3.36 Crore Section 69A Addition on Demonetisation Cash Deposits
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur upheld deletion of ₹3.36 crore Section 69A addition on cash deposits during demonetisation and ₹2.79 crore stock revaluation addition, accepting damaged guar gum valuation under AS-2.The
rows.summary:
This ITAT Jodhpur ruling for Assessment Year 2017-18 is a case-law update rather than a new rule, but it is important for compliance because it confirms how inventory write-downs and demonetization-period cash deposits were treated on the facts of this case. The Tribunal upheld deletion of a **₹2,79,03,981** addition relating to damaged guar gum stock after accepting the assessee’s position that, under **Accounting Standard 2 (AS-2)**, inventories must be valued at the **lower of cost and net realizable value (NRV)** and that damaged inventory may legitimately be written down where recovery at cost is no longer expected. The assessee was a manufacturer/trader of agricultural products, mainly **guar gum, Churi, and Korma**; its factory and stock had been taken over by the bank after the Phalodi account became an **NPA**, and the stock was said to have deteriorated due to **rain, germs, bacteria, and alleged negligence while under bank possession**, forcing conversion of damaged guar gum into Churi/Korma rather than sale as normal guar gum. The Assessing Officer had rejected the assessee’s valuation and instead used an **internet website** to adopt an NRV of **₹82.58 per kg**, but the Tribunal agreed with the deletion of that adjustment, reinforcing that valuation must be based on proper accounting principles and evidence rather than a mechanically applied external internet reference.

The Tribunal also upheld deletion of the Revenue’s **₹3,36,49,500** addition under **Section 69A** for cash deposits made during the **demonetization period**. In practical compliance terms, the decision indicates that cash deposits during demonetization are not automatically taxable as unexplained money if the taxpayer can substantiate the source and surrounding facts to the Tribunal’s satisfaction; the Revenue’s appeal was dismissed on this point. The document does **not** announce any new filing deadline, reporting format, or procedural change, but it is a useful precedent for finance/compliance teams documenting inventory impairment/write-downs and maintaining clear support for cash-in-hand and deposit trails, especially where cash deposits coincide with demonetization or other unusual business disruptions.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Upholds LIBOR Plus 300 Basis Points for Foreign-Currency Loans
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi dismisses both appeals, upholding LIBOR+300 for foreign-currency loans, excluding unsuitable comparables and deleting receivables and Section 14A adjustments.The post ITAT Delhi Upholds LIB
rows.summary:
The Delhi ITAT dismissed both the assessee’s and the Revenue’s cross-appeals for AY 2013-14 in the case of **ACIT v. Acme Cleantech Solutions Pvt. Ltd.**, in a combined order because the facts in both matters were common. The dispute arose from the assessee’s return filed on **30.11.2013** declaring income of **INR 23,85,28,970**, which led to a transfer-pricing reference because the company had international transactions with Associated Enterprises. The TPO made aggregate transfer-pricing adjustments of **INR 60,57,12,301**, broken down into **INR 47,52,09,333** for a loan transaction, **INR 11,02,91,500** for the manufacturing segment, and **INR 2,02,11,468** for receivables; the Assessing Officer then added those adjustments and also made a further **section 14A disallowance of INR 3,14,18,961**, resulting in assessed income of **INR 87,56,60,232**.

The key compliance point in the ruling is the interest benchmarking on **foreign-currency loans**. The TPO had applied **SBI PLR of 12.6%** even though the assessee had charged only **6.5% to 9.5%**, while the CIT(A) held that the correct benchmark was **LIBOR plus 300 basis points**. The assessee supported this position by relying on **CIT v. Cotton Naturals (I) Pvt. Ltd.**, and the Tribunal followed its own prior orders for **AYs 2011-12 and 2012-13**, where it had already held that loans repayable in **US dollars** should be benchmarked against **LIBOR plus an appropriate margin**, not domestic rupee lending rates like SBI PLR. The Tribunal therefore upheld the LIBOR-based approach for the foreign-currency loan transaction.

For the compliance team, this decision reinforces that where an intra-group loan is denominated and repayable in a foreign currency, transfer-pricing support should generally use a **LIBOR-based benchmark plus a reasonable spread** rather than an Indian domestic prime lending rate, and documentation should clearly show the loan currency, repayment currency, and basis for the chosen margin. The order also confirms that the matter covered both transfer-pricing adjustments and a **section 14A** disallowance, although the document excerpt does not provide separate substantive relief details beyond noting that the cross-appeals were dismissed and the CIT(A)’s position on the loan interest benchmark was sustained.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Deletes ₹4.26 Crore Section 14A Disallowance Against PNB Gilts
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi upheld relief to PNB Gilts on Section 14A, interest disallowance and ₹6.56 crore diminution in securities held as stock-in-trade.The post ITAT Deletes ₹4.26 Crore Section 14A Disallowance A
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi held in favor of PNB Gilts Ltd. and dismissed the Revenue’s appeals for Assessment Years 2012-13 and 2013-14, thereby upholding the relief granted by the CIT(A). For AY 2012-13, the Assessing Officer had attempted to make three major additions: a disallowance of ₹4.26 crore under Section 14A read with Rule 8D, a further disallowance of ₹30.61 lakh under Section 36(1)(iii), and a ₹6.56 crore adjustment for diminution in the market value of securities held as stock-in-trade. The Tribunal found that PNB Gilts, an RBI-registered NBFC and Primary Dealer, held the securities in its ordinary securities-trading business as stock-in-trade, not as investment assets, and that it had substantial interest-free funds of ₹577.64 crore, far exceeding the securities that generated exempt income; it also had net positive interest income, which supported the conclusion that the securities were not funded out of interest-bearing borrowings.

On the Section 14A issue, the Tribunal emphasized that Rule 8D cannot be applied mechanically and requires a valid, reasoned satisfaction by the Assessing Officer before disallowance is made; on these facts, the existence of ample interest-free funds meant the presumption favored the assessee. The separate disallowance under Section 36(1)(iii) was also rejected because the borrowings were used for business purposes, and the same interest cost could not effectively be disallowed twice through overlapping provisions.
