The ₹6.56 crore diminution claim was allowed because the securities were consistently valued at cost or market value, whichever was lower, in line with RBI guidelines and recognized accounting principles, so the loss was treated as a legitimate valuation loss rather than an unascertained provision. For compliance purposes, the ruling reinforces that entities holding securities as stock-in-trade should maintain clear evidence of business purpose, funding sources, and consistent valuation methodology, and that any Section 14A/Rule 8D disallowance must be supported by recorded satisfaction and cannot ignore substantial interest-free funds.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Jodhpur Restores 12AB Registration Application for RPT Act Exemption Examination
rows.desc: ITAT Jodhpur restores 12AB and 80G applications, directing CIT(E) to examine exemption from Rajasthan Public Trust Act registration.The post ITAT Jodhpur Restores 12AB Registration Application for RPT
rows.summary:
The ITAT Jodhpur dealt with two connected appeals by Veera Devi Ramchandra Jhanwar Charitable Trust against the Commissioner of Income-tax (Exemption), Jaipur, who had refused both 12AB registration and 80G(5) approval under the Income-tax Act, 1961. The trust was already registered under section 12AA from 11.11.2011 pursuant to an order dated 22.02.2012, and its stated charitable object was operating “Veera Seva Sadan Dharamshala” at P.B.M. Hospital, Bikaner to provide low-cost accommodation and related facilities to poor and needy patients and their attendants on a “No Profit No Loss” basis. During the registration/approval proceedings, the CIT(E) demanded that the trust produce registration under the Rajasthan Public Trust Act, 1959 (RPT Act) or otherwise prove that it was exempt from that State registration requirement.

The trust argued that it fell within the exemption under section 77(1) of the RPT Act because the Dharamshala was under government administration/control, and therefore separate RPT Act registration was not required. The CIT(E) nevertheless rejected the applications, but the Tribunal found that this issue needed proper examination on the merits and that the trust should not be denied 12AB/80G consideration without a clear determination of whether the RPT Act registration requirement actually applied or whether the statutory exemption covered it.

As a result, the ITAT restored the trust’s 12AB registration application back to the CIT(E) for fresh adjudication specifically on the RPT Act exemption question, and the 80G(5) approval matter was also disposed of in line with that remand. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that charitable entities seeking Income-tax Act registration/approval may be required to address State public trust registration requirements where the authority believes such registration is relevant, but a claim of exemption under the applicable State law must be examined before adverse action is taken. No new tax rate, monetary threshold, or general filing deadline was laid down in this order; the key requirement is that the exemption issue under section 77(1) of the RPT Act must be properly evaluated in the registration process before final denial.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 263 Cannot Import Later Restrictions into AY 2022-23: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai quashes Section 263 revision, holding later Finance Act 2023 restrictions cannot govern AY 2022-23 loan repayment application.The post Section 263 Cannot Import Later Restrictions into AY
rows.summary:
This order concerns four related appeals by Smt. Abha Bansal, Shri Pankaj Bansal, Shri Basant Bansal, and Shri Roop Kumar Bansal against separate but similar revisionary orders passed by the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax (Central), Gurgaon on 24.03.2021 for Assessment Year 2017–18 under section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal was heard on 19.05.2021 and decided on 31.05.2021 by the ITAT Delhi Bench “A” through video conferencing. From the excerpt provided, the key compliance issue is that the Pr. CIT attempted to revise the original assessment under section 263, and the assessees challenged that revision on multiple grounds; the document indicates that the parties primarily argued the lead case of Smt. Abha Bansal, with the other three appeals treated as connected matters.

For a compliance team, the material point is that the document is a judicial review of whether the revisionary jurisdiction under section 263 was properly exercised for AY 2017–18. The affected entities are the four named individual taxpayers, each with Gurgaon addresses and PANs listed in the order, and the respondent authority is the Pr. CIT (Central), Gurgaon. The excerpt does not yet state the substantive basis on which the original assessment was revised, nor the tribunal’s final conclusion, but it clearly confirms that the challenge is to the legality of the section 263 order dated 24.03.2021, so any compliance takeaway would depend on the tribunal’s later reasoning about whether the assessment order was erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue.

The title supplied with the document indicates the legal theme being discussed: section 263 cannot import later restrictions into AY 2022–23, suggesting the underlying principle is that revisionary powers or later statutory constraints should not be retroactively applied to an earlier assessment year. However, because the body excerpt provided stops at the start of the hearing discussion, no specific threshold, amendment, procedural deadline, or operational compliance instruction is set out in the text shown here. A complete compliance assessment would require the remainder of the order to determine exactly what the Pr. CIT directed, what the assessees’ objections were, and whether the Tribunal upheld or quashed the revision.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Administrative & Judicial Developments
rows.desc: Review major GST changes from September 2025 to September 2026 covering Finance Act amendments, rates, refunds, GSTAT appeals and judgments.The post Recent Updates in GST: A Review of Statutory, Admin
rows.summary:
The document reviews GST developments in India from September 2025 to September 2026 and says this was one of the most significant periods of change since GST began in July 2017. On the legislative side, the Finance Act, 2026 amended rules on post-supply discounts, credit notes, provisional refunds, and appellate arrangements, and it also omitted Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act, which had governed intermediary services; however, the amendments to Sections 15, 34, and 54 of the CGST Act are not yet effective because they still await notification, so compliance teams should not treat those particular changes as operative until the government notifies them.  

On tax rates, the rate rationalisation recommended by the 56th GST Council was completed by withdrawing compensation cess and moving specified tobacco and pan masala products into the 40% GST slab, which is a material pricing, invoicing, and tax-computation change for businesses dealing in those goods. The report also notes that the system’s refund regime was expanded to allow more risk-based provisional refunds, meaning eligible taxpayers may receive provisional refund relief under a wider set of circumstances than before, but the operational details depend on the revised administrative framework.  

On filings and compliance mechanics, the return architecture has become more verification-driven: taxpayers are increasingly expected to reconcile data before filing using GSTR-1A, GSTR-2B, and the Invoice Management System. For compliance teams, that means supplier invoices, outward supply reporting, and input tax credit claims should be checked more tightly before return submission, because the new workflow is designed to surface mismatches earlier and reduce post-filing disputes. The document also says GSTAT benches have become operational, which means appellate remedies are now more practically available, and revised limitation dates have been set for legacy appeals, so any old matters must be checked against the new appeal deadline framework rather than assumed to remain open.  

The judicial developments summarized in the document clarify that buyers can face exposure where suppliers fail to deposit tax, so companies cannot rely solely on vendor invoicing and must maintain stronger vendor due-diligence and reconciliation controls. The courts also clarified the statutory timelines for detention orders and held that penalty-related pre-deposit requirements apply prospectively, which affects how and when taxpayers must deposit amounts before pursuing certain appeals or challenges. Finally, the document flags that the 57th GST Council meeting was scheduled for 12 September 2026 and that proposals on ITC protection, corporate guarantees, blocked credit, registration, refunds, and small-business compliance were under consideration, but it expressly warns that these remain proposals only and are not enforceable law unless and until formally implemented.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corruption Controls
rows.desc: Low fees, limited time and market concentration weaken audit quality. Here is how stronger audits can help India prevent corruption and protect savings.The post How Underpriced Audits Weaken Anti-Corr
rows.summary:
The document argues that audit quality is being weakened by persistent underpricing, market concentration, and unrealistic time pressures, which in turn undermines audits as an anti-corruption control over bank deposits, investments, provident funds, companies, and cooperative societies. It cites reported data that between FY2018 and FY2023 the market value of Nifty 500 companies rose by about 92%, but audit fees for those companies increased only 28%, implying that audit remuneration has not kept pace with the growth and complexity of the work. It also notes that six large audit networks now audit about two-thirds of Nifty 500 companies, creating concentration risk and reducing the breadth of independent scrutiny across the market.

The piece highlights that the problem is more severe in cooperative societies, rural branches, and local bodies, where auditors may have only a few days to review cash-heavy, paper-based records; the practical concern is that such compressed timelines make meaningful verification difficult even if the formal audit requirement is met. For smaller practitioners, it says chartered accountants are generally restricted from undertaking business activities without ICAI permission, which constrains diversification and may affect the viability of smaller audit firms. It also criticizes the revised tax-audit ceiling for treating assignments of very different size and complexity as a single audit each, rather than calibrating limits to risk and difficulty.

From a compliance perspective, the document does not announce a new binding rule with a specific statutory effective date or deadline; instead, it recommends policy and supervisory changes to strengthen audit quality. Those proposed changes include requiring disclosure of the actual time available to complete an audit, scrutinizing abnormally low audit fees, building stronger mid-sized audit firms to reduce reliance on the largest networks, and setting audit ceilings based on risk and complexity rather than a flat count. It further calls for fair remuneration and realistic timelines for rural and cooperative audits, while emphasizing that higher fees alone do not guarantee quality if conflicts of interest, rushed work, and concentration remain unaddressed.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaulting Sellers
rows.desc: Why are bona fide buyers denied GST input tax credit when sellers fail to deposit tax? Analysis of Sections 16(2)(c) and 76 of the CGST Act.The post Why GST Department Targets Buyers Instead of Defaul
rows.summary:
The document explains that under Section 16(2)(c) of the CGST Act, a buyer’s claim to Input Tax Credit (ITC) is conditional on the supplier actually paying the GST charged to the government. That means a bona fide purchaser can still be required to reverse ITC even if it has a genuine invoice, actually received the goods or services, paid the full consideration including GST, and filed its own returns correctly, if the supplier fails to deposit the tax. In parallel, Section 76 gives the GST department a direct remedy against the person who collected tax but did not remit it, allowing recovery of the unpaid tax along with applicable interest and penalty.  

The document emphasizes that, in practice, GST authorities often proceed against compliant buyers rather than defaulting sellers because buyers are easier to identify, trace, and recover from—they typically remain active in the GST system, have assets, and are more administratively accessible—while defaulting suppliers may have shut down, disappeared, or operated through shell entities. It also notes that automated matching of GSTR-2B and GSTR-3B makes buyer-side enforcement simpler than a full investigation and recovery action against the supplier.  

The Supreme Court’s decision in Bhandari Scrap Traders is described as upholding the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), treating ITC as a statutory benefit that can be made conditional by Parliament, including on the supplier’s payment of tax. Even so, the document says fairness concerns remain, because a compliant buyer may lose credit despite having acted properly. The author argues that enforcement should, as a policy matter, prioritize recovery from the defaulting supplier under Section 76 and only deny ITC where there is collusion, fraud, or an inability to prove the genuineness of the transaction.  

There are no specific amendment dates, filing deadlines, or numerical thresholds in the text, but there is a clear compliance message: until the law or binding precedent changes the sequencing of these remedies, buyers should preserve robust evidence of due diligence and transaction genuineness, including supplier verification records, invoices, proof of receipt of goods or services, e-way bills, transport documentation, banking/payment records, and reconciliation of returns and ITC claims. This is especially important for responding to GST notices that may seek ITC reversal based on the supplier’s non-payment, even where the buyer itself has complied with its own filing and payment obligations.

rows.summary:
HDFC Bank forecasts that India’s balance of payments will still record a surplus of about **USD 60–65 billion in FY27**, even though the **current account deficit (CAD) is expected to widen to roughly 1.1%–1.3% of GDP**. The key assumption in the report is that **strong inflows through special Reserve Bank of India (RBI) schemes** will be sufficient to offset **weaker capital flows**, preserving an overall BoP surplus despite the larger CAD.

For compliance purposes, this is **not a new regulatory requirement or rule change**; it is an **economic/financial outlook** relevant to treasury, FX, and capital-flow planning. The only specific quantitative forward-looking indicators in the document are the **USD 60–65 billion BoP surplus forecast for FY27** and the **1.1%–1.3% of GDP CAD estimate**. No entity-specific obligations, filing deadlines, procedural changes, or enforcement requirements are described in the article.

Photo: Finance MinistryPress Trust of India New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Sep 07 2026 | 11:23 PM IST @media (min-width:1100px) and (max-width:1280px) { .storymeta .meta-info { flex: 0 0 45%; } } Listen to This ArticleThe government has decided to keep in abeyance the implementation of the performance-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for employees of public sector banks (PSBs) for 2025-26 following a representation by bank employees seeking a review of its existing structure.Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman met a delegation of bank employees representing different PSBs, led by the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, which raised several issues concerning the banking sector and employees, the finance ministry said in a statement on Monday.The delegation sought, among other things, a review of ex-gratia, medical facilities for retired employees and changes in the existing PLI structure applicable to PSB empl
rows.summary:
The government has put the performance-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for public sector bank (PSB) employees for FY 2025-26 into abeyance, meaning it will not be implemented for now, after a representation from bank employees asking for a review of the scheme’s current structure. This decision came after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman met a delegation of bank employees representing multiple PSBs, led by the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, who raised broader sector and employee concerns with the Finance Ministry.  

The employees’ delegation specifically requested review of the existing PLI structure, along with other matters such as ex-gratia payments and medical facilities for retired employees. The document does not state any revised PLI formula, new eligibility thresholds, payout rates, or an alternate implementation date; it only says the FY26 PLI scheme is being held in abeyance pending review.  

For compliance purposes, the affected parties are employees of public sector banks and, operationally, the PSBs themselves and the government bodies responsible for administering employee compensation schemes. The immediate obligation is to pause implementation of the FY26 PLI scheme rather than proceed under the current structure, and to await further government direction after the review.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India held a 30-day variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auction on Monday for a notified amount of ₹7 trillion, but banks showed weak interest and submitted only ₹2.59 trillion in bids, well below market expectations of up to ₹5 trillion. This 30-day auction was notable because it allowed premature reversal for the first time in a VRRR operation, yet banks still appeared unwilling to lock up funds for the full term. In response, the RBI announced a separate ₹5 trillion overnight VRRR auction, which drew stronger participation of ₹3.53 trillion.

For compliance and treasury monitoring purposes, the key point is that the RBI is actively using VRRR operations to absorb a very large liquidity surplus in the banking system, which stood at a record ₹11.16 trillion on Sunday according to RBI data. There is no direct new regulatory filing requirement described in the article, but banks and liquidity managers should note the auction sizes, the weak response to the 30-day tenor, and the availability of premature reversal in the 30-day VRRR, since these factors may affect short-term funding strategy, surplus placement decisions, and internal liquidity management assumptions.

rows.summary:
Bank of Baroda revised its FY27 macro view upward after stronger-than-expected first-quarter performance: it now expects India’s FY27 GDP growth to be in the 7.0%–7.2% range, up from its July estimate of 6.6%–6.8%. The revision is based on Q1FY27 GDP growth of 7.8% year on year, compared with 6.9% in the same quarter a year earlier, alongside GVA growth of 8.2%, private consumption growth of 9.9%, and investment growth of 20%. For compliance and risk-monitoring purposes, the article does not announce a regulatory filing or new legal obligation; rather, it is an economic outlook update that flags two downside-risk variables that could affect business conditions: a sub-normal monsoon and a fresh spike in oil prices.

The bank says those two factors are increasing upside risk to inflation and the fiscal deficit, which would matter for treasury, pricing, lending, and macro scenario planning even though no direct compliance deadline is stated. The piece also notes that Bank of Baroda economist Sonal Badhan characterized the strong growth as evidence of “strong domestic fundamentals” despite volatile global conditions. In short, the actionable takeaway is that Bank of Baroda has tightened its FY27 growth assumptions upward while warning that weather-related agricultural stress and higher oil premiums could worsen inflation and public-finance conditions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 30-day variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auction on Monday saw sharply weaker demand because of a technical glitch on the RBI’s e-Kuber portal, which is the normal electronic platform used for such auctions. The RBI had notified ₹7 trillion for the mop-up operation, but only ₹2.59 trillion of bids were received, far below market expectations of as much as ₹5 trillion. According to market participants, the e-Kuber system developed a technical issue and the RBI shifted bidding to another platform; some banks were not aware of the switch in time and were therefore unable to participate.

For compliance and treasury teams, the key operational takeaway is that participation in RBI liquidity-management auctions may be disrupted by platform changes, and institutions relying on e-Kuber need contingency monitoring so they do not miss a bidding window if the submission venue changes unexpectedly. The article does not report any change in the auction rules, eligibility, pricing mechanism, or a formal compliance deadline; it describes an incident on Sep. 7, 2026, with no substantive regulatory directive issued in the text.

rows.summary:
State Bank of India and Bank of Baroda disclosed in separate regulatory filings that they have received strike notices from the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU), a grouping representing seven bank employees’ and officers’ unions/associations, and warned that banking operations could be disrupted if the strikes go ahead. The UFBU has called for strikes on **September 11, September 28, 29 and 30, 2026**, followed by an **indefinite strike beginning October 26, 2026**. The filings indicate the banks are taking steps to maintain normal branch and office operations on the strike days, but they have expressly flagged the risk of service disruption.

The strike call is tied to UFBU demands including a **five-day working week** and related incentives. For compliance and operations teams, the practical issue is not a new regulatory requirement imposed on the banks, but a labor action that may affect branch staffing, customer service, transaction processing, and other routine banking functions on the announced dates. rows.summary: RBL Bank’s board has approved establishing a $1 billion Euro Medium Term Note (EMTN) programme to raise overseas debt, with the bank saying it may issue foreign-currency bonds, notes, or other permitted debt securities in one or more transactions depending on market conditions. The programme is being set up under Regulation S of the US Securities Act of 1933, which indicates the securities are intended for offshore issuance/exempt distribution rather than a domestic public offering. The approval is explicitly subject to all applicable regulatory, statutory, and other approvals, so the bank cannot proceed with issuances until those clearances are obtained. The document does not specify a final issuance date, pricing, maturity, or use of proceeds; it only confirms the authority to raise up to $1 billion under the programme on a phased basis as market conditions permit. For compliance purposes, the key point is that this creates a new overseas borrowing framework for RBL Bank, and any actual drawdown under it will need to be checked against the relevant securities, banking, and cross-border issuance approvals and disclosure requirements at the time of each transaction.

To support that fundraising, the board also approved the establishment of a **Euro Medium Term Note (EMTN) Programme**, which will be carried out under **Regulation S of the U.S. Securities Act of 1933**.

rows.title: Exclusive: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank ropes in Manmohan Shetty as CFO
rows.desc: Articles 1 min read Exclusive: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank ropes in Manmohan Shetty as CFO Manmohan Shetty, who most recently served as CFO of IREP Credit Capital (now Viksit Capital) and previously spent nearly nine years with Barclays, is set to join Utkarsh Small Finance Bank as its Chief Financial Officer, two people aware of the discussion told ETBFSI. The bank’s board meeting is scheduled for September 19, with approval for Shetty’s appointment expected to be taken up at the meeting. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Sep 8, 2026 at 01:36 AM IST var news_msid = 133895833; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is set to appoint Manmohan Shetty as its Chief Financial Officer, subject to approval by the bank’s board, which is scheduled to meet on September 19, according to a person familiar with the development and an Utkarsh SFB spokesperson.“The board meeting is scheduled for September 19th and one of the agenda is the approvals on the CFO appointment,” the Utkarsh SFB spokesperson told ETBFSI.Shetty will succeed Sarju Kumar Pravin Simaria, who has been serving as the bank’s CFO since September 2022 and was elevated as Whole time Director in June 2026. The document reports that the one-year median marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) for scheduled commercial banks in India rose to **8.70% in August** from **8.60% in July**, and for the first time in **14 months** this moved **above its year-ago level** of **8.60%**. This increase occurred even though the **repo rate stayed unchanged at 5.25%**, and despite a sharp improvement in banking system liquidity, suggesting persistent funding-cost pressure rather than a broad rate cycle driven by monetary tightening.

The rise was **not broad-based**: it was driven **entirely by foreign banks**, whose one-year median MCLR increased to **7.33% in August from 7.20% in July**. By contrast, the one-year median MCLR for **public sector banks** remained unchanged at **8.80%**, and for **private sector banks** remained unchanged at **9.35%**. For compliance and treasury teams, this means the rate movement is concentrated in a subset of banks and does not reflect a uniform market-wide repricing.

The article also notes that system liquidity improved materially, with **surplus liquidity rising to around Rs 6.7 lakh crore by August 31**, compared with **Rs 2.5 lakh crore at the end of July** and **Rs 1.4 lakh crore at the end of June**. This improvement was largely attributed to the **conversion of Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits into rupees**, which eased near-term funding pressure on banks. A related point in the article is that banks’ **fresh spreads recovered in July**, with the spread for scheduled commercial banks **widening by 8 basis points**. There are no explicit new regulatory deadlines, filing requirements, or compliance procedures announced in the text; the document is primarily a market update indicating that lending-rate pressure persists for some banks despite easier liquidity conditions.

NPCI is working on the framework and that it could be unveiled at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai. The exact technical architecture, however, has not been publicly detailed by NPCI. rows.summary:
NPCI is developing a new framework called the Unified Agent Protocol (UAP) that would let AI agents initiate UPI payments on a user’s behalf, but only within user-defined rules and spending limits rather than with unrestricted access to a bank account. The intended first use case is low-value, frequent consumer purchases such as groceries, with more advanced transaction types potentially added later. In practice, a user could set conditions such as “buy this item only if the price drops below a specified amount” or impose daily/transaction caps for routine purchases, and the AI agent would be expected to trigger payment only when those conditions are met.

For compliance purposes, the key shift is that UPI would move from a model requiring the user to approve each individual payment to one where automated payment initiation is permitted inside a clearly bounded authorization framework. The article does not provide technical specifications, but says NPCI is working on the framework and it may be unveiled at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai. No exact launch date, implementation deadline, or formal rule text is given in the document.

The piece also notes that NPCI already operates mechanisms that could support this architecture, specifically UPI Circle, which allows a primary user to delegate payment authority to another user, and UPI Reserve Pay, which allows funds to be blocked. From a compliance perspective, entities offering UPI-linked products or agentic payment functionality should monitor the UAP rollout because it implies new controls around user authorization, transaction limits, and conditional payment execution for AI-driven payments.

rows.summary:
This article is not a regulatory change notice or a new compliance requirement; it is a financial impact analysis of the RBI’s special FCNR(B) swap scheme and what it may cost the central bank. The key update is that banks had mobilized **$127.23 billion** through **FCNR(B) deposits by August 31**, far above the earlier working assumption of **$65–70 billion**, which means any prior cost estimate based on the smaller corpus is understated if applied directly to the final mobilisation. The article cites an earlier SBI Research estimate that a **five-year hedging cost of about $10.5 billion** would arise from a **$70 billion FCNR(B) corpus** assuming a **3% annual hedging cost**, and another estimate that the total potential cost could be about **Rs 36,000 crore over three to five years** based on a **3% hedging cost** applied to roughly **Rs 12 lakh crore** raised through foreign-currency schemes.

The total mobilisation under the RBI’s special swap facility is stated as **$136.38 billion**, consisting of **$127.23 billion in FCNR(B) deposits**, plus **$5.26 billion in overseas foreign-currency borrowings** and **$3.89 billion in external commercial borrowings**. The article emphasizes that the **$10.5 billion** estimate should **not** be used mechanically for the larger final corpus because it was built on different assumptions about corpus size, hedging cost, and maturity profile. It also notes that the **gross hedging cost is not necessarily the final net cost to RBI**, because returns earned on the foreign-currency assets funded by these inflows may offset part of the expense; the eventual impact will depend on **swap pricing, maturities, and asset returns**.

For a compliance team at a bank, the practical takeaway is that this story reflects the scale and financial implications of participation in the FCNR(B) swap framework, but it does **not** announce any new filing, conduct, or reporting obligation. The only operative “deadline” referenced is the mobilisation snapshot date of **August 31**, and the article’s focus is the RBI’s exposure rather than any change in requirements for banks or deposit-taking entities.

The document says the Reserve Bank of India’s special FCNR(B) foreign-currency deposit mobilisation window has now closed, after banks raised an exceptional $127.23 billion in FCNR(B) deposits by August 31 under the RBI’s special foreign-currency swap facility. Total inflows under the scheme reached $136.4 billion as of August 31, and while the mobilisation window ended on August 31, banks are still permitted to execute the related swaps with the RBI until September 11.  

For compliance and treasury teams, the key point is that the scheme provided a temporary and unusual funding and liquidity boost that may not reflect underlying deposit strength. Deposit growth rose to 15.4% year-on-year in July, then moderated to 14.7% by August 15, while credit growth remained higher at 18.3%, meaning the credit-deposit gap is still a live issue. The article warns that once the FCNR(B) windfall fades, banks’ ability to sustain deposit growth will depend on normal domestic mobilisation—especially retail and term deposits—rather than special offshore inflows.  

The article also notes that private-sector banks mobilised nearly half of the FCNR(B) deposits, so they benefited disproportionately from the scheme and currently have more room to support lending and less immediate funding pressure than banks that raised less. In practical terms, the compliance implication is not a new regulatory filing requirement, but a shift in supervisory and risk focus: banks should expect closer attention on whether their domestic deposit franchise is strong enough to support continuing credit expansion after the FCNR(B) window has ended.

For compliance teams at banks, payment firms, fintech investors, and acquisition targets, the practical takeaway is that the market is moving toward **larger, infrastructure-heavy, and strategically consolidated payment businesses**, with growing investor attention also extending to **embedded finance, AI-driven payments, and agentic commerce** where AI systems may participate in shopping and payment workflows. The report suggests these areas are becoming more relevant for deal review, product governance, and control frameworks because the technology and transaction models are evolving quickly.  

By contrast, **insurtech investment fell to $3.7 billion across just 124 deals**, showing that funding for that segment is becoming more selective. The document does not impose a regulatory deadline or new legal requirement, but it signals a clear market trend that compliance functions should watch closely when assessing **M&A activity, product development, AI-enabled payment tools, and sector-specific investment exposure**.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India is reconsidering its draft proposal to impose a blanket ban on revolving credit facilities offered by non-bank lenders/NBFCs, after industry feedback suggested the measure would affect far more of the NBFC sector than the RBI initially expected. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu met with NBFC representatives and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to hear concerns, and the central bank has already received about 350 industry feedback submissions on the draft proposal.

The main compliance issue under discussion is whether the RBI will proceed with a full prohibition on revolving credit or instead move to a partial restriction. Industry participants say the RBI originally believed the impact would be limited to only three or four NBFCs, but the consultation response indicates that a much broader set of lenders could be caught by the rule. One specific carve-out drawing repeated attention is an exemption for supply chain financing, which the industry has urged the RBI to preserve.

No final contours have been issued yet, so there is no confirmed operative rule to implement at this stage. However, sources cited in the article suggest the final guidelines may be issued in roughly two months, which is the only timeline provided. For compliance teams at NBFCs and other non-bank lenders, the key takeaway is that revolving credit products remain under active regulatory review, and firms offering such facilities should be prepared for either a narrower restriction or a broader ban depending on the RBI’s final decision, with supply chain financing potentially treated differently.

Niva Bupa Health Insurance is increasing health insurance premiums by about 8-9% per year to keep pace with medical inflation, and management expects this pattern to continue as medical costs rise. CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said the company prefers these smaller, regular annual increases over larger jumps every few years, indicating an ongoing pricing strategy rather than a one-time adjustment.

Ujjivan Small Finance Bank’s leadership has changed after managing director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal retired early on health grounds, creating a continuity watchpoint for the bank’s long-term FY30 strategy. rows.title: Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.
rows.summary:
The article says NBFCs have asked the Reserve Bank of India to clarify whether loan recovery calls qualify as “service calls” that may be made using the TRAI-mandated 1600 numbering series. Industry representatives raised the issue with RBI Deputy Governor S. C. Murmu, arguing that while sales calls should clearly remain outside the 1600 series, it is still unclear whether recovery calls are covered; this matters because customers are increasingly blocking calls originating from the 1600 series.

The underlying regulatory framework is that the Department of Telecommunications had allocated the 1600 series for service and transactional voice calls by government and BFSI entities, and TRAI later made migration to this series mandatory in a phased manner for RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities. TRAI’s objective was to help consumers distinguish legitimate regulated-financial calls from spam, promotional, and potentially fraudulent calls. For RBI-regulated entities, the compliance deadlines were staggered: commercial banks had to move to the 1600 series by January 1, 2026; large NBFCs with assets above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks, and small finance banks by February 1, 2026; and remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks, and other covered entities by March 1, 2026.

For compliance purposes, the key unresolved point is whether debt collection/recovery outreach can be treated as a permissible service call under the 1600 framework or whether it must be handled outside that series. The document does not indicate that any rule has changed yet; rather, it reports an industry request for RBI guidance because the current implementation is creating operational uncertainty and call-blocking risk for regulated lenders.

Rajagopal Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited, Sundaram Towers, 1 st and 2 nd floor 46, Whites Road, Royapettah, Chennai, 600014 Dear Sir, Sub: Request for Informal Guidance by way of interpretive letter under the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 in connection with the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 (“AIF Regulations”) Ref: Your letter dated April 23, 2025 1. Please clarify whether during the extended period, the close-ended Alternative Investment Fund is permitted only to liquidate its existing portfolio investments or allowed to make investments in portfolio companies. Page 2 of 4 2. Our Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the issues raised in your letter are as under: 2.1. In terms of Regulation 13(5) of AIF Regulations, extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Inve
rows.summary:
SEBI has issued an informal guidance letter dated **July 9, 2025** in response to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s request regarding the **extension of tenure for close-ended Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)** under the **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**. The applicant, which is a SEBI-registered portfolio manager (**registration no. INP000006271**) and the investment manager for **Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust** (Category III AIF, **registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291**) and **Sundaram Category II AIF** (**registration no. IN/AIF2/17-18/0340**), asked whether, during the extended period of a close-ended AIF, the fund may only liquidate existing investments or whether it may also make new investments in portfolio companies.

SEBI’s comment cites **Regulation 13(5)** of the AIF Regulations, which allows a close-ended AIF’s tenure to be **extended for up to two years** if approved by **two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment** in the AIF. SEBI’s guidance indicates that, during the extended tenure, the AIF is **not restricted only to liquidation** of its existing portfolio; rather, it is also **permitted to make investments in portfolio companies**. This means compliance teams should treat the extension period as a continued investment period, not a wind-down-only period, unless the fund’s own constitutive documents or other applicable rules impose stricter limits. The letter is issued as an **interpretive response under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003**, and addresses the specific operational question raised by the applicant for its close-ended AIFs.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on introduction of “Single Window Automatic & Generalised Access for Trusted Foreign Investors (SWAGAT-FI)” framework for FPIs and FVCIs [Click here to see rationale for rejection of comments]
rows.summary:
The paper proposes SEBI’s “Single Window Automatic & Generalised Access for Trusted Foreign Investors (SWAGAT-FI)” framework for FPIs and FVCIs, aimed at easing access for qualifying foreign investors while retaining regulatory verification. One key change concerns identification of SWAGAT-FIs: existing FPIs will have to demonstrate that they meet the eligibility conditions, including diversification, independence of fund managers, confirmation from the relevant regulator, blind-pool structure, and the absence of segregated portfolios. SEBI rejected the objection that this would add undue burden, stating that the verification approach will be aligned with the existing exemption-style checks already used under the Additional Disclosure Framework, which is already familiar to industry participants.

The consultation also addresses periodic re-KYC and fee payment timing. SEBI is retaining the requirement for re-KYC, including the obligation to capture material changes such as changes in UBOs, because these changes may otherwise remain undiscovered. The proposal to eliminate additional re-KYC was not accepted; instead, the framework keeps re-KYC in place for FPIs on the same general basis as other investor types. On fees, the document clarifies that there is not currently a “yearly fee” in the sense suggested by commenters; the only change is that the fee block period is being extended from 3 years to 10 years, and this 10-year block is being aligned with the re-KYC cycle.

A later point in the consultation indicates that SEBI considered comments against facilitating “single demat…” arrangements, but the excerpt is truncated before the full proposal and final response are visible, so the document provided does not allow a complete summary of that item. Based on the visible text alone, the material compliance takeaways are that firms falling within FPI/FVCI channels should expect a new SWAGAT-FI eligibility validation process, continued re-KYC obligations, ongoing reporting of material changes, and a longer 10-year fee block period rather than annual fee collection.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this paper signals a possible **change in corporate action handling procedures**, especially around coordination of board approval, record date scheduling, allotment/credit of bonus shares, and exchange/listing readiness so trading can start on **T+2**. Until SEBI issues a final circular/regulation, firms should treat this as a proposal under consultation and monitor for the final prescribed timeline and any detailed procedural requirements that may follow.

The document does not set out final operational conditions, thresholds, or timelines in the text provided, beyond inviting comments through SEBI’s public comment process.

Any eventual rule would likely require AIF managers to track whether an investee company qualifies as “infrastructure,” confirm the AIF category is **I or II**, and ensure any encumbrance is used only for the permitted purpose of facilitating the investee company’s debt raise. Until SEBI issues a final amendment, existing AIF restrictions remain in force and no immediate compliance change is mandated by this paper alone.

rows.title: Consultation Paper on Review of Voluntary Delisting norms under SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021  Addendum- Executive Summary
rows.summary:
SEBI’s consultation paper on reviewing the voluntary delisting framework under the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 proposes four substantive changes that would affect delisting mechanics for listed companies and their acquirers. First, the current rule allowing a counter-offer only when the acquirer plus tendered public shareholding reaches at least 90% of paid-up capital would be relaxed: a counter-offer could be made when combined holdings/tendered shares are below 90% but still at or above 75% of paid-up capital. For such a counter-offer, the proposed floor price would be the volume weighted average price of the shares tendered by willing shareholders in the failed delisting offer.

Second, the paper proposes adding “Adjusted Book Value” as an additional input in determining floor price, alongside the existing pricing parameters, and says this would apply to both frequently traded and infrequently traded shares. Third, SEBI is considering allowing delisting at a fixed price as an alternative to the reverse book building process, but only for companies whose shares are frequently traded; this would create a second route for determining the exit price instead of relying solely on reverse book building. Fourth, the reference date used to compute the floor price would change from the date of the board meeting approving the delisting proposal to the date of the initial public announcement, which could materially affect pricing calculations depending on market movement between those dates.

The document is an executive summary of a consultation paper placed on SEBI’s website on August 14, 2023 for public comments; it does not itself set an operative effective date or final compliance deadline, because these are proposed amendments under consultation rather than finalized regulatory changes.

rows.title: Consultation paper on proposal for introduction of the concept of General Information Document (GID) and Key Information Document (KID), mandatory listing of debt securities of listed issuers and other reforms under the NCS Regulations
rows.summary:
This document is a **consultation paper published on 9 February 2023** seeking public comments on proposed reforms to the **NCS Regulations** (the regime governing the listing of debt securities). It does **not itself introduce final binding requirements**, but it signals a package of proposed changes that compliance teams of issuers, debt-listing entities, and other NCS-regulated market participants should track closely because the consultation specifically covers two new disclosure concepts — a **General Information Document (GID)** and a **Key Information Document (KID)** — as well as **mandatory listing of debt securities issued by already listed issuers** and other related regulatory reforms.

The core proposal is to create a **two-stage disclosure framework** for debt securities: a broader **GID** intended to contain general issuer/programme information, and a more focused **KID** intended to provide the key transaction-specific facts that investors need before investing. The purpose appears to be to standardize and streamline information delivery for debt offerings, improve transparency, and reduce duplication across multiple issuances or programmes. Compliance teams should expect that if these proposals are adopted, they would need to prepare and maintain these documents in addition to existing offering/listing materials, ensure the disclosures are accurate and current, and align internal approval workflows so that the required information is available before any public offering or listing step.

The paper also proposes **mandatory listing of debt securities of issuers whose equity securities are already listed**, which would materially change issuance and compliance practices for listed companies that currently issue debt without necessarily listing it under the NCS framework. If adopted, this would mean such issuers could no longer treat debt issuance as outside the listing regime; instead, those securities would have to be listed, bringing with it the associated disclosure, filing, and ongoing compliance obligations under the NCS Regulations. For compliance purposes, the practical implication is that listed corporates would need to review debt-issuance policies, securities issuance timetables, board and committee approvals, and ongoing reporting controls to ensure any future debt issuance is captured and processed through the listing channel.

The document as provided does **not specify final effective dates, deadlines, thresholds, or rates**, because it is a consultation notice rather than an operative rule text. The key action for affected entities is therefore to **review the proposed GID/KID framework and mandatory-debt-listing concept and submit comments during the consultation period**, then prepare for implementation once the regulator finalizes the reforms.

The stated purpose of the framework is to strengthen RE cyber defenses against evolving threats, align SEBI requirements with industry standards, promote more efficient audit practices, and improve overall compliance. This document is not the framework itself, but a set of FAQs prepared after SEBI received queries and feedback from REs; it is intended to give practical guidance and clarification on how to apply the CSCRF and the related Framework for Adoption of Cloud Services by SEBI REs.

The FAQs are organized around the main compliance areas that REs need to operationalize: governance and CISO responsibilities, how REs are categorized by thresholds, asset inventory and classification of critical versus non-critical systems, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) and patch management, cyber audit timelines, the Cyber Capability Index (CCI), Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), outsourcing rules, cloud service providers and hosted services, COTS product testing, log management and data security, ISO 27001 certification, SOC and Market-SOC requirements, threat intelligence, DC-DR drills, response and recovery, and classification/handling of cybersecurity incidents. From a compliance perspective, this means affected entities need to review the CSCRF obligations across the full security lifecycle, including governance, technology controls, incident readiness, third-party and cloud risk, and assurance activities.

A key point for compliance teams is that these FAQs are expressly guidance only: SEBI states that the explanations and clarifications in the FAQ document should not be treated as an interpretation of the CSCRF itself or as a binding opinion or decision of SEBI. In other words, the binding obligations are in the underlying CSCRF circular and related framework, and the FAQs should be used to understand SEBI’s intent and implementation expectations, not as a substitute for the actual legal requirements. The document excerpt provided does not include any specific deadlines, numerical thresholds, or technical rates beyond the citation and issue date of the CSCRF circular, so compliance teams should cross-check the FAQs against the original circular and any annexures for precise applicability, implementation dates, and control requirements.

rows.summary:
The document sets out the rights and obligations of a beneficial owner and a depository participant (DP) under the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, and all related SEBI circulars, rules, regulations, depository bye-laws, business rules, operating instructions, and applicable government notifications in force from time to time. The DP must keep all beneficial-owner information from the account-opening form and supporting documents strictly confidential and may disclose it only where required by statutory, legal, or regulatory authority, while the beneficial owner must immediately notify the DP in writing of any change in the details previously provided in the account-opening form or later furnished to the DP.  

On fees and charges, the beneficial owner is required to pay only those charges for dematerialized holding, transfer, and depository services that have been mutually agreed between the DP and the beneficial owner and stated in the DP’s tariff sheet; the document specifically notes that no charges are payable for opening a demat account. Overall, the operational compliance themes are account-opening controls, ongoing KYC/documentation discipline, confidentiality of client records, mandatory client notification of changes, and adherence to the applicable tariff/fee regime, including any special rules for Basic Services Demat Accounts.

rows.title: Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI)
rows.summary:
The document appears to summarize SEBI’s responses to comments on proposed changes for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), and it indicates that SEBI is **not accepting several requests to relax the compliance framework**. On the proposal relating to **identification/validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs**, commenters asked that existing FPIs not be required to provide additional proof because it would increase burden and paperwork; SEBI **disagreed**, saying the verification requirements will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry has already implemented. In practical terms, FPIs seeking the relevant status will still need to demonstrate the required conditions—such as diversification, independence of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios—but SEBI’s stated approach is to use a familiar verification model rather than introduce an entirely new process.

On **re-KYC and fee/payment periodicity**, commenters wanted the current periodicity to remain unchanged and opposed additional re-KYC requirements, arguing that material changes such as UBO updates would be caught through ordinary monitoring and that longer fee blocks would reduce SEBI’s flexibility. SEBI **disagreed with removing the re-KYC requirement**, stating that **material change reporting obligations remain in force** and that the additional re-KYC requirement is being retained for FPIs, consistent with treatment of other investors. The document also clarifies that there is **no yearly fee requirement currently**; instead, the proposal is to **increase the fee block period from 3 years to 10 years**, and this 10-year block is intended to **coincide with the re-KYC cycle**, rather than changing the underlying ability of SEBI to adjust fees.

A third item begins addressing comments that **FPIs should not be allowed to facilitate single demat accounts**, but the text provided is truncated, so the specific final regulatory outcome for that point is not visible in the excerpt. Based on the visible portions, the compliance takeaway is that SEBI is **preserving core identity, ownership, and status-verification controls for FPIs**, while trying to implement them through standardized existing frameworks rather than eliminating the obligations.

rows.title: Information Technology Department (ITD)
rows.summary:
This document is not a regulatory change notice or a rule requiring action; it is a general description of the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (SEBI) Information Technology Department (ITD) and its technology mandate. It states that ITD is responsible for enabling SEBI’s technology landscape and partnering with all SEBI departments to deliver enterprise-wide systems such as portals and gateways, network infrastructure, private cloud infrastructure, mail and messaging solutions, a data lake, document management system, and SAP-based solutions.

For a compliance team, the relevant takeaway is that ITD supports digital interfaces used by market intermediaries for regulations, compliance, and reporting, and it also develops data warehouse capabilities used for surveillance, inspections, and supervision. The title further indicates ITD’s role in building data analytics capabilities, implementing cybersecurity and IT resilience measures for market infrastructure to support uninterrupted trading and investor-data privacy, conducting IT inspections and audits of market infrastructure institutions (MIIs) and intermediaries, creating frameworks for information exchange with government agencies, and enabling market innovation through SEBI’s Innovation Sandbox Framework.

No deadlines, effective dates, thresholds, fees, or specific compliance obligations are stated in the provided content, and no particular regulated entity is newly required to take action based on this text alone. As a result, this should be treated as an informational overview of ITD’s functions rather than a binding compliance requirement or policy update.

rows.title:
The Information Technology Department (ITD) of SEBI is the enabler of technology landscape in the organisation. ITD is committed to its vision of leveraging technology in partnership with every department of SEBI to achieve the following goals: 
1.	Development and implementation of Enterprise wide solutions like Portals and gateways, Network Infrastructure, Private Cloud Infrastructure, Mail and messaging solution, Data lake, Document Management system, SAP Solution etc. 
2.	Facilitating Ease of doing Business for market intermediaries by enhancing the digital interfaces between them and SEBI in respect of a large range of functions such as Regulations, Compliance and Reporting. 
3.	Developing Data Warehouse system for surveillance, inspections and supervision activities. 
4.	Driving data analytics practice at SEBI. 
5.	Ensuring deployment of strong cyber security measures and information technology (IT) resilience in the market Infrastructure to facilitate uninterrupted trading and privacy of investor data. 
6.	Undertaking IT inspections and audit for MIIs and intermediaries. 
7.	Development of framework for information interchange with various government agencies. 
8.	Facilitating innovation in markets through SEBI’s Innovation Sandbox Framework.

rows.title: Settlement Application
rows.summary:
This document describes the online **SEBI Settlement Application** process and the required supporting filings for applicants seeking settlement under SEBI’s settlement framework. It states that once the **non-refundable settlement application fee** is paid online, the applicant must **physically submit the printed settlement application together with all required documents, including proof of payment, to the SEBI Settlement Division within 7 calendar days** from the date the payment is successfully made. It also directs applicants to **refer to SEBI Circular dated June 18, 2019** before filing.

The application form requires the applicant to choose the **type of application** from the available categories: **Summary Settlement (SS), Suo Motu (SM), Pre-SCN, Post-SCN, Post Appeal (SAT), Post SAT Order (SO), or Settlement with Confidentiality (SC)**. The form asks for the relevant proceeding identifiers depending on the case type, including **Show Cause Notice number/date, Summary Settlement Notice number/date, SAT appeal number, and Appeal number**. It also requires the applicant to provide the **matter to which the application relates**, and includes controls to **save or withdraw** the application details.

For each applicant, the form requires entry of **name, PAN number, applicant type, and proposed settlement amount**, along with documentary uploads. The settlement amount entered **cannot be less than ₹3 lakhs**, as expressly required under the Settlement Regulations. The applicant must upload **certified true copies of the ITRs for the last 3 financial years** in **PDF format only, up to 20 MB**, and a **certified true copy of the PAN card** in **PDF format only, up to 500 KB**. These requirements apply to the applicant whether the applicant is an **individual or a body corporate**.

The form also requires a detailed **correspondence address**, the applicant’s **GST number**, **state/territory selection**, **10-digit phone number**, and a **primary email address**, with the email noted as the address that will be used for all communications with the entity. Overall, the compliance obligation is not just to complete the online submission, but to ensure the offline physical filing is sent to SEBI within the 7-day window and that all required identification, tax, and payment documents are accurate, complete, and in the specified file formats and size limits.

rows.title: Settlement Calculator BETA
rows.summary:
The document is an introductory description of SEBI’s **Settlement Calculator (BETA)**, which is built to estimate an **indicative settlement amount** under the **SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations, 2018**, using the computation matrix in **Schedule II** and factors under **Regulation 10**. It is explicitly stated that the calculator is only a guide: the final settlement amount can be modified by the **Internal Committee**, **High Powered Advisory Committee**, and the **Panel of Whole Time Members**, and in some cases SEBI may also impose **non-monetary settlement terms** under **Regulation 9**.

For compliance purposes, the core monetary floor is that the **Indicative Amount (IA)** cannot be lower than **Rs. 3 lakh for a first-time applicant** or **Rs. 7 lakh for other applicants**. A “first time applicant” is defined as a person against whom **no order has been passed by the adjudicating officer or SEBI**, and who has **never obtained a settlement order from SEBI** as of the date of the current application. The document also says the **Settlement Amount (SA)** is comprised of the IA plus any applicable adjustments under Regulation 10.

The calculator requires use of a **proceeding conversion factor (PCF)** depending on the **stage at which the relevant proceeding is pending** when the settlement application is filed. It further provides that, where a business or activity is **corporatized, converted into an LLP or partnership, or merged/taken over by new management**, the historical record of the erstwhile entity is treated as the record of the new entity. This means compliance obligations and past conduct do not reset simply because the entity form or ownership changes. The excerpt cuts off after mentioning “considerations including insolvency, change of name…,” so those additional conditions are referenced but not fully visible in the provided text.

rows.title: Adjudication Order in the matter of trading activities of certain entities in the scrip of Veer Global Infraconstruction Limited.[Corrigendum]
rows.summary:
This corrigendum amends a prior adjudication order, Ref. No. Order/SM/RG/2026-27/32369-32379, concerning trading activities in the scrip of Veer Global Infraconstruction Limited. The only substantive correction is to paras 31.2 and 32.2 of the original order: the original text had incorrectly referred to synchronised trades of “Patch 1,” and those references must instead be read as synchronised trades in “Patch 2” for para 31.2 and “Patch 3” for para 32.2. No other findings, conclusions, penalties, or directions in the original order are changed.

For Patch 2, the corrected data show a single synchronised trade between Mrs Bhavana Sahay and Mr Ranjan Sahay for 1,000 shares, with a sum of LTP difference of Rs. -17.90, occurring over 1 day and 1 trade, representing 0.64% of market volume. The order states that the suspected group entities, through this one synchronised trade, contributed 0.64% to market volume and Rs. -17.90 to net LTP.

For Patch 3, the corrected data show 11 synchronised trades among the suspected entities, with the following counterparties and quantities: Mrs Bhavana Sahay / Mrs Rita Kumar for 2,000 shares (Rs. 0.00 LTP difference, 2 days, 2 trades, 0.52% of market volume); Mr Ranjan Sahay / Mrs Bhavana Sahay for 2,000 shares (Rs. -5.05, 2 days, 2 trades, 0.52%); Mrs Shahnaj Khatoon / Mrs Rita Kumar for 4,000 shares (Rs. 13.70, 4 days, 4 trades, 1.04%); and Mrs Rita Kumar / Mrs Bhavana Sahay for 4,000 shares (Rs. -12.45, 4 days, 4 trades, 1.04%). In total, the patch 3 synchronised trades amounted to 15,000 shares, 11 days, 15 trades, 3.89% of market volume, and a cumulative LTP difference of Rs. 13.15; the order specifically states that through 11 synchronised trades among themselves, the entities contributed 3.89% to market volume and Rs. 13.15 to LTP.

The corrigendum itself was issued on April 27, 2026, in Mumbai, by the Adjudicating Officer, Sudeep Mishra. It must be read together with the original adjudication order, and the document directs that the original order is to always be read with this corrigendum while all other contents remain unchanged. A copy of the corrigendum is to be served on the Noticee and also on the Securities and Exchange Board of India.

rows.title: Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 2 Entries
rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/253 DOR.AML.REC.219/14.06.001/2026-27 September 07, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir, Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 2 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended as on December 29, 2025) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16446, dated September 04, 2026 wherein the Security Council pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al‑Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and underline in the entries below on its ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 A. Individuals QDi.431 Name: 1: SANAULLAH 2: GHAFARI 3: na 4: na Name (original script): ثناء ﷲ غفار
rows.summary:
This RBI communication requires regulated entities to continue implementing Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 in line with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 (dated November 28, 2025, as amended on December 29, 2025), meaning banks and other covered financial institutions must ensure they do not maintain accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved terrorism-related lists circulated under UAPA. The letter is addressed to commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, non-banking financial companies, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions. It specifically updates the UN Security Council’s 1267/1989 ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list based on UNSC press release SC/16446 dated September 4, 2026, which amended two entries on the sanctions list; the measures attached to listed persons/entities are the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo under UN Security Council Resolution 2734 (2024).

The document does not create a new sanctions framework, but it does require compliance teams to treat the updated UNSC list as operative and to screen/compare customer and counterparty names against the amended entries. The first amended individual listed in the excerpt is QDi.431, named Sanaullah Ghafari (original script: ثناء ﷲ غفار), indicating that the entry has been revised as shown in the UNSC notice. Because the RBI cites the UAPA Section 51A obligation and the KYC Directions, regulated entities must ensure they have no accounts in the names of any individuals/entities appearing on the circulated lists and must act on the updated designation information immediately upon receipt of this communication. The practical compliance action is to refresh sanctions screening/watchlists against the revised UNSC list and investigate any potential matches involving the amended entries without delay.
