The compliance chapter specifically covers the **Inter-Governmental Agreement (IGA) with the United States under FATCA**, with a dedicated **registration requirement**, so affected institutions must make sure their FATCA registration obligations are satisfied and maintained where applicable.

The directions further impose **human-resource and capacity-building** obligations, including a chapter on **certifications** and a specific provision on **staff rotation and audit**, which suggests compliance expectations for training/qualification records, role rotation controls, and related audit review. The document also includes a **repeal and other provisions** chapter, meaning some earlier RBI directions may be superseded or transitioned by this 2025 framework; compliance teams should therefore verify which prior instructions are repealed, amended, or carried forward. The excerpt provided does **not** include the operative text of the chapters, so specific numeric thresholds, filing deadlines, frequencies, or dates of phased implementation are not visible here; however, the effective date is tied to the **November 28, 2025** issuance unless the body of the directions states otherwise in the omitted sections.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025** establish a revised outsourcing risk-management framework for the entities covered by the directions, with the stated purpose of strengthening governance, accountability, and controls over outsourced activities, especially **outsourcing of information technology (IT) services**. The document is organized as a binding directions framework beginning with **Chapter I (Preliminary)**, which sets out the short title, commencement, applicability/scope, and definitions, followed by **Chapter II**, which assigns specific oversight responsibilities to the **Board**, and **Chapter III**, which addresses IT outsourcing in detail. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that outsourcing is not treated as a purely operational procurement matter; it is a regulated risk area requiring formal board-approved policy, senior management oversight, and defined internal control arrangements.

The document specifically requires each covered institution to have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and for the Board to retain responsibility for governance over outsourced arrangements. The Board’s role includes approving the policy and ensuring that management puts in place effective controls, while senior management is responsible for implementation and monitoring. The directions also create a structured governance framework for **outsourcing of IT services**, requiring the institution to maintain accountability for outsourced functions rather than transferring responsibility to service providers. This means the institution must be able to demonstrate oversight over the outsourced provider, the associated risks, and the control environment.

Within the IT outsourcing chapter, the directions call for an explicit **outsourcing policy**, a defined role for **senior management**, and a defined role for the **IT function** in overseeing outsourced technology arrangements. The policy is intended to govern authorization, accountability, oversight, and risk management for outsourced IT services, and the framework indicates that institutions must maintain internal ownership of the risk even where the service is performed externally. The outline of the chapter also shows a dedicated **Risk Management Framework**, signaling that institutions will need formal processes to identify, assess, mitigate, and monitor outsourcing-related risks rather than relying on ad hoc vendor management.

From the material provided, the document’s operative scope is centered on **All India Financial Institutions**, and the compliance obligation is to align outsourcing practices with the RBI’s prescribed governance and risk-management expectations. The excerpt does not provide the detailed substantive clauses beyond the chapter headings and section titles, so no specific numerical thresholds, deadlines, or rates are visible in the supplied content. However, the structure makes clear that affected institutions should expect mandatory board-level policy approval, documented management responsibilities, and formal controls around outsourced IT services as core compliance requirements under the 2025 directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “All India Financial Institutions – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025” set a consolidated conduct framework for all AIFIs, replacing the prior pre-existing directions on Fair Practices Code, loan penalties, prepayment charges, and recovery-agent conduct once these 2025 Directions became operative. The document is addressed to all All India Financial Institutions and places direct responsibility on their boards to approve, oversee, and periodically review policies and internal controls that ensure fair, transparent, and responsible customer treatment across the lending lifecycle.

AIFI boards must institutionalize governance for responsible business conduct rather than treating it as a purely operational matter. The Directions require board-approved policies on fair practices and responsible lending, effective complaint-handling and monitoring mechanisms, and clear internal accountability for ensuring compliance by branches, employees, and outsourced agents; the board is expected to review the effectiveness of these arrangements and satisfy itself that the institution’s conduct is aligned with regulatory expectations. The institution must also maintain sufficient documentation and oversight to evidence compliance with the RBI’s conduct rules.

On lending conduct, the Directions require a Fair Practices Code that makes loan terms, fees, interest, and borrower obligations transparent and non-misleading from sanction through closure. The institution must communicate sanction decisions and loan conditions clearly, avoid unfair or coercive collection practices, and ensure that loan documents and disclosures are understandable and accessible to borrowers. The document also standardizes treatment of penal charges in loan accounts: any penal charge must be reasonable, transparent, and linked to borrower non-compliance rather than being used as an additional source of income through hidden or compound charges. The RBI specifically requires that penal charges be clearly disclosed in the loan agreement and communicated at the time of sanction, and that they not be applied in a manner that is punitive, arbitrary, or opaque.

The Directions also regulate pre-payment charges on loans, requiring AIFIs to apply the RBI’s restrictions on when such charges may or may not be levied. Where pre-payment charges are prohibited under the applicable RBI framework, they cannot be imposed directly or indirectly, and institutions must ensure that product design, documentation, and collection systems do not circumvent this restriction. AIFI recovery-agent arrangements are subject to explicit conduct obligations: the institution remains responsible for the behavior of agents, must put in place controls over engagement, training, monitoring, and borrower-contact rules, and must prevent harassment, intimidation, or misrepresentation in recovery activity.

A separate miscellaneous provision requires compliance with the Supreme Court’s order dated April 30, 2025 in the matters of Pragya Prasun and Ors. v. Union of India and Ors. (W.P.(C) 289 of 2024) and Amar Jain v. Union of India and Ors. (W.P.(C) 49 of 2025), meaning affected institutions must align their practices with that judicial direction in addition to RBI’s conduct rules. The Directions also include provisions for “declaration of calamity,” under which institutions must adopt measures consistent with RBI requirements when borrowers are affected by a notified calamity, typically involving relief-oriented treatment of loan obligations and operational flexibility.

The document is dated November 28, 2025 and is marked “Updated as on July 1, 2026,” so compliance teams should treat the July 1, 2026 version as the operative text reflected in the update. It also contains repeal and saving provisions, preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework to the extent specified, while making clear that other applicable laws are not displaced by these Directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Know Your Customer (KYC) Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/335; DOR.AML.REC.No.254/14.01.011/2025-26, issued **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through December 29, 2025**) set out the KYC/AML framework applicable to covered **All India Financial Institutions**. From the table of contents alone, the document is structured to require these institutions to maintain board-approved policies and controls, define customer acceptance standards, implement risk management, perform customer identification and customer due diligence, and continue due diligence over the life of the relationship. It also specifically addresses special CDD treatment for **individuals, sole proprietary firms, legal entities, and beneficial owners**, which signals that the directions are not generic—they are intended to govern onboarding, verification, and ongoing monitoring across multiple customer types.

For compliance teams, the document’s material significance is that it appears to codify a full lifecycle KYC regime: institutions must establish a **customer acceptance policy**, a **risk management framework**, and a **customer identification procedure (CIP)** before or at onboarding, then apply **customer due diligence (CDD)** measures tailored to the nature of the customer and the risk posed. The presence of separate sections for **legal entities** and **beneficial ownership** means the institutions must look through entity structures and identify the natural persons who ultimately control or own the customer, rather than relying only on incorporation documents. The “ongoing due diligence” section indicates that KYC is not a one-time onboarding exercise; firms must periodically refresh and monitor customer information and transaction behavior over time.

The excerpt provided does **not** include the operative text of the requirements, so specific thresholds, documentary standards, periodic review frequencies, monetary limits, or exact timelines for implementation cannot be confirmed from the excerpt itself. However, the title and structure clearly indicate a binding RBI direction applicable to the covered institutions, and the updated date of **December 29, 2025** suggests compliance teams should use the consolidated version rather than the original issuance alone. In practice, a compliance officer should treat this as a directive to confirm that internal KYC/AML policies, customer onboarding workflows, beneficial ownership checks, and ongoing monitoring procedures are aligned to the final RBI text in each of the listed chapters.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“All India Financial Institutions – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025**, and this version is marked **“Updated as on April 1, 2026.”** It sets the mandatory financial-statement presentation, disclosure, accounting guidance, and consolidated prudential reporting framework for **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, so compliance teams at covered entities need to ensure their statutory financial reporting, notes to accounts, and group reporting are aligned to these directions rather than relying only on generic accounting standards.

The directions prescribe the **required balance sheet and profit and loss account format** and also govern the **preparation of consolidated financial statements**. They then provide **guidance on specific issues under certain accounting standards**, meaning AIFIs must apply RBI-prescribed interpretations or presentation rules where these directions speak to an accounting topic. The document also contains a detailed **“Notes to Accounts” disclosure regime**, organized into general presentation rules and mandatory disclosure requirements, which indicates that compliance is not limited to statement formats but extends to the content, structure, and completeness of footnote disclosures.

A separate chapter imposes **Consolidated Prudential Reporting (CPR)** requirements. For CPR, the directions specify the **scope of entities covered, the reporting frequency, the required format, and other consolidation instructions**, so relevant institutions must identify which consolidated group entities fall within RBI’s prudential consolidation perimeter and ensure the reports are prepared on the cadence and in the template mandated by RBI. Even from the table of contents alone, it is clear that this is a comprehensive reporting instruction set affecting both standalone and consolidated reporting processes, with a compliance obligation to monitor RBI-specified presentation, disclosure, and consolidation rules as of the updated effective reference date of **April 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** to create a standardized, transparent, and non-discriminatory process—consistent with natural justice—for classifying borrowers as **wilful defaulters** and for disseminating information about such defaulters so other lenders are warned and do not extend further institutional finance. The Directions are issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**, and they apply to **All India Financial Institutions** (the document’s regulated entities). The stated structure of the Directions shows they cover: the board’s role, treatment of wilful defaulters, reporting of wilful defaulters and **large defaulters**, preventive measures, auditor responsibilities, and repeal/transition provisions, with annexed reporting formats for large-defaulter lists and wilful-default data.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive change is that regulated institutions must follow the RBI’s prescribed procedure before branding a borrower a wilful defaulter, rather than using ad hoc internal classifications. The document specifically requires a **fair process** that includes principles of natural justice, and it establishes a formal mechanism to **collect and share credit information** on wilful defaulters so that lenders are cautioned against extending fresh finance. It also adds a separate reporting obligation for **large defaulters**, with a dedicated Annex I format for submitting the list of such defaulters, alongside Annex II for reporting wilful default cases.  

The Directions also assign governance responsibility to the institution’s **Board**, which must oversee the framework for identifying and handling wilful defaulters and ensure implementation of the preventive and reporting controls. In addition, the document contemplates a role for **auditors** in the preventive-control framework, indicating that compliance should not be treated only as a lending or recovery function but also as an internal-control and assurance issue. The presence of a distinct chapter on preventive measures indicates institutions are expected to maintain procedures that deter misuse of funds, detect default behavior early, and support accurate classification and reporting.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is identified as **DOR/2025-26/333** and **DOR.FIN.REC.No.252/20-16-003/2025-26**. The excerpt provided does not include the full operative commencement clause, so the exact effective date and any transition timelines cannot be confirmed from the supplied text; however, the Directions are clearly intended to take effect as the governing RBI framework for wilful-defaulter and large-defaulter treatment for all in-scope All India Financial Institutions. A compliance team should therefore review internal credit, recovery, reporting, board-governance, and audit procedures against the final text and the two annexed reporting templates to ensure the institution can identify, classify, notify, report, and share information on affected borrowers in the manner RBI prescribes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“All India Financial Institutions – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025”** (dated **November 28, 2025**, and **updated as on July 1, 2026**) sets out the RBI’s framework for how specified **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** must identify, report, and resolve borrower stress, and what additional provisioning applies if resolution is delayed or not implemented properly. In practice, the document requires covered institutions to maintain **board-approved policies** for handling stressed assets, establish processes for **early identification of stress**, make the required **disclosures**, and remain subject to **supervisory review** by RBI. The directions appear organized around a formal **review period**, an **Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA)** process where multiple lenders are involved, and a structured **resolution plan** requirement, indicating that the institution cannot simply delay action once stress is identified.

For compliance teams, the most important operational point is that the RBI is replacing ad hoc workout behavior with a prescribed, time-bound resolution framework: once an account shows signs of stress, the institution must escalate it through its internal governance process and, where applicable, coordinate with other lenders through an ICA and resolution plan. The document also introduces or reinforces **additional provisioning** consequences when there is **delayed implementation of a resolution plan**, meaning that failure to execute the required solution within the specified timeframe can create a direct capital/provisioning hit. Because the title and structure indicate applicability to **AIFIs**, compliance should assume this is relevant to RBI-regulated all-India development/financial institutions rather than ordinary commercial banks unless the institution is explicitly brought within scope elsewhere in the text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions, 2025** (updated through **July 01, 2026**) set the prudential rules that covered all-India financial institutions must follow for recognizing income, classifying assets, and making provisions. The directions apply to the institutions covered by the RBI’s definition in the document and replace/organize the framework under which they must identify non-performing assets, disclose asset quality, and maintain board-approved governance over lending and credit risk practices. The document is structured as binding directions effective from **November 28, 2025**, with later updates reflected through **July 01, 2026**.

At a compliance level, the directions require the **Board** to play a direct oversight role in prudential lending, asset classification, and provisioning policy, rather than leaving these as purely operational decisions. The institutions must also implement prudence in lending and consumer education measures and meet specified disclosure requirements, meaning compliance teams need to ensure credit policies, customer-facing communications, and reporting controls are aligned with the RBI framework. The directions are not merely accounting guidance: they govern how loans are treated when repayment weakness emerges, when income can no longer be recognized, and what provisioning must be charged against exposures that deteriorate.

The core substantive change area is **asset classification**, including the rules for when an account becomes a **non-performing asset (NPA)**, how such accounts are categorized, and how accounts can be upgraded after they are cured. The document includes detailed instructions on general asset classification, classification as NPA, accounts regularized near the balance sheet date, specific classification cases, NPA categories, and the conditions for upgradation of NPA loan accounts. Compliance officers should treat these sections as the operative rules for determining whether a credit exposure may continue to be treated as performing, what internal triggers must move it into NPA status, and how to document any subsequent regularization or upgrade.

Although the table of contents in the provided text does not show the numerical thresholds or provisioning percentages, the directions clearly contemplate a separate **Chapter IV – Provisioning Norms**, which indicates that the institutions must make provisions in accordance with RBI-prescribed standards once assets are classified as impaired or non-performing. In practice, this means compliance and finance teams need to ensure the institution’s systems, MIS, and accounting controls can automatically reflect the RBI’s recognition/classification/provisioning outcomes, including around balance-sheet date cutoffs and any special treatment for accounts that are regularized close to reporting dates. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025** under reference **DOR/2025-26/330 / DOR.LRG.REC.No.249/13-10-005/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025**. Based on the material shown, this is a new ALM and liquidity-risk framework for **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**, and it is organized to require formal board oversight, an ALM governance structure, and liquidity risk management procedures. The document’s structure indicates that it applies to AIFIs generally and covers the institution’s internal controls, reporting architecture, ALCO composition, and ALM process, rather than being a narrow one-off instruction.

At the board level, the directions require the **Board of Directors** to have explicit responsibility for ALM and liquidity risk oversight, including approving policies, setting limits, and conducting reviews. This means the board cannot treat ALM as an operational matter alone; it must formally approve the institution’s ALM framework and periodically reassess whether the policies and limits remain appropriate. Compliance teams should expect documented board approval, evidence of periodic review, and a clear allocation of responsibility to senior management for implementation.

The governance chapter requires an **ALM information system** capable of producing the data needed to manage assets, liabilities, and associated risks, along with an organized ALM function and an appropriately constituted **Asset-Liability Committee (ALCO)**. The document signals that the ALCO must be properly composed and integrated into the institution’s risk-management process, so firms will need a formal committee structure, meeting cadence, reporting lines, and escalation procedures. In practice, this typically means the institution must maintain reliable maturity-mismatch, liquidity, and cash-flow data, and use it to make management decisions rather than relying on ad hoc reporting.

The liquidity-risk chapter indicates that institutions must actively manage **liquidity risk** through a formalized process, which is likely to include monitoring cash flows, maintaining controls over funding concentrations and maturity mismatches, and establishing internal triggers for action. Although the excerpt provided does not show the detailed thresholds or ratios, the title and chapter outline make clear that the directions impose a structured liquidity-risk framework with ongoing monitoring and governance obligations. Compliance officers should therefore treat this as requiring policy updates, committee charters, reporting templates, and evidence that management regularly tests and reviews the institution’s liquidity position.

The table of contents also shows a **Chapter V on Miscellaneous** and subsequent sections beyond the excerpt, which likely contain additional operational or reporting requirements; however, the text provided does not include those details, so no specific deadlines, numerical limits, or transitional provisions can be confirmed from the excerpt alone. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the available content is that RBI is mandating a formal, board-supervised ALM and liquidity-risk regime for AIFIs, with documented governance, management information systems, committee oversight, and ongoing policy review as core obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“All India Financial Institutions – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025**. These Directions set the prudential framework for how **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** must manage their investment portfolios, covering board oversight, investment policy, portfolio classification, valuation, shifting between categories, and related operational controls. The document appears to replace or consolidate earlier investment-portfolio guidance into a single Directions-based regime, so compliance teams should treat it as the governing RBI framework for AIFI investment accounting and operations once it takes effect.

At a high level, the Directions require each covered institution to have a **board-approved investment policy** and clear internal governance for investment decisions, classification, valuation, and periodic review. The policy framework is expected to define how investments are booked into the prescribed buckets—**Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS), and Held for Trading (HFT)**—and how movements between these buckets are controlled and documented. Compliance teams should assume the RBI is emphasizing disciplined categorization at inception, consistency in valuation methodology, and board-level accountability for monitoring the portfolio rather than allowing ad hoc trading/valuation practices.

The document specifically addresses **classification of investments** and the rules for **shifting among categories**, which is significant because those decisions directly affect reported earnings, valuation treatment, and capital/risk outcomes. HTM investments are treated differently from AFS and HFT positions, and the Directions include separate valuation rules for each bucket. The presence of a dedicated chapter on shifting indicates that transfers between HTM, AFS, and HFT are not unrestricted and must be done under defined conditions and supervisory expectations, with appropriate recording and governance controls.

The valuation chapter indicates that each category has its own valuation treatment, with **HTM**, **AFS**, and **HFT** addressed separately. For compliance purposes, the material point is that institutions must not apply a single blanket valuation method across the portfolio; instead, they must value holdings in accordance with the category into which each security is classified. This creates an obligation to maintain accurate books, market-data processes, and end-of-period valuation controls so that classification and measurement remain aligned.

The table of contents also shows that the Directions include provisions on **short title and commencement, applicability, definitions, and the role of the board**, which means the document is likely meant to be operationally complete and enforceable across all relevant AIFIs from its commencement date. However, the excerpt provided does **not** include the actual commencement/effective date, any transition period, or the detailed numerical thresholds, rates, haircuts, or classification limits that may appear later in the text. A compliance officer should therefore review the full Directions for any implementation deadline, any restrictions on the percentage of securities permitted in HTM, any reclassification frequency or limits, and any specific valuation or provisioning rules that would affect accounting and regulatory reporting.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Securitisation Transactions Directions, 2025** (DOR/2025-26/328, DOR.STR.REC.247/21.04.177/2025-26) were issued on **November 28, 2025** and set out the prudential framework for securitisation transactions undertaken by **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**. The document is structured as a comprehensive rulebook covering which assets may be securitised, how much exposure the originator must retain, origination and disclosure standards, the conditions for the special purpose entity, treatment of representations and warranties, accounting requirements, and special capital-treatment rules for **simple, transparent and comparable (STC)** securitisations. The immediate compliance significance is that it governs both the structuring of new securitisation transactions and the ongoing treatment of retained and originated exposures, so affected institutions will need to review transaction structures, internal policy, and reporting/accounting processes against the RBI requirements.

For compliance teams, the key operational focus is Chapter II, which requires that only **eligible assets** may be securitised and that originators meet a **Minimum Retention Requirement (MRR)** for securitised exposures. The directions also require compliance with specified **origination standards**, prescribe how **payment priorities and observability** must be arranged, and impose a **limit on total retained exposures by originators** to prevent excessive risk concentration after securitisation. In addition, the rules address **issuance and listing** requirements, meaning the transaction documents and any securities issued in connection with the securitisation must satisfy the RBI’s prescribed conditions, and they separately require that the **special purpose entity (SPE)** used in the transaction meet defined criteria before the securitisation can be treated as compliant.

The directions further impose substantive obligations around **representations and warranties**, indicating the originator’s continuing responsibilities in relation to the securitised assets, and they include **accounting provisions** that affect how these transactions must be recognized and reported in financial statements. Chapter III introduces a separate framework for **STC securitisations** for **regulatory capital purposes**, meaning transactions that meet the STC criteria may receive specific prudential treatment, but only if they satisfy the RBI’s detailed conditions. Compliance officers should treat the document as a full regulatory framework rather than a narrow disclosure rule: it affects transaction eligibility, structuring, risk retention, documentation, entity form, and accounting treatment, and any AIFI engaging in securitisation should map its current and planned transactions to these directions before execution.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“All India Financial Institutions – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** as **DOR/2025-26/327 / DOR.STR.REC.246/21.04.048/2025-26**. The document is a consolidated prudential framework governing how **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** may **transfer loan exposures, transfer stressed loans, enter co-lending arrangements, and participate in consortium/multiple banking lending structures**. From a compliance perspective, the key point is that it establishes a single set of RBI requirements for credit risk transfer/distribution activities, replacing or superseding prior fragmented instructions, and it is structured into separate parts for **loan transfers**, **co-lending**, and **other lending/risk-sharing arrangements**.

For **loan transfers**, the Directions distinguish between **transfers of loans that are not in default** and **transfers of stressed loans**. AIFIs engaging in these transactions must follow the new general conditions and the specific rules applicable to the relevant loan category, which indicates that compliance must be assessed differently depending on whether the exposure is performing or stressed. The framework implies that institutions will need to verify the status of the exposure, apply the applicable transfer conditions, and comply with the RBI’s procedural and prudential requirements before moving exposures off balance sheet or otherwise distributing risk.

The Directions also separately regulate **co-lending arrangements**, meaning AIFIs participating in shared lending structures must comply with dedicated prudential norms under the new Part B. This signals that co-lending is not treated as a purely commercial arrangement; it is subject to RBI compliance expectations around how the arrangement is structured and monitored. In practical terms, compliance teams should review whether their institution’s co-lending documentation, allocation of credit risk, servicing arrangements, and internal controls align with the RBI’s specified prudential framework.

In addition, the Directions cover **lending under consortium and multiple banking arrangements**, indicating that risk distribution in syndicated or multi-lender lending structures is also brought within the regulatory perimeter. The document’s organization suggests that institutions involved in shared credit exposures must ensure their processes are consistent not only with loan-transfer rules but also with the rules applicable to lender-to-lender participation and risk allocation. The final part, **“Repeal and Other Provisions,”** indicates that the new Directions likely replace prior RBI guidance on these topics and may contain transition or saving provisions that compliance teams will need to identify and implement. No operative thresholds, percentages, fees, or explicit effective dates beyond the issuance date are shown in the provided excerpt, so those details would need to be confirmed from the full text and annexes before updating policies or procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and **take effect immediately upon issuance** (dated **November 28, 2025**). They apply to the five specified **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, and NaBFID**. The document replaces RBI’s concentration-risk rules for these entities with a formal framework governing how much exposure an AIFI may have to a single borrower, group, sector, or other concentrated counterparty/asset class, and it is intended to control concentration risk in the institutions’ lending and investment books.

At a high level, the Directions require AIFIs to operate under a **large exposures framework** and to observe specific prudential limits for exposures that may otherwise be permitted but remain concentration-sensitive. Compliance teams should expect the rules to define the exposure-measurement methodology, aggregation principles, and the treatment of on-balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet exposures so that related exposures are captured consistently for limit monitoring. The Directions are not limited to loans alone; they are aimed at the institution’s broader exposure profile, so any business line that creates credit or counterparty exposure must be assessed under the framework.

The document also sets out **“other permitted exposures and prudential limits”** in a separate chapter, indicating that certain exposures may be allowed if they fall within specified caps and conditions rather than being prohibited outright. For a compliance officer, the key obligation is to ensure the AIFI has internal controls, reporting, and board/senior-management oversight sufficient to identify concentration build-up before limits are breached and to manage exceptions or corrective actions in line with RBI requirements. Because the Directions are effective immediately, affected AIFIs would need to align their policies, exposure-monitoring systems, internal limits, and compliance reporting processes without waiting for a phased implementation date.

Finally, the Directions include a **repeal and other provisions** chapter, meaning prior RBI concentration-risk instructions for AIFIs are being superseded to the extent stated in the new instrument. The document’s structure also shows an **Annex I**, which likely contains technical or operational detail that may be important for implementation. Since the excerpt provided does not include the operative chapter text, the exact numerical exposure caps, sectoral thresholds, or exception criteria are not visible here; however, from the title and framework, the compliance implication is that all five AIFIs must immediately review existing exposure policies and compare them to the new RBI concentration-risk regime to identify any required limit changes, monitoring enhancements, or reporting updates.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions (Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025** are a consolidated prudential framework for AIFIs covering how credit risk must be governed, evaluated, restricted, and secured. The document states that AIFIs’ credit exposures are broad and interconnected, so the RBI is using a mix of **board-approved policies, regulatory prohibitions/restrictions, borrower identification requirements, security-interest filing requirements, and working-capital rules** to control risk. It is issued as **DOR/2025-26/325** on **November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated as on July 01, 2026**.

At a governance level, the directions require AIFIs to maintain **board-approved credit risk policies** and formal credit-risk evaluation processes. The document includes a dedicated chapter on **Credit Risk Evaluation**, indicating that institutions must assess borrower and exposure risk in a structured manner rather than relying on ad hoc underwriting. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that credit decisions and limits must be anchored in documented, board-sanctioned policies and risk assessment standards, not only business judgment.

The directions also contain a chapter on **Regulatory Restrictions**, which signals that certain credit exposures or activities are subject to RBI-imposed limits or prohibitions. Although the chapter title alone does not list every restriction in the excerpt, its placement in the framework means compliance teams should expect explicit controls on prohibited or restricted lending behaviors and ensure loan origination and portfolio monitoring systems can enforce them. The document also expressly covers **Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements for borrowers**, which means affected borrowers must be identified through LEI-based processes where applicable, so onboarding and ongoing KYC/credit administration should verify and record LEIs as required.

A separate chapter requires **filing of security interest in CERSAI** for collateral relating to **immovable property other than equitable mortgage, movable assets, and intangible assets**. That means the institution must ensure that relevant security interests are properly registered in the central registry, not merely documented internally, so that perfection and enforceability requirements are met. Compliance teams should treat this as a control obligation tied to documentation, filing, and post-disbursement tracking of security creation and registration.

The directions also address **working capital finance and revolving facilities**, indicating special prudential treatment for such products. This implies institutions must apply the RBI’s prescribed rules for structuring, monitoring, and managing drawdowns/utilization under working-capital and revolving exposures, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all credit process. Finally, the document includes a **repeal and savings** chapter and notes that **Chapter III has been deleted**, which means some prior provisions were replaced or removed and compliance teams should rely on the consolidated text rather than older circulars.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“All India Financial Institutions – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025”** (dated **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through July 1, 2026**) set out the RBI’s binding framework for how **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** must participate in the credit information ecosystem and report borrower data to **Credit Information Companies (CICs)**. The document is aimed at the AIFIs covered by the RBI’s credit reporting regime and governs both their **membership/participation obligations in CICs** and the **operational standards for reporting, correcting, updating, and using credit information**.

At a high level, the Directions require covered institutions to report credit information in the **prescribed RBI formats**, within the **specified timelines**, and to maintain ongoing quality and accuracy of the data they submit. The document also establishes procedures for handling **rejected data**, monitoring and reviewing the institution’s **Data Quality Index (DQI)**, and correcting errors in a borrower’s **Credit Information Report (CIR)** when issues are identified. In addition, it addresses how credit information may be used in **credit appraisal**, and it contains requirements for the **display of information** as well as the relationship between these Directions and any other instructions issued by RBI’s Department of Regulation.

From a compliance standpoint, the key obligation is that AIFIs must not only become and remain compliant members of the CIC framework, but must also ensure their credit reporting systems can produce accurate, timely, and complete submissions in the exact formats and with the review/rectification processes mandated by RBI. The Directions indicate that reporting is not a one-time requirement: institutions must continuously update credit information, address any rejected records, and engage with the RBI-prescribed process for data quality review and CIR correction whenever discrepancies arise. Because the document is an RBI direction, failure to comply would likely affect both regulatory compliance status and the institution’s operational ability to rely on and contribute to the credit bureau system.

The table of contents shows that the document is organized into chapters covering: **Preliminary matters (short title, commencement, applicability, definitions)**; **membership of CICs**; **credit information reporting and dissemination**; and a **Technical Working Group** section, indicating that the RBI has also contemplated governance/coordination arrangements around implementation. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that this is a comprehensive reporting and data-governance regime for AIFIs, and the institution should verify that its internal policies, vendor/system controls, reporting calendars, error-resolution workflows, and borrower dispute correction procedures align with the RBI’s prescribed standards in the full directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “All India Financial Institutions – Credit Facilities” Directions, 2025 (DOR/2025-26/323; DOR.CRE.REC.242/07-01-007/2025-26) were issued on November 28, 2025 and are marked updated through July 15, 2026. They establish a consolidated compliance framework for All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) in relation to credit facilities, with significant requirements around board governance, digital lending, project finance, real estate exposure, and other lending controls. For a compliance team, the key point is that these directions are binding operating instructions for affected AIFIs and cover both direct lending and lending conducted through digital and third-party arrangements.

A major component of the directions is the digital lending framework in Chapter III, which imposes requirements on AIFI–LSP (lending service provider) arrangements, customer protection, technology/data controls, reporting of credit information, and default-loss sharing. The directions require AIFIs to have board-approved policies governing digital lending and to ensure that customer-facing and backend processes meet RBI standards, including how digital lending apps are used, how customer consent and disclosures are handled, how data is collected and stored, and how credit information is reported. Where AIFIs use LSPs or digital lending apps (DLAs), they must ensure the arrangements are compliant, monitored, and subject to governance controls; the document also contemplates loss-sharing arrangements in the event of borrower default and sets procedural requirements for those structures.

The document also contains a dedicated chapter on project finance, indicating that AIFIs must follow RBI-prescribed rules for project lending across project phases. Although the excerpt shown does not include the substantive project-finance thresholds or tests, the structure makes clear that compliance obligations will be tied to project life-cycle stages and that AIFIs must align appraisal, disbursement, monitoring, and any restructuring/recognition practices with the prescribed framework. Because the directions are issued as a comprehensive credit-facilities code, they likely replace or supersede prior fragmented guidance in the relevant areas, so compliance teams should treat them as the controlling standard for policies, contracts, system controls, and supervisory reporting.

In practical terms, the institution should verify that its board has approved updated policies, that all digital lending partner contracts and user journeys are aligned to RBI requirements, that any credit-information reporting processes and borrower communications are compliant, and that project finance and other specialized lending books are being managed under the exact criteria and procedures in the 2025 Directions as updated through July 15, 2026. If your institution is an AIFI or uses an AIFI as a lender/financier, these directions are directly relevant; if you rely on third-party service providers for origination, underwriting support, collections, or app-based lending, those arrangements should be reviewed immediately for regulatory alignment.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions– Resource Raising Norms) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “All India Financial Institutions – Resource Raising Norms” Directions, 2025 were issued on November 28, 2025 and establish a consolidated framework for how All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) may raise resources through specified liabilities and market instruments. The document’s primary compliance impact is to replace prior RBI directions on this subject, while preserving actions already taken under the old framework to the extent they are consistent with the new Directions. It is organized around an “Umbrella Limit” (UL) for resource raising and then sets instrument-specific rules for term deposits, term money borrowings, certificates of deposit, commercial papers, and bonds.

The Directions apply to AIFIs, which are the institutions the RBI regulates under this framework, and they govern only the forms of resource raising expressly permitted in Chapter II. The document does not merely restate general principles; it prescribes the actual instruments and limits that may be used, meaning compliance teams must verify that each liability issuance or borrowing falls within the allowed instrument type and within the applicable cap or conditions under the Directions. The existence of a single umbrella limit indicates that the institution’s aggregate resource raising is controlled at a portfolio level, rather than only by instrument-by-instrument permissions.

For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is to map any planned funding activity to the specified instrument rules in the Directions: term deposits (TDs), term money borrowings, certificates of deposit (CDs), commercial papers (CPs), and bonds. Each of these categories is separately addressed, so a firm must check not only whether it is permitted to use the instrument, but also whether the instrument meets the RBI’s structural requirements and falls within the broader resource-raising framework. The Directions also make clear that other laws continue to apply unless specifically barred, so institutions must comply simultaneously with these RBI norms and any relevant securities, company law, or borrowing regulations.

The repeal-and-saving clause is important for transition management: prior RBI norms on AIFI resource raising are repealed, but anything done, action taken, or liability created under the repealed framework is generally preserved if it is not inconsistent with the 2025 Directions. Compliance teams should therefore review outstanding deposits, borrowings, CDs, CPs, and bonds that were issued under earlier rules to confirm they remain valid and operationally compliant under the new framework, especially where renewals, rollovers, or amendments are contemplated. The document excerpt provided does not include the detailed numerical caps, maturity ranges, issuance conditions, or procedural filing requirements for each instrument, so those details would need to be checked in the full text of the chapters referenced in the table of contents.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 16, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the prudential capital adequacy framework for All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) and is the governing document for how these institutions must measure, classify, maintain, and report regulatory capital. It is issued as **DOR/2025-26/321 / DOR.CAP.REC.240/21-01-002/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated through June 16, 2026**. From the table of contents alone, the document clearly covers the full capital regime, including applicability and definitions, board-approved policy requirements, scope of consolidation/application, and the detailed composition of **Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1), Additional Tier 1 (AT1), and Tier 2 capital**, as well as the specific loss-absorbency requirements for AT1 instruments at their trigger point and for all non-equity regulatory capital instruments at the point of non-viability.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this is not merely a reporting template; it is a comprehensive prudential standard that will govern which items can be counted as regulatory capital and under what conditions they remain eligible. The document expressly requires **board-approved policies** and board review of specified capital-related documents, and it establishes the **scope of application** of the capital adequacy framework, meaning the institution must determine whether the rules apply on a solo, consolidated, or otherwise defined basis as prescribed in the body of the directions. It also divides capital into **CET1, AT1, and Tier 2**, implying that the institution must monitor instrument eligibility against RBI criteria rather than relying on accounting treatment alone, and must ensure that each instrument meets the applicable permanence, subordination, loss-absorption, and other regulatory conditions.

The table of contents shows that a dedicated section addresses **minimum requirements to ensure loss absorbency** for AT1 instruments when a specified trigger is reached and for all non-equity regulatory capital instruments at the **point of non-viability (PONV)**. That means compliance must confirm that capital instruments contain the required contractual terms for write-down or conversion at trigger/PONV and that issuance documentation, investor disclosures, and internal capital management procedures align with those requirements before instruments are issued or recognized as capital. Because this is an RBI prudential framework for AIFIs, the institutions affected are the regulated all-India financial institutions within RBI’s scope, and the obligations are ongoing capital adequacy and governance obligations rather than one-time filing requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 27, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **All India Financial Institutions – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated through **April 27, 2026**) sets the framework under which **All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)** may undertake financial services directly or through subsidiaries and branches, and it replaces prior guidance subject to the document’s repeal-and-saving provisions. It applies to the entities covered by the RBI’s AIFI framework and is structured to govern both **prudential limits on investments** and the **procedure for seeking RBI approval** before expanding into financial services activities.

On the prudential side, the directions require AIFIs to follow RBI-prescribed limits and conditions for investments made in connection with financial services activities, rather than treating such activity as unrestricted. The document also establishes a formal **application process** for permission, meaning an AIFI must seek regulatory approval in the manner specified before undertaking the relevant activity, rather than proceeding solely on an internal decision. Compliance teams should treat this as a prior-approval and ongoing compliance framework, not a one-time authorization.

For group structures, the directions specifically address the **relationship with subsidiaries**, meaning any financial-services activity carried on through a subsidiary remains subject to RBI governance expectations for how the parent AIFI controls, monitors, and interfaces with that subsidiary. The directions also cover **operations of subsidiaries and branches in foreign jurisdictions and in International Financial Services Centers (IFSCs)**, so any cross-border or IFSC presence must be reviewed against the RBI’s conditions before launch or expansion. In practical terms, this means compliance must assess not only the legal entity performing the activity, but also where it is performed and whether it is through a subsidiary or branch.

The repeal-and-saving chapter indicates that earlier instructions on the subject are superseded to the extent provided in this instrument, while preserving any actions or rights saved by the RBI’s transitional language. The directions also state that **other applicable laws are not barred**, so RBI compliance does not eliminate the need to comply with company law, sectoral regulations, foreign exchange rules, securities laws, or host-country requirements where relevant. Because the text provided is only the table of contents rather than the operative clauses, the summary above reflects the document’s stated scope and structure, but not any clause-level thresholds or numerical caps beyond the issuance and update dates included in the title block.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on February 26, 2026)
rows.summary:
The document is the Reserve Bank of India’s consolidated **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025**, issued on **November 28, 2025** and shown as **updated through February 26, 2026**. It is framed under the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and is intended to regulate NBFC conduct in the public interest, including to protect investors and depositors. The table of contents shows that the directions are organized into: general preliminary provisions; miscellaneous instructions for **NBFCs in the Base Layer**; miscellaneous instructions for **NBFCs in the Middle Layer**; specific directions for **NBFC-Factors and NBFC-ICCs registered under the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011**; specific directions for **Infrastructure Debt Funds – NBFCs (IDF-NBFCs)**; and repeal/other provisions.

Based on the excerpt provided, the text clearly establishes that the directions are **binding supervisory directions** for the covered NBFC categories, but the excerpt does not yet include the substantive operational requirements, thresholds, reporting forms, or implementation dates contained later in the chapters. The only date information visible here is the issuance date (**November 28, 2025**) and the update date (**February 26, 2026**). From the material shown, the compliance significance is that an NBFC must check which layer or product category it falls into—Base Layer, Middle Layer, factoring/ICC, or IDF-NBFC—because the document is structured to impose category-specific obligations rather than one uniform rule set.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 05, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NOFHC) Directions, 2025** set out the regulatory framework for **non-operative financial holding companies that own/hold stakes in regulated financial entities**, with the directions issued on **November 28, 2025** and updated as of **December 05, 2025**. The document establishes the basics of **registration, regulatory structure, shareholding requirements, corporate governance, prudential norms, and exposure limits** for NOFHCs, and it applies to entities that fall within the RBI’s NOFHC framework under the directions’ applicability provisions.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the directions impose an RBI-supervised structure for NOFHCs, meaning affected groups must ensure the holding company is set up and maintained in the manner prescribed by RBI, including compliance with the **registration requirements** and the **shareholding framework** for the NOFHC and the entities underneath it. The document also places specific emphasis on **corporate governance at the NOFHC level**, so governance arrangements, board oversight, control mechanisms, and internal compliance processes must align with the RBI’s expectations rather than treating the NOFHC as a passive holding vehicle.

The directions further prescribe **prudential norms** for the NOFHC both **on a stand-alone basis** and **on a consolidated basis**, which means compliance is not limited to the parent holding company alone but extends to the overall group structure where consolidation is required. In addition, the document sets out **exposure norms** for both stand-alone and consolidated NOFHCs, indicating that the holding company and the group must monitor and remain within RBI-prescribed limits on exposures; compliance teams should therefore ensure aggregation, measurement, and reporting systems can track exposures at both levels. Any group using or operating through an NOFHC should review the detailed chapters on registration, governance, prudential requirements, and exposure limits to determine the exact operational restrictions and ongoing reporting obligations that apply to its structure.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under sections **45JA, 45L, and 45M of the RBI Act, 1934**, and states that the Directions are mandatory for **every NBFC-MFI**. The document is structured to regulate **registration, qualifying assets, permissible activities, prudential norms, shareholding and corporate governance, risk management, miscellaneous compliance, and repeal/transitional treatment**, with the stated policy goal of ensuring NBFC-MFIs are not conducted in a manner detrimental to investors or contrary to public interest. 

From the text provided, the Directions specifically apply to **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institutions (NBFC-MFIs)** and are intended to replace/organize prior RBI instructions through an express **repeal and other provisions** chapter. The document makes clear that it is a comprehensive regulatory framework for the sector, covering both ongoing conduct and institutional governance, rather than a narrow amendment to one rule. 

Because the excerpt ends at the beginning of Chapter I, the specific operative requirements, thresholds, ratios, deadlines, and procedural obligations are **not visible in the text supplied**. The only concrete dates and identifiers present are the **issue date (November 28, 2025)** and the circular/reference numbers **DOR/2025-26/371** and **DOR.FIN.REC.290/03-10-038/2025-26**. If you share the remaining chapters, I can produce a full compliance-focused summary including the exact asset criteria, exposure limits, governance requirements, reporting timelines, and any transition dates.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Peer to Peer Lending Platform) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Peer to Peer Lending Platform) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, to apply to **every Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) carrying on the business of a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Lending Platform**. The document is a consolidated regulatory framework issued under the RBI Act, 1934 (including sections **45IA, 45JA, 45L, and 45M**) and is intended to replace and formalize the compliance obligations for NBFC-P2P operators. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025

The directions also require **reporting and disclosures**, which means affected NBFCs should expect continuing compliance obligations to document green-deposit mobilisation, deployment, verification results, and impact metrics in a manner suitable for regulators and stakeholders. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set replaces and consolidates the conduct requirements for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) under the “Responsible Business Conduct” framework, with the document issued on **November 28, 2025** and updated through **July 1, 2026**. It applies to NBFCs covered by the RBI’s NBFC regulatory framework and is organized around board oversight, fair lending practices, customer disclosures, pricing/penalty rules, and loan servicing conduct. The compliance focus is on ensuring that NBFCs have board-approved policies and operational controls that make lending transparent, non-discriminatory, and customer-protective, especially for retail and personal lending.

A central requirement is that the **board** must approve and oversee the institution’s conduct framework, including policies that ensure fair treatment of borrowers, clear disclosures, grievance handling, and periodic review of compliance. NBFCs must maintain a **Fair Practices Code** and align loan origination and servicing with that code, meaning lending terms, communications, and recovery practices must be transparent and not misleading. The document also requires a **Key Facts Statement (KFS)** for loans and advances, so borrowers receive a standardized summary of key terms before or at disbursement, including pricing and charges; the document emphasizes that critical loan terms must be disclosed clearly and in a manner borrowers can understand.

The directions impose specific conduct rules on loan pricing and customer charges. **Penal charges** in loan accounts are regulated so that NBFCs cannot use punitive charges as a disguised interest-rate increase; such charges must be clearly disclosed and applied only for genuine non-compliance, not as a revenue substitute. The framework also addresses **reset of floating interest rates on EMI-based personal loans**, requiring NBFCs to disclose and manage resets in a way that prevents unexpected shocks to borrowers and ensures borrowers understand how their EMI, tenor, or other loan conditions may change when rates move. Similarly, the rules on **pre-payment charges** restrict or regulate charges for early repayment, with the compliance expectation that borrowers are told upfront whether prepayment is permitted and what costs, if any, apply.

The document also strengthens borrower protection at closure of a loan, especially for **personal loans**: upon **repayment or settlement**, NBFCs must promptly release the borrower’s **movable or immovable property documents** and follow a defined process for returning collateral/documents, reducing the risk of unnecessary retention after debt discharge. Separate conduct guidance applies to **lending against gold and silver collateral**, indicating that NBFCs must follow specific customer-protection and conduct standards in valuation, custody, and handling of pledged precious-metal assets. Overall, compliance teams should treat this as a borrower-conduct and disclosure regime: review board policies, loan documentation, pricing and penalty mechanics, EMI reset communications, prepayment terms, collateral release workflows, and gold/silver lending procedures to ensure they match the RBI’s prescribed conduct requirements as updated through **July 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025**, effective **November 28, 2025** and updated **as on July 1, 2026**, to require a **transparent, non-discriminatory wilful-default classification process** that follows **natural justice** and to ensure that information on wilful defaulters is shared so lenders can avoid extending further institutional finance to them. The Directions apply to **NBFCs** and are issued under RBI’s powers under **Section 45JA and Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**.

For compliance purposes, the document establishes a formal regime for identifying, classifying, reporting, and preventing wilful default within NBFCs. It also introduces requirements for handling **“large defaulters”** and provides for standardized reporting to RBI using specified annexed formats: **Annex I** for submission of the **list of large defaulters** and **Annex II** for submission of **data on cases of wilful default**. The stated policy objective is not just internal classification, but dissemination of relevant credit information so that the market is warned and additional institutional credit is not extended to such borrowers.

The document’s structure shows that compliance obligations are organized around several operational areas: the **Board’s role**, the **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting obligations for wilful and large defaulters**, and **preventive measures/auditor involvement**. This indicates that NBFCs must have board-level oversight, internal procedures for classification and escalation, reporting processes that match the RBI-prescribed formats, and controls designed to prevent misclassification or improper credit extensions to flagged borrowers.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds or procedural steps from the later chapters, the title and introduction make clear that the Directions are intended to govern both the **decision-making process for wilful-default classification** and the **subsequent reporting/dissemination obligations**. A compliance team should therefore treat these Directions as requiring a documented internal policy, fairness-oriented borrower treatment, board supervision, and timely regulatory reporting of both wilful default cases and large defaulters in the formats specified by RBI.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and noted as **updated as on July 1, 2026**) set a formal stress-resolution framework for certain NBFCs, with the main regime applying to **non-deposit-taking NBFCs with asset size of ₹500 crore or more** and to **all deposit-taking NBFCs**. The document establishes the legal structure for identifying stressed assets early, mandating board-approved resolution policies, and requiring disclosures and supervisory review by RBI. It is organized to cover definitions, governance and policy requirements, early detection and reporting of stress, and the mechanics of resolution through a review period, inter-creditor coordination, and an approved resolution plan.

For affected NBFCs, the directions require a **board-approved policy** for resolution of stressed assets and impose obligations for **early identification and reporting of stress** rather than waiting for default to become severe. The document also requires specified **disclosures** and subjects the institution’s actions to **supervisory review**, meaning compliance teams must expect RBI scrutiny of both process and outcomes. In practice, this means the NBFC must have documented internal triggers, escalation procedures, governance oversight, and reporting controls that allow stressed accounts to be identified and handled in a structured and auditable manner.

The resolution process itself is built around a defined **Review Period**, during which lenders/workout participants are expected to assess the account and finalize a workable plan. Where multiple creditors are involved, the directions require an **Inter Creditor Agreement (ICA)** so that the lenders can coordinate decision-making and implement the resolution plan consistently. The framework then contemplates a formal **Resolution Plan** that must be prepared and implemented within the regulatory process, rather than ad hoc restructuring outside the prescribed structure.

A key compliance implication is that this is not merely guidance on loan workout; it is a **prescriptive RBI directions framework** that can affect capital, provisioning, governance, and reporting obligations for covered NBFCs. Because the content provided here is a table-of-contents excerpt rather than the full operative text, no specific provisioning percentages, review-period lengths, or deadline dates can be extracted from the excerpt itself; however, the document clearly signals that those operational requirements are contained in the later chapters, including **additional provisioning** rules. Compliance teams should therefore treat the directions as immediately relevant to covered NBFCs and ensure they are reviewing the full text for the detailed triggers, timelines, provisioning norms, and any implementation deadlines tied to the July 1, 2026 updated version.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
