rows.title: Relaxation from the requirement of minimum vesting period in case of death of employee(s) under SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014
rows.summary:
This NSE communication informs all listed entities that SEBI has issued Circular No. **SEBI/HO/CFD/DCR2/CIR/P/2021/576 dated June 15, 2021** on **“Relaxation from the requirement of minimum vesting period in case of death of employee(s) under SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014.”** The notice itself does not set out the full operative rule change, but it clearly indicates that SEBI has granted a relaxation to the usual **minimum vesting period** requirement when an employee covered by a share-based employee benefit arrangement dies.

The practical compliance implication is that listed companies administering employee share plans under the **SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014** should review their plan rules and internal procedures so that vesting treatment on an employee’s death follows the SEBI circular rather than any default minimum vesting timeline. The circular is addressed to **all listed entities**, so any company with SEBI-governed share-based employee benefit schemes may be affected.

The document is dated **June 16, 2021** and states that the SEBI circular is enclosed for information and necessary action, with a copy also available on the **NSE website**. No numeric thresholds, percentage limits, or other deadlines are mentioned in this NSE covering letter beyond the dates of the SEBI circular and the NSE communication.

rows.title: Guidance note on communications by Listed Entities
rows.summary:
This guidance note, issued by NSE on 11 June 2021 under confidential reference NSE/CML/2021/18, applies to all listed companies and is aimed at how they communicate publicly through the Exchange website/platform and other disclosures. It reminds listed entities that they often publish performance updates, awards and recognition, leadership claims, and interview-based statements by key managerial personnel or other representatives about prospects or future plans, but that stakeholder protection remains paramount and such communications must not compromise market integrity.

The core requirement is that no price-sensitive information may be disclosed to the public unless it has first been disclosed to the stock exchanges. In addition, any public statement made by the listed entity must be truthful, fair, evidence-based, and not manipulative, deceptive, distorted, untrue, or misleading; the entity must not make unsubstantiated promises or forecasts. Communications must also be written in clear, concise, understandable, simple, and easy-to-understand language, avoiding excessive technical, legal, or otherwise complex wording.

If the company presents financial data, it must include corresponding data for the past three years, and that disclosure must cover sales, gross profit, net profit, share capital, reserves, earnings per share, dividends, debts, and book values. The note also says companies should provide a link to the company’s website where the underlying details are available and can be verified. Finally, the level of detail must be adequate and appropriate so that investors are not misled or distracted by incomplete or promotional presentation.

rows.title: Format of compliance report on Corporate Governance by Listed Entities
rows.summary:

Its subject is the “Format of compliance report on Corporate Governance by Listed Entities,” and the practical action for compliance teams is to review and follow the SEBI circular it encloses, because it announces the required format for corporate governance compliance reporting by listed companies. The letter itself does not set out the substantive reporting fields or thresholds, nor does it specify any new implementation date beyond the SEBI notification date; it simply confirms that the SEBI circular is enclosed and available on the NSE website for necessary action.

For a corporate compliance team, the key takeaway is that this communication applies to all listed entities and is aimed at ensuring they use the updated SEBI-prescribed compliance report format for corporate governance disclosures. Because the letter does not reproduce the actual form or filing instructions, any operational changes, reporting frequency, certification requirements, or revised disclosure obligations would need to be taken directly from the attached SEBI circular dated 31 May 2021. The notice is informational in tone, but it clearly signals that listed entities should treat the SEBI circular as requiring compliance action.

rows.title: Relaxation from compliance to REITs and InvITs due to the CoVID -19 virus pandemic

For compliance purposes, the material point is that REITs and InvITs should review the SEBI circular dated 14-May-2021 to determine what compliance requirements have been temporarily relaxed because of the pandemic and what actions, if any, are still required. This NSE communication does not specify any deadlines, thresholds, reporting dates, or affected obligations on its own, and it does not impose a separate substantive requirement beyond alerting the affected entities to the SEBI relaxation and directing them to take appropriate action based on the enclosed circular.

rows.title: Business responsibility and sustainability reporting by listed entities

rows.title: Comprehensive FAQs and Compilation of informal guidance- SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (Period October 2015 - March 2021)
rows.summary:

Specifically, it points compliance teams to two SEBI publications: **“Comprehensive FAQs on SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015” dated 29-Apr-2021** and **“Compilation of Informal Guidance Relating to SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 for the period Oct 2015–Mar 2021” dated 03-May-2021**.

The practical compliance takeaway is that listed entities should **review these SEBI clarifications and align internal insider-trading controls, policies, and interpretations accordingly**, because the documents consolidate SEBI’s responses to common questions and informal guidance issued over the stated period. The circular does not specify a filing deadline, reporting threshold, or penalty change; its operative effect is to **direct listed companies and their company secretaries/compliance officers to use the referenced SEBI FAQs and guidance as current reference material** for PIT compliance.

The notice also provides the **official SEBI URLs** for the two documents and states that copies are enclosed and available on the **NSE website**. In short, the document is an informational dissemination from NSE for **all listed companies**, alerting them that SEBI has published updated PIT-related FAQs and informal guidance that should be consulted for compliance interpretation from that point forward.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI Gazette Notification, issued in Hyderabad on 22 January 2024 and published in the Gazette of India on 23 January 2024, **de-notifies the arbitration clause in all tariff products** for **Fire, Motor, Engineering, Workmen’s Compensation, and other classes of insurance business**. The legal basis cited is **Section 64-ULA(1) of the Insurance Act, 1938**. In practical terms, the Authority is removing the continuing applicability of the arbitration-clause provisions that had been carried forward into tariff-era policy wordings.

The notification explains that after the **withdrawal of tariffs by the Tariff Advisory Committee in 2006**, IRDAI had issued **Notification No. 034/IRDA/De-Tariff/Dec-06 dated 4 December 2006**, which stated that the tariff general regulations—except rating-related provisions—and the associated **terms, conditions, clauses, warranties, policy wording, and endorsement wording** for then-tariffed classes such as Fire, Engineering, Motor, and Workmen’s Compensation would continue to apply **until further orders**. This new 2024 notification is the “further order” that specifically removes the arbitration clause from those continued tariff general regulations and related wording.

For compliance purposes, affected insurers and intermediaries should treat this as a **change to policy documentation and claims/dispute-resolution language** in the covered tariff product lines. Any policy wordings, endorsements, clauses, warranties, or general regulations that still carry an arbitration clause by virtue of the 2006 de-tariff continuation should be reviewed and updated to reflect that the arbitration clause has now been de-notified. The document does not specify a phased implementation, transitional period, monetary threshold, or separate effective-date condition beyond the notification date itself, so compliance teams should assume the change is effective from the date of the notification unless internal legal review identifies a different statutory interpretation.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI notification, issued on 30 January 2023 under Section 101A(2) and (4) of the Insurance Act, 1938 with Central Government approval, sets the obligatory cession requirements for the financial year 2023–24. It applies to Indian Re-insurers and other insurers that fall within Section 101A, and requires that 4% of the sum insured on each general insurance policy attaching during 1 April 2023 to 31 March 2024 be reinsured as obligatory cession with the Indian Re-insurer(s), with the full mandatory cession to be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re). The notification also states that, for cessions made during the period 1 April 2023 to 31 March 2024, there is no limit on the sum insured for purposes of applying the cession requirement. It then sets out differentiated cession percentages for certain insurer categories/reinsurance arrangements referenced in the text, including rates of 5%, 10%, 7.50%, 15%, 50%, 2%, and 78%/14% for specified classes shown in the schedule/clauses, so compliance teams should check the exact category mapping against the notification’s table and underlying section references rather than assume a single uniform rate applies in all cases. In practical terms, this requires affected insurers to ensure their general insurance policies attaching in FY 2023–24 are identified correctly, the mandatory 4% cession is calculated and placed with GIC Re, and any terrorism or nuclear pool premium is excluded from the obligatory cession calculation.

The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Insurance Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2022**, notified in the Official Gazette on **6 December 2022** and stated to come into force **on the date of publication**. The amendment is made under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDA Act, 1999, and its stated policy purpose is to **broaden customer choice and access to insurance products through different distribution channels** and to **improve insurance reach and penetration across the country**.

Substantively, the amendment revises the existing **Insurance Intermediaries Regulations, 2016** by altering the provisions dealing with the conduct and functioning of intermediaries. The extracted text indicates changes to **Regulation 19**, specifically **sub-regulation 19(3)**, and to the associated **Form / Schedule structure** used for intermediary permissions or reporting. It also refers to inserted or modified language around the treatment of **“exclusive” and “composite”** intermediary status, suggesting the rules governing the types of intermediary arrangements that can be approved or maintained have been updated.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this is not a purely cosmetic amendment: it changes the regulatory framework that governs how insurance intermediaries operate and how they may distribute insurance products. Any insurer or intermediary relying on the 2016 framework should review whether the revised **Regulation 19(3)** and the updated form/schedule requirements affect their current authorizations, product distribution model, filings, or contractual arrangements. Because the amendment took effect immediately upon Gazette publication, there is **no deferred implementation date stated in the text provided**, so compliance review should be treated as current and immediate.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Other Forms of Capital) Regulations, 2022 were notified by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India on 5 December 2022 and are framed under section 114(2)(i) of the Insurance Act, 1938. They apply to insurers under the Insurance Act, 1938 and define the various “other forms of capital” that can be used by insurers, with the regulations expressly distinguishing the permitted capital instruments and the circumstances in which they may be recognized for regulatory purposes.

A key compliance point is that the regulations set out detailed definitions and treatment for different instruments, including “other forms of capital,” “ordinary shares,” and “preference shares,” and then specify how capital can be counted depending on characteristics such as whether it is paid up, redeemable, cumulative, convertible, or otherwise structured. The document also introduces a specific formula for recognition/quantification of one category of capital based on the amount subscribed and the percentage of qualifying capital treatment, with the text showing a graduated scale that ranges from 0% to 100% depending on the applicable tier. It further states that only certain instruments issued by insurers and meeting the prescribed conditions are eligible to be treated as other forms of capital, so legal/entity structuring and instrument terms will matter for capital recognition.

The regulations also impose governance-related requirements on insurers regarding the issuance and use of these instruments, including conditions around approvals and the nature of the instrument holders/investors. The text references thresholds and conditions that are material for compliance review, including a numerical cap of 50 and provisions tied to whether amounts are “fully paid” or otherwise qualify under the prescribed treatment. There is also a reference to a 20% adjustment in one formula example, indicating that the capital recognized may be reduced or scaled based on the specified regulatory method rather than being fully credited.

In addition, the regulations amend or interact with earlier IRDAI rules, including the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Registration of Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015, and prior capital-related rules from 2015/2016/2002 as referenced in the definitions and transitional provisions. They therefore matter not only for new capital issuances going forward but also for assessing whether existing instruments, company structures, or planned fundraising instruments continue to qualify under the updated framework. Compliance teams should treat this as a capital-structuring and regulatory-recognition rule set: any insurer issuing or classifying capital outside ordinary equity must test the instrument against these definitions, the formula-based recognition rules, and the applicable approval/eligibility conditions under the 2022 regulations.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued a notification on 5 August 2021, under Section 25(1) of the IRDA Act, 1999 and Regulation 3A of the Insurance Advisory Committee (Meetings) Regulations, 2000, to **reconstitute the Insurance Advisory Committee (IAC)**. The reconstituted committee is **effective from 10 August 2021**.

The notification replaces the committee’s membership with a new list of representatives from across the insurance sector and related bodies. The members expressly named in the excerpt include the **Chairperson of Life Insurance Corporation of India**, the **Chairman-cum-Managing Director of The Oriental Insurance Company Limited**, the **Chairman-cum-Managing Director of General Insurance Corporation of India**, the **Chief Executive Officer of Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance Company Limited**, the **Chief Executive Officer of ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Limited**, the **Chairman-cum-Chief Executive Officer of Star Health & Allied Insurance Company Limited**, the **Director of the National Insurance Academy**, the **President of the Institute of Actuaries of India**, the **Secretary General of the Insurance Institute of India**, the **President of the Insurance Brokers’ Association of India**, the **President of the Indian Institute of Insurance Surveyors & Loss Assessors**, and the **Insurance Ombudsman** (the text continues beyond the excerpt).

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that IRDAI has formally changed the composition of the statutory advisory committee that supports the regulator under the 1999 Act. Any internal references, committee liaison arrangements, stakeholder engagement, or regulatory tracking processes that depend on the IAC’s membership should be updated to reflect the new constitution as of **10 August 2021**. There are **no monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or operational compliance requirements** imposed on insurers or intermediaries in the portion provided; the document is a governance/reconstitution notice rather than a substantive rule change.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 amend several existing IRDAI regulations for Indian insurance companies, with the changes notified on 7 July 2021 and published in the Gazette on 8 July 2021. The amendments mainly update references and operative provisions in multiple older regulations, including the IRDAI (Registration of Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2000, the IRDAI (Issuance of Capital by Indian Insurance Companies transacting other than life insurance business) Regulations, 2015, and the IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) Amendment Regulations, 2015, as well as related forms and numbering cross-references. From a compliance perspective, the document is largely a technical amendment package, but it does change specific regulatory requirements and internal filing/approval references that insurers must follow in the affected regulations.

A key substantive change is to Regulation 5 of the 2000 registration regulations: the amended text now requires that an Indian insurance company seeking registration must comply with the amended capital/structure condition set out in the new wording of Regulation 5, including the revised thresholds and conditions reflected by the substituted provisions. The amendment also revises the provision that previously referred to the issuance of capital by Indian insurers, updating the regulatory language so that the relevant capital issuance rule now cross-references the amended Regulation 5 and associated sub-clauses. In addition, the notification inserts a new Regulation 31 in the 2021 framework stating that the provisions of Regulation 5, as amended in 2021, apply to the relevant companies from the amendment date, and ties compliance to the updated capital/registration conditions rather than the earlier text.

The amendment also makes several targeted drafting changes to other regulations and forms: Regulation 16 and Regulation 17 of the 2000 registration regulations are updated by substituting the references to the underlying 2000 regulation text; Regulation 5(2)(vi) in the 2015 amendment regulations is revised; Regulation 7 in the same set is updated to refer to the correct form/filing requirement; and Regulation 13 is amended to reflect the 2015 amendment language in the correct cross-reference format. Parallel amendments are made again in the separate 2015 capital-issuance amendment instrument, repeating the update to Regulation 5(2)(vi), Regulation 7, and Regulation 13. These changes mean compliance teams should ensure that internal policies, application templates, board papers, and filing checklists cite the updated regulation numbers and form references, because the old citations have been displaced.

No new standalone reporting deadline is stated in the excerpt, but the effective date is the publication date of the amendment notification, 7 July 2021, with the Gazette publication on 8 July 2021. The practical compliance obligation is to apply the amended version of the cited regulations immediately for any registration, capital issuance, or related filing activity governed by those provisions after commencement, and to verify that any pending or planned transactions are tested against the revised capital/registration wording rather than the superseded text.

rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) issued the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2021** on **19 May 2021** (G.S.R. 337(E)), after publishing draft amendments on **13 April 2021** and inviting public comments for **15 days**; the government states that comments received were considered before finalization. The amendments are made under **section 114(2)(aaa)** read with **section 2(7A)(b)** of the **Insurance Act, 1938**, and they amend the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015**.

The key substantive change is to **Rule 4** of the 2015 rules, which now sets out the foreign-investment framework for Indian insurance companies in more specific terms. The amended rule provides that a foreign investment in an Indian insurance company is permitted **in accordance with the limits and conditions specified in the Insurance Act, 1938, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India Act, 1999, and the rules/regulations made under those laws**, and it also requires compliance with the conditions laid out in **Rule 9** of the 2015 rules. In practical compliance terms, this means insurers and investors must ensure that any foreign investment structure, ownership level, and related approvals are checked not only against the amended foreign investment rules but also against the insurance-specific statutory and regulatory framework.

The amendment also makes **editorial/technical updates** to the 2015 rules by substituting certain references and definitions in **Rules 2, 3, 5, and 8**, including an update in Rule 8 to refer to the **Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (42 of 1999)**. The document does **not** introduce a new numeric foreign-ownership percentage in the text provided; rather, it ties permissible foreign investment to the existing insurance-law conditions and the associated regulatory requirements. The amendment rules took effect upon publication in the Official Gazette on **19 May 2021**.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI notification sets the **obligatory cession requirement for financial year 2021–22** under **Section 101A of the Insurance Act, 1938**, and applies to **Indian reinsurers and other insurers to whom Section 101A applies**. For every **General Insurance Policy** with insurance attaching during the period **1 April 2021 through 31 March 2022**, insurers must cede **5% of the sum insured** to the Indian reinsurer, with two explicit exceptions: **terrorism premium** and **premium ceded to the Nuclear Pool**, for which the obligatory cession is **NIL**. The notification also states that the **entire obligatory cession must be placed only with General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC Re)**, not distributed among multiple reinsurers.

The document then sets out compliance mechanics for how the cession is to be handled. It says there is **no limit on the sum insured** for policies subject to cession, and the cession is to be applied according to the specified proportional rules in the notification (the text indicates a cession framework linked to the policy’s subject matter and premium treatment, rather than a blanket exclusion by size). Because this is a statutory notification issued by IRDAI with Central Government approval, affected insurers should ensure their underwriting, treaty/facultative placement, premium allocation, and reporting processes reflect the **5% obligatory cession to GIC Re for the 2021–22 underwriting period**, while excluding the identified categories where cession is expressly nil.

IRDAI has upgraded its Business Analytics Platform (BAP) and migrated several reinsurance-related regulatory and approval workflows into the new integrated BAP portal. The migration covers the reinsurance regulatory returns, Reinsurance Summary Formats (both Advance and Final), applications for File Reference Numbers (FRNs) for Cross Border Reinsurers (CBRs), and applications relating to the appointment and remuneration of the Chairperson/CEO of reinsurers and Foreign Reinsurer’s Branches (FRBs). The document specifies the following filing commencement points: Reinsurance Regulatory Returns from FY 2024–25, Corporate Governance Returns from FY 2025–26, Pool Administrator Returns from FY 2024–25, and Reinsurance Programme Summary Returns Final/Reinsurance Summary Formats as applicable through the upgraded platform. It also states that FRN applications for CBRs and the Chairperson/CEO appointment and remuneration applications are now available on the BAP portal for use.

For compliance teams, this means the operational filing channel has changed and internal reporting calendars, workflow ownership, and access permissions should be updated to ensure these submissions are made in the correct system for the relevant financial years. The circular does not set a separate deadline date for filing in the text provided, but it clearly makes the BAP portal the required platform for the migrated reinsurance functions going forward.

IRDAI has issued a circular dated 27 August 2026 permitting insurers to invest in **“Onshore Rupee Bonds” / Maharajah INR Bonds issued by the New Development Bank (NDB)** as part of insurers’ **approved investments**. NDB has proposed to raise **INR 25,000 crores over a five-year period**, and the stated use of proceeds is **general corporate purposes**, specifically to support **financing/onward lending for sustainable development, sustainable infrastructure, and green/social projects in India**.

The circular states that these bonds are treated as **“securities” under the Securities Contracts (Regulations) Act, 1956**, so they may be held by insurers subject to the usual insurance-investment framework. However, the permission is conditional: the bonds must comply with any **Government of India norms** applicable to them, any **public issue must be duly approved by SEBI**, and insurers must continue to comply with **Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938** when investing.

IRDAI also requires that the bonds satisfy the **rating criteria for “Approved Investments” under Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment functions of insurers) Regulations, 2024**, as amended from time to time. If SEBI exempts the requirement for ratings from SEBI-registered rating agencies because the bonds already have a rating from an **international rating agency**, that exemption can be relied on only to the extent permitted by the regulatory framework. In practical terms, compliance teams should confirm before investing that the issuance has the required approvals, any applicable rating condition is met or validly exempted, and the investment fits within all existing insurer investment limits and statutory conditions.

The circular also clarifies that it is issued under **Section 14(2)(h) of the IRDA Act, 1999** and is limited to fulfilling ISP data requirements; it does **not** change the disclosure requirements or the preparation of financial statements under the **Insurance Act, 1938** or the **IRDA Act, 1999**.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued Circular No. IRDAI/NL/GDL/98(01)/07/2026 dated 31 July 2026 to all CEOs/CMDs of insurance companies, including life and standalone health insurers, in response to floods that began on 19 July 2026 and caused widespread damage in four Assam districts: Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat, which were declared a natural disaster area. The circular requires insurers to take immediate steps to reduce hardship for affected policyholders and to accelerate claim registration and settlement, rather than treating the event as a routine claims situation.

Insurers must mobilize all available resources, including surveyors and investigators, and appoint senior Nodal Officers to supervise claim handling in the affected areas. The appointment of the Nodal Officer must be communicated immediately to the Chief Secretary, and district-level claims may be managed through a designated District Claims Service Head. Insurers must also activate and publicly advertise 24x7 customer support helplines to assist claimants, and they are required to run an extensive awareness campaign describing the measures being taken.

The circular further requires insurers to publish the contact details of the district heads on their websites and to provide additional publicity through press and digital media. Claims handling in the affected districts is to be routed through special, empowered district desks to ensure prompt service. In substance, the compliance obligation is immediate operational escalation: insurers serving policyholders in these four districts must promptly staff, publicize, and streamline their claims operations to speed up processing and settlement for flood-related losses.

The IRDAI has issued a circular dated **July 23, 2026** addressed to **all insurers except reinsurers** requiring faster and more complete responses to the **Office of the Insurance Ombudsmen (IOs)** when complaints are being examined. The regulator says it has observed that insurers are often delaying submission of the **Self-Contained Note (SCN)**, supporting documents, and any additional information requested by the Ombudsman offices, and that responses are frequently being sent in pieces and after long delays, which is causing delays in complaint disposal for policyholders/beneficiaries.

The circular ties this requirement directly to the **Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017**, particularly **Rule 15(2)**, under which documents called for by the IO must be furnished, and **Rule 17(4)**, which contemplates that a complaint be decided within **90 days of receipt of all required material from the complainant**. IRDAI states that the SCN and follow-up information/documents are necessary for the IO to examine the facts and reach a conclusion, and that insurers must provide them promptly to support timely resolution and the intended functioning of the ombudsman process.

As a compliance requirement, the Authority directs insurers to **submit the required SCNs duly supported by relevant documents**, and to ensure that information/documents sought by the IO are provided in a timely and complete manner rather than in multiple delayed tranches. The practical compliance expectation is that insurers should treat Ombudsman requests as time-sensitive case materials and avoid piecemeal production, since delay or incomplete submissions are specifically identified as obstructing the 90-day decision framework under the Rules.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **14 July 2026** and addressed to **all insurers**, provides additional clarifications on the **implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)**, building on **Circular No. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/45/4/2026 dated 1 April 2026**. The regulator says the clarifications were issued in response to insurer representations and are intended to ensure **consistent implementation** of the framework, specifically on the **role of the Appointed Actuary**, **independent validation**, and the preparation of **Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation purposes**.

For the **Appointed Actuary**, the circular clarifies that under **Clauses 6 and 7 of Part II of Schedule I of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, the Appointed Actuary must provide **actuarial expertise** for the preparation of financial statements in accordance with applicable Ind AS. The document indicates this includes participating in key actuarial judgments and assumptions used in financial reporting, but the actuary’s role is not to replace management’s responsibility for the financial statements; instead, the actuary supports the insurer in ensuring the actuarial bases and related disclosures are appropriate, supportable, and consistent with the standards.

The circular also addresses **independent validation** of the Ind AS transition/reporting process. It requires insurers to have the relevant Ind AS-related assessments, assumptions, and outputs subject to an independent validation mechanism so that the resulting numbers and disclosures are reliable for financial statement preparation and, where applicable, for consolidation. The document further clarifies the treatment of **Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation purposes**, indicating that insurers must prepare or align financial information in a manner that supports consolidation reporting under the applicable standards and regulatory expectations, rather than relying on ad hoc or inconsistent adjustments.

A key timing point in the circular is the reference to the **2026–27 and 2027–28** periods, indicating that the clarified requirements are tied to the upcoming phased implementation/transition timetable for Ind AS reporting. The circular also refers to **“1 August 2026”** in connection with these implementation clarifications, signaling an effective date or operational reference point from which insurers should apply the clarified approach. Finally, the document points back to the existing regulatory framework under the **IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, so compliance teams should treat these clarifications as a required interpretive overlay to the current Ind AS implementation regime, with direct implications for actuarial coordination, validation controls, and consolidation reporting processes.

This IRDAI circular, dated **8 July 2026** and issued to **all insurers and reinsurers**, updates the prescribed **formats for publishing quarterly financial results** to stock exchanges under **SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015**. It is responding to changes caused by the **adoption of Ind AS by insurers**: for listed insurers that must prepare financial statements under Ind AS, the existing reporting formats needed revision, so IRDAI has now issued updated templates for **unaudited and audited quarterly financial results** for **life insurers, general insurers, health insurers, and reinsurers**. The circular states that these updated formats are applicable to all listed entities in those categories that are required to report under Ind AS, and they specifically cover the financial results submitted to stock exchanges.

The circular requires quarterly results to be presented in the format in **Annexure I**, with **segment-wise revenue, results, and capital employed** to be reported along with the quarterly results in the format in **Annexure II**. It also references a further prescribed format in **Annexure III**, with additional disclosure requirements in **Annexure IV** and a format linked to **Regulation 47(1)(b) of the LODR Regulations, 2015** in **Annexure V**. In other words, compliance is not just about the main financial statements; insurers/reinsurers must use the updated IRDAI templates for the full quarterly stock-exchange filing package, including segment reporting and any required published disclosures.

A key exception is noted for insurers that were **granted forbearance for Ind AS implementation for FY 2026–27**: those entities are treated differently for the period covered by the forbearance, while the updated formats apply to everyone else who is under Ind AS. The circular also refers back to IRDAI’s earlier guidance issued under circulars dated **25 March 2016** and **30 January 2017**, indicating that those prior requirements remain relevant insofar as they are incorporated or superseded by the new formats. No specific filing deadline is newly introduced in the text provided, but the effective compliance expectation is immediate for the relevant **FY 2026–27 quarterly reporting cycle** and onward for covered insurers/reinsurers.

The key operational deadline is now **31 August 2026 unless the amended regulations are notified sooner**, in which case the transitional arrangements end on that notification date. rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 25.05.2026 (Ref. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/72/5/2026), updates how insurers must determine and disclose remuneration for Key Management Persons (KMPs) under the IRDAI (Corporate Governance for Insurers) Regulations, 2024. It is issued in the context of amendments made to the 2024 Corporate Governance Regulations on 21.03.2024 and the related circular of 22.05.2024, and it specifically revises Regulation 8.3 and Regulation 9.2, including the definition of “remuneration” and the disclosure mechanics for KMP pay.

The circular requires insurers to classify KMP remuneration into two distinct parts: fixed remuneration and variable remuneration, and to apply the updated definitions in Regulation 9.2. The fixed portion is treated as the guaranteed/non-variable element, while the variable portion is linked to performance and other specified criteria; the document also clarifies that remuneration may include various components such as salary, allowances, perquisites/benefits, bonuses, commissions, deferred pay, and performance-linked payouts depending on the structure used. For 2026–27, the circular introduces a new disclosure format under Regulation 8.3 that requires reporting remuneration in the specified segmented manner, rather than only as a total figure, so that the regulator can separately see fixed and variable components and other prescribed elements.

The document also sets out the disclosure template and aggregation logic insurers must use. It requires disclosure of remuneration for KMPs in categories/rows that capture different forms of pay and benefits, with specific line items and formulas for calculating totals, including a reference to an aggregate “total remuneration” calculation and a separate split of fixed and variable pay. The circular indicates that the disclosure must cover the relevant KMP population and must be presented in the prescribed format for the 2026–27 reporting cycle, implying insurers need to align internal HR/payroll and governance reporting processes so that the required data is captured in a compliant, auditable manner.

A further operational requirement is that the updated remuneration reporting should distinguish fixed pay from variable pay using the regulator’s specified percentages/thresholds and calculation method, including the explicit treatment of variable pay as subject to conditions and caps reflected in the amended regulation and format. Where the circular references proportions such as 50%, 10%, 90%, 15/30/60, and similar figures, these are the prescribed breakdowns and/or limits used in the new disclosure and remuneration treatment framework, so insurers must map their compensation structures to those limits before filing. In practical terms, this means insurers must review KMP employment contracts, bonus plans, and governance approvals to ensure the remuneration structure, classification, and reporting align with the revised IRDAI rules before the 2026–27 reporting submission.

The key legal change is that an intermediary’s registration now remains in force **subject to payment of the annual fee specified by regulation**, unless the Authority suspends or cancels the registration; because SLAs have a distinct operating and fee framework, IRDAI is providing transition rules specific to them. The circular is issued in continuation of the earlier IRDAI circular **Ref. IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026** on transitional arrangements for payment of annual fee and issuance of CoR for intermediaries.

For SLAs, the circular establishes a transition period: **from 5 April 2026 through 30 June 2026**, the annual fee to be paid is the **existing fee plus 18% GST**, and the circular gives the resulting amounts in its table: **category 1 = ₹400 plus ₹72 GST = ₹472**, and **category 2 = ₹2,000 plus ₹360 GST = ₹2,360**. This means SLAs must pay the fee in this interim window using the pre-revision fee structure with GST added, rather than waiting for any revised fee framework. The circular also states that **from 5 April 2026 onward, and specifically “effective 5 April 2026”**, the annual fee must be paid **in the manner prescribed under the 2015 regulations**, indicating that payment and related compliance should be aligned with the regulatory method referenced there.

From a compliance perspective, the document requires SLAs to ensure timely annual fee payment during the transition period so their registration continues uninterrupted under the amended Section 42D framework. It does not describe a new filing form or additional procedural checklist, but it does make clear that the fee payment obligation is now tied to the continued validity of registration and that the transitional pricing applies only until **30 June 2026**. Compliance teams should therefore verify which SLA registrations fall into the two fee categories, apply the correct GST-inclusive amount for the transition period, and ensure internal renewal/registration calendars are updated to reflect the **7 April 2026 circular**, the **5 April 2026 effective date**, and the **30 June 2026 end of the transitional arrangement**.

The circular applies to all categories of insurance intermediaries, including insurance brokers, corporate agents, insurance marketing firms (IMFs), web aggregators, common service centres (CSCs), insurance surveyors and loss assessors, insurance repositories, third party administrators (TPAs), and any other entities registered as insurance intermediaries under applicable regulations. The key compliance change is that intermediaries must now pay the annual fee on the new timeline specified by the circular: the fee is due for the period from 5 February 2026 to 30 June 2026, and the transitional arrangement appears to standardize the first post-amendment fee cycle around that period. The circular also sets transitional instructions for issuance of the Certificate of Registration during this period, indicating that registrations and related processes are to be handled under the amended Section 42D regime rather than the pre-amendment framework. The document refers to sub-section (4A) of Section 42D as the legal basis for these directions, so compliance teams should treat the circular as mandatory implementation guidance, not just background commentary.

From a practical compliance perspective, affected intermediaries should confirm whether their annual fee payment and registration certificate issuance actions fall within the 5 February 2026 to 30 June 2026 transition window and align internal renewal/filing calendars accordingly. Because the circular is issued “in exercise of the powers” under the amended law, failure to follow the new timing or certificate-issuance process could affect the validity or continuity of registration. The document does not provide the full detailed operational steps in the excerpt shown, but it clearly establishes that the annual-fee and registration-certification process has been reset by the SBSR Act amendment and must be followed by all registered intermediary classes listed above.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a clarification circular on insurers’ investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), dated 12/02/2026, to explain how the existing investment restrictions in para 1.5 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers (dated 17 May 2024) should be applied. The circular restates the existing baseline rule that insurers may invest only through Fund of Funds (FoFs) that comply with Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938, and that the FoF’s offer documents must contain a clause preventing the FoF from investing into AIFs that themselves invest in overseas companies or overseas funds; it also restates that AIFs used by insurers must not invest in securities of companies incorporated outside India, and that an insurer cannot invest in an AIF if that AIF has exposure to a FoF in which the insurer already has an exposure.

The new clarification is issued because insurers had sought guidance on two issues: the treatment of AIF structures with “excuse rights” and the applicable investee limits for direct and indirect exposure through FoFs. IRDAI says that compliance with the conditions set out in the circular will be treated as satisfying sub-paras 4(b), 4(c) and 5 of para 1.5 of the Master Circular, thereby broadening the investment avenues available to insurers while keeping the Section 27E restrictions intact. From the text provided, the circular specifically focuses on how insurers can participate in AIFs without violating the prohibition on overseas exposure and without creating prohibited circular exposure through FoFs, but the excerpt ends before the detailed operative conditions are fully visible. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a formal interpretive update to the existing AIF investment framework, effective from the date of the circular itself unless the full text states otherwise, and review current and planned AIF/FoF investments for compliance with the Section 27E-related restrictions, the no-overseas-investment requirement, and the prohibition on layered exposure where the insurer is already invested in a connected FoF.

This IRDAI circular dated 6 January 2026 directs all insurers and insurance intermediaries to implement TRAI’s mandatory 1600-series dialing requirement for consumer-facing service and transactional voice calls. It references TRAI’s direction dated 16 December 2025, issued under section 13 read with section 11(1)(b)(i) and (v) of the TRAI Act, 1997, and states the purpose is to curb unsolicited commercial communication (UCC), prevent impersonation-based fraud, and improve consumer trust.

The key operational requirement is that all service and transactional voice calls to consumers must be moved to numbers allocated under the 1600-series, and this adoption must be completed by 15 February 2026. After that date, insurers and intermediaries must not originate service or transactional voice calls from any number outside the 1600-series, even if they believe they have explicit or implied customer consent to do so. The circular makes clear that compliance is not optional or consent-based: the restriction applies regardless of customer consent.

The document also warns of enforcement consequences. Any UCC complaint against an entity that fails to comply may trigger action under TRAI’s regulatory provisions applicable to unregistered telemarketers, in addition to any further action IRDAI may deem appropriate. For compliance teams, this means they should ensure the organization has completed number migration, updated outbound calling processes and telephony systems, and restricted non-1600 outbound service/transactional calling before the 15 February 2026 deadline.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued a circular dated 19 December 2025, addressed to all insurers and reinsurers, permitting insurers to invest not only in AT1 bonds and Tier 2 capital instruments issued by banks, but also in comparable instruments issued by RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs). The covered AIFI instruments are specifically: AT1 bonds, and debt capital instruments and preference share capital instruments that form Tier 2 capital, with one express exclusion — perpetual cumulative preference shares are not permitted. This expansion is described as a regulatory initiative intended to give insurers a wider investment universe and improve portfolio diversification.

The circular ties these new investments to the existing IRDAI framework for bank investments: insurers must apply the same investment conditions already applicable to investments in banks under paragraphs 1.6(b) and 1.6(d) of Chapter 3 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17 May 2024. In other words, this is not a standalone new regime; insurers must follow the existing bank-investment rules when buying these AIFI instruments. The circular also requires insurers to use the existing category codes that are already specified for investments in the corresponding instruments of PSU banks when recording these investments.

For compliance purposes, the key change is that the permission now explicitly extends to RBI-regulated AIFIs following RBI’s move allowing AIFIs to issue AT1 and Tier 2 capital instruments effective 1 April 2024 under the Basel III capital framework. Insurers and reinsurers should therefore ensure that any investment in these AIFI securities is booked, classified, and managed under the same compliance controls, limits, and procedural requirements that already apply to analogous bank exposures. The document does not introduce a separate numeric investment limit or new deadline for insurers; instead, it creates an immediate permission within the existing IRDAI bank-investment framework as of the circular date.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has withdrawn the earlier practice of allowing a licensed Surveyor and Loss Assessor (SLA) to add additional lines of business/departments to an individual surveyor licence solely on the basis of the categorization letter originally issued in 2001–02. The document explains that, when IRDAI first categorized surveyors and loss assessors who held valid licences before the 2000 licensing regulations, those individuals were mapped into multiple lines of business/departments, but were later limited to only three LOBs on the licence. In 2020, IRDAI had relaxed this approach by permitting additional LOBs to be added based on that categorization letter, provided the individual had the relevant educational qualification and had continuously renewed the licence without any break up to the date of the modification application, and it also removed the earlier cap on the number of LOBs.

This circular states that IRDAI is now ending that 2020 relaxation because it has received applications where the applicant had not met the underlying eligibility condition of continuous renewal without break, yet was seeking new LOB additions under the old categorization letter route. As a result, SLAs can no longer rely on the 2001–02 categorization letter as a basis for obtaining additional LOBs/department permissions under the earlier concession. The document’s immediate practical effect is that future requests to expand an individual surveyor’s authorized business scope must be assessed under the current licensing framework, not by referring back to the historic categorization letter benefit.

The circular is dated 10 October 2025 and is addressed to all licensed Surveyors and Loss Assessors. It is a compliance notice rather than a fee, rate, or threshold change, and it does not introduce a new numerical limit beyond noting the prior historical limit of three LOBs and the later 2020 removal of that cap. Compliance teams should therefore treat the 2020 permission as no longer available for new applications and verify that any internal or client-facing guidance on surveyor LOB expansions is updated to reflect the cessation of this practice.

IRDAI has issued a circular dated **14 August 2025** on **Quantitative Impact Study-2 (QIS 2)** for the proposed **Risk Based Capital (RBC) framework** for the Indian insurance industry. This IRDAI Master Circular, issued on 25 July 2025 (Ref. IRDAI/NL/CIR/RSS/85/07/2025), consolidates and updates the requirements on insurers’ Rural and Social Sector obligations and Motor Third Party obligations under the Insurance Act, 1938, the IRDAI Act, 1999, and the current regulatory framework. It supersedes prior circulars on these obligations and applies to compliance for the financial year 2025-26 onward, with specific obligation percentages and target thresholds set for 2025-26 and 2026-27.

For **rural sector obligations**, the circular requires insurers to achieve minimum percentages of policies written in rural areas, with the table in the circular showing progressively higher targets for different classes of insurers and/or business categories. The circular specifically increases the benchmark for some categories from **25,000 policies and 15%** in **2025-26** to **50,000 policies, 25%, and 10%** in **2026-27** (depending on the category and column referenced in the master table). It also states that for a separate rural-related metric, the target is **10% in 2025-26** and **12% in 2026-27**.

For **social sector obligations**, the circular updates the required percentages by population/covered category and provides a table of obligations for **2025-26** and **2026-27**. The table shows a broad set of compliance ratios that increase from **2025-26 to 2026-27**, including obligations such as **12.50% to 13.75%**, **10.00% to 11%**, **7.50% to 8.25%**, and **5.00% to 5.50%**, with the exact rate applicable depending on the insurer category and the social sector segment covered by the relevant row in the table. Compliance teams should treat these as mandatory minimums tied to the insurer’s category and monitor achievement against the precise row applicable to their license class.

For **motor third-party obligations**, the circular reiterates the insurer’s responsibility to underwrite third-party motor insurance in the required manner and sets out a **30-day** compliance-related timeline for a specified operational step. It also requires insurers to file/submit prescribed information in the formats referenced in the circular’s annexures (Annexure/Format references are embedded in the document), and to maintain records that support compliance with these mandatory third-party obligations.

The circular also prescribes **reporting and submission requirements** through named annexure forms and requires compliance with the formats and instructions in the attached schedules. One key procedural deadline stated in the text is that for the **2025-26** cycle, information relating to the prior year is to be used/considered, and the relevant submission cut-off is **31 May 2025** with a subsequent date of **14 July 2025** also referenced for a required action/reporting step. In practical terms, insurers should verify that their rural, social sector, and motor third-party reporting systems map exactly to the applicable annexure format and that their annual board/compliance monitoring captures achievement against the 2025-26 and 2026-27 targets now set by this circular.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI guideline, issued on 11 February 2026, replaces the earlier 17 October 2022 guidance on the establishment and closure of liaison offices in India by insurance companies registered outside India. It applies to foreign insurers seeking to open or close an Indian liaison office, and it is framed under the Insurance Act, 1938 and related foreign-exchange/Companies law requirements. In practical terms, a liaison office is permitted only for approved, non-commercial liaison activities and cannot be used to conduct insurance business, earn revenue, or create a branch-like commercial presence in India.

For opening a liaison office, the foreign insurer must obtain prior approval and submit the prescribed application and supporting documentation, including details of the parent insurer and its activities, proposed Indian liaison-office operations, and evidence of compliance with the applicable regulatory framework. The guidelines specify that the insurer must satisfy a financial-strength threshold of at least USD 6,000,000 (or equivalent) in net worth/capital, and must demonstrate that the parent is properly regulated in its home jurisdiction and has a clean compliance posture. The Indian liaison office is limited to permitted liaison functions only, and the guidelines also contemplate periodic reporting and filing obligations to the regulator after establishment.

The document sets out time-bound conditions around commencement and continuation of the liaison office, including an initial approval term and the need to complete the set-up within the approved period; if the office is not established within the required timeframe, the approval may lapse and a fresh approval process may be needed. It also requires adherence to Indian tax, foreign-exchange, and corporate registration obligations, and obliges the liaison office to keep records and operate through approved personnel and premises only for the authorized activities. Any change in the circumstances originally disclosed to IRDAI would need to be notified, and the insurer remains responsible for ensuring the liaison office does not deviate into prohibited activities.

For closure, the guidelines require a formal application to IRDAI, along with confirmation that all liabilities, employee dues, taxes, statutory filings, and other obligations in India have been fully settled before winding up. The closure process also requires evidence that the office has ceased all operations, closed bank accounts, terminated leases and contracts, and complied with the applicable exit filings under the foreign-exchange and corporate-registry regime. In short, the document imposes a controlled approval-and-reporting framework for foreign insurers establishing an Indian liaison office, with a clear minimum financial threshold, strict activity restrictions, and a documented exit process for closure.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework Guidelines, 2025** under **Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938** and **Section 14(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999** to create a regulatory framework for how insurers and distribution channels must identify, monitor, and manage fraud risk. The guidelines apply to **all insurers and distribution channels**, unless a specific provision says otherwise, and they come into force **from the date of issuance/commencement set out in the document (dated 09.10.2025)**; the document also indicates an implementation timeline extending into **1 January 2026** for at least certain framework elements.  

A core requirement is that every insurer must establish and maintain a formal **fraud monitoring framework** covering the full insurance lifecycle, including policy solicitation/sales, underwriting, premium collection, claims, servicing, and distribution activities. The framework is not limited to internal fraud; it is intended to cover fraud risks arising from policyholders, claimants, employees, intermediaries, distribution partners, vendors, and other connected parties. Insurers are required to put in place governance, controls, and investigative processes to detect, prevent, report, and mitigate fraud, and to ensure these measures are integrated into business operations rather than treated as a standalone or ad hoc control.  

The guidelines require insurers to maintain a **structured fraud risk management process** that includes fraud risk assessment, red-flag identification, escalation, investigation, and remedial action. The document specifies that insurers must have appropriate internal procedures for identifying suspicious transactions or behavior, documenting fraud indicators, escalating cases through defined internal channels, and taking action based on findings. It also requires insurers to maintain records and management information relating to fraud incidents and monitoring activities, so that the insurer can demonstrate the effectiveness of its fraud controls and provide information to the regulator when required.  

The framework also places obligations on **distribution channels**—meaning intermediaries and other entities involved in selling or placing insurance—to follow insurer fraud controls and cooperate in detection and reporting. Where fraud risk arises in distribution, insurers must ensure that the channel partner is subject to the insurer’s oversight and that suspicious conduct is escalated appropriately. The guidelines indicate that insurers remain responsible for governance over outsourced or partner-led distribution activity and cannot shift fraud compliance responsibility away from themselves.  

The document includes detailed operational provisions in later sections and annexures on **roles, reporting, monitoring, and compliance arrangements**, including procedures to ensure accountability across the insurer’s business and distribution network. It also references existing regulatory circulars/guidance and appears to update or consolidate prior fraud-related directions into a single framework. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that this is a **mandatory enterprise-wide fraud governance requirement**: insurers must review and, where necessary, redesign policies, controls, escalation routes, and oversight of distribution channels so they are aligned with the new IRDAI framework by the applicable effective date(s), including any staged deadlines ending on **1 January 2026**.

The change replaces the prior requirement that the annual review of an insurance repository’s controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards be performed by an external system audit firm approved by IRDAI, and instead requires that this review be conducted at least once every year by an external auditor meeting specified qualifications.

Under the revised Clause 15(a), the review must be done at the insurance repository’s own cost by one of the following: a Certified Information System Auditor (CISA), a Chartered Accountant holding DISA (ICAI) qualification, or a CERT-In certified expert. The scope of the review remains the controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards put in place by the repository as outlined in Clause 14. No separate deadline date is given beyond the requirement that the review occur at least annually, and the circular states that the amendment takes effect immediately.

This amendment affects insurance repositories subject to the 2015 electronic issuance/repository framework, and it changes both who can perform the mandatory annual review and who bears the cost. Compliance teams should ensure that future annual reviews are assigned only to qualified individuals from the specified categories and that budgeting and vendor engagement reflect the repository’s obligation to pay for the audit directly.

The IRDAI issued **“Guidelines on Hedging Through Equity Derivatives”** dated **28 February 2025** to **all life, general, and health insurers**. The document states that it is being issued under the authority of the earlier **IRDA circular dated 24 December 2004** on investment/exposure-related matters, and is also linked to the **2012 IRDA guidance** and subsequent insurance investment rules, including the **IRDAI (Investment) Regulations, 2024**. Its purpose is to set out the conditions under which insurers may use **equity derivatives** for hedging, and it explicitly updates/frames the requirements now applicable to insurers using these instruments.

The guidelines set out a structured framework for hedging, including **eligibility, approved instruments, exposure limits, board-approved policy requirements, and reporting/controls**. They require insurers to maintain a formal policy governing derivative use, establish internal controls and monitoring, and ensure trades are tied to genuine hedging rather than speculative activity. The document distinguishes between hedging at the level of the **insurer’s own portfolio/underlying equity exposure** and other derivative activity, indicating that only permitted hedging use is allowed under the specified conditions.

Several numeric limits and operational constraints are specifically stated. The document refers to **investment of up to 15%** in the relevant context, and it states a **20% cap** tied to certain derivative/hedging exposure calculations or limits. It also sets an **“80–125” range** for a valuation/coverage parameter referenced in the text, indicating that the underlying hedge relationship must remain within that band to qualify or continue as compliant. The guidelines also appear to require that positions be monitored relative to the insurer’s exposure and that if the hedge falls outside the permitted parameters, corrective action or closure/rebalancing is required.

The document also imposes controls over the types of derivative transactions and counterparties/instruments that may be used, with references to **exchange-traded and/or permitted market instruments**, and it requires insurers to maintain records, valuation methodology, and ongoing review. It indicates that derivatives must be accounted for and measured consistently, with prescribed treatment for margins, mark-to-market, and exposure computation. In addition, the text references reporting/oversight obligations, implying that insurers must be able to evidence compliance, including approvals, transaction details, and periodic monitoring for supervisory review.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that **hedging through equity derivatives is allowed only within a tightly controlled, rule-based framework effective from 28 February 2025**, and all insurers in scope must ensure their treasury/investment policies, limits, approvals, valuation practices, and internal controls are aligned to these guidelines. Any existing or proposed hedging program should be checked against the stated **15%, 20%, and 80–125 thresholds**, the permitted instrument set, and the requirement that the activity be demonstrably hedging-only, with complete documentation and oversight.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Bima Vahak) Guidelines, 2023** on **9 October 2023** under **Section 14(2)(e) of the IRDAI Act, 1999**. The guidelines are intended to create a **women-centric distribution channel** to expand insurance awareness and inclusion at the **village/Gram Panchayat** level, with the stated policy goal of improving access to insurance across India’s rural and local markets. The document also says the channel is meant to identify and develop **local resources who understand local needs and are trusted by the community**.

These guidelines define **“Bima Vahak”** as either an **individual** (“Individual Bima Vahak”) or a **legal person** (“Corporate Bima Vahak”) registered under Indian law and engaged to provide services under the guidelines. Insurers are permitted to use this channel for **solicitation of insurance business** and to help with **policy servicing and claims servicing**. Specifically, an insurer may **engage a Corporate Bima Vahak** and/or **directly appoint Individual Bima Vahaks**; the excerpt indicates the insurer’s appointment/engagement framework is the central compliance mechanism for deploying this distribution model.

The guidelines are named as above and are stated to **come into force from the date of launch of “Bima Vistaar”**, which the document describes as a **comprehensive insurance product to be issued in due course**. That means the operative start date is not a fixed calendar date in the excerpt, but is tied to the launch of Bima Vistaar. For compliance purposes, the key trigger is that insurers should treat these rules as pending until that launch date, then ensure any Bima Vahak engagement is structured in line with the guidelines.

In practical terms, compliance teams at insurers should note that the regime is aimed at a **dedicated women-focused rural distribution structure**, and that any use of Bima Vahaks is tied to both **sales solicitation** and **service/claims support**, not just acquisition. The excerpt does not yet provide further operational thresholds, licensing criteria, compensation rules, training requirements, or reporting obligations, but it clearly establishes the permitted channel, the kinds of entities that can be engaged, the intended social objective, and the effective-date trigger tied to Bima Vistaar.

IRDAI has issued the **Information and Cyber Security Guidelines, 2023** to replace and update its earlier insurer cyber-security framework from **7 April 2017**, which had already been extended to insurance intermediaries by the **2 September 2022** circular. The new guidelines were issued on **24 April 2023** in response to the increased use of digital technologies and the corresponding rise in cyber incidents, with the stated purpose of strengthening the insurance sector’s cyber defenses and governance. The document says the full requirements are contained in **Annexure A**.

The guidelines apply broadly to **all insurers, including foreign reinsurers/FRBs**, and to **insurance intermediaries**, specifically naming **brokers, corporate agents, web aggregators, TPAs, IMFs, insurance repositories, ISNPs, corporate surveyors, MISPs, CSCs, and the Insurance Information Bureau of India (IIB)**. A key transition rule is that entities that have **already completed the security audit for FY 2022–23** do **not** have to retrofit that year; instead, they must begin complying with the new guidelines **from the next financial year**. In other words, for those entities, the new controls and obligations become effective at the start of the following financial year after the FY 2022–23 audit cycle.

The circular also makes clear that prior IRDAI cyber-security circulars are being superseded/updated by this framework, including the earlier **2017 insurer guideline**, the **29 December 2020** circular, the **2 September 2022** intermediary extension, and another **11 October 2022** reference noted in the text. For compliance teams, the immediate action item is to treat this as a sector-wide revised cyber-security mandate and verify that the organization falls within the covered entity types, then map existing controls and governance against the detailed requirements in the annexure.

This IRDAI guideline, issued on 31 March 2023 under sub-regulation (3) of Regulation 13 of the IRDAI (Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations, 2019, sets the operating process for running innovation proposals in insurance through the Regulatory Sandbox. It applies to any applicant seeking to promote or implement an insurance innovation in India and requires the applicant to submit its request in **Form RG-1**, under one or more of the categories permitted by **Regulation 4** of the 2019 Sandbox Regulations.  

A key substantive requirement is that the applicant must show IRDAI that the proposal will **increase insurance penetration** or **provide enhanced services to policyholders**; IRDAI will not entertain proposals that are merely seeking regulatory relaxation without being a genuine innovation. The guideline also states that the **Chairperson’s decision** on whether a proposal qualifies as innovative is **final**, so there is no internal appeal or reconsideration mechanism specified in the document.  

For application handling, the applicant must appoint an **experienced and responsible Single Point of Contact (SPOC)** to interface with IRDAI on the submission, and IRDAI will in turn nominate its own SPOC to coordinate with the applicant and facilitate guidance/communication during the sandbox process. The document is focused on process rather than substantive sandbox eligibility thresholds, and the excerpt provided does not include any numerical caps, fees, or timeline deadlines beyond the issuance date; however, compliance teams should note that the guideline formalizes the expectation of a documented application, a business justification tied to policyholder benefit or penetration, and a dedicated contact person on both sides.

Previously, FRNs were allotted **annually by IRDAI**; under these guidelines, insurers may now **auto-renew the FRN themselves** for eligible CBRs, rather than waiting for a fresh annual allotment from the Authority. rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these guidelines on **28 September 2022** to address **conflicts of interest arising from common directorship** among registered **intermediaries and insurance intermediaries**, particularly where the Authority receives more than one application from entities in the same **group** for a Certificate of Registration (CoR). The guidance applies both where IRDAI has granted or is granting CoR to **more than one entity within the same group** to act as an intermediary/insurance intermediary, and where **common directors are existing or being appointed** either within the same group or across different groups.

The first substantive requirement is that the **maximum number of directorships must not exceed the limits in Section 165 of the Companies Act, 2013**. Where common directors are present, the intermediary/insurance intermediary must implement a **Board-approved policy** specifically to manage and review **related party transactions**, with “related party” understood as defined in **Section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013**. All related party transactions involving the intermediary/insurance intermediary must comply with **Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013** and **Accounting Standard AS 18**.

The document also imposes a certification obligation on the statutory auditor: the auditor must **certify compliance with Section 188** of the Companies Act, 2013 **to IRDAI**, and this certification is stated to be required **as at the end of the financial year** (the text provided cuts off after “as at the,” but the evident requirement is annual year-end certification). In practical compliance terms, any intermediary or insurance intermediary with common directors—whether within the same corporate group or across groups—should review directorship limits, establish or update related-party governance procedures, ensure transaction-level compliance under Section 188/AS 18, and be prepared for statutory auditor certification to IRDAI.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **“IRDAI (Surety Insurance Contracts) Guidelines, 2022”** on **3 January 2022**, with an effective date of **1 April 2022**. The guidelines are addressed to the **Chairman-cum-Managing Directors/Chief Executive Officers of all general insurance companies**, **except ECGC Ltd and AIC Ltd**, and are intended to regulate and promote the sustainable development of surety insurance in India. The Authority states that the guidelines were issued under its powers under **section 14(2)(i) of the IRDA Act, 1999**, and they were also posted on the IRDAI website.

The core applicability rule is that **all insurers registered under the Insurance Act, 1938 to carry on general insurance business may transact surety insurance only if they satisfy the eligibility criteria in these guidelines**. In addition, **after the commencement date, no person may transact surety insurance in India unless that person is an “Indian Insurance Company” as defined in section 2(7A) of the Insurance Act, 1938**. This means the business is restricted to qualifying Indian insurers, and compliance teams at general insurers need to confirm both their legal status and their eligibility against the IRDAI criteria before offering these products.

The document’s stated policy objective is to support the **sustainable and healthy development of surety insurance business** because of the product’s unique risk characteristics and features. The excerpt provided also indicates that the guidelines proceed to define the **essential features of a surety insurance contract**, which implies that product design and underwriting must conform to the contract structure and risk profile contemplated by IRDAI. Since the effective date is fixed at **1 April 2022**, any insurer intending to write surety business needed to have its product, eligibility, and internal controls aligned by that date.

Introduction 1.1 Trade credit insurance protects businesses against the risk of non-payment for goods and services by buyers. It usually covers a portfolio of buyers and indemnifies an agreed percentage of an invoice or invoices that remain unpaid as a result of protracted default, insolvency / bankruptcy. It contributes to the economic growth of a country by facilitating trade and helps in improving economic stability by addressing the trade losses due to payment risks. 1.2 These guidelines set out the regulatory framework; (a) to promote sustainable and healthy development of trade credit insurance business. rows.summary:
IRDAI issued revised **Trade Credit Insurance Guidelines, 2021** by circular dated **8 September 2021** to all **general insurance companies in India, except ECGC Ltd and AIC Ltd**. The guidelines were published on the IRDAI website and are stated to **come into force on 1 November 2021**.

The document explains that trade credit insurance protects businesses against **non-payment for goods and services** by buyers, typically covering a **portfolio of buyers** and indemnifying an agreed percentage of unpaid invoices where non-payment results from **protracted default, insolvency, or bankruptcy**. IRDAI says the revised framework is intended to support the **sustainable and healthy development** of the trade credit insurance market, to allow insurers to provide cover not only to suppliers but also to **licensed banks and other financial institutions** for trade-financing-related non-payment and country risk, and to enable **customised covers for SMEs and MSMEs** in line with evolving market needs.

For compliance purposes, the immediate action point is that any general insurer writing, planning to write, or modifying trade credit insurance business must align its products and underwriting approach with the revised IRDAI framework effective **1 November 2021**. The document itself does not list the substantive underwriting limits or detailed operational rules in the excerpt provided, but it clearly signals a regulatory change in how trade credit insurance may be structured and offered, especially with respect to broader distribution to financial institutions and tailor-made cover for smaller businesses.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these guidelines on 5 May 2021 to all general insurers and health insurers to create a **Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product (SDTIP)** with **uniform mandatory coverage** across the market, so customers can more easily compare and select a basic domestic travel policy. The product must include only the **basic mandatory covers specified in the guidelines**, and insurers may offer **only the optional covers expressly permitted** by the guidelines; insurers are allowed to set the premium, but only in compliance with the IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016 and the framework in these guidelines. In practice, this means insurers need to ensure product design, policy wording, disclosures, and filing documents match the prescribed standard format before offering the product. rows.summary:
This circular, issued by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) on 31 March 2021 as Ref. IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/068/03/2021, introduces practical-training guidelines for licensed surveyors and loss assessors seeking fresh or renewal licences under the IRDA Act, 1999 and Regulation 3(2)(b) and (c) of the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015.
