IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/288/12/2020), so compliance teams should treat it as a supplement/clarification to the existing licensing-training framework rather than a standalone policy.

The document requires **institutional practical training of two months** with either the **National Insurance Academy (NIA)** or the **Insurance Institute of India (III)**. This training must cover core insurance and survey/loss-assessment concepts, including introduction to different types of policies, endorsements, insurance terminology, and the nature of cover, so the requirement is not just attendance-based but substantive exposure to insurance products and documentation.

The circular is specifically addressed to **all licensed surveyors and loss assessors**, and the training requirement applies where the individual is seeking **fresh or renewal licence** to act in that capacity. In practical compliance terms, any applicant falling into that category will need to ensure completion of this two-month institutional training at the approved institutions before the licence process can be completed, and internal licensing trackers should be updated to reflect this prerequisite.

Because the visible portion of the document indicates a structured training curriculum, compliance officers should also expect that the practical-training obligation may be more detailed than a single classroom module and may include multiple components within the two-month period. Based on the text provided, the key hard requirement that can be stated with certainty is the **two-month institutional training at NIA or III**, with the subject matter centered on foundational insurance-policy and surveyor/loss-assessor knowledge.

rows.title: NFRA Circular on Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees

All listed companies 2. Companies and bodies corporate as specified in Rule 3 of NFRA Rules, 2018 3. Auditors of the above companies Subject: Effective Communication Between Statutory Auditors and Those Charged with Governance, Including Audit Committees In the course of discharging of NFRA’s statutory functions, it has been noticed that there is a need to strengthen the communications between Statutory Auditors (Auditors), Those Charged with Governance (TCWG), including Audit Committees (ACs), in line with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013), the Standards on Auditing (SAs) prescribed under CA 2013, and other relevant Rules and Regulations. 2. Provisions of CA 2013 and other Relevant Rules: The CA 2013 has placed certain important obligations on the Board of Directors (BOD or the ‘Board’), Independent Directors (IDs), Audit Committees and Statutory Auditors of Companies in respect of Accounts and Audit of Companies. 2.1 Board of Directors: Section 134 of CA 2013 and related Rules require that the financial statements, including the consolidated financial statements, if any, be approved by the Board of Directors. A report by the Board shall be attached to the financial statements, which shall include, inter alia, an important statement called Directors’ Responsibility Statement. According to sub-section 5 of Section 134, this statement shall disclose the Board’s assertions regarding certain critical aspects, such as adherence to applicable accounting standards; selection and application of accounting policies and making of judgements/estimates on reasonable and prudent basis; maintenance of adequate records for safeguarding the assets of the company and preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; preparation of accounts on a going concern basis; implementation of adequate
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 07.01.2026, is addressed to all listed companies, companies and bodies corporate covered under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the statutory auditors of those entities. It does not create a new standalone legal regime, but signals NFRA’s expectation that communication between statutory auditors and those charged with governance (TCWG), including audit committees, be materially strengthened and brought into closer alignment with the Companies Act, 2013, the Standards on Auditing under that Act, and related rules and regulations.

The circular explains that the Companies Act, 2013 already imposes key responsibilities on the board of directors, independent directors, audit committees, and auditors in relation to financial statements and audit. It specifically highlights Section 134, under which the board must approve the financial statements, including consolidated financial statements where applicable, and attach a board’s report that includes the Directors’ Responsibility Statement. That statement must cover the board’s assertions that applicable accounting standards have been followed; accounting policies have been selected and applied with reasonable and prudent judgment/estimates; adequate records are maintained to safeguard assets and prevent and detect fraud and other irregularities; the accounts have been prepared on a going-concern basis; and adequate internal financial controls are in place and operating effectively.

The compliance message is that auditors and governance bodies must treat these statutory obligations as requiring more effective and timely two-way communication during the audit and financial reporting process, particularly with the audit committee. While the excerpt provided does not yet set out any new numeric thresholds, filing deadlines, or penalties, it clearly indicates NFRA has observed deficiencies in current practice and is issuing the circular to reinforce existing statutory and audit-standard-based communication requirements. Compliance teams should therefore expect a heightened supervisory expectation that management, the board, audit committees, and auditors actively exchange information on matters affecting financial statements, internal controls, and audit findings, rather than treating audit committee interaction as merely formal or periodic.

As of now, the auditors are required to ensure adherence to the following sets of Standards and Codes to remain compliant with the extant laws in India: a) Standard on Quality Control (SQC); b) 35 SAs addressing various aspects during the entire life cycle of an audit; and c) Code of Ethics including Independence standards. 2. Audit of SFS, where the company has branches, and the audit of CFS of companies with subsidiaries, associates etc, called as audit of Group Financial Statements (GFS), requires special considerations by the auditor (called Principal Auditor), who is ultimately responsible for issue of group audit opinion, and also by the auditors (called Other Auditor) engaged to undertake audit of components such as branches and subsidiaries etc. ‘SA 600 - Using the Work of Another Auditor’ deals with the requirements in the audit of GFS. 3. In the contemporary business and economic environment, there are audit areas of material and/or significant risk in almost all the audits of GFS due to the following features (this list is not exhaustive). a. Complex group structures including special purpose vehicles, auto pilot structures, cross holdings of interests across group entities and shared servi
rows.summary:
The NFRA’s circular dated 3 October 2024 addresses the responsibilities of the principal auditor and other auditors in group audits for entities covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018. It reiterates that statutory audits of both standalone financial statements and consolidated financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013 must comply with the Standards on Auditing, the Standard on Quality Control, and the Code of Ethics, including independence requirements. The circular explains that audits of group financial statements—such as audits of companies with branches, subsidiaries, associates, and other components—require special attention because the principal auditor remains ultimately responsible for the group audit opinion, even where component work is performed by other auditors, and that SA 600 governs the use of another auditor’s work.

The document’s central point is that group audits often involve material or significant-risk areas because of modern group structures and business arrangements. It specifically notes complex structures such as special purpose vehicles, “auto pilot” structures, cross-holdings, and shared-services arrangements as examples of the kinds of group features that can make audit risk higher and component reliance more difficult. The circular is therefore aimed at ensuring that auditors treat group audits as a heightened compliance and audit-quality area, with the principal auditor actively managing and overseeing the work of other auditors rather than merely relying on their reports.

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that audit teams involved in group audits must ensure full adherence to the applicable auditing framework, with documented compliance to the quality-control standards, the 35 standards on auditing, and ethical/independence requirements. The circular is directed to auditors of entities under NFRA’s jurisdiction and is intended to reinforce the existing legal and professional duties in group audit engagements, especially where the work of component auditors is used in forming the final group opinion. No monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or new reporting forms are set out in the excerpt provided, but the effective date of the circular itself is 3 October 2024.

rows.desc: / Government of India / National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25013/2/2023 Dated 26.06.2023 Circular To 1. Auditors of the Entities Regulated by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) Subject: Statutory Auditors’ Responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company In course of discharge of its statutory functions, NFRA has noticed that auditors are not fulfilling their statutory responsibilities relating to reporting of fraud as mandated under the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013) read with the relevant Rules and the applicable Standards on Auditing (SAs). 2 The CA 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO) and the Standards on Auditing (SAs) place mandatory reporting obligations on auditors to report fraud and/or suspected fraud to the Central Government and the Board/Audit Committee. 2.1 Section 143 (12) of CA 2013 and related Rules places certain reporting obligations on the auditor, in relation to frauds: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving such amount or amounts as may be prescribed, is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, the auditor shall report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed: ....” Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014, prescribes detailed steps that need to be followed by the auditor if he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud, which involves or is expected to involve individually an amount of rupees one crore or above, is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees. The auditor is required to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee and to the Central Government in the form of a statement as specified in Form ADT-4. 2.2 Clause (xi) of Companies
rows.summary:
The NFRA has issued this circular because it has observed that statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated entities are not consistently carrying out their legal duties to report fraud, or suspected fraud, as required under the Companies Act, 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO), and the applicable Standards on Auditing. The circular is addressed to auditors of entities regulated by NFRA and reiterates that these reporting duties are mandatory, not discretionary.  

For fraud involving a company’s officers or employees, section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires an auditor who, in the course of audit work, has reason to believe that a fraud offence has been or is being committed to report the matter to the Central Government within the prescribed time and in the prescribed manner. Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 specifies the process where the suspected or actual fraud involves, or is expected to involve, an amount of **₹1 crore or more**: the auditor must report first to the **Board or Audit Committee** and also report to the **Central Government** in **Form ADT-4**.  

The circular also points auditors to the separate reporting obligation under **Clause (xi)** of the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, which requires disclosure of fraud and suspected fraud matters in the auditor’s reporting. In substance, NFRA is reminding auditors that fraud-related reporting must be completed through the correct statutory channels, using the prescribed form and process, whenever the threshold and legal test under the rules are met.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that auditors of NFRA-regulated entities must ensure they have procedures to identify, document, escalate, and report any fraud or suspected fraud meeting the statutory threshold, and they must not limit themselves to internal reporting alone. The circular signals NFRA scrutiny of auditor non-compliance in this area and reinforces that failure to report as required under section 143(12), Rule 13, CARO, and the SAs may constitute a breach of statutory audit responsibilities.

Auditors of the above companies Subject: Instances of non-compliance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind ASs) on Accounting Policies for measurement of Revenue from Contracts with Customers and Trade Receivables As per sub-section 2(b) of section 132 of the Companies Act 2013 (the Act) read with rule 4(2)( c) of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules 2018 (NFRA Rules 2018), the National Financial Reporting Authority is mandated to monitor and enforce compliance with accounting standards and auditing standards. Further, NFRA is required by sub-section 2( d) of section 132 of the Act read with rule 4(2) (g) of NFRA Rules, to perform such other functions and duties as may be necessary or incidental to the aforesaid functions and duties. 2. NFRA monitors compliance with accounting standards by Companies as part of its review of published financial statements of companies. During its recent review, instances of apparent non­ compliance with the prescriptions of the Ind ASs in the critical areas of Revenue Recognition and Measurement, and Initial Measurement of corresponding Trade Receivables have come to light. In order to ensure adherence to high-quality Ind AS Reporting Framework, which is substantially aligned with globally accepted IFRS Standards, the instances of non-compliance are highlighted below for the urgent attention of the Company Management/Audit Committees and the Statutory Auditors. Revenue from Contracts with Customers - Recognition and Measurement 3. Para 46 of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, requires that the entity shall recognise as revenue the amount of the transaction price, excluding the estimates of variable conside
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 29 March 2023, is addressed to all listed companies, unlisted companies covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the auditors of those companies. It states that, in exercising NFRA’s statutory mandate under section 132(2)(b) and 132(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 4(2)(c) and 4(2)(g) of the NFRA Rules, NFRA has identified apparent non-compliance in recent financial statement reviews in two linked areas: revenue recognition/measurement and the initial measurement of the related trade receivables.

The circular specifically flags compliance issues under Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, beginning with paragraph 46, which requires revenue to be recognized at the transaction price, excluding estimated variable consideration until the amount can be reliably determined in accordance with the standard. NFRA says these are critical areas because they affect both how revenue is measured and how the corresponding receivables are initially recorded, and it highlights the concern to the company’s management, audit committee, and statutory auditors for urgent attention. The document makes clear that the issue is not a general accounting reminder but a warning based on NFRA’s review findings that some companies are not following the prescribed Ind AS requirements.

For compliance purposes, the affected population is broad: every listed company and every unlisted company that falls within NFRA Rule 3 is expected to ensure its revenue policies, estimates, and trade receivables accounting are fully consistent with Ind AS 115. The circular does not introduce a new quantitative threshold, fee, or deadline, but it does require immediate review of existing accounting policies and practices, especially around transaction price determination, treatment of variable consideration, and the measurement of receivables arising from customer contracts. Management, audit committees, and statutory auditors should treat the circular as a prompt to verify that the company’s Ind AS 115 policy documentation, estimates, and financial statement presentation are compliant and supportable under the standard.

rows.summary:
NFRA Order No. 24/2024, dated 21 October 2024, disposes of the show-cause notice issued on 13 October 2023 to CA Chirag Doshi (ICAI Membership No. 119079), who was the Engagement Partner for the statutory audit of Ushdev International Limited (UIL) for FY 2017–18. The order is issued under Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11(6) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and it concerns NFRA’s suo motu examination of the auditor’s professional conduct in relation to a public interest entity.  

The order states that although the auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on both the financial statements and the internal financial controls over financial reporting for FY 2017–18, he nevertheless failed in key audit responsibilities. NFRA found that he did not exercise due diligence and acted with gross negligence in meeting his obligation to identify and report fraud under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and SA 240, despite there being several indicators of fraud. NFRA also concluded that he failed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in the course of the audit.  

For a compliance team, the practical significance is that the order reinforces that a disclaimer of opinion does not relieve an engagement partner of the duty to perform fraud-risk procedures, respond appropriately to fraud indicators, or gather sufficient appropriate evidence before concluding an audit. It also shows that NFRA is actively using its powers to scrutinize auditors’ conduct in prior-period audits of public interest entities, and that failures tied to fraud reporting and audit evidence can be treated as serious professional misconduct. The excerpt provided does not include the final penalty or sanctions section, so any monetary penalty, debarment period, or other disciplinary consequence is not visible in the supplied text.

rows.title: Request for public comments – Draft SA 600 (Revised)
rows.desc: SA 600 (REVISED) Request for Public Comments by 30.10.2024 (Refer accompanying note on NFRA website) SA 600 (Revised), SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS—AUDITS OF GROUP FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (INCLUDING THE WORK OF COMPONENT AUDITORS) (Applicable to PIEs under Rule 3 of NFRA Rules 2018 except PSUs, PSBs and PSIs and their branches) Introduction Scope of this SA 1. The Standards on Auditing (SAs) apply to an audit of group financial statements (a group audit). This SA deals with special considerations that apply to a group audit, including in those circumstances when component auditors are involved. The requirements and guidance in this SA refer to, or expand on, the application of other relevant SAs to a group audit, in particular SA 220 (Revised), 1 SA 230, 2 SA 300, 3 SA 315 (Revised), 4 and SA 330. 5 (Ref: Para. A1–A2) 2. Group financial statements include the financial information of more than one entity or business unit through a consolidation process, as described in paragraph 14(k). The term consolidation process as used in this SA refers not only to the preparation of consolidated financial statements in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, but also to the presentation of combined financial statements, and to the aggregation of the financial information of entities or business units such as branches or divisions. (Ref: Para. A3–A5, A27) 3. rows.summary:
NFRA has issued a draft revision of SA 600, “Special Considerations—Audits of Group Financial Statements (Including the Work of Component Auditors),” for public comment, with comments due by 30.10.2024. The draft applies to audits of group financial statements for PIEs under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, but specifically excludes PSUs, PSBs, PSIs, and their branches. The standard explains that group financial statements cover more than one entity or business unit brought together through a consolidation process, and that this includes not only consolidated financial statements under the relevant reporting framework but also combined financial statements and aggregation of information from branches, divisions, or similar units.

The revised SA 600 is intended to address the special risks and responsibilities that arise in group audits, especially where component auditors are involved. It cross-references and builds on other auditing standards, particularly SA 220 (Revised), SA 230, SA 300, SA 315 (Revised), and SA 330, meaning group audit teams must apply those standards with the additional requirements in SA 600. The document also notes that the guidance may be useful outside a formal group audit when the engagement team includes individuals from another firm—for example, for attending physical inventory counts, inspecting property, plant and equipment, or performing procedures at a remote shared service center.

For compliance teams, the immediate action item is the consultation deadline: public comments must be submitted by 30 October 2024. Substantively, the draft signals heightened focus on how group structures are organized and how auditors evaluate and coordinate work across components, so affected PIEs should expect tighter scrutiny over consolidation structures, the involvement of component auditors, and audit planning and supervision in group engagements.

rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued an invitation for public comment dated 16 January 2023 to statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated Public Interest Entities (PIEs) on the proposal to require publication of Annual Transparency Reports (ATR) by auditors/audit firms. The notice explains that because auditors of PIEs play a critical role in the financial reporting supply chain, and because audit quality increasingly depends on robust professional and operational capabilities, regulators in some overseas jurisdictions already require audit firms auditing PIEs to prepare and publish annual transparency reports. NFRA notes that Indian companies are now important participants in the global economy and implies that Indian audit firms and PIEs should align with higher transparency expectations seen internationally.  

The document is a consultation notice rather than a final rule, so it does not itself create an enforceable compliance obligation or set a specific effective date, deadline, filing format, or threshold in the text provided. However, the subject matter makes clear that the contemplated requirement would affect statutory auditors and audit firms serving NFRA-regulated PIEs, and would likely require them to disclose information annually about their firm’s capabilities, resources, governance, quality-related arrangements, and possibly other transparency information comparable to overseas ATR regimes. Compliance teams at affected audit firms should treat this as an early policy signal that public annual disclosure obligations for PIE auditors may be introduced, and should monitor NFRA’s next consultation or final issuance for the precise content, timing, and scope of any mandatory ATR requirement.

rows.summary:
This document is a **Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)** from the **National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)** dated **28.09.2021** to the **Secretary, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)** regarding **ICAI’s recommendations for revising the existing Accounting Standards under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013**. It records that ICAI had submitted an Approach Paper and draft revised texts for **18 revised Accounting Standards**, as part of a broader project expected to result in **32 revised Accounting Standards** in total, intended for companies **not required to follow Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)**. NFRA notes the historical context: the revision project was developed after Ind AS implementation for certain classes of companies, and ICAI’s 2020 revision of its 2014–15 approach paper reflects the view that accounting recognition and measurement should, as far as possible, be broadly the same across companies.

The core compliance point is that the **revised ASs will apply to companies for which Ind AS is not mandatory**, meaning the regime will cover a **large number of Micro, Small and Medium-size Companies (MSMCs)** and will **replace the existing Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules**. NFRA emphasizes that this is not a minor technical update: because these standards are intended for a very large non-Ind AS population, the revision could have a **significant economic and administrative impact** on affected entities. The letter indicates NFRA is evaluating ICAI’s recommendations in light of that broad impact, especially because the changes would govern financial reporting for companies outside the Ind AS framework.

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that organizations **not currently on Ind AS** should monitor the final outcome of this standards-revision exercise, because their accounting and reporting policies may need to change once the revised ASs are notified. The document itself does **not** set a new effective date, transition date, or threshold numbers for application in this excerpt, but it clearly signals that the revised standards are intended to become the **mandatory baseline** for non-Ind AS companies. The key obligation area is therefore readiness for updated accounting recognition/measurement requirements once NFRA/MCA complete the revision process and the revised standards are formally prescribed.

The report explains that financial reporting is viewed as a “supply chain” involving auditors, preparers, users, regulators, academics, and other stakeholders, and it assesses NFRA’s role in each part of that chain. In practical compliance terms, the document signals an expected shift toward more structured engagement by NFRA, stronger transparency around its decision-making and enforcement approach, and greater emphasis on audit quality measurement and firm-level evaluation. It also specifically points to settlement and remediation mechanisms for disciplinary matters, suggesting that entities subject to NFRA oversight may face not only enforcement but also processes aimed at corrective action and resolution.

No binding deadlines, numeric thresholds, fee rates, or immediate filing obligations are set out in the text provided. rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule, set to become effective on December 15, 2026.
rows.desc: At September 9 Open Meeting, PCAOB to Consider Adopting Amendments to Quality Control Standard WASHINGTON, Sep. 3, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) will hold an open meeting at 10:00 a.m. ET on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. At the meeting, the Board will consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, and related proposed amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule set to become effective on December 15, 2026. The meeting is open to the public and will take place in the PCAOB’s Multi-Purpose Room (301) at 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC. The public may also view the meeting via a livestream on the PCAOB’s event page, and a recording will be available after the meeting concludes.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. Related Topics About the PCAOB
rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced that it will hold an open meeting on September 9, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET in Washington, DC, with a public livestream and later recording available on its event page. At that meeting, the Board will consider adopting proposed amendments to QC 1000, **A Firm’s System of Quality Control**, along with related amendments to PCAOB forms and the QC reporting rule. The notice states that these proposed amendments are set to become effective on **December 15, 2026**, so firms subject to PCAOB oversight should treat that as the operative implementation date.

For compliance purposes, the affected entities are PCAOB-regulated audit firms, particularly those performing audits of public companies and brokers/dealers registered with the SEC. The document does not describe the substantive content of the amendments themselves, but it does make clear that the Board is moving from proposal toward adoption of changes to the firm-level quality control framework and associated reporting mechanics. A compliance team should therefore monitor the September 9 action closely, because final adoption would likely require updates to internal quality control systems, any PCAOB form filings tied to QC reporting, and related implementation planning ahead of the December 15, 2026 effective date.

rows.title: The PCAOB posted select materials shared for discussion purposes with the Inspections Modernization Council for its meetings in July and August 2026.
rows.desc: PCAOB Posts Discussion Materials From Summer 2026 Meetings of the Inspections Modernization Council WASHINGTON, Aug. 24, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today posted select materials shared for discussion purposes with the Inspections Modernization Council (IMC) for its meetings in July and August 2026. The discussion materials – which address topics including the development of a QC-informed inspection approach, use of technology, inspection reporting, and remediation – are available at the IMC’s page on the PCAOB website.Launched in May 2026, the IMC is a resource group composed of outside parties with capital markets expertise and knowledge of the PCAOB’s inspection activities. The IMC’s objective is to provide perspectives to inform the PCAOB’s efforts to modernize its inspection program, as part of the PCAOB’s continued efforts to improve audit quality.“The PCAOB’s inspection program has contributed meaningfully to improving audit quality over time, and, to build on these accomplishments, we need to continue to evolve,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “Since its formation, the IMC has provided us with excellent input to inform our work in this area, and we thank all IMC members for sharing their time and perspectives.”The PCAOB is posting the IMC discussion materials as part of its commitment to transparency and stakeholder engagement as it works on inspections modernization. Stakeholders with questions or ideas regarding the PCAOB’s inspections modernization efforts are encouraged to contact the PCAOB at [email protected].Note: the materials posted today were prepared by PCAOB staff for discussion purposes. Except for the Board’s authorization to share and post the materials, the materials have not otherwise been approved, adopted, requested, directed, selected, or authorized by the Board.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order

For compliance teams, the main takeaway is that the PCAOB is actively shaping potential changes to how it inspects audit firms and is soliciting transparency and stakeholder input as part of that process. The Inspections Modernization Council itself was launched in May 2026 and is an external resource group made up of people with capital markets expertise and knowledge of PCAOB inspection activities, intended to provide perspectives that inform the PCAOB’s modernization efforts. The PCAOB says its goal is to continue improving audit quality by evolving the inspection program, and it explicitly encourages stakeholders with questions or ideas about inspections modernization to contact the PCAOB at [email protected].

No effective date, deadline, threshold, fee, or mandatory compliance action is announced in this posting. However, firms subject to PCAOB inspection should treat this as a signal that changes may be coming in inspection methodology, reporting expectations, and remediation review processes, and should monitor the PCAOB website and related releases for any formal proposals or adopted requirements that may follow from these discussions.

rows.title: A new PCAOB staff resource, QC 1000 Questions and Answers, provides answers to questions about certain matters related to the implementation of QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control.

rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George Kostolampros as General Counsel.
rows.desc: George Kostolampros Named PCAOB General Counsel WASHINGTON, Jul. 1, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George Kostolampros has been appointed the PCAOB’s General Counsel. As General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros will provide legal advice and counsel on all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC). “OGC’s work underpins the PCAOB’s ability to execute its mission to protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We are grateful that George is joining us to fill this critical leadership role.” Mr. Kostolampros brings more than 25 years of experience advising organizations and senior leaders on complex legal, regulatory, governance, compliance, and risk-management matters. Prior to his appointment as General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. Before returning to private practice, he served as Senior Counsel in the Division of Enforcement at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Kostolampros received his J.D., magna cum laude, from Widener University School of Law and his B.A. from Syracuse University. “I am honored to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the talented OGC staff to advance the PCAOB’s priorities and mission,” said Mr. Kostolampros. Matt Goldin, who was named Acting General Counsel in January 2026, will resume his role as Deputy General Counsel, advising the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assisting with OGC’s management. “Matt is a valued member of the OGC team, and we thank him for his distinguished service as Acting General Counsel,” said Chairman Logothetis.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corp

rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of Dr. Ying Li Compton as its Chief Economist and Director of the Office of Economic and Risk Analysis.
rows.desc: Dr. Ying Li Compton Named PCAOB Chief Economist and Director of Its Office of Economic and Risk Analysis WASHINGTON, Jun. 29, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced the appointment of Dr. Ying Li Compton as the PCAOB's Chief Economist and Director of its Office of Economic and Risk Analysis (OERA). At the PCAOB, OERA conducts independent, evidence-based economic and risk analyses to inform the organization’s oversight activities, including inspections, investigations, rulemaking, standard setting, and post-implementation reviews. “Evidence-based economic and risk analyses are critical to strengthening the PCAOB’s oversight and, by extension, its ability to accomplish its investor-protection mission,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “Dr. Compton brings to the PCAOB a strong combination of analytical experience and accounting expertise.” Dr. Compton joins the PCAOB from PwC International Limited, where she served as a managing director advising the Global Assurance Leadership Team. Before that, she was chief of staff to the PwC US Assurance Leader. Prior to joining PwC, Dr. Compton served as Senior Accounting and Economic Advisor to the Chief Accountant in the SEC’s Office of the Chief Accountant, after beginning her time at the agency as a financial economist in the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis. Previously, Dr. Compton worked as an assistant professor of accounting at the George Washington University and Baruch College. The PCAOB announced on June 29, 2026 that Dr. Ying Li Compton has been appointed Chief Economist and Director of the Office of Economic and Risk Analysis (OERA). OERA’s role is to provide independent, evidence-based economic and risk analysis that supports PCAOB oversight work, including inspections, investigations, rulemaking, standard setting, and post-implementation reviews; the announcement is an internal leadership change and does not itself impose a new compliance rule, filing requirement, or deadline on registrants or audit firms. rows.title: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB after more than 17 years of service.
rows.desc: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich to Depart the PCAOB WASHINGTON, Jun. 26, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB on July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. “I have greatly valued Barb’s expert advice – her accomplishments at the PCAOB have been extraordinary,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We thank her for her leadership and dedication, and we wish her well as she embarks on a new professional opportunity.” Ms. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009. After serving in several roles at the PCAOB – including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor – she was named Chief Auditor in October 2022. During her tenure as Chief Auditor, the PCAOB adopted several new standards that represented important milestones in the PCAOB’s work to improve audit quality and protect investors. Most notably, the PCAOB in May 2024 adopted QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control. The standard, which will become effective December 15, 2026, features a risk-based approach designed to drive continuous improvement in audit quality. Additionally, Ms. Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, the creation of resources to help audit firms with implementation of new standards, the launch of the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process through which registered public accounting firms can submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. “It has been an honor to advance the PCAOB’s investor-protection mission, together with my talented colleagues in the Office of the Chief Auditor and so many others across the PCAOB,” said Ms. Vanich. The PCAOB is beginning a search to fill the Chief Auditor
rows.summary:

The notice also highlights several substantive PCAOB initiatives completed or advanced under Vanich’s tenure, especially **QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control**, which the PCAOB **adopted in May 2024** and which is scheduled to become **effective December 15, 2026**. That standard is described as using a **risk-based approach** intended to drive continuous improvement in audit quality, making its effective date a key compliance deadline for affected audit firms.

The announcement also notes that Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, implementation resources for audit firms, the **Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program**, the PCAOB’s **first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting**, and the creation of a **Firm Consultation Process** allowing **registered public accounting firms** to submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. For a corporate compliance team, the main takeaway is to continue monitoring PCAOB communications and implementation guidance, especially as the **December 15, 2026** effective date for **QC 1000** approaches and leadership transitions at the PCAOB may affect timing, interpretation, or outreach related to audit-quality and quality-control requirements.

rows.title: The PCAOB today announced the establishment of a Firm Consultation Process designed to provide timely and consistent guidance from PCAOB staff.

rows.summary:
On June 25, 2026, the PCAOB announced a new **Firm Consultation Process**, administered by the **Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA)**, to give registered public accounting firms more timely and consistent staff guidance on PCAOB requirements. The process is not a rule change or new substantive audit standard; instead, it creates a formal channel for firms to **submit questions directly to OCA staff** and receive **informal staff views** on the **implementation of new standards** and the **application of existing standards**.  

The consultation process is available only to **registered public accounting firms**, and it covers the interpretation and application of **PCAOB auditing, attestation, and quality control standards**, along with the **related rules and forms**, and the PCAOB’s **ethics and independence standards and rules**. If a firm wants to use the process, it must submit a request by completing the **Consultation Intake Form**. The PCAOB stated that it **does not plan to make consultation requests public**, although it may later issue **public guidance** if questions are commonly asked or broadly useful.  

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that firms now have a more structured mechanism to seek PCAOB staff input before finalizing interpretations or implementation approaches, which may help reduce inconsistency across engagements and support compliance with evolving PCAOB requirements. The announcement does not specify a filing deadline, approval timeline, or mandatory use requirement, and it does not impose a new compliance obligation beyond the submission process if a firm chooses to consult.

rows.title: The PCAOB has launched an open comment period for stakeholders to provide input on its standard-setting and research agendas.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued **Release No. 2026-005 on June 23, 2026** to open a **public comment period** seeking stakeholder input on its **standard-setting and research agendas**. The document does **not** itself adopt a new auditing rule or impose an immediate compliance requirement on registrants or auditors; rather, it asks firms, investors, audit committees, preparers, and other interested parties to comment on **which topics the PCAOB should prioritize** in future standard-setting and research work.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the PCAOB is signaling where future requirements may emerge and is inviting feedback on the most pressing audit-related issues. The agenda discussion specifically highlights **data and technology**, with focused attention on **artificial intelligence** and **digital assets**, indicating these are likely areas of regulatory development or updated guidance. The release also discusses the PCAOB’s **approach to standard setting**, including its **conceptual framework**, its **standard-setting process**, and its consideration of **other standard setters** and **possible alignment with international auditing standards**.

Because this is a request for comment rather than a final standard, the practical obligation is external-facing: organizations that want to influence future PCAOB rulemaking should review the agenda and submit comments during the open comment period. The document’s material significance is that it may foreshadow future auditing standards affecting how audits are performed in technology-heavy areas, especially where AI tools or digital assets are involved, but it does not specify new thresholds, rates, deadlines for compliance, or effective dates for substantive obligations in the excerpt provided.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced on June 15, 2026 that George G. Demos has been appointed Director of its Division of Enforcement and Investigations (DEI). For compliance teams, the practical significance is that the PCAOB’s enforcement function is now under the leadership of a former SEC enforcement attorney and litigation partner with direct experience handling accounting fraud, insider trading, market manipulation, and internal corporate investigations, which may signal continued or increased focus on audit-related misconduct and securities-law compliance.

The announcement does not create any new substantive rule, deadline, or filing obligation, and it does not change the underlying enforcement standards. However, it does confirm a leadership transition that may affect the tone, pace, and priorities of PCAOB enforcement and investigative activity. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 11, 2026 Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers summarizes its 2025 oversight of audits of SEC-registered broker-dealers that are required to file audited financial statements with the SEC. The report confirms that the PCAOB has statutory authority over the auditors of these broker-dealers and that its inspection program is intended to promote investor protection and audit quality by evaluating whether PCAOB-registered firms are performing these audits in compliance with applicable standards and rules. This report is issued under PCAOB Rule 4020T, which governs interim inspection reporting for broker-dealer audits.

The document does not announce a new substantive rule change, but it does describe the compliance framework broker-dealers and their auditors operate under. It notes that under Exchange Act Rule 17a-5, SEC-registered broker-dealers generally must file annual financial reports with the SEC, including financial statements subject to audit by a PCAOB-registered firm. The annual report’s stated purpose is to provide information on the PCAOB’s 2025 inspection approach and a summary of inspection observations, which means compliance teams should use it as guidance on areas where auditors were found deficient or where risks were elevated.

The report organizes its findings around 2025 inspection results, selected firms and engagements, and observations from inspections, along with the PCAOB standards and rules associated with those observations. While the excerpt provided does not include the specific deficiencies or statistics, the report signals that broker-dealer audit oversight remains an active compliance focus and that firms auditing broker-dealers should expect PCAOB scrutiny of audit execution, documentation, and conformity with PCAOB standards. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that broker-dealers must continue using qualified PCAOB-registered auditors for their annual audited filings, and those auditors should ensure their broker-dealer audit work is aligned with PCAOB requirements because inspection findings may affect regulatory posture, audit quality assessments, and supervisory expectations.

rows.title: The PCAOB will hold an open meeting to consider issuing proposed amendments related to QC 1000, the PCAOB’s quality control standard, for public comment.

rows.summary:

For compliance teams, the key point is that this announcement signals an upcoming PCAOB effort to gather market input on inspection modernization, which could lead to future changes in inspection methods, expectations, or related oversight practices, although no immediate substantive compliance obligations are imposed by this announcement itself.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued an order on January 13, 2026, imposing sanctions on Zwick CPA, PLLC and its owner Jack Zwick, CPA, based on violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audit of one issuer client’s financial statements. The Board censured both the firm and Zwick and revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, which means the firm cannot continue practicing before the PCAOB as a registered public accounting firm unless it later reapplies and is approved. The order also bars Zwick from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, although he may file a petition for Board consent to re-associate only after three years from the date of the order; similarly, the firm may reapply for registration only after three years from the date of the order.

Financially, the PCAOB imposed a civil money penalty of $50,000, assessed jointly and severally against the firm and Zwick. In addition to the monetary penalty, the firm must complete specified remedial quality-control measures before submitting any future registration application, and it must provide evidence of those measures with any such application. Zwick must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education focused on PCAOB auditing standards, on top of any CPE required for his professional license, before he can file any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 order against Deloitte Accountants B.V. (“Deloitte Netherlands”) imposes a formal censure, a $3 million civil money penalty, and required remedial measures because the firm violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards over several years in connection with its internal training program. The order was issued under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1); Deloitte Netherlands submitted an Offer of Settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205, and the PCAOB accepted it. The document makes clear that the sanctions are based on findings of misconduct related to the firm’s training environment, and the firm consented to the order for purposes of the proceeding while not admitting or denying the findings, except as to PCAOB jurisdiction.

The order requires Deloitte Netherlands to implement additional remedial actions described in Section IV of the order, meaning the firm must take corrective steps beyond paying the penalty and accepting the censure. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 Order permanently sanctions both Michael T. Studer, CPA P.C. and Michael T. Studer, CPA for audit-quality and supervision failures in connection with an issuer audit. The Board censured both respondents, permanently revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, permanently barred Studer from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $20,000 civil money penalty against the firm and Studer jointly and severally. The stated basis for the sanctions is that they violated PCAOB rules and standards during the audit of an issuer’s financial statements, Studer failed to properly supervise the engagement team, the firm failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR), the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards, and Studer directly and substantially contributed to the EQR and quality control violations.

For compliance teams, the key point is that the order is a final PCAOB disciplinary action affecting a registered public accounting firm and its CPA principal. No broader industry-wide rule change is announced in this excerpt; the document is an enforcement order imposing firm- and individual-specific sanctions for failures in audit supervision, EQR, and quality control.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 12, 2025 Order against Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) and partner Kristofer Heaton is a disciplinary action based on findings that the firm failed to timely assemble and retain complete and final audit documentation for five issuer audits, that Heaton did not adequately perform engagement quality reviews on those same five audits, and that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards. As sanctions, the PCAOB censured both respondents, revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, barred Heaton from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, and imposed civil money penalties of $35,000 on the firm and $25,000 on Heaton. The order also imposes forward-looking remedial conditions: if the firm later seeks to reapply for PCAOB registration, it must first complete certain remedial measures described in Section IV of the Order, and Heaton must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education beyond any CPE required by his professional license before he may file a petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm.

The order specifies a two-year waiting period from the date of the Order before either the firm may reapply for registration or Heaton may petition for consent to associate again. The affected activities are audits of issuers, so the action is relevant to registered public accounting firms, partners performing EQRs, and any firm with PCAOB inspection/registration obligations. For compliance teams, the key takeaways are that the PCAOB treated failures in audit file completion, EQR performance, and quality control as sanctionable violations, and it paired the sanctions with reinstatement hurdles—remedial steps for any future firm registration application and a mandatory 40-hour CPE condition for Heaton before any future association request.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered an April 22, 2025 disciplinary order against registered public accounting firm Adeptus Partners LLC and partner Howard S. Krant, CPA, based on violations tied to supervision, audit review, and quality control in connection with the audits of two issuers. The Board censured both Adeptus and Krant; suspended Krant from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm for one year starting on the date of the Order; imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty on Krant; imposed a $75,000 civil money penalty on Adeptus; and required Adeptus to retain an independent consultant to review its quality-control system and make recommendations as specified in Section IV of the Order. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 25, 2025 order against James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner, Yu-Ching James Pai, imposes significant disciplinary sanctions for audit-related violations involving two audits of one issuer client. The Board found that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in performing those audits, and that the firm specifically failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR). The order also states that the firm filed inaccurate PCAOB Form APs in connection with those engagements, which is a separate reporting/compliance failure.

As sanctions, the PCAOB censured both the firm and Pai, revoked the firm’s registration, barred Pai from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $40,000 civil money penalty jointly and severally on the firm and Pai. In addition, the firm is required to undertake remedial actions to its system of quality control before it can submit any future registration application, and it must provide evidence of those remedial measures with any future application. Pai is required to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, on top of any CPE required for licensing, before he may file a petition for PCAOB consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm.

The order provides that the firm may reapply for PCAOB registration only after three years from the date of the order, and Pai may file a petition for Board consent to associate only after three years from the same date. For compliance teams, the key takeaways are that the PCAOB treated the audit failures, missing EQR, and inaccurate Form AP filings as serious violations warranting revocation, a personal bar, monetary penalty, and mandatory remediation/CPE conditions tied to any future re-entry into the PCAOB-regulated practice environment.

The Board based these sanctions on findings that Sellers violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards in connection with two issuer audits and also violated auditor independence requirements in one of those audits. The document does not describe the underlying audit failures in detail, but it makes clear that the misconduct involved two issuer audits and included at least one independence violation, which is especially significant because independence requirements apply to the audit engagement and the firm’s ability to issue an informative, accurate, and independent audit report. The proceeding was instituted to protect investors and the public interest, indicating that the PCAOB treated these violations as serious professional conduct failures rather than isolated technical errors.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a disciplinary order against former engagement partner Natalie Murphy, CPA, based on misconduct tied to issuer audit work and her cooperation with a PCAOB inspection of Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah). The Board censured Murphy, barred her from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education before she can even petition for PCAOB consent to associate with a registered firm; any such petition cannot be filed until five years after the date of the Order, February 25, 2025.

For compliance purposes, the order underscores that engagement partners and other personnel at registered public accounting firms must provide truthful, complete, and timely responses during PCAOB inspections, and must properly document post-completion changes to audit workpapers and finalize audit files within the required retention timeline.

The practical effect is that Murphy is prohibited from working in any capacity that would constitute being “associated with” a registered public accounting firm unless and until the PCAOB grants consent after the five-year period and she satisfies the additional 40-hour CPE شرط. The order is aimed at protecting investors and reinforcing the PCAOB’s expectations for audit documentation integrity, timely file completion, and full cooperation with inspection staff.
